overview: Berkshire bought its Washington Post Company stake (about $10.6 million) in mid-1973 at roughly a quarter of business value and never added to it. Buffett repeatedly credited Kay Graham's buybacks and management, called the stake a permanent holding in 1986, and cited it as a model of Mr. Market's bargains and honest shareholder treatment. From 1988 to 1991 he warned of lower upside and a secular decline in media value, while still preferring WPC to other media firms. The shares stayed at 1,727,765 in holdings tables through 2008; in 2014 Berkshire exchanged its Graham Holdings stock for operating businesses.
stance_basis: praised (management, buybacks, price paid) in letters 1981-2003; caution on media economics 1988-1991; never criticized the company

timeline.point: 1977 holdings table: 934,300 Class B shares, cost $10.6 million, market $33.4 million (000s omitted).
timeline.quote: 934,300 The Washington Post Company Class B

timeline.point: WPC is one of four holdings whose undistributed earnings, unrecorded by Berkshire, exceed reported operating earnings.
timeline.quote: our share of undistributed and therefore unrecorded earnings probably will total well over $35 million in 1982

timeline.point: Washington Post and GEICO are Berkshire's two largest unrealized gains, both tied to Buffett's earliest business connections.
timeline.quote: Our two largest unrealized gains are in Washington Post and GEICO

timeline.point: Buffett credits WPC's large repurchases at bargain prices with materially enhancing Berkshire's interest.
timeline.quote: We have prospered in a very major way - as have other shareholders - by the large share repurchases of GEICO, Washington Post, and General Foods, our three largest holdings.

timeline.point: The 1973 purchase was made at no more than one-fourth of per-share business value, an attitude learned from Ben Graham.
timeline.quote: We bought all of our WPC holdings in mid-1973 at a price of not more than one-fourth of the then per-share business value of the enterprise.

timeline.point: By yearend 1974 the holding showed a loss of about 25%, market $8 million versus $10.6 million cost.
timeline.quote: by yearend 1974 our WPC holding showed a loss of about 25%, with market value at $8 million against our cost of $10.6 million.

timeline.point: About $160 million of extra gain over other media stocks is credited to Kay Graham's managerial decisions.
timeline.quote: The extra $160 million or so we gained through ownership of WPC came, in very large part, from the superior nature of the managerial decisions made by Kay

timeline.point: Buffett intends to hold indefinitely but warns that at a $1.8 billion valuation future gains cannot match the past.
timeline.quote: there is no way that the value can progress from that level at a rate anywhere close to the rate possible when the company's valuation was only $100 million.

timeline.point: WPC named one of three permanent holdings that would not be sold even if overpriced.
timeline.quote: we expect to keep permanently our three primary holdings, Capital Cities/ABC, Inc., GEICO Corporation, and The Washington Post.

timeline.point: Example of Mr. Market's bargains: bought at $5.63 a share; 1987 per-share earnings were $10.30.
timeline.quote: we purchased our Washington Post stock in 1973 at $5.63 per share, and per-share operating earnings in 1987 after taxes were $10.30.

timeline.point: Industry conditions for the three permanent holdings are less favorable; upside looks less exciting at current prices.
timeline.quote: But, at current prices, their upside potential looks considerably less exciting to us today than it did some years ago.

timeline.point: The two media holdings' market prices fell in 1990 for good reasons tied to industry developments.
timeline.quote: The market prices of the two media companies have since fallen significantly - for good reasons relating to evolutionary industry developments

timeline.point: Intrinsic value of Berkshire's media investments, including WPC, declined materially from secular change; holdings kept as permanent.
timeline.quote: the intrinsic value of this investment has declined materially because of the secular transformation that the industry is experiencing.

timeline.point: Strong balance sheets and managements make WPC and Cap Cities preferable to any other media holding.
timeline.quote: The strong balance sheets and strong managements of Cap Cities and Washington Post leave us more comfortable with these investments than we would be with holdings in any other media companies.

timeline.point: On Katharine Graham's retirement: the roughly $10 million stake now yields $7 million in dividends and is worth over $400 million.
timeline.quote: Our holding now garners $7 million a year in dividends and is worth over $400 million.

timeline.point: Buffett recalls the WPC investment turning $10 million into $500 million.
timeline.quote: a company that much later made it possible for Berkshire to turn $10 million into $500 million.

timeline.point: Past repurchases by WPC at very low prices benefited Berkshire more than repurchases at today's prices.
timeline.quote: the repurchases that Coca-Cola, The Washington Post and Wells Fargo made in past years at very low prices benefitted Berkshire far more than do today's repurchases

timeline.point: WPC praised for objectively reviewing its acquisitions three years after making them.
timeline.quote: A notable exception to this never-look-back approach is that of The Washington Post Company, which unfailingly and objectively reviews its acquisitions three years after they are made.

timeline.point: The WPC position has not changed since 1973; the 2003 table shows 18.1% ownership worth $1,367 million.
timeline.quote: we last changed our position in Coca-Cola in 1994, American Express in 1998, Gillette in 1989, Washington Post in 1973

timeline.point: Buffett reproduces his 1975 memo to Katharine Graham on pension promises and investment policy.
timeline.quote: In 1975, I wrote a memo to Katharine Graham, then chairman of The Washington Post Company, about the pitfalls of pension promises and the importance of investment policy.

timeline.point: Berkshire exchanged its Graham Holdings (formerly WPC) stock for operating businesses in 2014.
timeline.quote: we were pleased to exchange our Phillips 66 and Graham Holdings stock for operating businesses last year

overview: Apart from a 1996 note that World Book launched a CD-ROM with IBM, IBM appears only in the 2011-2016 letters. In 2011 Berkshire bought 63.9 million shares for $10.9 billion; Buffett praised IBM's financial management, said he was 'late to the IBM party' and argued long-term holders should want a low stock price during buybacks. IBM was one of the 'Big Four' through 2015, with ownership raised to 8.4%. Holdings tables show market value below cost at yearend 2014, 2015 and 2016. In 2014 he also listed IBM among once-dominant firms that fell through bureaucracy. The letters in this corpus do not discuss selling IBM.
stance_basis: praised as a 'Big Four' holding in letters 2011-2015; 2016 only a table row; no later verdict in the letters

timeline.point: No investment yet: World Book's new CD-ROM product was launched in association with IBM.
timeline.quote: when it was launched in association with IBM.

timeline.point: Major 2011 purchase: 63.9 million IBM shares at a cost of $10.9 billion.
timeline.quote: 63.9 million shares of IBM that cost us $10.9 billion.

timeline.point: Buffett praises Gerstner and Palmisano and calls IBM's financial management unmatched.
timeline.quote: I can think of no major company that has had better financial management

timeline.point: Because IBM will repurchase about $50 billion of stock, Berkshire should hope its price stays low.
timeline.quote: We should wish for IBM's stock price to languish throughout the five years.

timeline.point: Success depends mainly on IBM's future earnings, secondarily on how many shares it buys back.
timeline.quote: In the end, the success of our IBM investment will be determined primarily by its future earnings.

timeline.point: Buffett read IBM reports for 50 years before his thinking crystallized in March 2011.
timeline.quote: As was the case with Coca-Cola in 1988 and the railroads in 2006, I was late to the IBM party.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought more IBM in 2012, lifting ownership from 5.5% to 6.0%.
timeline.quote: IBM (6.0% versus 5.5%)

timeline.point: IBM's non-GAAP 'adjusted operating earnings' that exclude purchase-accounting charges are the right focus.
timeline.quote: IBM has made many small acquisitions in recent years and now regularly reports "adjusted operating earnings,"

timeline.point: Further purchases raised ownership to 6.3%.
timeline.quote: IBM (6.3% versus 6.0%)

timeline.point: More shares bought in 2014; ownership 7.8%. Table shows cost $13,157 million, market $12,349 million.
timeline.quote: We purchased additional shares of IBM (increasing our ownership to 7.8% versus 6.3% at yearend 2013).

timeline.point: IBM named, from the distant past, among giants that fell through arrogance, bureaucracy and complacency.
timeline.quote: In their glory days, General Motors, IBM, Sears Roebuck and U.S. Steel sat atop huge industries.

timeline.point: Ownership raised to 8.4%; table shows cost $13,791 million versus market $11,152 million.
timeline.quote: We purchased additional shares of IBM (increasing our ownership to 8.4% versus 7.8% at yearend 2014)

timeline.point: The Big Four, IBM included, have returns on tangible equity from excellent to staggering.
timeline.quote: Their returns on tangible equity range from excellent to staggering.

timeline.point: 2016 table only: 81,232,303 shares, 8.5%, cost $13,815 million, market $13,484 million; no text comment.
timeline.quote: International Business Machines Corp.

overview: Berkshire acquired Dexter Shoe in November 1993 for 25,203 Berkshire Class A shares. Buffett then called it one of the best-managed companies he had seen. By 1999 low-cost imports were hurting it; in 2000 he called the price a mistake and wrote off the remaining goodwill. In 2001 he listed three errors: buying it, paying in stock and delaying changes. H.H. Brown's managers turned it around in 2002. From 2007 on he called it his worst deal: its value went to zero, and the shares given were worth $3.5 billion (2007), $5.7 billion (2014) and over $6 billion (2016).
stance_basis: praised in the 1993 letter; problems 1999-2002; called his worst deal or a disaster in 2000, 2001, 2007, 2014, 2015 and 2016

timeline.point: Berkshire issued 25,203 shares to acquire Dexter Shoe.
timeline.quote: we issued 25,203 shares when we acquired Dexter Shoe

timeline.point: At purchase Buffett praises Dexter as exceptionally well managed.
timeline.quote: Dexter, I can assure you, needs no fixing: It is one of the best-managed companies Charlie and I have seen in our business lifetimes.

timeline.point: Dexter and H.H. Brown's U.S. plants are said to compete well against imports from low-wage countries.
timeline.quote: But someone forgot to tell this to the ingenious managements of Dexter and H. H. Brown

timeline.point: Buffett presents the stock-for-stock deal as sound for the sellers.
timeline.quote: trade a 100% interest in a single terrific business for a smaller interest in a large group of terrific businesses.

timeline.point: Shoe group earnings fell in 1995; Buffett calls it a cyclical, not secular, problem.
timeline.quote: we believe you should view last year's figures as reflecting a cyclical problem, not a secular one.

timeline.point: Dexter is the exception in a good year; imports supply about 93% of U.S. shoes.
timeline.quote: The exception was Dexter Shoe, and there the shortfall did not occur because of managerial problems

timeline.point: Buffett calls the purchase price a mistake, compounded by paying in Berkshire shares.
timeline.quote: I clearly made a mistake in paying what I did for Dexter in 1993.

timeline.point: All remaining accounting goodwill from the Dexter deal is written off.
timeline.quote: we charged off all the remaining accounting goodwill that was attributable to the Dexter transaction.

timeline.point: Shoes lost $46.2 million pre-tax; Buffett owns three Dexter decisions as his mistakes.
timeline.quote: I concluded that Dexter could continue to cope with that problem, and I was wrong.

timeline.point: Under H.H. Brown's Frank Rooney and Jim Issler, Dexter was turned around; shoes earned $24 million.
timeline.quote: the Dexter operation has been turned around.

timeline.point: Paying $433 million in stock made the true cost $3.5 billion, 1.6% of Berkshire.
timeline.quote: In essence, I gave away 1.6% of a wonderful business – one now valued at $220 billion – to buy a worthless business.

timeline.point: Dexter is called his worst deal to date.
timeline.quote: To date, Dexter is the worst deal that I've made.

timeline.point: Value went to zero; the shares given are now worth about $5.7 billion.
timeline.quote: As a financial disaster, this one deserves a spot in the Guinness Book of World Records.

timeline.point: Low-cost Asian competition folded Dexter; Berkshire lost its entire investment and 1,600 workers lost jobs.
timeline.quote: our once-prosperous Dexter operation folded, putting 1,600 employees in a small Maine town out of work.

timeline.point: Bought for $434 million in 1993; the 25,203 shares given were worth over $6 billion by yearend 2016.
timeline.quote: giving the sellers 25,203 shares of Berkshire that at yearend 2016 were worth more than $6 billion.

overview: Purchases of the five Japanese trading houses (Itochu, Marubeni, Mitsubishi, Mitsui, Sumitomo) began on July 4, 2019. The 2020 and 2021 letters show some of them only in holdings tables. The 2023 and 2024 letters discuss them in text: about 9% owned with a 9.9% pledged cap, later relaxed. Cost was ¥1.6 trillion versus ¥2.9 trillion market (2023), and $13.8 billion versus $23.5 billion (2024). Most of the position is financed with yen debt to stay roughly currency-neutral. Buffett praises their shareholder-friendly buybacks, modest pay and capital use, and expects to hold for many decades.
stance_basis: praised in the 2023 and 2024 letters (the only text discussions); 2020-2021 appear only as table rows

timeline.point: First appearance: 2020 holdings table lists Itochu, 5.1% owned, cost $1,862 million, market $2,336 million.
timeline.quote: Itochu Corporation

timeline.point: 2021 table lists ITOCHU (5.6%), Mitsubishi (5.5%) and Mitsui (5.7%).
timeline.quote: Mitsubishi Corporation

timeline.point: Holdings raised in all five after a Tokyo visit; about 9% of each, with a pledge not to exceed 9.9%.
timeline.quote: Berkshire now owns about 9% of each of the five.

timeline.point: Cost versus yearend market value for the five, in yen.
timeline.quote: Our cost for the five totals ¥1.6 trillion, and the yearend market value of the five was ¥2.9 trillion.

timeline.point: No currency forecasts: the position is financed mostly with yen bonds.
timeline.quote: Berkshire has financed most of its Japanese position with the proceeds from ¥1.3 trillion of bonds.

timeline.point: The five have bought back shares at attractive prices and are praised for shareholder policies.
timeline.quote: follow shareholder-friendly policies that are much superior to those customarily practiced in the U.S.

timeline.point: Purchases began July 4, 2019; building positions at Berkshire's size takes patience.
timeline.quote: Our Japanese purchases began on July 4, 2019.

timeline.point: First bought because prices were amazingly low; admiration has grown since.
timeline.quote: As the years have passed, our admiration for these companies has consistently grown.

timeline.point: Yearend 2024: cost $13.8 billion, market value $23.5 billion; ownership cap relaxed.
timeline.quote: At yearend, Berkshire's aggregate cost (in dollars) was $13.8 billion and the market value of our holdings totaled $23.5 billion.

timeline.point: Buffett expects a holding period of many decades and further cooperation with the five.
timeline.quote: I expect that Greg and his eventual successors will be holding this Japanese position for many decades

timeline.point: Expected 2025 dividends of about $812 million against about $135 million of yen-debt interest.
timeline.quote: the annual dividend income expected from the Japanese investments in 2025 will total about $812 million

overview: Insurance is the sector Buffett discusses most, in every letter from 1977 to 2024, and he calls it Berkshire's core business. His view of the industry stays negative throughout: a commodity product, chronic underwriting losses, unreliable reserves and subnormal returns. His view of Berkshire's own insurance changed. It was poor in 1982-1984, then from 1990 he called it Berkshire's greatest opportunity and core strength, valued by cheap float. Float grew from about $16-20 million in 1967 (figures vary by letter) to $171 billion in 2024. Setbacks were 1999-2001 (General Re, September 11) and 2017. Recurring themes: discipline over volume, capital strength for huge risks, and catastrophe and reserving dangers.
stance_basis: industry economics criticized in letters 1977-2019 (commodity, subnormal returns); Berkshire's own insurance praised as core strength or greatest opportunity in letters 1990-2024; own results called poor in 1982-1984, 1999-2001 and 2017
coverage_note: decade method: 301 tagged passages read in full (1970s 74 = all, 1980s 47, 1990s 49, 2000s 50, 2010s 44, 2020s 37 = all) plus 18 untagged passages found by corpus search; the rest via annotation summaries and stance quotes

timeline.point: Entry in 1967 via National Indemnity for about $8.6 million; premiums $22 million then, $151 million in 1977.
timeline.quote: It was early in 1967 that we made our entry into this industry through the purchase of National Indemnity Company and National Fire and Marine Insurance Company

timeline.point: Insurance is a commodity whose results depend on managers.
timeline.quote: Insurance companies offer standardized policies which can be copied by anyone. Their only products are promises.

timeline.point: He predicts that industry combined ratios will be permanently higher.
timeline.quote: we expect that competition will create a new threshold of tolerance for underwriting losses, and that combined ratios will average higher in the future than in the past.

timeline.point: Industry structure: excess capacity plus a commodity product.
timeline.quote: a textbook case of an industry usually faced with the deadly combination of excess capacity and a "commodity" product.

timeline.point: Berkshire's own underwriting was worse than the industry's for three years running.
timeline.quote: Our own combined ratio in 1984 was a humbling 134.

timeline.point: Capital strength became an advantage when the market tightened; volume tripled.
timeline.quote: Our premium volume more than tripled last year, following a long period of stagnation.

timeline.point: Total indifference to volume when prices are inadequate.
timeline.quote: In 1989, we will be perfectly willing to write five times as much business as we write in 1988 - or only one-fifth as much.

timeline.point: Insurance is called the business with the greatest potential.
timeline.quote: it is the one - among all the fine businesses we own - that has the greatest potential.

timeline.point: Super-cat worst case about $600 million after tax; volatility accepted.
timeline.quote: If you are not comfortable with this level of exposure, the time to sell your Berkshire stock is now, not after the inevitable mega-catastrophe.

timeline.point: With all of GEICO, insurance doubled and became the core strength.
timeline.quote: More than ever, insurance is our core strength.

timeline.point: Float compounded 25.4% a year; its average cost over 32 years was below zero.
timeline.quote: Our average cost over the 32 years has been well under zero.

timeline.point: September 11 and General Re's lapses pushed float cost to 12.8%.
timeline.quote: Our float cost therefore came in at a staggering 12.8%.

timeline.point: General Re broke all three underwriting rules.
timeline.quote: In the past I have assured you that General Re was underwriting with discipline – and I have been proven wrong.

timeline.point: Industry returns are poor because the product is a commodity.
timeline.quote: Insurers have generally earned poor returns for a simple reason: They sell a commodity-like product.

timeline.point: Six straight underwriting profits; insurance called the core of Berkshire.
timeline.quote: Our insurance operation, the core business of Berkshire, is an economic powerhouse.

timeline.point: Industry will keep earning subnormal returns.
timeline.quote: will continue its dismal record of earning subnormal returns as compared to other businesses.

timeline.point: After 14 profitable years, hurricanes caused a $3.2 billion underwriting loss.
timeline.quote: My warning became fact in 2017, as we lost $3.2 billion pre-tax from underwriting.

timeline.point: Insurance suits Berkshire's capital and integrity.
timeline.quote: The insurance business is made to order for Berkshire.

timeline.point: Shrink rather than underprice.
timeline.quote: We must never write inadequately-priced policies in order to stay in the game. That policy is corporate suicide.

timeline.point: Two decades: $32 billion after-tax underwriting profit; float grew from $46 billion to $171 billion.
timeline.quote: Over the past two decades, our insurance business has generated $32 billion of after-tax profits from underwriting

overview: General Re Securities was the derivatives dealer Berkshire inherited with General Re in 1998. Buffett judged it dangerous from the start, failed to sell it, and began liquidating it in early 2002 with 23,218 contracts and 884 counterparties. The wind-down cost $173 million pre-tax in 2002, $99 million in 2003, $44 million in 2004, $104 million in 2005 and $5 million in 2006, $409 million in all, by which time 197 contracts remained. He used it as a warning about derivatives accounting ("mark-to-myth"), correlated counterparty risk and trader incentives, and blamed himself for dithering instead of closing it at once.

timeline.point: Gen Re Securities is placed in the finance segment and described as in long run-off.
timeline.quote: General Re Securities (which is in a run-off mode that will continue for an extended period)

timeline.point: Unit lost $173 million pre-tax, partly from faulty but standard earlier accounting.
timeline.quote: This entity lost $173 million pre-tax last year, a result that, in part, is a belated acknowledgment of faulty, albeit standard, accounting it used in earlier periods.

timeline.point: He never wanted the dealer, could not sell it and is terminating it; exiting derivatives is slow.
timeline.quote: a derivatives dealer that Charlie and I didn’t want, judging it to be dangerous. We failed in our attempts to sell the operation, however, and are now terminating it.

timeline.point: Large receivables from many counterparties can go bad together in a crisis.
timeline.quote: At Gen Re Securities, we still have $6.5 billion of receivables, though we’ve been in a liquidation mode for nearly a year.

timeline.point: After two years 7,580 of 23,218 tickets remained; losses of $173 million (2002) and $99 million (2003) despite benign markets.
timeline.quote: The shrinking of this business has been costly. We’ve had pre-tax losses of $173 million in 2002 and $99 million in 2003.

timeline.point: He confesses that acting faster would have saved about $100 million.
timeline.quote: I’m sure I could have saved you $100 million or so, pre-tax, if I had acted more promptly to shut down Gen Re Securities.

timeline.point: Munger would have closed it swiftly; Buffett dithered.
timeline.quote: Charlie would have moved swiftly to close down Gen Re Securities – no question about that. I, however, dithered.

timeline.point: Wind-down continues: 2,890 contracts left; loss of $44 million in 2004.
timeline.quote: we still had 2,890 contracts outstanding at yearend, down from 23,218 at the peak. Like Hell, derivative trading is easy to enter but difficult to leave.

timeline.point: Fuzzy marks feed trader bonuses, so phantom profits are common.
timeline.quote: In the interim the marks influence the managerial and trading bonuses that are paid annually. It’s small wonder that phantom profits are often recorded.

timeline.point: Another $104 million lost cutting contracts to 741; cumulative losses $404 million.
timeline.quote: We lost $104 million pre-tax last year in our continuing attempt to exit Gen Re’s derivative operation. Our aggregate losses since we began this endeavor total $404 million.

timeline.point: He faults himself for wasting years trying to sell it; the lesson is to act immediately.
timeline.quote: Fault me for dithering. (Charlie calls it thumb-sucking.) When a problem exists, whether in personnel or in business operations, the time to act is now.

timeline.point: Final report: 197 contracts left, $5 million loss in 2006, $409 million cumulative.
timeline.quote: Our cumulative pre-tax loss from this operation totals $409 million, but only $5 million occurred in 2006.

overview: A minor, mostly tabular topic. In 1977-1986 Berkshire's insurers held Kaiser Aluminum, Alcoa, Cleveland-Cliffs and Handy & Harman, and Wesco's Precision Steel appeared in the earnings tables. In 1980 Buffett said the aluminum stakes gave Berkshire more economic exposure than most controlled businesses; a year later he admitted his rosy aluminum view had reversed about 180 degrees. Later he used steel and aluminum as examples of commodity industries with subnormal returns, while praising Precision Steel's manager for good returns in a tough industry. In 2004 MidAmerican wrote off a zinc recovery project. POSCO was held from 2006 to about 2012, appearing only in holdings tables.

timeline.point: Holdings table lists Kaiser Aluminum & Chemical (cost $11.2 million, market $10.0 million) among insurance equity holdings.
timeline.quote: 324,580 Kaiser Aluminum& Chemical Corporation ... 11,218 9,981

timeline.point: Handy & Harman (precious metals) becomes a major holding; Precision Steel first shows in earnings table.
Stakes of about 3% of Kaiser and 1.25% of Alcoa give Berkshire a larger economic interest in aluminum than in most operating businesses it controls.
timeline.quote: we have a much larger economic interest in the aluminum business than in practically any of the operating businesses we control

timeline.point: He admits his optimistic 1980 view on aluminum was wrong, citing it as a miscalculation.
timeline.quote: last year your Chairman volunteered his expert opinion on the rosy future of the aluminum business. Several minor adjustments to that opinion - now aggregating approximately 180 degrees - have since been required.

timeline.point: Praises Dave Hillstrom for consistently good returns at Precision Steel Warehouse despite an extremely competitive industry.
timeline.quote: Precision operates in an extremely competitive industry, yet Dave consistently achieves good returns on invested capital.

timeline.point: Commodity industries like steel or insurance earn subnormal profits except when capacity is short.
timeline.quote: whether the product being sold is steel or insurance policies - is certain to cause subnormal profitability in all circumstances but one: a shortage of usable capacity.

timeline.point: Berkshire's returns came from managers in prosaic fields, including steel warehousing, not from industry economics.
timeline.quote: a group of businesses operating in such prosaic fields as furniture retailing, candy, vacuum cleaners, and even steel warehousing.

timeline.point: Steel earnings were valued low because they 'bob around' rather than grow.
timeline.quote: whereas steel earnings clearly fell in the bob-around category.

timeline.point: MidAmerican wrote off its zinc recovery project from geothermal brine; mining prospects 'tease' developers.
timeline.quote: But in mining, just as in oil exploration, prospects have a way of “teasing” their developers, and every time one problem was solved, another popped up. In September, we threw in the towel.

timeline.point: POSCO appears among the large equity holdings (about 4% of the company).
timeline.quote: POSCO

timeline.point: POSCO still listed among large holdings, 3,947,555 shares.

overview: Mostly about Berkshire's leasing businesses. Early mentions are thin (a 1981 GATX holding, a 1982 note on regulated trucking prices). In 2001 Berkshire bought trailer lessor XTRA, calling trailer leasing cyclical but able to earn decent returns. XTRA tracked the economy: poor in the 2002-03 recession, rebounding in 2004-06, hit again in 2009, and recovering as leasing earnings rose from $13 million (2009) to $155 million (2011). From 2007 Marmon's Union Tank Car added a big railcar fleet, worth more than book in his view, a business he likes despite demand swings. In 2014 Berkshire bought Van Tuyl's dealerships; he later noted driverless cars as a risk to them. BYD appears in holdings tables.

timeline.point: GATX (railcar lessor) listed among insurance equity holdings, below cost.
Bought XTRA after Tiger Fund sold its block; trailer leasing called cyclical but able to earn decent returns.
timeline.quote: Trailer leasing is a cyclical business but one in which we should earn decent returns over time.

timeline.point: XTRA and CORT earned poorly in the recession but remain leaders; modest improvement expected.
timeline.quote: Both operations have had poor earnings during the past two years as the recession caused demand to drop considerably more than was anticipated.

timeline.point: XTRA narrowed to trailer leasing, cut overhead and returned to decent profits under new CEO Bill Franz.
timeline.quote: XTRA disposed of its container and intermodal businesses in order to concentrate on trailer leasing, long its strong suit.

timeline.point: Trailer utilization fell and XTRA's earnings dropped; still called a good, ably run business.
timeline.quote: Utilization of trailers was down considerably in 2007 and that led to a drop in earnings at XTRA.

timeline.point: Marmon acquisition brings Union Tank Car, 94,000 leased rail cars costing $5.1 billion.
timeline.quote: Marmon’s largest operation is Union Tank Car, which together with a Canadian counterpart owns 94,000 rail cars that are leased to various shippers.

timeline.point: Recession hit trailer and furniture leasing hard with no rebound yet.
timeline.quote: how severely our furniture (CORT) and trailer (XTRA) leasing operations have been hit by the recession.

timeline.point: XTRA utilization rose from 63% to 75%, lifting pre-tax earnings to $35 million from $17 million.
timeline.quote: XTRA increased the utilization of its equipment from 63% in 2009 to 75% in 2010, thereby raising pre-tax earnings to $35 million from $17 million in 2009.

timeline.point: Combined leasing pre-tax earnings: $13 million (2009), $53 million (2010), $155 million (2011).
timeline.quote: Their combined pre-tax earnings were $13 million in 2009, $53 million in 2010 and $155 million in 2011

timeline.point: XTRA spent $256 million on new equipment, over double depreciation, while rivals hesitated.
timeline.quote: Our expenditures for new rental equipment at XTRA totaled $256 million in 2012, more than double its depreciation expense.

timeline.point: Bought Van Tuyl's 78 dealerships; plans to grow the auto group by buying more at sensible prices.
timeline.quote: Our purchase was recently completed, and we are now “car guys.”

timeline.point: Marmon's rail fleet is carried at a bargain cost and worth well above book.
timeline.quote: Marmon’s rail fleet is worth considerably more than the $5 billion figure at which it is carried on our books.

timeline.point: Driverless cars could eventually hurt GEICO and the auto dealerships.
timeline.quote: GEICO’s premium volume may shrink because of driverless cars. This development could hurt our auto dealerships as well.

timeline.point: Railcar demand slowed (utilization 91% vs 97%), but he still likes the business and expects decent returns.
timeline.quote: Big swings in railcar demand have occurred in the past and they will continue. Nevertheless, we very much like this business and expect decent returns on equity capital over the years.

timeline.point: Berkshire Hathaway Automotive ranked among the next five subsidiaries that together earned $1.9 billion.
timeline.quote: (Berkshire Hathaway Automotive, Johns Manville, NetJets, Shaw and TTI) earned $1.9 billion last year

overview: Buffett treats American Express as a classic great franchise. In 1980 and 1989 he cited its 1964 salad-oil scandal as a solvable blow to an exceptional business. Berkshire bought $300 million of Amex Percs in 1991. In 1994 he leaned toward selling because of card competition, but was persuaded the corporate card was a terrific franchise and bought up to about 10% by 1995. The holding was essentially unchanged after 1998, while Amex buybacks lifted Berkshire's stake from 12.6% to about 20%. It was one of the 'Big Four' in 2011-2015. By 2022-2023 dividends had grown from $41 million to $302 million, and Berkshire's share of earnings exceeded the $1.3 billion cost.

timeline.point: Amex in 1964 (salad-oil scandal) was an extraordinary franchise hit by a fiscal blow that did not destroy its economics, like GEICO later.
timeline.quote: Both were one-of-a-kind companies, temporarily reeling from the effects of a fiscal blow that did not destroy their exceptional underlying economics.

timeline.point: Great opportunities arise when a marvelous business hits a huge but solvable one-time problem, as at Amex and GEICO.
timeline.quote: a great investment opportunity occurs when a marvelous business encounters a one-time huge, but solvable, problem as was the case many years back at both American Express and GEICO.

timeline.point: Bought $300 million of Amex 'Percs', 8.85% dividend, converting in three years with capped upside and no floor.
timeline.quote: it is a "Perc," which carries a fixed dividend of 8.85% on our $300 million cost.

timeline.point: Enlarged Amex holding; partnership once put 40% of capital into Amex after the salad-oil scandal.
timeline.quote: we put about 40% of Buffett Partnership Ltd.'s capital into the stock - the largest investment the partnership had ever made.

timeline.point: Raised ownership to about 10%, the only change among top holdings.
timeline.quote: The sixth was American Express, in which we increased our ownership to about 10%.

timeline.point: In 1994 he leaned toward selling because of card competition led by Visa, despite a strong CEO in Harvey Golub.
timeline.quote: Amex faced relentless competition from a multitude of card-issuers, led by Visa. Weighing the arguments, I leaned toward sale.

timeline.point: Hertz's CEO convinced him the corporate card was a terrific franchise; he bought to 10%, now a $3 billion gain.
timeline.quote: Frank had convinced me that Amex's corporate card was a terrific franchise, and I had decided not to sell. On the back nine I turned buyer

timeline.point: Amex position last changed in 1998; among six largest holdings.
timeline.quote: we last changed our position in Coca-Cola in 1994, American Express in 1998

timeline.point: Names Amex CEO Ken Chenault among giant-company managers he greatly admires; Amex per-share earnings rose 18% in 2006.
timeline.quote: There are many giantcompany managers whom I greatly admire; Ken Chenault of American Express

timeline.point: Amex (13.0%) counted among four exceptional companies held as partnership interests, not trading securities.
timeline.quote: We view these holdings as partnership interests in wonderful businesses, not as marketable securities to be bought or sold based on their near-term prospects.

timeline.point: Amex buybacks lifted Berkshire's stake from 14.8% to 15.6% at no cost.
timeline.quote: our interest in American Express increased from 14.8% to 15.6%.

timeline.point: Holding unchanged for eight years while buybacks raised ownership from 12.6% to 17.9%; share of earnings $1.2 billion vs $1.3 billion cost.
timeline.quote: Berkshire’s portion of the $6.9 billion earned by American Express was $1.2 billion, about 96% of the $1.3 billion we paid for our stake in the company.

timeline.point: Purchases completed in 1995 for $1.3 billion; annual dividends grew from $41 million to $302 million; holding worth $22 billion.
timeline.quote: Annual dividends received from this investment have grown from $41 million to $302 million.

timeline.point: No trades for over two decades; Berkshire's share of 2023 Amex earnings exceeded the original cost. Lesson: stick with a wonderful business.
timeline.quote: When you find a truly wonderful business, stick with it. Patience pays, and one wonderful business can offset the many mediocre decisions that are inevitable.

timeline.point: Amex named among highly profitable household-name minority holdings.
timeline.quote: very large and highly profitable businesses with household names such as Apple, American Express, Coca-Cola and Moody’s.

overview: Berkshire built a stake in Burlington Northern Santa Fe in 2007-2008 (17.5%, then over 20%) and bought the whole railroad in early 2010, its largest purchase, paying about 30% of the cost in shares. Buffett called it a close decision and an 'all-in wager' on the U.S. economy. He praised it in every letter from 2009 to 2024 as an essential national artery, fuel-efficient against trucking, with strong interest coverage and value above book. The caveats: 2014 service failures and lost share to Union Pacific; depreciation that understates real capital needs; and, in 2023, earnings below his expectations and margins that slipped against peers, giving an acceptable but smaller return than reported earnings suggest.

timeline.point: Burlington Northern Santa Fe appears as a new major holding: 17.5% of the company, cost $4.7 billion.
timeline.quote:
Burlington Northern Santa Fe..................
17.5
4,731
5,063

timeline.point: Stake rose above 20%, mainly through further buying, so BNSF moved to equity accounting.
timeline.quote: Burlington Northern has also repurchased shares, but our increase to 20% primarily occurred because we continued to buy this stock.

timeline.point: Railroad compared with utilities: essential service, heavy investment beyond depreciation, need for wise regulators.
timeline.quote: In both cases we provide fundamental services that are, and will remain, essential to the economic well-being of our customers, the communities we serve, and indeed the nation.

timeline.point: Paying 30% in Berkshire stock was offset by deploying $22 billion cash in a business he liked; still a close call.
timeline.quote: But the final decision was a close one. If we had needed to use more stock to make the acquisition, it would in fact have made no sense.

timeline.point: Purchase working out better than expected, raising normal earning power by nearly 40% pre-tax.
timeline.quote: The highlight of 2010 was our acquisition of Burlington Northern Santa Fe, a purchase that’s working out even better than I expected.

timeline.point: Railroads hold a cost and environmental edge over trucking; BNSF is three times more fuel-efficient.
timeline.quote: railroads have major cost and environmental advantages over trucking, their main competitor.

timeline.point: BNSF and MidAmerican carry $20 billion of goodwill, yet intrinsic value is far greater than book.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I believe current intrinsic value is far greater than book value.

timeline.point: BNSF is worth considerably more than carrying value; funds were better used there than for dividends or buybacks.
timeline.quote: BNSF is a case in point: It is now worth considerably more than our carrying value.

timeline.point: He recalls calling the deal an all-in bet on the U.S. economy.
timeline.quote: At the time, I called the transaction an “all-in wager on the economic future of the United States.”

timeline.point: Service failures disappointed shippers; BNSF lost share and Union Pacific's earnings beat it by a record amount; $6 billion capex planned for 2015.
timeline.quote: But our service problems exceeded Union Pacific’s last year, and we lost market share as a result. Moreover, U.P.’s earnings beat ours by a record amount.

timeline.point: Service improved dramatically; record capex of about $5.8 billion was money well spent.
timeline.quote: After a poor performance in 2014, our BNSF railroad dramatically improved its service to customers last year.

timeline.point: Railroad depreciation understates real capital needs, so GAAP earnings exceed economic earnings.
timeline.quote: You should also subtract something to reflect BNSF’s inadequate depreciation charge.

timeline.point: Despite heavy capital needs, BNSF counted among his better purchases.
timeline.quote: All that said, Charlie and I love our railroad, which was one of our better purchases.

timeline.point: Since 2010 BNSF invested $41 billion and paid Berkshire $41.8 billion in dividends; margin rose despite a 7% volume drop.
timeline.quote: Nevertheless, BNSF has paid substantial dividends to Berkshire – $41.8 billion in total.

timeline.point: Record earnings of $6 billion; he predicts BNSF will be a key asset a century from now.
timeline.quote: Your railroad had record earnings of $6 billion in 2021.

timeline.point: Earnings fell more than expected; capex beyond depreciation of $22 billion leaves an acceptable but smaller-than-apparent return.
timeline.quote: Consequently, Berkshire is receiving an acceptable return on its purchase price, though less than it might appear, and also a pittance on the replacement value of the property.

timeline.point: Margins slipped against all five major peers since the purchase; he believes they can improve.
timeline.quote: its profit margins have slipped relative to all five since our purchase.

timeline.point: Operating earnings table: BNSF $5,031 million in 2024 vs $5,087 million in 2023.

overview: Management and governance run through every letter from 1977 to 2024. Buffett holds two consistent positions. He praises Berkshire's owner-minded managers and runs the company by delegating heavily: no budgets or staff departments, pay tied to each unit's own results with a capital charge, and directors with large purchased stakes, token fees and no D&O insurance. He also criticizes common corporate practice: empire-building acquisitions, value-diluting stock deals, fixed-price options and their non-expensing, fee-dependent 'independent' directors, consultant-driven CEO pay, earnings guidance and manipulation, and price-blind buybacks. The critique peaked in 2002-2006 after the bubble. Over time he added owner-capitalism board rules, executive sessions, a whistleblower line and succession planning, and in 2024 admitted misjudging some managers.
note: Stance 'mixed' because the theme is consistently positive about Berkshire's own managers and governance and consistently negative about prevailing U.S. corporate practice, in every decade from the 1970s to the 2020s.

timeline.point: Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test of management.
timeline.quote: The primary test of managerial economic performance is the achievement of a high earnings rate on equity capital employed (without undue leverage, accounting gimmickry, etc.) and not the achievement of consistent gains in earnings per share.

timeline.point: Berkshire centralizes capital decisions and delegates operations.
timeline.quote: Your company is run on the principle of centralization of financial decisions at the top (the very top, it might be added), and rather extreme delegation of operating authority

timeline.point: High-premium takeovers driven by animal spirits and size.
timeline.quote: we would rather buy 10% of Wonderful Business T at X per share than 100% of T at 2X per share. Most corporate managers prefer just the reverse

timeline.point: Owner-related principles: shareholders as partners.
timeline.quote: Although our form is corporate, our attitude is partnership.

timeline.point: Fixed-price options don't align managers with owners.
timeline.quote: No owner has ever escaped the burden of capital costs, whereas a holder of a fixed-price option bears no capital costs at all.

timeline.point: Inadequate CEOs keep their jobs; boards rarely hold them to account.
timeline.quote: The supreme irony of business management is that it is far easier for an inadequate CEO to keep his job than it is for an inadequate subordinate.

timeline.point: The institutional imperative undermines rational decisions.
timeline.quote: I thought then that decent, intelligent, and experienced managers would automatically make rational business decisions. But I learned over time that isn't so.

timeline.point: Options are compensation and must be expensed.
timeline.quote: If options aren't a form of compensation, what are they? If compensation isn't an expense, what is it?

timeline.point: Directors should act for an absentee owner and replace mediocre management.
timeline.quote: I believe directors should behave as if there is a single absentee owner, whose long-term interest they should try to further in all proper ways.

timeline.point: True alignment shares downside too.
timeline.quote: In our book, alignment means being a partner in both directions, not just on the upside.

timeline.point: Managers told to run businesses for a century, ignoring accounting optics.
timeline.quote: We want our managers to think about what counts, not how it will be counted.

timeline.point: Post-bubble: managers' norms fell as prices rose; CEO pay is the acid test of reform.
timeline.quote: The acid test for reform will be CEO compensation.

timeline.point: Berkshire board model: owner-capitalism.
timeline.quote: The bottom line for our directors: You win, they win big; you lose, they lose big. Our approach might be called owner-capitalism.

timeline.point: Executive pay often wildly out of line with performance.
timeline.quote: Too often, executive compensation in the U.S. is ridiculously out of line with performance.

timeline.point: Failed financial-firm CEOs and directors should face real penalties.
timeline.quote: CEOs and, in many cases, directors have long benefitted from oversized financial carrots; some meaningful sticks now need to be part of their employment picture as well.

timeline.point: Reputation over money in the memo to managers.
timeline.quote: We can afford to lose money – even a lot of money. But we can’t afford to lose reputation – even a shred of reputation.

timeline.point: Stock deals must not give more value than they get.
timeline.quote: The intrinsic value of the shares you give in an acquisition must not be greater than the intrinsic value of the business you receive.

timeline.point: Director pay now compromises independence.
timeline.quote: Director compensation has now soared to a level that inevitably makes pay a subconscious factor affecting the behavior of many non-wealthy members.

timeline.point: Numbers manipulation called a shame of capitalism.
timeline.quote: “Bold imaginative accounting,” as a CEO once described his deception to me, has become one of the shames of capitalism.

timeline.point: Admits personnel mistakes; delay in correcting them is the cardinal sin.
timeline.quote: A decent batting average in personnel decisions is all that can be hoped for. The cardinal sin is delaying the correction of mistakes

overview: Buffett treated the high inflation of 1977-1982 as the central threat to real returns for Berkshire's owners. He argued that inflation combined with income taxes (an 'investor's misery index' and an 'inflation tax') could turn a 20% return on equity into zero or negative real gains, that it raised insurance loss costs (monetary and 'social' inflation), made long-term fixed-rate bonds unsound, and acted as a 'corporate tapeworm' forcing low-return businesses to retain earnings. He welcomed Volcker's efforts in 1981 but stayed pessimistic; in 1983 he showed that businesses with economic goodwill and few tangible assets weather inflation best, and in 1984 he still warned of future high inflation.
note: Stance is about inflation's effects (negative in every tagged letter 1977-1981). 1983 and 1984 passages on goodwill and inflation and on the dollar outlook are not tagged with the event but were read and quoted.

timeline.point: Insurance costs rise about 1% a month from monetary and 'social' inflation, so underwriting margins shrink unless rates keep pace.
timeline.quote: We estimate that costs involved in the insurance areas in which we operate rise at close to 1% per month.

timeline.point: Even a 20% compounded gain in net worth may give owners almost no after-tax purchasing power gain at a 14% inflation rate.
timeline.quote: your after-tax purchasing power gain is likely to be very close to zero at a 14% inflation rate.

timeline.point: He defines an 'investor's misery index' (inflation plus taxes) and says Berkshire has no corporate solution.
timeline.quote: We have no corporate solution to this problem; high inflation rates will not help us earn higher rates of return on equity.

timeline.point: Long-term fixed-rate bonds are unsuitable in an inflationary world; Berkshire avoids them.
timeline.quote: Overall, we opt for Polonius (slightly restated): “Neither a short-term borrower nor a long-term lender be.”

timeline.point: High inflation acts as a tax on capital that makes much corporate investment unwise for taxable owners.
timeline.quote: High rates of inflation create a tax on capital that makes much corporate investment unwise - at least if measured by the criterion of a positive real investment return to owners.

timeline.point: Berkshire is not an inflation-indexed business; inflation does not raise its return on equity.
timeline.quote: Only a few businesses come close to exhibiting this ability. And Berkshire Hathaway isn’t one of them.

timeline.point: Acquisition preference shifts to cash-generating businesses, since inflation forces many companies to spend all internal funds to stand still.
timeline.quote: Our acquisition preferences run toward businesses that generate cash, not those that consume it.

timeline.point: He applauds Volcker and notes moderating price indices, but stays negative on long-term inflation.
timeline.quote: Nevertheless, our views regarding long-term inflationary trends are as negative as ever. Like virginity, a stable price level seems capable of maintenance, but not of restoration.

timeline.point: Inflation forces low-return businesses to retain all earnings just to keep unit volume.
timeline.quote: For inflation acts as a gigantic corporate tapeworm.

timeline.point: Looking back, the businesses that did best through the inflation combined lasting intangibles with few tangible assets, unlike asset-heavy ones.
timeline.quote: During inflation, Goodwill is the gift that keeps giving.

timeline.point: Although inflation had dropped, he still expects substantial inflation and avoids most long-term bonds.
timeline.quote: We believe substantial inflation lies ahead, although we have no idea what the average rate will turn out to be.

overview: Buffett discussed arbitrage mainly in the 1985-1989 letters. Berkshire's insurance units used it as a higher-return alternative to Treasury bills when cash exceeded ideas, taking only a few large, publicly announced deals and never trading on rumors. He estimated average pre-tax arbitrage returns of at least 25% (1987), reported about $78 million pre-tax gain on $147 million in 1988 (Arcata and RJR Nabisco as examples), and set out four questions for judging a deal. He used the 63-year Graham-Newman/Buffett record against efficient-market theory, but warned that arbitrage guarantees nothing. He then stayed out in 1989 because takeover excesses made deals look like a greater-fool game. Later mentions (General Dynamics 1992, diversification 1993, Rockwood 2007) are brief.
note: Mixed: positive about Berkshire's own arbitrage results 1986-1988 and Graham's method, but always framed as a cash substitute with real risk, and he withdrew in 1989 citing takeover excesses.

timeline.point: Beatrice is a short-term arbitrage holding, used only in announced deals when Berkshire has more money than ideas.
timeline.quote: We sometimes enter the arbitrage field when we have more money than ideas, but only to participate in announced mergers and sales.

timeline.point: Arbitrage is a short-term parking place for money, better than T-bills so far, but one bad deal could change the record.
timeline.quote: To date, our returns from the funds committed to arbitrage have been many times higher than they would have been had we left those funds in Treasury Bills.

timeline.point: He estimates long-run pre-tax arbitrage returns of at least 25% a year, with a warning about bad experiences like late 1987.
timeline.quote: I believe that overall we have averaged annual pre-tax returns of at least 25% from arbitrage.

timeline.point: Unusually large arbitrage profits in 1988.
timeline.quote: Our pretax gain was about $78 million on average invested funds of about $147 million.

timeline.point: His four-question framework for judging an arbitrage situation.
timeline.quote: To evaluate arbitrage situations you must answer four questions: (1) How likely is it that the promised event will indeed occur? (2) How long will your money be tied up?

timeline.point: Arcata deal: a 15% annual return despite delays, later boosted by the redwood claim settlement.
timeline.quote: our 15% annual rate of return excluding any value for the redwood claim - was more than satisfactory.

timeline.point: Berkshire takes only publicly announced deals and does not trade on rumors.
timeline.quote: We do not trade on rumors or try to guess takeover candidates.

timeline.point: Graham-Newman, Buffett Partnership and Berkshire arbitrage returns averaged about 20% or more over 63 years, evidence against efficient-market theory.
timeline.quote: Unleveraged returns averaged 20% per year.

timeline.point: Warning: arbitrage is not a guaranteed-profit style; discipline matters more than the category.
timeline.quote: Investing in arbitrage situations, per se, is no better a strategy than selecting a portfolio by throwing darts.

timeline.point: Berkshire did little arbitrage in 1989 because many deals made no economic sense.
timeline.quote: arbitraging such deals comes too close to playing the greater-fool game.

timeline.point: General Dynamics began as a Dutch-tender arbitrage and became a long-term holding.
timeline.quote: In short order, I dumped my arbitrage thoughts and decided that Berkshire should become a long-term investor with Bill.

timeline.point: Arbitrage, unlike concentrated investing, needs wide diversification across independent bets.
timeline.quote: our efforts in arbitrage over the years - require wide diversification.

overview: For decades Buffett kept technology outside Berkshire's circle of competence. From 1982 his acquisition criteria excluded businesses with 'lots of technology', and in 1993 and 1999 he said he could not judge which tech firms had durable advantages, so Berkshire owned no tech stocks. In 2000 he condemned the dot-com bubble as a wealth transfer through 'bubble companies'. His view changed in 2011 with a $10.9 billion IBM stake, praised for its financial management and buybacks, held as one of the 'Big Four' through 2015. From 2016 Apple became a major holding; by 2020 it was tied with BNSF as Berkshire's second most valuable asset. He stressed that Apple's buybacks raised Berkshire's share at no cost.
note: Cautious or negative on tech investing 1982-2000 (outside circle of competence; dot-com bubble), positive on specific holdings IBM 2011-2015 and Apple 2016-2023. Many tagged 2011-2021 passages are holdings tables. 1982, 1991, 1996, 2007, 2022 and 2023 passages are untagged but read and used.

timeline.point: Acquisition criteria exclude technology-heavy businesses; the line is repeated in later letters.
timeline.quote: simple businesses (if there’s lots of technology, we won’t understand it),

timeline.point: Missing high-tech winners such as Apple is not counted as a mistake; he will never develop the competence to spot them early.
timeline.quote: We will never develop the competence to spot such businesses early.

timeline.point: Fast-moving technology does not allow reliable evaluation of long-term economics.
timeline.quote: For example, a business that must deal with fast-moving technology is not going to lend itself to reliable evaluations of its long-term economics.

timeline.point: Berkshire owns no tech stocks because he cannot tell which tech firms have durable advantages.
timeline.quote: This explains, by the way, why we don’t own stocks of tech companies, even though we share the general view that our society will be transformed by their products and services.

timeline.point: The dot-com bubble created 'bubble companies' that transferred wealth from the public to promoters.
timeline.quote: The fact is that a bubble market has allowed the creation of bubble companies, entities designed more with an eye to making money off investors rather than for them.

timeline.point: Capital-light growth like Microsoft's or Google's is the ideal economic model.
timeline.quote: It’s far better to have an ever-increasing stream of earnings with virtually no major capital requirements. Ask Microsoft or Google.

timeline.point: Berkshire buys 63.9 million IBM shares for $10.9 billion, his first major tech investment.
timeline.quote: 63.9 million shares of IBM that cost us $10.9 billion.

timeline.point: He praises IBM's financial management and buybacks.
timeline.quote: Indeed, I can think of no major company that has had better financial management, a skill that has materially increased the gains enjoyed by IBM shareholders.

timeline.point: IBM stake raised to 8.4% as one of the 'Big Four' investees.
timeline.quote: We purchased additional shares of IBM (increasing our ownership to 8.4% versus 7.8% at yearend 2014)

timeline.point: Apple, bought from late 2016 for $36 billion, is tied with BNSF as Berkshire's second most valuable asset.
timeline.quote: Our second and third most valuable assets – it’s pretty much a toss-up at this point – are Berkshire’s 100% ownership of BNSF, America’s largest railroad measured by freight volume, and our 5.4% ownership of Apple.

timeline.point: Apple's buybacks raised Berkshire's stake at no cost.
timeline.quote: That increase was costless to us, coming about because Apple has continuously repurchased its shares, thereby substantially shrinking the number it now has outstanding.

timeline.point: Berkshire's share of Apple's earnings far exceeds the dividends in GAAP; he praises Tim Cook.
timeline.quote: Yet our “share” of Apple’s earnings amounted to a staggering $5.6 billion.

timeline.point: Apple remains a huge commitment compared with Coca-Cola and American Express.
timeline.quote: These are not huge commitments like our Apple position.

overview: Berkshire bought Clayton Homes in 2003 for $1.7 billion. Buffett saw it as the class act of an industry ruined by reckless lending. Berkshire borrowed to fund Clayton's loan book at its cost plus one point, and Clayton stopped securitizing and kept its loans. With that backing it bought Oakwood and kept lending through 2008-2009. Its market share rose from about 13-14% to about half. Buffett praised CEO Kevin Clayton every year and said the loans to low-FICO borrowers performed well because of down payments and payments geared to income. His concerns were the industry's slump and the funding and rate disadvantages created by government policy (2008-2010). From 2017 to 2019 Clayton ranked among Berkshire's top non-insurance earners.
note: Positive on Clayton and its management in every letter 2003-2020; negative on the manufactured-housing industry's past practices and on the financing disadvantages imposed by government policy.

timeline.point: Clayton behaved better than competitors in an industry wrecked by bad lending and securitization.
timeline.quote: Much of its volume a few years back came from buyers who shouldn’t have bought, financed by lenders who shouldn’t have lent.

timeline.point: Clayton stops securitizing and keeps its loans, funded by Berkshire borrowing re-lent at cost plus one point.
timeline.quote: So Clayton has begun to retain its loans.

timeline.point: He expects the loan portfolio to grow and deliver significant earnings.
timeline.quote: Clayton’s loan portfolio will likely grow to at least $5 billion in not too many years and, with sensible credit standards in place, should deliver significant earnings.

timeline.point: Clayton completes the Oakwood acquisition and becomes the industry's largest producer; Kevin Clayton praised.
timeline.quote: He is a prototype Berkshire manager.

timeline.point: Clayton is the star of the finance sector and the only industry player earning significant money.
timeline.quote: The star of our finance sector is Clayton Homes, masterfully run by Kevin Clayton.

timeline.point: Despite the industry's lowest sales since 1962, Clayton earns $513 million pre-tax.
timeline.quote: Yet Clayton earned $513 million pre-tax and paid Berkshire an additional $86 million as a fee

timeline.point: Clayton's subprime-like borrowers keep paying through the housing crash.
timeline.quote: Clayton’s 198,888 borrowers, however, have continued to pay normally throughout the housing crash, handing us no unexpected losses.

timeline.point: Government-guaranteed competitors' cheaper funding threatens Clayton's lending.
timeline.quote: At the moment, it is much better to be a financial cripple with a government guarantee than a Gibraltar without one.

timeline.point: The rate gap between factory-built and site-built home mortgages will keep Clayton below its potential.
timeline.quote: Even under these conditions, I believe Clayton will operate profitably in coming years, though well below its potential.

timeline.point: Down payments and payments geared to income kept Clayton solvent and buyers in their homes.
timeline.quote: This policy kept Clayton solvent and also kept buyers in their homes.

timeline.point: Manufactured housing is in a depression, but Clayton stays profitable thanks to its mortgage portfolio.
timeline.quote: Despite these difficult times, Clayton has continued to operate profitably, largely because its mortgage portfolio has performed well under trying circumstances.

timeline.point: Market share rose from 14% at purchase to about 45%.
timeline.quote: When we purchased Clayton in 2003 for $1.7 billion, its share was 14%.

timeline.point: Clayton keeps 100% of the risk on the mortgages it originates.
timeline.quote: At Clayton, our risk retention was, and is, 100%.

timeline.point: He calls the Clayton-Berkshire relationship a partnership with real synergies.
timeline.quote: Clayton and Berkshire have been a wonderful partnership.

timeline.point: Clayton holds 49% of the manufactured-home market and expands into site-built homes.
timeline.quote: All told, Clayton accounted for 49% of the manufactured-home market last year.

timeline.point: Clayton earns more than $1 billion pre-tax a year.
timeline.quote: Today, Clayton and Pilot each have annual pre-tax earnings of more than $1 billion.

overview: Railroads appear in the letters only from 2007, when BNSF was a stock holding (bought from 2006, 20%+ by 2008). In late 2009 Berkshire bought all of BNSF, its largest purchase, for $22 billion cash plus 6.1% more shares. Buffett called it an all-in bet on America and said it lifted normal earning power by nearly 40% pre-tax. He described BNSF as the economy's main freight artery, more fuel-efficient than trucks, and a regulated, capital-intensive business with a social compact that needs heavy reinvestment. Faults he admitted: poor 2014 service, GAAP depreciation that overstates railroad earnings, and in 2023 slipping margins, wage pressure and spending of $22 billion beyond depreciation. He still calls BNSF a century-long asset.
note: Positive on BNSF in every letter 2009-2024, with stated reservations: service failures and lost share in 2014, depreciation that understates true costs (2015-2017, 2023), and 2023 earnings below his expectation with margins lagging peers. 2022 notes he and Munger 'hated railroad stocks for decades' before changing their view. No railroad passages before 2007.

timeline.point: BNSF appears as a large marketable holding: 17.5% of the company at a cost of $4,731 million.
timeline.quote: Burlington Northern Santa Fe

timeline.point: BNSF stake passes 20% mainly through continued buying and is carried at equity value.
timeline.quote: Burlington Northern has also repurchased shares, but our increase to 20% primarily occurred because we continued to buy this stock.

timeline.point: Paying 30% of the BNSF cost in stock was a close call, accepted to deploy $22 billion of cash in a business he understood.
timeline.quote: In the end, Charlie and I decided that the disadvantage of paying 30% of the price through stock was offset by the opportunity the acquisition gave us to deploy $22 billion of cash

timeline.point: BNSF resembles the utilities: an essential service needing heavy investment and a social compact with regulators.
timeline.quote: We see a “social compact” existing between the public and our railroad business, just as is the case with our utilities.

timeline.point: BNSF is working out better than expected and raises normal earning power substantially.
timeline.quote: It now appears that owning this railroad will increase Berkshire’s “normal” earning power by nearly 40% pre-tax and by well over 30% after-tax.

timeline.point: Rail has cost and environmental advantages over trucking.
timeline.quote: Both of us are enthusiastic about BNSF’s future because railroads have major cost and environmental advantages over trucking, their main competitor.

timeline.point: BNSF carries about 15% of US inter-city freight ton-miles: the economy's largest artery.
timeline.quote: It is no exaggeration to characterize railroads as the circulatory system of our economy. Your railroad is the largest artery.

timeline.point: BNSF is worth considerably more than its carrying value; buying it beat dividends or repurchases.
timeline.quote: BNSF is a case in point: It is now worth considerably more than our carrying value.

timeline.point: BNSF's service failed many customers; it lost share to Union Pacific and plans $6 billion of capital spending.
timeline.quote: During the year, BNSF disappointed many of its customers.

timeline.point: Service recovered and BNSF earned a record $6.8 billion pre-tax.
timeline.quote: BNSF, however, maintained volume, and pre-tax income rose to a record $6.8 billion*

timeline.point: GAAP depreciation understates the railroad's true costs, but he loves the railroad.
timeline.quote: All that said, Charlie and I love our railroad, which was one of our better purchases.

timeline.point: BNSF has paid Berkshire $41.8 billion of dividends since purchase despite heavy investment.
timeline.quote: Nevertheless, BNSF has paid substantial dividends to Berkshire – $41.8 billion in total.

timeline.point: BNSF had record earnings of $6 billion; he predicts it will be a key asset a century from now.
timeline.quote: Your railroad had record earnings of $6 billion in 2021.

timeline.point: Munger's lesson: they hated railroad stocks for decades and were slow to see the change.
timeline.quote: Warren and I hated railroad stocks for decades, but the world changed and finally the country had four huge railroads of vital importance to the American economy.

timeline.point: BNSF earns an acceptable return on its price but a pittance on replacement value; margins slipped versus peers.
timeline.quote: Consequently, Berkshire is receiving an acceptable return on its purchase price, though less than it might appear, and also a pittance on the replacement value of the property.

timeline.point: Railroad and utility earnings improved in aggregate, but both have much left to accomplish.
timeline.quote: Both, however, have much left to accomplish.

overview: Across 1977-2024 Buffett treats accounting as 'the beginning, not the end' of valuation. He consistently argues that reported earnings miss the retained earnings of minority investees (look-through earnings from 1989), that goodwill amortization usually is not a real cost while depreciation is, and that owner earnings beat GAAP for valuation. He attacked misleading practices in every decade: 'cash flow' and EBITDA, insurers' loss-reserve games, unexpensed stock options (1992-2004), restructuring charges and earnings management (1998), pro-forma and 'adjusted' earnings, and fanciful pension assumptions. He backed some reforms (option expensing, goodwill impairment-only, mark-to-market) and opposed others. From 2017 he rejected the rule putting unrealized gains into net income and told owners to use operating earnings.
note: Mixed: critical of specific GAAP rules and of managements' and auditors' manipulation in every decade 1978-2024, yet he calls accounting the indispensable language of business, reconciles to audited GAAP and supports some rules (option expensing, mark-to-market, asymmetric goodwill write-downs). Built from six decade parts; 208 of 719 tagged passages read in full, the rest from the annotation layer.

timeline.point: Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the test of managerial performance.
timeline.quote: The primary test of managerial economic performance is the achievement of a high earnings rate on equity capital employed (without undue leverage, accounting gimmickry, etc.) and not the achievement of consistent gains in earnings per share.

timeline.point: Unreported retained earnings of investees exceed Berkshire's reported operating earnings.
timeline.quote: Thus, conventional accounting only allows less than half of our earnings “iceberg” to appear above the surface, in plain view.

timeline.point: Accounting numbers start, but do not finish, a valuation.
timeline.quote: accounting numbers are the beginning, not the end, of business valuation.

timeline.point: See's goodwill amortization was not a true economic cost.
timeline.quote: One reality is that the amortization charges that have been deducted as costs in the earnings statement each year since acquisition of See’s were not true economic costs.

timeline.point: Owner earnings, not GAAP, matter for valuation.
timeline.quote: we consider the owner earnings figure, not the GAAP figure, to be the relevant item for valuation purposes

timeline.point: Insurers' reported earnings, including Berkshire's, deserve suspicion.
timeline.quote: You should be very suspicious of any earnings figures reported by insurers (including our own, as we have unfortunately proved to you in the past).

timeline.point: He introduces look-through earnings.
timeline.quote: In our view, Berkshire's fundamental earning power is best measured by a "look-through" approach

timeline.point: Options are compensation and belong in expenses.
timeline.quote: If options aren't a form of compensation, what are they? If compensation isn't an expense, what is it?

timeline.point: Restructuring charges are often used to manipulate earnings.
timeline.quote: The distortion du jour is the “restructuring charge,” an accounting entry that can, of course, be legitimate but that too often is a device for manipulating earnings.

timeline.point: Goodwill amortization charges are usually spurious.
timeline.quote: we agree with the many managers who argue that goodwill amortization charges are usually spurious.

timeline.point: Investors should beware weak accounting such as unexpensed options.
timeline.quote: Three suggestions for investors: First, beware of companies displaying weak accounting.

timeline.point: EBITDA wrongly implies depreciation is not an expense.
timeline.quote: Trumpeting EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) is a particularly pernicious practice.

timeline.point: Berkshire's net income is almost always meaningless.
timeline.quote: Important though that number may be at most companies, it is almost always meaningless at Berkshire.

timeline.point: Stock-based compensation is a real expense.
timeline.quote: “Stock-based compensation” is the most egregious example. The very name says it all: “compensation.”

timeline.point: Putting unrealized gains in net income will make the bottom line useless.
timeline.quote: For analytical purposes, Berkshire’s “bottom-line” will be useless.

timeline.point: GAAP net income is worse than useless; Berkshire reports operating earnings.
timeline.quote: So sanctified, this worse-than-useless “net income” figure quickly gets transmitted throughout the world via the internet and media.

overview: CORT, the national leader in 'rent-to-rent' office and apartment furniture, was bought for Wesco (80%-owned by Berkshire) in late 1999-2000 for about $386 million in cash. He called it a fine though unglamorous business with an outstanding manager (Paul Arnold) at a sensible price. Its earnings were weak in the 2001-2003 recession and still 'inadequate' in 2004, improved significantly in 2006, were hit hard again in the 2008-09 recession (a $3 million pre-tax loss in 2009), and recovered to $18 million in 2010. From 2007 to 2016 he repeatedly described it as a good business and an industry leader. Basis: discussed in 13 letters 2000-2016; consistently positive on the franchise, candid about cyclical earnings.

timeline.point: Buffett learned of CORT from an unrelated broker's fax in November 1999, read its SEC filings that day and quickly saw the ingredients for a purchase.
timeline.quote: a fine though unglamorous business, an outstanding manager, and a price (going by that on the failed deal) that made sense.

timeline.point: CORT was bought through Wesco for about $386 million in cash; Buffett expected it to beat original expectations.
timeline.quote: We quickly purchased CORT for Wesco, our 80%-owned subsidiary, paying about $386 million in cash.

timeline.point: Recession hit the leasing businesses: earnings were poor for two years, but CORT and XTRA stayed leaders and a modest improvement was expected.
timeline.quote: They remain leaders in their fields, and I expect at least a modest improvement in their earnings this year.

timeline.point: Leasing rebounded in 2004, but CORT's earnings were still not good enough.
timeline.quote: At CORT (office furniture), earnings remain inadequate, but are trending upward.

timeline.point: CORT's earnings improved significantly in 2006; Berkshire looked for tuck-in acquisitions for Paul Arnold to run.
timeline.quote: CORT’s earnings improved significantly last year

timeline.point: Buffett grouped CORT with Clayton and XTRA as good, well-run businesses that make tuck-in acquisitions.
timeline.quote: Clayton, XTRA and CORT are all good businesses, very ably run by Kevin Clayton, Bill Franz and Paul Arnold.

timeline.point: The 2008-09 recession hit CORT severely; its competitive position stayed strong but no rebound was visible yet.
timeline.quote: The table also illustrates how severely our furniture (CORT) and trailer (XTRA) leasing operations have been hit by the recession.

timeline.point: Business picked up and operations were tightened in 2010, turning a 2009 loss into a profit.
timeline.quote: The combination increased its pre-tax results from a loss of $3 million in 2009 to $18 million of profit in 2010.

timeline.point: Combined CORT and XTRA pre-tax earnings tracked the non-housing recovery: $13 million (2009), $53 million (2010), $155 million (2011).
timeline.quote: Their combined pre-tax earnings were $13 million in 2009, $53 million in 2010 and $155 million in 2011

timeline.point: CORT and XTRA described as leaders in their industries under new managers, with Berkshire funding equipment purchases.
timeline.quote: CORT and XTRA are leaders in their industries as well. And Jeff Pederson and Bill Franz will keep them on top.

timeline.point: CORT and XTRA had substantially increased earnings as the economy strengthened, helped by investing more in equipment than competitors.
timeline.quote: These companies are industry leaders and have substantially increased their earnings as the American economy has gained strength.

timeline.point: CORT was still named among Berkshire's leasing operations, each a leader in its field.
timeline.quote: Each is the leader in its field.

overview: Wesco Financial (Mutual Savings, Precision Steel, later Wes-FIC, KBS and CORT) was 80% owned by Blue Chip Stamps, so Berkshire's economic share was about 46-48% until the 1983 Blue Chip merger raised it to 80%. Most mentions are structural: earnings tables, equity-method accounting, holdings excluding Wesco's minority, and pointers to Charlie Munger's Wesco letters (praised for explaining the savings-and-loan crisis and banking). Buffett's direct comments are favorable: good progress in 1977, a superb repositioning of Mutual Savings, Louie Vincenti as a marvelous manager, Precision Steel's good returns. In the 1990s-2000 Wesco became a vehicle for small insurance (KBS) and the CORT purchase. Basis: discussed in about 21 letters 1977-2000 (one 2019 board list); mildly positive, mostly descriptive.

timeline.point: Wesco, 80% owned by Blue Chip Stamps and run by Louis Vincenti, made good progress in 1977.
timeline.quote: Both Wesco Financial Corp., an 80% owned subsidiary of Blue Chip Stamps, managed by Louis Vincenti, and See’s Candies, a 99% owned subsidiary, managed by Chuck Huggins, made good progress in 1977.

timeline.point: Through its ~58% stake in Blue Chip, Berkshire's equity in Wesco's earnings was about 46%.
timeline.quote: Thus, Berkshire’s equity in Wesco’s earnings is about 46%.

timeline.point: Wesco, controlled but only 48% owned, was reported by the equity method as a one-line entry.
timeline.quote: for example, Wesco Financial, controlled by Berkshire but only 48% owned - are included via a one-line entry in the owner’s Statement of Earnings.

timeline.point: Buffett praised Vincenti and Munger for repositioning Wesco's Mutual Savings and Loan.
timeline.quote: particularly note the superb job done by Louie Vincenti and Charlie Munger in repositioning Mutual Savings and Loan.

timeline.point: After the 1983 Blue Chip merger, Berkshire's net interest in Wesco rose from 48% to 80%.
timeline.quote: Berkshire’s net interest in Wesco was 48% during 1982 and the first six months of 1983, and 80% for the balance of 1983.

timeline.point: Munger succeeded Vincenti as Wesco chairman in late 1983.
timeline.quote: Charlie replaced Louie Vincenti as Chairman of Wesco late in 1983 when health forced Louie’s retirement at age 77.

timeline.point: Wesco formed Wes-FIC, which took two-sevenths of the Fireman's Fund quota-share reinsurance business written by National Indemnity.
timeline.quote: two-sevenths of it is passed along to Wesco-Financial Insurance Company (“Wes-FIC”), a new company organized by our 80%-owned subsidiary, Wesco Financial Corporation.

timeline.point: Buffett pointed shareholders to Munger's Wesco letter on the savings-and-loan crisis and praised Precision Steel's returns.
