timeline.quote: Precision operates in an extremely competitive industry, yet Dave consistently achieves good returns on invested capital.

timeline.point: Wesco's Mutual Savings resigned from the U.S. League of Savings Institutions in protest at its policies.
timeline.quote: which conveyed our disgust with its policies and our consequent decision to resign.

timeline.point: Kansas Bankers Surety was placed in Wesco because of its small size and Wesco's wish to expand in insurance.
timeline.quote: Because of its relatively small size, we placed KBS with Wesco, our 80%-owned subsidiary, which has wanted to expand its insurance operations.

timeline.point: CORT was bought for Wesco for about $386 million in cash.
timeline.quote: We quickly purchased CORT for Wesco, our 80%-owned subsidiary, paying about $386 million in cash.

overview: Berkshire bought $10.9 million of Capital Cities in 1977, sold it at about $43 a share in 1978-80, then in early 1986 bought 3 million shares at $172.50 to help finance the $3.5 billion ABC acquisition, letting CEO Tom Murphy vote the block. He called its management the best of any public company and made it a permanent holding. From 1988 he saw less upside at current prices, and in 1991 secular change cut media intrinsic value, softened by low debt and strong managers. He sold a third in 1993 at $630 (later calling it a mistake) and swapped the rest for Disney stock and cash in 1996. Basis: discussed in 23 letters 1977-2024; consistently positive on people and business.

timeline.point: First purchase: $10.9 million in 1977; Buffett judged the stock cheaper than buying such properties directly and preferred its managers to control.
timeline.quote: Capital Cities possesses both extraordinary properties and extraordinary management. And these management skills extend equally to operations and employment of corporate capital.

timeline.point: Tom Murphy saluted as a managerial superstar strong in both acquisitions and operations.
timeline.quote: especially Tom Murphy at Capital Cities Communications (a real managerial “twofer”

timeline.point: In March 1985 Berkshire agreed to buy 3 million shares at $172.50, contingent on Cap Cities acquiring ABC.
timeline.quote: Our admiration for the management of Capital Cities, led by Tom Murphy and Dan Burke, has been expressed several times in previous annual reports. Quite simply, they are tops in both ability and integrity.

timeline.point: Purchase completed after yearend; Buffett rated Cap Cities' management the best of any public company.
timeline.quote: I’ve been on record for many years about the management of Cap Cities: I think it is the best of any publicly-owned company in the country.

timeline.point: The stake helped finance the $3.5 billion ABC deal; Buffett expected unexciting ABC economics for years and was willing to wait.
timeline.quote: For Cap Cities, ABC is a major undertaking whose economics are likely to be unexciting over the next few years. This bothers us not an iota; we can be very patient.

timeline.point: He admitted paying a full price in a media mania, years after selling the stock at $43 in 1978-80.
timeline.quote: Our Cap Cities purchase was made at a full price, reflecting the very considerable enthusiasm for both media stocks and media properties

timeline.point: Cap Cities named one of three permanent holdings, not to be sold even if overpriced.
timeline.quote: we expect to keep permanently our three primary holdings, Capital Cities/ABC, Inc., GEICO Corporation, and The Washington Post.

timeline.point: Industry conditions for the permanent holdings had worsened; managers superb but upside less exciting at current prices.
timeline.quote: All of these companies have superb management and strong properties. But, at current prices, their upside potential looks considerably less exciting to us today than it did some years ago.

timeline.point: Example of retained earnings missing from GAAP: Berkshire's 17% share of Cap Cities' earnings was over $83 million, but only about $530,000 was reported.
timeline.quote: The extreme case is Capital Cities/ABC, Inc. Our 17% share of the company's earnings amounted to more than $83 million last year.

timeline.point: Secular change reduced media intrinsic value, but strong balance sheets and managers made Cap Cities and Washington Post the media holdings he was most comfortable with.
timeline.quote: The strong balance sheets and strong managements of Cap Cities and Washington Post leave us more comfortable with these investments than we would be with holdings in any other media companies.

timeline.point: Sold one-third of the stake in late 1993 at $630 a share, a $297 million after-tax profit, far above the look-through retained earnings.
timeline.quote: in 1986 we bought three million shares of Capital Cities/ABC for $172.50 per share and late last year sold one-third of that holding for $630 per share.

timeline.point: Buffett called the 1993 sale a mistake once the price rose to $85.25 (post-split), second only to USAir.
timeline.quote: Late in 1993 I sold 10 million shares of Cap Cities at $63; at year-end 1994, the price was $85.25.

timeline.point: Dan Burke retired, credited with record earnings after tough industry years.
timeline.quote: But their skill as managers allowed the businesses they ran to emerge from these periods with record earnings, added luster, and bright prospects.

timeline.point: In early 1996 the Cap Cities shares were exchanged for Disney stock and cash.
timeline.quote: we exchanged our Cap Cities shares for a combination of cash and Disney stock.

timeline.point: Buffett said the shares he sold in 1993 for $635 million would have brought $1.27 billion in the Disney merger.
timeline.quote: And don't later be as dumb as I was two years ago when I sold one-third of our holdings in Cap Cities for $635 million

timeline.point: Recalled turning down Murphy's offer of the Dallas-Fort Worth NBC station for $35 million, a See's-like business.
timeline.quote: In effect Murph whispered “buy” into my ear. But I didn’t listen.

timeline.point: Murphy and Burke later described as the best managerial duo Buffett and Munger ever saw.
timeline.quote: These two were the best managerial duo – both in what they accomplished and how they did it – that Charlie and I ever witnessed.

overview: From 1978 to 2023 Buffett consistently rejected short-term forecasts of stock prices, interest rates, currencies and the economy: useless, 'poison', a waste of time. His rule is to price, not time, purchases and to be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful (1986, repeated 2004, 2006, 2016). He did make explicit forecasts in narrower areas: insurance-industry combined ratios (1977-1987), inflation and long bonds (1984-87), the dollar (2003-05, with caveats), and long-run return expectations (1992, 1999, 2007: lower future equity returns). He admitted not acting on Bubble-era overvaluation (2004). Basis: tagged in 37 letters 1977-2023; consistently negative on market timing and macro prediction, with no change in view.

timeline.point: Early statement that no one can forecast short-term stock prices; Berkshire relies on long-term value of holdings instead.
timeline.quote: successfully forecasting short term stock price movements is something we think neither we nor anyone else can do.

timeline.point: Meanwhile he made explicit insurance-cycle forecasts, e.g. an industry combined ratio near 105 over five years.
timeline.quote: Our forecast is for an average combined ratio for the industry in the 105 area over the next five years.

timeline.point: Short-term stock and bond forecasts called useless.
timeline.quote: We believe that short-term forecasts of stock or bond prices are useless. The forecasts may tell you a great deal about the forecaster; they tell you nothing about the future.

timeline.point: Expected substantial future inflation and avoided long-term bonds, while admitting no idea of the rate.
timeline.quote: We believe substantial inflation lies ahead, although we have no idea what the average rate will turn out to be.

timeline.point: Finding no attractive equities was explicitly not a market call; the fear-and-greed rule was stated.
timeline.quote: we simply attempt to be fearful when others are greedy and to be greedy only when others are fearful.

timeline.point: No ability to forecast interest rates; Berkshire borrows when conditions are benign to be ready for opportunities.
timeline.quote: We have no ability to forecast interest rates and - maintaining our usual open-minded spirit - believe that no one else can.

timeline.point: New stock commitments reflect long-term business views, never market opinions.
timeline.quote: We do not have, never have had, and never will have an opinion about where the stock market, interest rates, or business activity will be a year from now.

timeline.point: Despite calling forecasts poison, he predicted lower stock returns for the coming decade because stocks had outrun their businesses.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I continue to believe that short-term market forecasts are poison and should be kept locked up in a safe place, away from children

timeline.point: Political and economic forecasts are ignored; the best purchases came at peaks of macro fear.
timeline.quote: We will continue to ignore political and economic forecasts, which are an expensive distraction for many investors and businessmen.

timeline.point: Price, not timing, guides purchases.
timeline.quote: We try to price, rather than time, purchases. In our view, it is folly to forego buying shares in an outstanding business whose long-term future is predictable

timeline.point: Not forecasting the market, but warned that investors' return expectations were wildly optimistic.
timeline.quote: We have never attempted to forecast what the stock market is going to do in the next month or the next year, and we are not trying to do that now.

timeline.point: Bearish on the dollar via currency positions, yet warned about macro forecasting.
timeline.quote: I should note that the cemetery for seers has a huge section set aside for macro forecasters.

timeline.point: Self-criticism: he talked about Bubble overvaluation but did not act.
timeline.quote: I underestimated just how severe the overvaluation was. I talked when I should have walked.

timeline.point: Even certain economic gloom does not imply a market direction.
timeline.quote: We’re certain, for example, that the economy will be in shambles throughout 2009 – and, for that matter, probably well beyond – but that conclusion does not tell us whether the stock market will rise or fall.

timeline.point: Media quoted only the gloomy half of that sentence; the Dow rose from 7,063 to 10,428.
timeline.quote: The Dow closed the day of the letter at 7,063 and finished the year at 10,428.

timeline.point: Dancing in and out of a favorable game is a terrible mistake.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I believe it’s a terrible mistake to try to dance in and out of it based upon the turn of tarot cards, the predictions of “experts,” or the ebb and flow of business

timeline.point: Macro opinions are a waste of time and dangerous.
timeline.quote: Forming macro opinions or listening to the macro or market predictions of others is a waste of time.

timeline.point: Nobody can say when chaos will occur.
timeline.quote: Market forecasters will fill your ear but will never fill your wallet.

timeline.point: Major declines will come at unknown times; widespread fear is an investor's friend.
timeline.quote: First, widespread fear is your friend as an investor, because it serves up bargain purchases. Second, personal fear is your enemy.

timeline.point: Expected stock buying is not a market call.
timeline.quote: My expectation of more stock purchases is not a market call. Charlie and I have no idea as to how stocks will behave next week or next year.

timeline.point: Interest-rate forecasting has never been Berkshire's game.
timeline.quote: Forecasting interest rates has never been our game, and Charlie and I have no idea what rates will average over the next year, or ten or thirty years.

timeline.point: Near-term economic and market forecasts called worse than useless.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I plead ignorance and firmly believe that near-term economic and market forecasts are worse than useless.

timeline.point: Currency moves cannot be forecast, so the Japanese stakes were funded with yen debt.
timeline.quote: Neither Greg nor I believe we can forecast market prices of major currencies.

overview: Early letters cover the forced Illinois bank divestiture, regulator-set insurance pricing, 'judicial inflation', the 1986 Tax Reform Act (net negative) and Proposition 103. From 1992 to 2004 he attacked Congress and CEOs for blocking option expensing, praised SEC chairmen Levitt and Donaldson, doubted most post-Enron governance rules, and warned about trade deficits. PUHCA limited MidAmerican until its 2005 repeal. In 2008-09 he criticized government-guaranteed competitors and the regulator that missed Fannie and Freddie, but backed the Fed's rescue. From 2009 he described a 'social compact' with utility and rail regulators; in 2023 he said that pact had broken in some states and called it his costly mistake. Basis: 38 letters 1978-2023; mixed.

timeline.point: The Bank Holding Company Act forced Berkshire to divest the Illinois National Bank by end-1980; the Fed barred shared officers after a spin-off.
timeline.quote: the Bank Holding Company Act of 1969 requires that we divest the bank by December 31, 1980.

timeline.point: Past insurance profitability came largely from regulator-sanctioned pricing that let insurers price their way to profit despite overcapacity.
timeline.quote: insurance companies could legally price their way to profitability even in the face of substantial overcapacity.

timeline.point: He called the large federal deficit dangerous and inflationary, with politicians avoiding it.
timeline.quote: But we believe that present fiscal policy - featuring a huge deficit - is both extremely dangerous and difficult to reverse.

timeline.point: The 1986 Tax Reform Act was judged a net negative for Berkshire and its shareholders.
timeline.quote: Although we find much to praise in the Act, the net financial effect for Berkshire is negative

timeline.point: California's Proposition 103 threatened below-cost auto rates, a risk mainly to GEICO's economic goodwill.
timeline.quote: If voters insist that auto insurance be priced below cost, it eventually must be sold by government.

timeline.point: Accounting regulators were criticized for yielding to executives on stock options.
timeline.quote: The accounting profession and the SEC should be shamed by the fact that they have long let themselves be muscled by business executives on the option-accounting issue.

timeline.point: USAir mistake tied to deregulation: revenues faced open competition while costs stayed at regulated-era levels.
timeline.quote: These costs, if left unchecked, portended disaster, however reassuring the airline's past record might be.

timeline.point: He backed SEC chairman Levitt's push against earnings management.
timeline.quote: A big piece of news, however, is that the SEC, led by its chairman, Arthur Levitt, seems determined to get corporate America to clean up its act.

timeline.point: PUHCA forced the MidAmerican deal to give Berkshire under 10% of the vote but about 76% of the equity.
timeline.quote: Acquisitions in the electric utility industry are complicated by a variety of regulations including the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935.

timeline.point: He doubted most post-Enron governance rules were worth their cost, while backing independent-director sessions.
timeline.quote: I doubt, however, that most of the other new governance rules and recommendations will provide benefits commensurate with the monetary and other costs they impose.

timeline.point: The Senate's 1994 vote against expensing options opened an era of anything-goes earnings reports.
timeline.quote: To its shame, the Senate voted 88-9 against expensing.

timeline.point: Regulated utility pricing endorsed as fair, while private managers find efficiencies government will not.
timeline.quote: Prices and earnings continue to be regulated in a fair manner by the government, just as they should be.

timeline.point: Bipartisan trade policies were pushing America toward foreign ownership.
timeline.quote: But that’s precisely where our trade policies, supported by Republicans and Democrats alike, are taking us.

timeline.point: PUHCA's 2005 repeal let Berkshire convert to voting control and consolidate MidAmerican.
timeline.quote: The Public Utility Holding Company Act (“PUHCA”) was repealed on August 8, 2005

timeline.point: Government guarantees gave weak lenders cheaper money than AAA-rated Berkshire, hurting Clayton.
timeline.quote: At the moment, it is much better to be a financial cripple with a government guarantee than a Gibraltar without one.

timeline.point: Despite criticizing OFHEO's failure on Fannie and Freddie, he supported the Fed's Bear Stearns rescue.
timeline.quote: In my opinion, the Fed was right to do so.

timeline.point: Government mortgage rules favored site-built homes, making factory-built home loans cost about 9% versus 5 1/4%.
timeline.quote: The residential mortgage market is shaped by government rules that are expressed by FHA, Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae.

timeline.point: Utilities and railroads described as a social compact: heavy investment in exchange for fair allowed returns.
timeline.quote: Wise regulation and wise investment are two sides of the same coin.

timeline.point: He repeatedly stated trust that governments will treat capital providers well enough to keep funds flowing.
timeline.quote: It is in the self-interest of governments to treat capital providers in a manner that will ensure the continued flow of funds to essential projects.

timeline.point: Clayton came through heavy post-crisis scrutiny with tiny fines, which Buffett cited with pride.
timeline.quote: Our total fines during this period were $38,200 and our refunds to customers $704,678.

timeline.point: The 2017 tax law added $29 billion to Berkshire's net worth.
timeline.quote: The remaining $29 billion was delivered to us in December when Congress rewrote the U.S. Tax Code.

timeline.point: BHE's western transmission project rested on trust in America's political, economic and judicial systems.
timeline.quote: BHE’s decision to proceed, it should be noted, was based upon its trust in America’s political, economic and judicial systems.

timeline.point: Rail wage increases set in Washington outran inflation goals and cut BNSF's earnings.
timeline.quote: wage increases, promulgated in Washington, were far beyond the country’s inflation goals.

timeline.point: View changed: the fixed-return utility pact broke in some states, and he called not anticipating it a costly mistake.
timeline.quote: and investors are becoming apprehensive that such ruptures may spread.

timeline.point: Buffett took responsibility for not foreseeing worse regulatory returns.
timeline.quote: I did not anticipate or even consider the adverse developments in regulatory returns and, along with Berkshire’s two partners at BHE, I made a costly mistake in not doing so.

overview: Buffett's yardstick shifted over time: operating return on equity (1977-81), per-share book and intrinsic value (from 1982-83), a modest edge over the S&P 500 (from 1992, explicit to 2018), then operating earnings and market price (from 2018). Book value per share compounded about 20-24% from 1964, peaking near 24.7% in 1998 and easing to 19.1% by 2017; market value compounded 19.9% versus 10.4% for the S&P over 1965-2024. Worst years were 1999 (+0.5%, his 'D') and 2008 (-9.6%). In every decade he warned that size would shrink returns, and he discounted bull-market or accounting-driven gains. Basis: discussed in all 48 letters 1977-2024; consistently proud of the record but more modest about the edge from the 2000s on.

timeline.point: Single-year performance measured by operating return on beginning equity: 19% in 1977.
timeline.quote: In 1977 our operating earnings on beginning equity capital amounted to 19%, slightly better than last year and above both our own long-term average and that of American industry in aggregate.

timeline.point: Book value compounded 20.5% from 1964 to 1979.
timeline.quote: At yearend 1979, book value with equity holdings carried at market value was $335.85 per share. The gain in book value comes to 20.5% compounded annually.

timeline.point: Return-on-equity yardstick dropped as returns fell to 9.8%; he admitted the move invites suspicion.
timeline.quote: You should be suspicious of such an assertion. Yardsticks seldom are discarded while yielding favorable readings.

timeline.point: Goal set as per-share intrinsic value growth above the average large corporation.
timeline.quote: Our long-term economic goal (subject to some qualifications mentioned later) is to maximize the average annual rate of gain in intrinsic business value on a per-share basis.

timeline.point: Size warnings began in earnest: the historical 22% rate is history.
timeline.quote: Our historical 22% rate is just that - history.

timeline.point: Corporate tax burdens Berkshire relative to the pre-tax S&P 500.
timeline.quote: Under present tax laws, a gain for the S&P of 18% delivers a corporate holder of that index a return well short of 13%.

timeline.point: Strong 1997 gain dismissed because the S&P rose almost as much.
timeline.quote: So what's our duck rating for 1997? The table on the facing page shows that though we paddled furiously last year, passive ducks that simply invested in the S&P Index rose almost as fast as we did.

timeline.point: 1999 was the worst absolute and relative year of his tenure.
timeline.quote: We had the worst absolute performance of my tenure and, compared to the S&P, the worst relative performance as well.

timeline.point: Past record will not be replicated: higher valuations and far more capital.
timeline.quote: One final thought about Berkshire: In the future we won’t come close to replicating our past record.

timeline.point: 2008 was the worst year for both Berkshire's book value and the S&P.
timeline.quote: Our decrease in net worth during 2008 was $11.5 billion, which reduced the per-share book value of both our Class A and Class B stock by 9.6%.

timeline.point: Beat the S&P in all 41 five-year periods through 2009 and in every down year, but the edge was shrinking.
timeline.quote: we have never had any five-year period beginning with 1965-69 and ending with 2005-09 – and there have been 41 of these – during which our gain in book value did not exceed the S&P’s gain.

timeline.point: Record vs the S&P now only satisfactory; exceptional results ruled out.
timeline.quote: The bountiful years, we want to emphasize, will never return. The huge sums of capital we currently manage eliminate any chance of exceptional performance.

timeline.point: At 50 years, intrinsic value gain roughly matched the 1,826,163% market-price gain.
timeline.quote: In our view, the increase in Berkshire’s per-share intrinsic value over the past 50 years is roughly equal to the 1,826,163% gain in market price of the company’s shares.

timeline.point: Book value retired as the headline metric; market price to be the long-run measure.
timeline.quote: The fact is that the annual change in Berkshire’s book value – which makes its farewell appearance on page 2 – is a metric that has lost the relevance it once had.

timeline.point: GAAP swings called misleading; operating earnings emphasized.
timeline.quote: The GAAP earnings are 100% misleading when viewed quarterly or even annually.

timeline.point: Size makes doubling Berkshire within five years impossible.
timeline.quote: Doubling our huge base is simply not possible within, say, a five-year period

timeline.point: 2024 operating earnings reached a record $47.4 billion.
timeline.quote: All told, we recorded operating earnings of $47.4 billion in 2024.

overview: Buffett treats gold, silver and commodities as non-productive assets, in contrast to farmland, which he values for its output. In 1979 he noted Berkshire's book value bought the same half ounce of gold as in 1964. In 1997 Berkshire bought 111.2 million ounces of silver on a supply-demand view (not inflation) and held oil derivative contracts. His fullest statement (2011) calls gold neither useful nor procreative and predicts productive assets will far outcompound it; 2013 recounts his 1986 farm purchase (10% normalized return, worth five times cost); 2018 shows gold returned under 1% of what American business delivered. Stance: negative on gold in 2011 and 2018, positive on productive farmland in 2011 and 2013, one tactical silver purchase in 1997.

timeline.point: Inflation measured in gold: Berkshire's book value bought about the same half ounce of gold in 1979 as in 1964; government can print money but not gold or oil.
timeline.quote: after we have plowed back all earnings along with much blood, sweat and tears, the book value produced will buy about the same half ounce.

timeline.point: Berkshire held oil derivative contracts (45.7 million barrels established 1994-95), bought when oil seemed modestly underpriced; by 1997 he had no opinion on oil.
timeline.quote: When we established our contracts, oil for future delivery seemed modestly underpriced. Today, though, we have no opinion as to its attractiveness.

timeline.point: Bought 111.2 million ounces of silver, a $97.4 million pre-tax mark-to-market gain in 1997, on falling bullion inventories; inflation expectations played no part.
timeline.quote: In recent years, bullion inventories have fallen materially, and last summer Charlie and I concluded that a higher price would be needed to establish equilibrium between supply and demand.

timeline.point: Explains disclosing the silver position (regulator questions) and says he will not normally report unconventional positions; some were eliminated and others added.
timeline.quote: questions about our silver position that we had received from regulatory authorities led us to believe that they wished us to publicly acknowledge this investment.

timeline.point: Gold is a non-productive asset bought on hope that others will pay more later; its price rise rests on the growing ranks of the fearful.
timeline.quote: Gold, however, has two significant shortcomings, being neither of much use nor procreative.

timeline.point: Pile A (all gold, $9.6 trillion at $1,750/oz) versus pile B (all U.S. cropland plus 16 Exxon Mobils, with $1 trillion left over).
timeline.quote: Can you imagine an investor with $9.6 trillion selecting pile A over pile B?

timeline.point: Predicts the gold pile will compound far below productive assets over a century.
timeline.quote: I'm confident, however, that the $9.6 trillion current valuation of pile A will compound over the century at a rate far inferior to that achieved by pile B.

timeline.point: Prefers productive assets such as businesses, farms and real estate, which retain purchasing power in inflation, over sterile assets like gold.
timeline.quote: My own preference - and you knew this was coming - is our third category: investment in productive assets, whether businesses, farms, or real estate.

timeline.point: Bought a 400-acre Nebraska farm from the FDIC in 1986 for $280,000 after the farm bubble burst, at a normalized return of about 10%.
timeline.quote: From these estimates, I calculated the normalized return from the farm to then be about 10%.

timeline.point: 28 years later the farm had tripled its earnings and was worth five times or more its cost; lesson: value an asset by its output, not price moves.
timeline.quote: Now, 28 years later, the farm has tripled its earnings and is worth five times or more what I paid.

timeline.point: $114.75 put into 3 1/4 ounces of gold in 1942 would be worth about $4,200, under 1% of an unmanaged investment in American business.
timeline.quote: You would now have an asset worth about $4,200, less than 1% of what would have been realized from a simple unmanaged investment in American business.

overview: Berkshire bought $700 million of Salomon Inc 9% convertible preferred in 1987, treating it as a fixed-income holding with a conversion option; Buffett backed CEO John Gutfreund's integrity while admitting no insight into investment banking. After the 1991 Treasury-bond scandal he served ten months as interim chairman (August 1991-June 1992) and credited Maughan, Denham and others with saving the firm. In 1995 he graded the conversion bet 'very poor' though the preferred delivered as a bond; Salomon's 1997 merger into Travelers made results 'far better than I anticipated'. Later letters (2010, 2022) cite Salomon as a lesson in facing bad news and a near-disaster escaped partly by luck. Salomon Brothers was also praised as Berkshire's banker (1987-1996).

timeline.point: Largest 1987 investment: $700 million of Salomon 9% convertible preferred, convertible at $38 a share, viewed mainly as a medium-term fixed-income security.
timeline.quote: By far our largest - and most publicized - investment in 1987 was a $700 million purchase of Salomon Inc 9% preferred stock.

timeline.point: No insight into investment-banking economics, hence the preferred structure; conviction rested on CEO John Gutfreund's ability and integrity.
timeline.quote: We, of course, have no special insights regarding the direction or future profitability of investment banking.

timeline.point: Admiration for Gutfreund reinforced; most of the preferred's value lies in its fixed-income characteristics, not the conversion right. Salomon directorships restricted Berkshire's RJR arbitrage.
timeline.quote: However, the overwhelming portion of the preferred's value resides in its fixed-income characteristics, not its equity characteristics.

timeline.point: Groups Salomon with USAir and Champion as industries he cannot forecast, so the preferred structure gives mediocre returns if industry economics are poor.
timeline.quote: we have no ability to forecast the economics of the investment banking business (in which we have a position through our 1987 purchase of Salomon convertible preferred), the airline industry, or the paper industry.

timeline.point: Salomon preferred assessed as worth about what Berkshire paid at yearend 1990; rebuts press valuing it only by conversion value.
timeline.quote: we can assess our holdings in Salomon and Champion at yearend 1990 as worth about what we paid, Gillette as worth somewhat more, and USAir as worth substantially less.

timeline.point: Elected interim chairman of Salomon on August 18, 1991, to protect Berkshire's investment.
timeline.quote: when I was elected Interim Chairman of Salomon Inc, it was a different story: I put my mouth where our money was.

timeline.point: Despite the scandal, he judged the preferred slightly up in value in 1991 on lower rates and a higher common price.
timeline.quote: Despite the company's travails, Charlie and I believe our Salomon preferred stock increased slightly in value during 1991.

timeline.point: Stepped down in June 1992 after ten months; Salomon Brothers posted record pre-tax earnings, 34% above the prior high, and its reputation recovered.
timeline.quote: Salomon Brothers, the securities subsidiary of Salomon Inc, reported record pre-tax earnings last year - 34% above the previous high.

timeline.point: Credits Maughan, Denham, Howard and Macfarlane with saving the firm.
timeline.quote: the firm very probably would not have survived.

timeline.point: Grades the decision to buy for the conversion option as very poor, though the preferred delivered as a fixed-income security; $140 million redeemed in 1995.
timeline.quote: That means my decision to go with Salomon because I saw value in the conversion option must be graded as very poor.

timeline.point: Praises Salomon Brothers' banking work on the Class B offering and exchangeable notes, which served Berkshire's goals against the firm's own fee interest.
timeline.quote: In the case of the 1996 transactions at Salomon Brothers, we more than got our money's worth.

timeline.point: Salomon merged into Travelers Group (Berkshire then held 23.7 million Travelers shares); final results far better than he expected two years earlier.
timeline.quote: Berkshire's final results from its Salomon investment won't be tallied for some time, but it is safe to say that they will be far better than I anticipated two years ago.

timeline.point: Uses Salomon as the lesson on facing bad news fast.
timeline.quote: A reluctance to face up immediately to bad news is what turned a problem at Salomon from one that could have easily been disposed of into one that almost caused the demise of a firm with 8,000 employees.

timeline.point: Lists Salomon among near-disasters escaped with luck in his capital-allocation report card.
timeline.quote: near-disasters at USAir and Salomon? I certainly do.)

overview: Buffett repeatedly says he cannot forecast interest rates or Fed actions (1987, 1994, 2019) and does not let them drive purchases, yet treats the long-term risk-free rate as the yardstick for all valuation (1981, 2000, 2021). In 1979-1987 he shunned long-term bonds despite 10-16% yields because of inflation risk. In 1997 he held $4.6 billion of zero-coupon Treasuries that gained as rates fell. From 2001 on, low rates appear mostly as a negative: they make insurance float less valuable (2001-2019), earn 'a pittance' on Berkshire's cash (2003, 2010) and make bonds 'return-free risk' (2011) and 'not the place to be' (2020), while lifting prices of stocks and other productive assets (1997, 2021). Higher Treasury-bill yields lifted investment income in 2023-2024.

timeline.point: High rates embed higher inflation forecasts, but he still refuses to lock in long-term bond yields, just as he would not fix a candy price for 2010.
timeline.quote: Overall, we opt for Polonius (slightly restated): "Neither a short-term borrower nor a long-term lender be."

timeline.point: High interest rates tempt insurers to write business at underwriting losses for investment income, so he expects higher combined ratios.
timeline.quote: Present interest rates encourage the obtaining of business at underwriting loss levels formerly regarded as totally unacceptable.

timeline.point: Applauds Volcker but stays negative on long-term inflation; 16% bond yields raise the 'crossbar' that a business's return on equity must clear.
timeline.quote: During the past year, long-term taxable bond yields exceeded 16% and long-term tax-exempts 14%.

timeline.point: Views a bond as a business; buyers of 1% tax-exempt bonds in 1946 paid par for an 'abominable' business.
timeline.quote: In effect, the buyer of those bonds at that time bought a "business" that earned about 1% on "book value"

timeline.point: Retains a general fear of long-term bonds even if current rates may compensate for inflation.
timeline.quote: While recognizing the possibility that we may be wrong and that present interest rates may adequately compensate for the inflationary risk, we retain a general fear of long-term bonds.

timeline.point: Cannot forecast rates, so Berkshire borrows when terms are non-oppressive; tight money tends to create the best acquisition chances.
timeline.quote: We have no ability to forecast interest rates and - maintaining our usual open-minded spirit - believe that no one else can.

timeline.point: Falling rates have cut the value of insurance float, so a given combined ratio now means a worse business than in the 1980s.
timeline.quote: As interest rates have fallen, however, the value of float has substantially declined.

timeline.point: Business purchases were made on business prospects, not on forecasts of the Fed or the economy.
timeline.quote: In each case, we pondered what the business was likely to do, not what the Dow, the Fed, or the economy might do.

timeline.point: Held $4.6 billion of long-term zero-coupon Treasuries; falling rates produced a $598.8 million unrealized pre-tax gain.
timeline.quote: Since rates fell in 1997, we ended the year with an unrealized pre-tax gain of $598.8 million in our zeros.

timeline.point: Stocks not overvalued if rates stayed at or below 6.89% and corporate returns held; lower rates make each dollar of earnings more valuable.
timeline.quote: So far, interest rates have fallen -- that's one requisite satisfied -- and returns on equity still remain exceptionally high.

timeline.point: Aesop's valuation axiom uses the long-term U.S. bond yield as the risk-free rate for discounting all assets.
timeline.quote: What is the risk-free interest rate (which we consider to be the yield on long-term U.S. bonds)?

timeline.point: The downward trend of rates turned once-tolerable underwriting losses into burdens.
timeline.quote: the downward trend of interest rates in recent years has transformed underwriting losses that formerly were tolerable into burdens that move insurance businesses deeply into the lemon category.

timeline.point: Rising U.S. rates relative to abroad gave direct currency positions a negative carry, so Berkshire shifted to foreign equities.
timeline.quote: As U.S. rates have risen relative to those of the rest of the world, holding most foreign currencies now involves a significant negative "carry."

timeline.point: Near-zero Treasury yields in late 2008 were a bubble comparable to the Internet and housing bubbles.
timeline.quote: But the U.S. Treasury bond bubble of late 2008 may be regarded as almost equally extraordinary.

timeline.point: $38 billion of cash earned a pittance; normal rates would add at least $500 million to investment income.
timeline.quote: At yearend we held $38 billion of cash equivalents that have been earning a pittance throughout 2010.

timeline.point: Current rates do not offset purchasing-power risk, so he dislikes currency-based investments.
timeline.quote: Bonds promoted as offering risk-free returns are now priced to deliver return-free risk.

timeline.point: Berkshire is asset-sensitive: its cash at short-term rates means rising rates help consolidated earnings even as they hurt Clayton's lend-long, borrow-short spread.
timeline.quote: Berkshire is - and always will be - heavily asset-sensitive and will consequently benefit from rising interest rates.

timeline.point: Still no rate forecasts, but at current rates and tax levels equities should far outperform long-term fixed-rate debt.
timeline.quote: it is almost certain that equities will over time perform far better than long-term, fixed-rate debt instruments.

timeline.point: The 10-year Treasury's 0.93% yield, down 94% from 15.8% in 1981, leaves bond investors facing a bleak future.
timeline.quote: And bonds are not the place to be these days.

timeline.point: Low long-term rates push up prices of all productive assets, leaving little that excites him in public markets.
timeline.quote: Long-term interest rates that are low push the prices of all productive investments upward, whether these are stocks, apartments, farms, oil wells, whatever.

timeline.point: Higher Treasury-bill yields and larger holdings gave a predictable large gain in investment income.
timeline.quote: We were aided by a predictable large gain in investment income as Treasury Bill yields improved

overview: Berkshire bought just under 10% of Wells Fargo in 1989-90 for $290 million, under five times after-tax earnings, during a bank-stock panic over California real estate; Buffett praised Carl Reichardt and Paul Hazen as the best managers in banking and stress-tested the loan book. 1991 earnings were break-even, which he had called a low-level possibility. The stake grew through the 1990s, was enlarged under Dick Kovacevich (2005) and again in 2011-2015, reaching about 10% by 2016. From 2004 to 2015 Wells Fargo was one of the 'Big Four' whose retained earnings he counted as value. He praised its crisis strength and faulted its GAAP core-deposit charge (2012). Stance: positive throughout 1990-2016; no commentary after 2019.

timeline.point: Raised the stake to just under 10% (the Fed limit); one-sixth bought in 1989, the rest in 1990.
timeline.quote: The exception was Wells Fargo, a superbly-managed, high-return banking operation in which we increased our ownership to just under 10%, the most we can own without the approval of the Federal Reserve Board.

timeline.point: Calls Reichardt and Hazen the best managers in banking, likened to Murphy and Burke at Capital Cities/ABC.
timeline.quote: With Wells Fargo, we think we have obtained the best managers in the business, Carl Reichardt and Paul Hazen.

timeline.point: Bought amid a bank-stock panic at a very low multiple.
timeline.quote: we purchased our 10% interest in Wells Fargo for $290 million, less than five times after-tax earnings, and less than three times pre-tax earnings.

timeline.point: Stress test: even if 10% of $48 billion of loans went bad at a 30% loss, the bank would roughly break even; he welcomed the near-50% price drop.
timeline.quote: we welcomed the decline because it allowed us to pick up many more shares at the new, panic prices.

timeline.point: Wells Fargo contributed break-even look-through earnings in 1991, the outcome he had called unlikely.
timeline.quote: we had a break-even result from our interest in Wells Fargo (dividends we received from the company were offset by negative retained earnings).

timeline.point: A 13% stake equals a $7 billion 'Berkshire Bank' earning about $100 million; Reichardt retired leaving record earnings.
timeline.quote: our 13% ownership translates into a $7 billion "Berkshire Bank" that earned about $100 million during 1994.

timeline.point: Wells Fargo's past repurchases at very low prices benefited Berkshire more than today's at loftier prices.
timeline.quote: the repurchases that Coca-Cola, The Washington Post and Wells Fargo made in past years at very low prices benefitted Berkshire far more than do today's repurchases, made at loftier prices.

timeline.point: Wells Fargo named one of the 'Big Four' with American Express, Coca-Cola and Gillette, held on average about 12.5 years.
timeline.quote: Let's look at how the businesses of our "Big Four" - American Express, Coca-Cola, Gillette and Wells Fargo - have fared since we bought into these companies.

timeline.point: Substantially increased holdings, crediting CEO Dick Kovacevich.
timeline.quote: we substantially increased our holdings in Wells Fargo, a company that Dick Kovacevich runs brilliantly

timeline.point: Earnings dipped slightly as the real estate bubble popped, but he judged intrinsic value still up.
timeline.quote: The fourth, Wells Fargo, had a small decline in earnings because of the popping of the real estate bubble. Nevertheless, I believe its intrinsic value increased, even if only by a minor amount.

timeline.point: Wells Fargo prospered through the recession but the Fed's dividend freeze kept its payout artificially low; expects dividends to rise by hundreds of millions.
timeline.quote: we would expect our annual dividends from just this one security to increase by several hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

timeline.point: Added $1 billion to the position; the bank's earnings, assets and capital were strong.
timeline.quote: The banking industry is back on its feet, and Wells Fargo is prospering. Its earnings are strong, its assets solid and its capital at record levels.

timeline.point: Criticizes GAAP's core-deposit amortization (about $1.5 billion) as understating Wells Fargo's real earnings.
timeline.quote: In no sense, except GAAP accounting, is this whopping charge an expense.

timeline.point: Bought more shares, taking ownership to 9.8% from 9.4%, within the Big Four whose returns he called excellent to staggering.
timeline.quote: We purchased additional shares of IBM (increasing our ownership to 8.4% versus 7.8% at yearend 2014) and Wells Fargo (going to 9.8% from 9.4%).

timeline.point: Wells Fargo, 9.8% owned, is one of the five largest holdings whose retained earnings he says matter more than dividends.
timeline.quote: Consider, as an indicator, these figures that cover only our five largest holdings.

timeline.point: Last appearance: 8.4% owned, cost $7,040 million, market $18,598 million, in the holdings table.
timeline.quote: Wells Fargo & Company

overview: This sector spans Blue Chip Stamps (1977-1985), Kirby within Scott Fetzer (1986-1996), and later CORT (2000), Pampered Chef (2002), McLane (2003), Business Wire (2006), TTI (2007) and Pilot Flying J (2017). Buffett's comments are mostly praise of managers and steady earnings growth: Kirby's unit gains, McLane's record but thin 1% margins, TTI's records and 673% earnings rise, Business Wire as one of Berkshire's best-run firms. The negatives: Blue Chip's trading-stamp sales collapsed from $102.5 million (1972) to $1.2 million (1991), and he admits misjudging trading-stamp economics (2000); CORT's earnings were poor in 2002-03 and recessions hit leasing in 2009. Stance: positive in most letters 1986-2021, with the stamp business and leasing cycles as exceptions.

timeline.point: Berkshire raised its stake in Blue Chip Stamps to about 36.5%; Blue Chip earned about $12.9 million from operations.
timeline.quote: We again increased our equity interest in Blue Chip Stamps, and owned approximately 36 1/2% at the end of 1977.

timeline.point: Berkshire's Blue Chip ownership went from 60% to 100% in mid-1983 after the merger, raising its Wesco interest to 80%.
timeline.quote: In 1982, Berkshire owned about 60% of Blue Chip Stamps whereas, in 1983, our ownership was 60% throughout the first six months and 100% thereafter.

timeline.point: Bought Scott Fetzer, owner of Kirby, for about $320 million as a prototype of the businesses Berkshire wants.
timeline.quote: Scott Fetzer is a prototype - understandable, large, well-managed, a good earner.

timeline.point: Kirby posted a fourth straight year of unit gains; its premium cleaner outlasts cheaper rivals.
timeline.quote: Kirby likewise recorded its fourth straight year of unit volume gains. Worldwide, unit sales grew 4% from 1985 and 33% from 1982.

timeline.point: Kirby export sales more than doubled in two years and rose to 20% of unit sales.
timeline.quote: International business has more than doubled in the last two years and quintupled in the past four; its share of unit sales has risen from 5% to 20%.

timeline.point: Blue Chip's trading-stamp business withered while its See's purchase flourished.
timeline.quote: The sales of trading stamps by Blue Chip thereafter declined from $102.5 million in 1972 to $1.2 million in 1991.

timeline.point: Bought CORT, the national leader in rent-to-rent furniture, for Wesco for about $386 million.
timeline.quote: I knew at once that we had the right ingredients for a purchase: a fine though unglamorous business, an outstanding manager, and a price (going by that on the failed deal) that made sense.

timeline.point: Admits he misjudged the economics of trading stamps, among other businesses.
timeline.quote: I'm the fellow, remember, who thought he understood the future economics of trading stamps, textiles, shoes and second-tier department stores.

timeline.point: Acquired The Pampered Chef, grown from $3,000 to over $700 million in annual sales through 67,000 kitchen consultants.
timeline.quote: Today - only 22 years later - TPC does more than $700 million of business annually, working through 67,000 kitchen consultants.

timeline.point: Bought McLane from Wal-Mart: about $23 billion of sales at roughly 1% pre-tax margins, with no due diligence.
timeline.quote: McLane has sales of about $23 billion, but operates on paper-thin margins - about 1% pre-tax - and will swell Berkshire's sales figures far more than our income.

timeline.point: CORT and XTRA leasing earnings poor for two years as the recession cut demand.
timeline.quote: Both operations have had poor earnings during the past two years as the recession caused demand to drop considerably more than was anticipated.

timeline.point: Agreed to buy Business Wire, which serves 25,000 clients in 150 countries, after its president wrote to him.
timeline.quote: By the time I finished Cathy's two-page letter, I felt Business Wire and Berkshire were a fit.

timeline.point: Agreed to buy TTI, an electronic-components distributor grown from $112,000 to $1.3 billion of sales, in one morning meeting.
timeline.quote: Paul and I met on the morning of November 15th and made a deal before lunch.

timeline.point: McLane was the main exception to the recession, with record pre-tax earnings of $344 million on $31.2 billion of sales.
timeline.quote: Grady Rosier led McLane to record pre-tax earnings of $344 million, which even so amounted to only slightly more than one cent per dollar on its huge sales of $31.2 billion.

timeline.point: Business Wire cited with See's as one of the best-run businesses, whose cash, with limited reinvestment needs, helped fund BNSF.
timeline.quote: See's Candies or Business Wire (two of our best-run businesses, but also two offering limited reinvestment opportunities)

timeline.point: McLane, bought in 2003 for $1.5 billion, set a $370 million pre-tax record and had earned $2.4 billion pre-tax since purchase.
timeline.quote: Since its purchase in 2003 for $1.5 billion, the company has had pre-tax earnings of $2.4 billion

timeline.point: Bought 38.6% of Pilot Flying J, the leading travel-center operator with about $20 billion of volume, with a contract to reach 80% in 2023.
timeline.quote: With about $20 billion in annual volume, the company is far and away the nation's leading travel-center operator.

timeline.point: TTI's volume reached $7.7 billion; since Berkshire bought it, employees rose from 2,387 to 8,043 and earnings 673%; TTI led Berkshire to BNSF.
timeline.quote: When Berkshire purchased TTI, the company employed 2,387. Now the number is 8,043. A large percentage of that growth took place in Fort Worth and environs. Earnings have increased 673%.

overview: Across all 48 letters (1977-2024) Buffett pairs eagerness to buy whole businesses with skepticism of most corporate acquisitions, which he says usually transfer value from acquirer shareholders (1981, 1994, 1995, 2017). His own approach shifted after failed bargain buys (Waumbec, 1979) to good businesses at fair prices (stated 1992), and from stock-financed deals to cash after admitting stock deals cost money (1997), with Dexter (1993) and General Re (1998) later called his worst errors. Constants: published criteria, no hostile deals or auctions, managers stay, buy to keep. Big buys ran from National Indemnity (1967) to GEICO, General Re, BNSF, Precision Castparts (overpaid, 2020) and Alleghany. Since about 2017 he says high prices and Berkshire's size limit deals.

timeline.point: Insurance growth since the 1967 National Indemnity purchase came from cash buys and start-ups, with no new Berkshire shares issued.
timeline.quote: In 1977 our aggregate insurance premium volume was $151 million. No additional shares of Berkshire Hathaway stock have been issued to achieve any of this growth.

timeline.point: Waumbec Mills, bought as a bargain, was a mistake that taught him to prefer good businesses at fair prices.
timeline.quote: "turnarounds" seldom turn, and that the same energies and talent are much better employed in a good business purchased at a fair price than in a poor business purchased at a bargain price.

timeline.point: Doubts high-premium takeovers driven by managers' belief in their own 'kiss'.
timeline.quote: We've observed many kisses but very few miracles.

timeline.point: Paying for acquisitions with undervalued stock destroys value.
timeline.quote: In effect, the acquirer must give up $2 of value to receive $1 of value.

timeline.point: Bought 90% of Nebraska Furniture Mart for $55 million without an audit, on the seller's word.
timeline.quote: We gave Mrs. B a check for $55 million and she gave us her word. That made for an even exchange.

timeline.point: Raised the minimum after-tax earnings for acquisitions from $5 million to $10 million after buying Fechheimer.
timeline.quote: Our threshold for minimum annual after-tax earnings of potential acquisitions has been moved up to $10 million from the $5 million level that prevailed when Bob wrote to me.

timeline.point: States his shift from cheap fair businesses to fair-priced good ones.
timeline.quote: I revised my strategy and tried to buy good businesses at fair prices rather than fair businesses at good prices.

timeline.point: Most major acquisitions reduce acquirer shareholders' wealth.
timeline.quote: But, alas, they usually reduce the wealth of the acquirer's shareholders, often to a substantial extent.

timeline.point: Even after three 1995 deals including GEICO's other half ($2.3 billion), he remains skeptical of deals generally.
timeline.quote: We believe most deals do damage to the shareholders of the acquiring company.

timeline.point: Confesses stock-financed mergers cost shareholders money; cash deals did far better.
timeline.quote: Though it hurts me to say it, when I've issued stock, I've cost you money.

timeline.point: Completed the $22 billion General Re acquisition, largely paid in stock.
timeline.quote: On December 21, we completed our $22 billion acquisition of General Re Corp.

timeline.point: Eight acquisitions for about $8 billion, 97% cash, no debt; negotiated deals give only reasonable returns outside crises.
timeline.quote: All told, these purchases have cost us about $8 billion, with 97% of that amount paid in cash and 3% in stock.

timeline.point: Berkshire buys to keep, unlike exit-minded LBO and private equity buyers.
timeline.quote: Unlike LBO operators and private equity firms, we have no "exit" strategy - we buy to keep.

timeline.point: First large foreign purchase: 80% of ISCAR for $4 billion.
timeline.quote: Berkshire purchased 80% of ISCAR for $4 billion.

timeline.point: Dexter, bought for stock, is his worst deal.
timeline.quote: To date, Dexter is the worst deal that I've made.

timeline.point: BNSF needed 6.1% new shares; more stock would have made the deal senseless.
timeline.quote: If we had needed to use more stock to make the acquisition, it would in fact have made no sense.

timeline.point: Overall acquisition record satisfactory, better than buybacks or dividends would have been, though size makes deals harder.
timeline.quote: Overall, however, our record is satisfactory

timeline.point: Bought Precision Castparts for more than $32 billion of cash.
timeline.quote: PCC fits perfectly into the Berkshire model and will substantially increase our normalized per-share earning power.

timeline.point: Issuing 21.8% more shares for General Re was a terrible mistake.
timeline.quote: It was, nevertheless, a terrible mistake on my part to issue 272,200 shares of Berkshire in buying General Re

timeline.point: Record prices and cheap debt fueled a buying frenzy that Berkshire stayed out of.
timeline.quote: Indeed, price seemed almost irrelevant to an army of optimistic purchasers.

timeline.point: $11 billion write-down: he overpaid for Precision Castparts.
timeline.quote: That year, Berkshire purchased Precision Castparts ("PCC"), and I paid too much for the company.

timeline.point: Size leaves only a handful of U.S. companies that could move the needle.
timeline.quote: There remain only a handful of companies in this country capable of truly moving the needle at Berkshire

timeline.point: Raised BHE ownership from about 92% to 100% for about $3.9 billion, mostly cash.
timeline.quote: at a cost of roughly $3.9 billion, of which $2.9 billion was paid in cash with a balance in Berkshire "B" shares.

overview: Buffett discussed underwriting and float in every letter 1977-2024 (merged from decade parts). He stayed negative on the industry: a commodity business with excess capacity, chronic underwriting losses, weak reserving and subnormal returns. His view of Berkshire's own results moved with them: poor in 1982-85 (combined ratios up to 134) and 1999-2001 (float costs 5.8%, 6%, 12.8%, General Re's failures), but from the late 1980s he made low-cost float the key measure, calling it better than free and worth more than equal net worth. Float grew from $19 million (1967) to $171 billion (2024), with underwriting profits in most years since 2003. He kept warning that catastrophes will bring bad years and Berkshire must shrink rather than underprice.

timeline.point: Expects to accept lower volume when rates turn inadequate, which requires unusual discipline.
timeline.quote: Unusual managerial discipline will be required, as it runs counter to normal institutional behavior to let the other fellow take away business - even at foolish prices.

timeline.point: Predicts high interest rates will lead insurers to tolerate underwriting losses.
timeline.quote: Managers decry the folly of underwriting at a loss to obtain investment income, but we believe that many will.

timeline.point: Calls insurance a commodity product with excess capacity.
timeline.quote: Insurance, therefore, would seem to be a textbook case of an industry usually faced with the deadly combination of excess capacity and a “commodity” product.

timeline.point: Berkshire's combined ratio hit 134, worse than the industry for a third year, partly from his reserving errors.
timeline.quote: Our own combined ratio in 1984 was a humbling 134.

timeline.point: Defines float and the break-even combined ratio once float income is counted.
timeline.quote: When the investment income that an insurer earns from holding on to policyholders’ funds ("the float") is taken into account, a combined ratio in the 107-112 range typically produces an overall break-even result

timeline.point: Total indifference to volume is a key Berkshire differentiator.
timeline.quote: In 1989, we will be perfectly willing to write five times as much business as we write in 1988 - or only one-fifth as much.

timeline.point: Adopts underwriting loss relative to float as the cost-of-funds measure.
timeline.quote: We believe a better measure, however, to be a comparison of underwriting loss to float developed.

timeline.point: Low-cost float has served as equity.
timeline.quote: Since our float has cost us virtually nothing over the years, it has in effect served as equity.

timeline.point: Float has been worth more than an equal amount of net worth.
timeline.quote: Though our float is shown on our balance sheet as a liability, it has had a value to Berkshire greater than an equal amount of net worth would have had.

timeline.point: A $1.4 billion underwriting loss gave a 5.8% float cost, judged extremely poor.
timeline.quote: In 1999, however, we incurred a $1.4 billion underwriting loss that left us with float cost of 5.8%.

timeline.point: September 11 pushed float cost to 12.8%, the worst since 1984.
timeline.quote: Our float cost therefore came in at a staggering 12.8%. It was our worst year in float cost since 1984

timeline.point: Underwriting discipline, not size, determines insurer profitability; few insurers are satisfactory.
timeline.quote: When property/casualty companies are judged by their cost of float, very few stack up as satisfactory businesses.

timeline.point: Admits misjudging General Re's discipline at the 1998 merger.
timeline.quote: I was dead wrong. Gen Re’s culture and practices had substantially changed

timeline.point: The industry almost always runs underwriting losses, unlike Berkshire in about half its years.
timeline.quote: In aggregate, the property-casualty industry almost invariably operates at an underwriting loss.

timeline.point: Paid $2.8 billion to hold $58.5 billion of float in a sixth straight profitable year.
timeline.quote: In fact, we were paid $2.8 billion to hold our float during 2008.

timeline.point: Float should be viewed as a revolving fund worth far more than book value implies.
timeline.quote: If float is both costless and long-enduring, the true value of this liability is far lower than the accounting liability.

timeline.point: Industry returns will stay subnormal and low rates will cut float earnings.
timeline.quote: Competitive dynamics almost guarantee that the insurance industry, despite the float income all its companies enjoy, will continue its dismal record of earning subnormal returns on tangible net worth

timeline.point: After 14 profitable years, a $3.2 billion underwriting loss from hurricanes.
timeline.quote: My warning became fact in 2017, as we lost $3.2 billion pre-tax from underwriting.

timeline.point: Float of $147 billion has cost less than nothing over 55 years.
timeline.quote: So far, this float has cost us less than nothing.

timeline.point: Berkshire must shrink rather than write underpriced policies.
timeline.quote: We must never write inadequately-priced policies in order to stay in the game. That policy is corporate suicide.

timeline.point: Underwriting earned $32 billion after tax over two decades as float grew to $171 billion.
timeline.quote: Meanwhile, our float has grown from $46 billion to $171 billion.

overview: Buffett consistently described Berkshire's owners as partners and shaped communication to attract long-term, business-minded holders: a candid CEO-written annual report (from 1979), the 1983 owner principles ('our attitude is partnership'), a no-split stance (1983, 1992), NYSE listing to cut trading costs (1988), the Owner's Manual (1996), simultaneous weekend Internet releases and no one-on-one talks with analysts or institutions (1998-2021). The shareholder-designated contributions program (1981-2002) drew about 95-97% participation each year and gave $197 million; he defended it as owners' money directed by owners, then reluctantly ended it in 2003 after abortion-related boycotts hurt Pampered Chef associates. He repeatedly praised the low-turnover owner base, e.g. the 2014 vote against a dividend and the 2020 'fifth bucket' of individual holders.

timeline.point: Owners are entitled to hear directly from the CEO; companies get the shareholders their communications seek.
timeline.quote: In large part, companies obtain the shareholder constituency that they seek and deserve.

timeline.point: Launches shareholder-designated charitable contributions; 95.6% of eligible shares responded and $1.78 million went to about 675 charities.
timeline.quote: Our new program enabling shareholders to designate the recipients of corporate charitable contributions was greeted with extraordinary enthusiasm.

timeline.point: Sets out the owner-manager principles after the Blue Chip merger, starting with the partnership attitude.
timeline.quote: Charlie Munger and I think of our shareholders as owner-partners, and of ourselves as managing partners.

timeline.point: Rejects a stock split, arguing it would downgrade the shareholder group and raise trading costs.
timeline.quote: Splitting the stock would increase that cost, downgrade the quality of our shareholder population, and encourage a market price less consistently related to intrinsic business value.

timeline.point: Offers shareholders an advisory vote on the contributions program, noting no precedent existed.
timeline.quote: Managers who put their trust in capitalism seem in no hurry to put their trust in capitalists.

timeline.point: Contrasts director-matched giving at other companies with Berkshire's owner-directed gifts.
timeline.quote: When A takes money from B to give to C and A is a legislator, the process is called taxation. But when A is an officer or director of a corporation, it is called philanthropy.

timeline.point: Lists on the NYSE to reduce transaction costs; wants the stock to trade near intrinsic value with little activity.
timeline.quote: First, we do not want to maximize the price at which Berkshire shares trade. We wish instead for them to trade in a narrow range centered at intrinsic business value

timeline.point: Defends the program as the owners' money; raises the designated amount from $8 to $10 per share.
timeline.quote: At Berkshire, we believe that the company's money is the owners' money, just as it would be in a closely-held corporation, partnership, or sole proprietorship.

timeline.point: Creates Class B shares to blunt high-commission unit trusts and keep shareholders informed and business-oriented.
timeline.quote: we are better off if we can blunt the merchandising efforts of the unit trusts - and that is the reason we are creating the B stock.

timeline.point: Reproduces the full Owner's Manual; believes Berkshire leads large companies in long-term holders.
timeline.quote: Berkshire probably ranks number one among large American corporations in the percentage of its shares held by owners with a long-term view.

timeline.point: Opposes selective disclosure; a one-share B holder equals large institutions, and earnings guidance seekers get public documents.
timeline.quote: At Berkshire, we regard the holder of one share of B stock as the equal of our large institutional investors.

timeline.point: Explains the program follows owners' choices on either side of the abortion issue, like a dividend donated more tax-efficiently.
timeline.quote: It’s as if we paid a dividend, which the shareholder then donated. Our form of disbursement, however, is more tax-efficient.

timeline.point: Ends the program after $197 million of gifts because boycotts hurt Pampered Chef's independent associates.
timeline.quote: We reluctantly terminated the program in 2003 because of controversy over the abortion issue.

timeline.point: Does not woo Wall Street; wants partners who understand the business, and restates principles for BNSF newcomers.
timeline.quote: Investors who buy and sell based upon media or analyst commentary are not for us.

timeline.point: B shareholders voted about 47 to 1 against paying a dividend, which he calls remarkable alignment.
timeline.quote: To have our fellow owners – large and small – be so in sync with our managerial philosophy is both remarkable and rewarding.

timeline.point: Treats all shareholders alike and releases data late Friday or Saturday; the small saver is foremost.
timeline.quote: There is no one more important to us than the shareholder of limited means who trusts us with a substantial portion of his or her savings.

timeline.point: Describes five ownership buckets and a special kinship with the million-plus individual long-term holders.
timeline.quote: We already have the investors we want and don’t think that they, on balance, would be upgraded by replacements.

timeline.point: Notes the buy-and-keep owner base limits repurchase opportunities but prefers these owners.
timeline.quote: Nevertheless, Charlie and I far prefer the owners we have, even though their admirable buy-and-keep attitudes limit the extent to which long-term shareholders can profit from opportunistic repurchases.

timeline.point: Writes for 'lifetime' shareholders entitled to good and bad news from the CEO, not an investor-relations officer.
timeline.quote: We cherish their presence and believe they are entitled to hear every year both the good and bad news, delivered directly from their CEO

overview: National Indemnity (NICO), bought with its sister National Fire & Marine from Jack Ringwalt in 1967 for $8.6 million, is the base of Berkshire's insurance business. Buffett praised it consistently: its traditional commercial auto and liability lines showed rare underwriting discipline under Phil Liesche and later Don Wurster, accepting falling volume (1986-1999) rather than underpricing, with a no-layoff policy. Results slipped in 1982-83 when prices fell. NICO also housed Ajit Jain's reinsurance division and large catastrophe covers. Later letters call NICO the world's largest P/C company by net worth and trace Berkshire's float, now over $100 billion, to the 1967 purchase. In 2014 he called buying it for Berkshire rather than his partnership a colossal mistake for his partners.

timeline.point: Insurance volume grew from $22 million in 1967 to $151 million without issuing shares; NICO's traditional lines had excellent underwriting margins.
timeline.quote: In that year their premium volume amounted to $22 million. In 1977 our aggregate insurance premium volume was $151 million.

timeline.point: Phil Liesche's NICO segment earned about $11 million underwriting profit on $90 million of premiums, Berkshire's top contributor.
timeline.quote: On about $90 million of earned premiums, an underwriting profit of approximately $11 million was realized, a truly extraordinary achievement

timeline.point: Praises NICO's willingness to cut volume rather than write unprofitable business, a discipline instilled by founder Jack Ringwalt.
timeline.quote: Phil Liesche is an exception: if business makes sense, he writes it; if it doesn’t, he rejects it.

timeline.point: Underwriting deteriorated sharply; NICO's traditional lines were now priced to guarantee losses.
timeline.quote: Lines that have been highly profitable for us in the past are now priced at levels that guarantee underwriting losses.

timeline.point: Calls NICO the most important operation in Berkshire's growth.
timeline.quote: National Indemnity has been the most important operation in Berkshire’s growth.

timeline.point: NICO's ad for large risks drew 600 replies and about $50 million of premiums, long-tail business still to be proven.
timeline.quote: it’s all long-tail business and it will be at least five years before we know whether this marketing success was also an underwriting success.

timeline.point: NICO's monthly volume rose from $5 million to $35 million as competitors fled, then fell as new competitors cut prices.
timeline.quote: Monthly volume is currently about $20 million and will continue to fall as new competitors surface and prices are cut.

timeline.point: NICO's traditional business ran a 74.2 combined ratio with large float relative to premiums.
timeline.quote: National Indemnity's traditional business had a combined ratio of 74.2 and, as usual, developed a large amount of float compared to premium volume.

timeline.point: NICO's reinsurance operation under Ajit Jain is the largest by size of individual risks assumed.
timeline.quote: Working with only 18 associates, Ajit manages one of the world’s largest reinsurance operations measured by assets, and the largest, based upon the size of individual risks assumed.

timeline.point: Says NICO overcame commodity insurance economics through pricing discipline; without it Berkshire might be worth half as much.
timeline.quote: Indeed, had we not made this acquisition, Berkshire would be lucky to be worth half of what it is today.

timeline.point: NICO accepted a long revenue decline from 1986 to 1999 rather than cut prices.
timeline.quote: But we instead consistently priced to make a profit, not to match our most optimistic competitor. We never left customers – but they left us.

timeline.point: Promises no layoffs for falling volume, since underpriced business is what NICO cannot survive.
timeline.quote: It can’t live, however, with underpriced business and the breakdown in underwriting discipline that accompanies it.

timeline.point: Ties eleven years of underwriting profit and float growth to $77 billion back to the 1967 purchase.
timeline.quote: And all of this all began with our 1967 purchase of National Indemnity for $8.6 million.

timeline.point: NICO's GAAP net worth of $111 billion exceeds any other insurer's; calls it Berkshire's best deal per page.
timeline.quote: National Indemnity today has GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles) net worth of $111 billion, which exceeds that of any other insurer in the world.

timeline.point: Admits buying NICO for Berkshire instead of his partnership was a colossal mistake for his partners.
timeline.quote: I opted to marry 100% of an excellent business (NICO) to a 61%-owned terrible business (Berkshire Hathaway)

timeline.point: The 1967 deal brought $19.4 million of float and an insurer that usually made underwriting profits.
timeline.quote: the insurance operation carried with it $19.4 million of “float” – money that belonged to others but was held by our two insurers.

timeline.point: NICO is the only company prepared to insure certain giant risks.
timeline.quote: Today National Indemnity is the only company in the world prepared to insure certain giant risks.

timeline.point: From the NICO purchase, Berkshire's float grew from $19 million to $147 billion.
timeline.quote: From an $8.6 million purchase of National Indemnity in 1967, Berkshire has become the world leader in insurance “float”

overview: Ajit Jain's reinsurance operation, begun in 1985-86 inside National Indemnity and named Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group (B-H Reinsurance) in 2002-2016 letters. Buffett praised it in every letter that discusses it: a tiny staff writing huge, unusual risks (super-cats, the $1 billion PepsiCo prize, terrorism covers, Equitas) and keeping all the risk, made possible by Berkshire's financial strength. Float grew from $6.3 billion (1999) to $13.4 billion (2002) and $45 billion (2016) with cumulative underwriting profits, though retroactive contracts deliberately book underwriting losses and super-cat results are lumpy (2005 and 2011 losses). He repeatedly warned of an occasional horrible year, cut volume when prices fell, and later noted run-off contracts make its float drift down.

timeline.point: Berkshire has become a large writer of super-catastrophe reinsurance, where its unmatched financial strength is a competitive advantage; results will be terrible in an occasional year.
timeline.quote: While we expect our super-cat business to produce satisfactory results over, say, a decade, we're sure it will produce absolutely terrible results in at least an occasional year

timeline.point: Rejects over 98% of business offered; calls Ajit Jain the best in the business.
timeline.quote: Ajit Jain, who runs our reinsurance operation, is simply the best in this business.

timeline.point: Warns a single good super-cat year proves nothing; true odds take decades to learn.
timeline.quote: In fact, it will take decades for us to find out whether our underwriting judgment has been sound.

timeline.point: Puts the worst-case super-cat loss at about $600 million after tax and tells uncomfortable holders to sell now.
timeline.quote: If you are not comfortable with this level of exposure, the time to sell your Berkshire stock is now, not after the inevitable mega-catastrophe.

timeline.point: Catastrophe bonds drove prices down, so Berkshire will write less super-cat business in 1998.
timeline.quote: has caused super-cat prices to deteriorate materially. Therefore, we will write less business in 1998.

timeline.point: Ajit built the business from scratch with an underwriting profit and $6.3 billion of float.
timeline.quote: He has from scratch built an outstanding reinsurance business, which during his tenure has earned an underwriting profit and now holds $6.3 billion of float.

timeline.point: After September 11 it wrote huge terrorism-related covers, retaining all risk while avoiding aggregating exposures.
timeline.quote: No one can match the speed with which Ajit can offer huge policies.

timeline.point: Float reached $13.4 billion with a $534 million underwriting profit even after a $428 million retroactive charge; accepts lumpy results.
timeline.quote: At Berkshire, we would rather earn a lumpy 15% over time than a smooth 12%.

timeline.point: Specializes in mammoth catastrophe risks; shareholders should expect an occasional horrible year.
timeline.quote: You should, therefore, expect his operation to have an occasional horrible year.

timeline.point: Took on the huge Equitas retroactive contract after reviewing Lloyd's legacy claims with Ajit.
timeline.quote: Ajit and I think the odds are in our favor. And should we be wrong, Berkshire can handle it.

timeline.point: A 31-person unit with very large transactions and fast execution.
timeline.quote: This may be one of the most remarkable businesses in the world, hard to characterize but easy to admire.

timeline.point: Wrote the $7.1 billion Lloyd's/Equitas premium and a life reinsurance contract that could bring $50 billion over 50 years.
timeline.quote: During 2009, he negotiated a life reinsurance contract that could produce $50 billion of premium for us over the next 50 or so years.

timeline.point: Float of $30 billion with significant underwriting profits built from a standing start.
timeline.quote: From a standing start in 1985, Ajit has created an insurance business with float of $30 billion and

timeline.point: Despite a $714 million underwriting loss in 2011, says Berkshire would profit overall even in a $250 billion industry catastrophe.
timeline.quote: Berkshire as a whole would likely record a moderate profit for the year because of its many streams of earnings.

timeline.point: Ajit launched Berkshire Hathaway Specialty Insurance in commercial lines.
timeline.quote: One venture materialized last June when he formed Berkshire Hathaway Specialty Insurance (“BHSI”).

timeline.point: Run-off contracts mean the division's float will drift down.
timeline.quote: National Indemnity’s reinsurance division, however, is party to a number of run-off contracts whose float drifts downward.

timeline.point: Underwriting profit $822 million on $45 billion of float; Ajit has created tens of billions of value.
timeline.quote: Since then, Ajit has created tens of billions of value for Berkshire shareholders.

overview: Oil and gas appears mostly through individual holdings rather than a sector thesis. In the 1980s Buffett owned Exxon (praising its buybacks), used the oil industry as an example of GAAP earnings overstating owner earnings, and profited from Texaco bonds bought in bankruptcy. Oil futures contracts (1994-99) gave modest gains. PetroChina, bought 2002-03 for $488 million, was sold in 2007 for $4 billion. In the 2008 letter he called his ConocoPhillips purchase near peak oil prices a major mistake costing several billion dollars. Later holdings included Exxon Mobil, Phillips 66, Chevron and, from 2019, Occidental Petroleum, which by 2023 he expected to hold indefinitely, praising its U.S. reserves and management while saying no one knows oil prices.

timeline.point: Lists OPEC-style foreign cartelization among the ways an industry can escape commodity pricing.
timeline.quote: “extralegally” through OPEC-style foreign cartelization (with tag-along benefits for domestic non-cartel operators).

timeline.point: Exxon, Berkshire's fourth-largest holding, praised for repurchasing its shares wisely and aggressively.
timeline.quote: Exxon, in which we have our fourth largest holding, has also wisely and aggressively repurchased shares

timeline.point: Uses major oil companies as a conspicuous example of GAAP earnings overstating owner earnings because maintenance capex exceeds depreciation.
timeline.quote: The oil industry has in recent years provided a conspicuous example of this phenomenon.

timeline.point: Bought Texaco bonds after its bankruptcy filing as the most attractive bond investment available.
timeline.quote: we regarded these issues as by far the most attractive bond investment available to us.

timeline.point: Sold nearly all the Texaco bonds at a pre-tax profit of about $22 million.
timeline.quote: During 1988, we sold practically all of these bonds at a pre-tax profit of about $22 million.
