timeline.point: Oil derivative contracts from 1994-95 produced a $61.9 million pre-tax gain; he now has no opinion on oil's attractiveness.
timeline.quote: When we established our contracts, oil for future delivery seemed modestly underpriced. Today, though, we have no opinion as to its attractiveness.

timeline.point: Sold PetroChina for $4 billion after buying 1.3% for $488 million when he thought it worth about $100 billion; higher oil prices and reserve growth lifted value.
timeline.quote: In the second half of last year, the market value of the company rose to $275 billion, about what we thought it was worth compared to other giant oil companies.

timeline.point: Calls buying ConocoPhillips near peak energy prices a major mistake of commission.
timeline.quote: I bought a large amount of ConocoPhillips stock when oil and gas prices were near their peak.

timeline.point: Still expects higher oil prices but admits the timing cost Berkshire several billion dollars.
timeline.quote: But so far I have been dead wrong. Even if prices should rise, moreover, the terrible timing of my purchase has cost Berkshire several billion dollars.

timeline.point: Uses Exxon Mobil as the example of a productive asset that beats gold over a century.
timeline.quote: plus 16 Exxon Mobils (the world’s most profitable company, one earning more than $40 billion annually).

timeline.point: BNSF and Marmon benefit from the resurgence of U.S. oil production; BNSF hauls about 10% of lower-48 output.
timeline.quote: At both BNSF and Marmon, we are benefitting from the resurgence of U.S. oil production.

timeline.point: Exchanged Phillips 66 stock for an operating business as part of the focus on operating earnings.
timeline.quote: That’s why we were pleased to exchange our Phillips 66 and Graham Holdings stock for operating businesses last year

timeline.point: Discloses a $10 billion Occidental Petroleum investment in preferred stock and warrants.
timeline.quote: Includes $10 billion investment in Occidental Petroleum Corporation consisting of preferred stock and warrants to buy common stock.

timeline.point: Holds 27.8% of Occidental indefinitely, liking its U.S. oil and gas holdings, but has no interest in buying or managing it.
timeline.quote: We particularly like its vast oil and gas holdings in the United States, as well as its leadership in carbon-capture initiatives

timeline.point: Praises shale ending U.S. energy dependence and Occidental's CEO, while disclaiming any oil-price forecast.
timeline.quote: No one knows what oil prices will do over the next month, year, or decade. But Vicki does know how to separate oil from rock

overview: Buffett treated the late-1990s tech/internet boom as speculation outside Berkshire's circle of competence. The 1999 letter warned that return expectations were unrealistic and a severe adjustment likely where speculation was concentrated. The 2000 letter called it a bubble market creating 'bubble companies' built to make money off investors. Later letters dated the end of 'The Great Bubble' to March 10, 2000, blamed loose accounting and declining CEO conduct, and found equities still unattractive. In 2003-2004 he admitted a mistake: he should have sold several large holdings during the Bubble ('I talked when I should have walked'). In 2008 and 2011 he grouped it with the housing bubble as bandwagon excess.

timeline.point: Says fast-changing industries are beyond Berkshire's circle of competence; it will not envy or emulate those whose predictive claims the market seems to validate.
timeline.quote: Predicting the long-term economics of companies that operate in fast-changing industries is simply far beyond our perimeter.

timeline.point: Warns equity returns will fall well below expectations and the market adjustment is likely to be severe where speculation is concentrated.
timeline.quote: If investor expectations become more realistic — and they almost certainly will — the market adjustment is apt to be severe, particularly in sectors in which speculation has been concentrated.

timeline.point: Dismisses explanations of the 'enchanted' manic market.
timeline.quote: if anyone starts explaining to you what is going on in the truly-manic portions of this “enchanted” market, you might remember still another line of song: “Fools give you reasons, wise men never try.”

timeline.point: Labels capital committed to new businesses and rapidly changing industries speculative, and speculation a game Berkshire will not play.
timeline.quote: But it is not a game in which Charlie and I wish to play. We bring nothing to the party, so why should we expect to take anything home?

timeline.point: Cites a December 1999 survey where investors expected 19% annual returns for the next decade as evidence of irrational expectations.
timeline.quote: Their answers averaged 19%. That, for sure, was an irrational expectation

timeline.point: Says money-losing businesses destroy value whatever their interim valuations.
timeline.quote: But value is destroyed, not created, by any business that loses money over its lifetime, no matter how high its interim valuation may get.

timeline.point: Describes bubble companies as designed to profit from investors via IPOs, a chain letter with investment bankers as postmen.
timeline.quote: a bubble market has allowed the creation of bubble companies, entities designed more with an eye to making money off investors rather than for them.

timeline.point: Lessons of the bubble's end: Wall Street sells whatever investors will buy; Berkshire does not try to pick winners among unproven enterprises.
timeline.quote: But a pin lies in wait for every bubble.

timeline.point: Dates the bubble's end to the NASDAQ peak on March 10, 2000, the same day Berkshire stock hit its lowest price since mid-1997.
timeline.quote: The Great Bubble ended on March 10, 2000 (though we didn’t realize that fact until some months later).

timeline.point: After three years of falling prices, still finds few attractive stocks, blaming the insane valuations of the Bubble.
timeline.quote: That dismal fact is testimony to the insanity of valuations reached during The Great Bubble. Unfortunately, the hangover may prove to be proportional to the binge.

timeline.point: Links the Bubble to falling managerial stewardship and to anything-goes accounting after option-expensing was blocked.
timeline.quote: As stock prices went up, the behavioral norms of managers went down.

timeline.point: Admits a big mistake in not selling several large holdings during the Bubble.
timeline.quote: I made a big mistake in not selling several of our larger holdings during The Great Bubble.

timeline.point: Repeats the self-criticism: market gains outstripped the businesses during the Bubble, and he did not act on his overvaluation views.
timeline.quote: I can properly be criticized for merely clucking about nose-bleed valuations during the Bubble rather than acting on my views.

timeline.point: Places the Internet bubble alongside the housing bubble and the late-2008 Treasury bond bubble.
timeline.quote: it will surely speak of the Internet bubble of the late 1990s and the housing bubble of the early 2000s.

timeline.point: Uses Internet stocks and houses as examples of bandwagon excess that inevitably pops.
timeline.quote: Over the past 15 years, both Internet stocks and houses have demonstrated the extraordinary excesses that can be created by combining an initially sensible thesis with well-publicized rising prices.

overview: Buffett treats pension and retiree-benefit promises as liabilities that accounting long hid and managers understate. In 1992 he welcomed the rule forcing companies to book post-retirement health costs and said Berkshire avoids acquisitions carrying such obligations. From 2002 he warned investors about fanciful pension return assumptions; in 2007 he showed why the average 8% S&P assumption was unrealistic given 5.3% Dow growth in the 20th century. From 2007 on he called public pension promises a fiscal time bomb, repeated in 2008, 2013 and 2016 (fees and poor returns). Berkshire subsidiaries' pension assets are managed by Todd Combs and Ted Weschler and excluded from the holdings tables.
stance_basis: critical of pension and retiree-benefit accounting, return assumptions and public pension funding in every letter that discusses it (1992, 2002, 2006-2008, 2013, 2016); no positive view of these practices is expressed
note: read = the 22 tagged passages plus 6 untagged corpus hits read in full (1978_p0031, 1978_p0032, 1978_p0035, 2010_p0160, 2012_p0022, 2020_p0029); holdings-table footnotes that only say pension-fund shares are excluded were skimmed, not counted

timeline.point: Pension managers bought stocks heavily at high prices (1971) and shunned them at lows (1974, 1978), despite having the longest investment horizon.
timeline.quote: in 1971, pension fund managers invested a record 122% of net funds available in equities - at full prices they couldn't buy enough of them

timeline.point: New GAAP rule forces recognition of post-retirement health liabilities; Berkshire has avoided buying companies with large such obligations, so its own liability is inconsequential.
timeline.quote: In making acquisitions, Charlie and I have tended to avoid companies with significant post-retirement liabilities.

timeline.point: He blames cash-basis accounting for reckless open-ended retiree health promises that understated liabilities.
timeline.quote: accounting rules did not, for so long, require the booking of post-retirement health costs as they were incurred.

timeline.point: Advice to investors: fanciful pension assumptions are a sign of weak accounting and of management taking the low road.
timeline.quote: If a company still does not expense options, or if its pension assumptions are fanciful, watch out.

timeline.point: Unrealistic return assumptions let private plans overstate earnings and public plans defer tax increases.
timeline.quote: private pension plans can temporarily overstate their earnings, and public pension plans can defer the need for increased taxes, by using investment assumptions that are likely to be out of reach.

timeline.point: S&P companies with pension plans assumed an average 8% return; he argues equities would need 9.2% after fees, which history does not support.
timeline.quote: For the 363 companies in the S&P that have pension plans, this assumption in 2006 averaged 8%.

timeline.point: High return assumptions exist because they raise reported earnings, with consequences arriving after the CEO retires.
timeline.quote: What is no puzzle, however, is why CEOs opt for a high investment assumption: It lets them report higher earnings.

timeline.point: Public pension promises are a long-fused fiscal time bomb for taxpayers.
timeline.quote: Public pension promises are huge and, in many cases, funding is woefully inadequate.

timeline.point: After 2008, city and state pension funding gaps add to local fiscal stress, relevant to municipal bond insurance.
timeline.quote: The gap between assets and a realistic actuarial valuation of present liabilities is simply staggering.

timeline.point: In his letter to managers, changes in post-retirement benefits are one of the few decisions subsidiaries must clear with him.
timeline.quote: The only items you need to clear with me are any changes in post-retirement benefits and any unusually large capital expenditures or acquisitions.

timeline.point: Todd Combs and Ted Weschler manage some subsidiaries' pension funds; these holdings are excluded from Berkshire's reported portfolio.
timeline.quote: Todd and Ted also manage the pension funds of certain Berkshire subsidiaries

timeline.point: Unaffordable public pension promises drive state and local financial problems; he reprints his 1975 memo on pension investment policy.
timeline.quote: Local and state financial problems are accelerating, in large part because public entities promised pensions they couldn't afford.

timeline.point: Public employee pension funds were hurt by high fees and poor results from seeking superior advice; taxpayers will cover shortfalls.
timeline.quote: Many of these funds are woefully underfunded, in part because they have suffered a double whammy: poor investment performance accompanied by huge fees.

timeline.point: Long-horizon investors such as pension funds mismeasure risk by their bond-to-stock ratio; bonds can raise risk.
timeline.quote: It is a terrible mistake for investors with long-term horizons - among them, pension funds, college endowments and savings-minded individuals - to measure their investment "risk" by their portfolio's ratio of bonds to stocks.

timeline.point: With 10-year Treasury yields near 0.93%, bond-dependent investors including pension funds face poor prospects.
timeline.quote: Fixed-income investors worldwide - whether pension funds, insurance companies or retirees - face a bleak future.

overview: Shaw, the world's largest carpet maker, came to Berkshire after a 2000 meeting about asbestos insurance for a merger partner; Berkshire bought 87.3% (closed January 2001) and the remaining 12.7% for Berkshire shares in early 2002, making Shaw its largest non-insurance business. Buffett praised Bob Shaw and Julian Saul for cost control and margins (pre-tax $292 million in 2001 to $424 million in 2002; 25.6% on tangible equity in 2004). From 2004-2005 raw-material and energy costs squeezed margins, and the 2007-2011 housing slump cut earnings of Shaw and its building-products peers sharply, which he called temporary. Vance Bell succeeded Bob Shaw in 2006 and bought U.S. Floors in 2016; Shaw stayed among Berkshire's mid-sized earners through 2019.
stance_basis: praised management and franchise in every letter discussing Shaw 2000-2017; earnings setbacks (2004-2005 costs, 2007-2011 housing) were described as cyclical with competitive position intact
note: read = the 31 tagged passages plus 3 untagged corpus hits read in full (2000_p0008, 2004_p0085, 2007_p0008); annual-meeting exhibit mentions of Shaw carpet in Clayton homes were skimmed and are not financial

timeline.point: A failed merger needing uncapped asbestos cover sparked Buffett's interest; Berkshire agreed to buy 87.3% of Shaw, with Bob Shaw and Julian Saul keeping at least 5%.
timeline.quote: Bob and Julian decided that if we didn't want to bet the ranch on the extent of the acquiree's liability, neither did they. So their deal died. But my interest in Shaw was sparked

timeline.point: Shaw had about $4 billion of sales and became Berkshire's largest business outside insurance.
timeline.quote: Shaw has annual sales of about $4 billion, and we own 87.3% of the company. Leaving aside our insurance operation, Shaw is by far our largest business.

timeline.point: After a strong first year, Berkshire exchanged 4,740 A shares for the 12.7% minority and owns all of Shaw.
timeline.quote: Shaw is our largest noninsurance operation and will play a big part in Berkshire's future.

timeline.point: Pre-tax earnings rose from $292 million to $424 million on productivity and cost control despite flat carpet prices.
timeline.quote: Carpet prices increased only 1% last year, but Shaw's productivity gains and excellent expense control delivered significantly improved margins.

timeline.point: Record year; the Dixie Group carpet purchase lifts volume toward $5 billion.
timeline.quote: Shaw Industries, the world's largest manufacturer of broadloom carpet, also had a record year.

timeline.point: Fiber cost increases of over $300 million narrowed margins, yet Shaw earned 25.6% on tangible equity.
timeline.quote: Despite these roadblocks, Shaw, led by Bob Shaw and Julian Saul, earned an outstanding 25.6% on tangible equity in 2004. The company is a powerhouse and has a bright future.

timeline.point: Shaw spent about $550 million on two vertical-integration acquisitions; results were respectable despite soaring petrochemical and gas costs.
timeline.quote: Shaw, our carpet operation, spent about $550 million last year on two purchases that furthered its vertical integration and should improve its profit margin in the future.

timeline.point: Bob Shaw retired at 75, succeeded by Vance Bell; housing weakness slowed carpet demand.
timeline.quote: Weakness in housing has caused the carpet business to slow. Shaw, however, remains a powerhouse and a major contributor to Berkshire's earnings.

timeline.point: The housing downturn cut Shaw's pre-tax earnings 27%; Buffett called the setbacks temporary.
timeline.quote: Shaw, Acme Brick, Johns Manville and MiTek were all hurt in 2007 by the sharp housing downturn, with their pre-tax earnings declining 27%, 41%, 38%, and 9% respectively.

timeline.point: Combined earnings of Shaw and the other construction businesses fell 82.5% from the 2006 peak, but their positions held.
timeline.quote: These businesses continue to bump along the bottom, though their competitive positions remain undented.

timeline.point: Profits still far below peak; Shaw planned $200 million of U.S. capital spending in 2011 in expectation of a housing recovery.
timeline.quote: Shaw will spend $200 million in 2011 on plant and equipment, all of it situated in America. These businesses entered the recession strong and will exit it stronger.

timeline.point: Housing-related companies including Shaw earned $513 million pre-tax, versus $1.8 billion in 2006; he expected housing to return.
timeline.quote: Housing will come back - you can be sure of that.

timeline.point: The U.S. Floors acquisition (late 2016) grew sales 40% and lifted Shaw's sales to $5.7 billion.
timeline.quote: With the purchase of USF, Shaw has substantially strengthened its position as an important and durable source of earnings for Berkshire.

timeline.point: Shaw remains in the third tier of five non-insurance earners, which together made $1.9 billion.
timeline.quote: The next five, similarly ranked and listed (Berkshire Hathaway Automotive, Johns Manville, NetJets, Shaw and TTI) earned $1.9 billion last year

overview: From 1979 to 1987 Buffett doubted the long-term value of the dollar and avoided long bonds; in 1987 he warned that the trade deficit was piling up dollar claim checks abroad and invited inflation. In 2002 he bought foreign currencies for the first time, reaching $21.4 billion of contracts in 12 currencies at end-2004, and argued that persistent current-account deficits were turning America into a 'Sharecropper's Society'. Negative carry led him to cut direct positions in 2005-2006 (total gain $2.2-2.3 billion). Later letters treat currency as inflation risk in currency-based assets (2011, 2014, 2024); in 2016 he called foreign claims of little importance, and in 2023-2024 he said he cannot forecast currencies and hedged the Japanese stakes with yen debt.
stance_basis: bearish on the dollar and alarmed by trade deficits in letters 1979-1987 and 2003-2007 (acting on it with currency contracts 2002-2007); from 2016 he downplayed foreign ownership and by 2023-2024 claimed no currency view, seeking currency-neutrality, while still warning that paper money can lose value
note: read = the 73 tagged passages plus 7 untagged corpus hits read in full (2011_p0110, 2011_p0114, 2014_p0106, 2014_p0107, 2014_p0108, 2024_p0026, 2024_p0032); 1985_p0039 and 1999_p0079 concern foreign low-wage competition (textiles, shoes) rather than currency

timeline.point: Currency stability may matter more to Berkshire owners' real returns than management's work; long dollar bonds may be obsolete.
timeline.quote: external conditions affecting the stability of currency may very well be the most important factor in determining whether there are any real rewards from your investment in Berkshire Hathaway.

timeline.point: He avoids most long-term bonds because he expects the dollar to keep losing value to inflation.
timeline.quote: That's because bonds are as sound as a dollar - and we view the longterm outlook for dollars as dismal.

timeline.point: Aversion to long bonds rests on legislators' control over currency value.
timeline.quote: Over time, the behavior of our currency will be determined by the behavior of our legislators.

timeline.point: The trade deficit is piling dollar claims in foreign hands; he likens U.S. policy to depending on the kindness of strangers and sees inflation pressure.
timeline.quote: Our enormous trade deficit is causing various forms of "claim checks" - U.S. government and corporate bonds, bank deposits, etc. - to pile up in the hands of foreigners at a distressing rate.

timeline.point: Berkshire entered foreign currencies in 2002 and enlarged the position in 2003 as he grew bearish on the dollar; about $12 billion of contracts in five currencies at yearend.
timeline.quote: During 2002 we entered the foreign currency market for the first time in my life, and in 2003 we enlarged our position, as I became increasingly bearish on the dollar.

timeline.point: Contracts reached $21.4 billion in 12 currencies; he stresses this is not doubt about America.
timeline.quote: Be clear on one point: In no way does our thinking about currencies rest on doubts about America.

timeline.point: Current-account deficits transfer U.S. wealth abroad; foreigners own a net $3 trillion and he projects about $11 trillion in a decade.
timeline.quote: A country that is now aspiring to an "Ownership Society" will not find happiness in - and I'll use hyperbole here for emphasis - a "Sharecropper's Society."

timeline.point: He admits macro calls are hard and he may be wrong, but would not hold a dollar-only policy if he owned all of Berkshire.
timeline.quote: macro-economics is a tough game in which few people, Charlie and I included, have demonstrated skill. We may well turn out to be wrong in our currency judgments.

timeline.point: Currency positions lost $955 million pre-tax in 2005 but were $2.0 billion ahead since inception.
timeline.quote: My conviction, however, cost Berkshire $955 million pre-tax in 2005.

timeline.point: Negative interest carry led him to reduce direct currency holdings and prefer foreign equities.
timeline.quote: We reduced our direct position in currencies somewhat during 2005.

timeline.point: Direct currency position nearly eliminated, with $2.2 billion total gain since 2002; he still expects the dollar to weaken.
timeline.quote: As our U.S. trade problems worsen, the probability that the dollar will weaken over time continues to be high.

timeline.point: The U.S. investment income account turned negative, which he had predicted.
timeline.quote: In effect, we've used up our bank account and turned to our credit card.

timeline.point: A falling dollar has not closed the trade gap; sovereign wealth funds buying U.S. assets follow from U.S. trade.
timeline.quote: So far, at least, a plunging dollar has not done much to bring our trade activity into balance.

timeline.point: Only one direct position (Brazilian real) remained; direct currency positions earned $2.3 billion over five years, plus Euro bond gains.
timeline.quote: Our direct currency positions have yielded $2.3 billion of pre-tax profits over the past five years

timeline.point: Currency-based investments look safe but lose purchasing power; the dollar fell 86% since 1965.
timeline.quote: Under today's conditions, therefore, I do not like currency-based investments.

timeline.point: Over fifty years, diversified American businesses were safer than Treasuries tied to the currency.
timeline.quote: currency-denominated instruments are riskier investments - far riskier investments - than widely-diversified stock portfolios

timeline.point: In contrast to 2004, he says foreign claims on U.S. wealth are offset by American assets abroad.
timeline.quote: Those holdings, however, are of little importance to our national balance sheet: Our citizens own assets abroad that are roughly comparable in value.

timeline.point: He says he cannot forecast major currencies, so the Japanese trading-company stakes are financed with ¥1.3 trillion of yen bonds.
timeline.quote: Neither Greg nor I believe we can forecast market prices of major currencies.

timeline.point: Yen borrowing aims at currency-neutrality; $2.3 billion of after-tax gains from dollar strength were recognized by yearend.
timeline.quote: Greg and I have no view on future foreign exchange rates and therefore seek a position approximating currency-neutrality.

timeline.point: Paper money can lose value through fiscal folly; fixed-coupon bonds offer no protection, so Berkshire stays in equities.
timeline.quote: Paper money can see its value evaporate if fiscal folly prevails.

overview: From 1980 Buffett pledged to run Berkshire with plenty of liquidity and moderate debt, accepting lower returns. In the 1980s idle money was parked in Treasury bills, arbitrage or medium-term tax-exempt bonds while he waited for opportunities. From 1998 large cash piles ($15 billion in 1998, $43 billion in 2004, $116 billion in 2017, $144 billion in 2021) appear as something he dislikes holding but will not deploy at poor prices. The 2008 crisis turned liquidity into an asset: Berkshire supplied $15.5-15.6 billion while others scrambled. He set a floor of $10 billion (2010), worked at $20 billion, raised it to $30 billion in 2021, holds Treasury bills, and avoids collateral calls, bank lines and material short-term debt.
stance_basis: ample liquidity is praised as non-negotiable in every decade (1980, 1987, 2008-2010, 2014, 2017-2018, 2021-2023), while large idle cash balances are called unwelcome and low-earning (1986, 1998, 2004, 2009, 2017, 2021); the view did not change, only the stated minimum rose from $10 billion (2010) to $20 billion and then $30 billion (2021)
note: untagged corpus hits (financial-strength remarks in insurance sections, Treasury-bill mentions in the investment-category lists) were checked in context and add nothing beyond the tagged passages; the 1990s have only three tagged passages

timeline.point: Berkshire will always keep ample liquidity, moderate well-structured debt and strong capital, even at some cost to return on equity.
timeline.quote: Under all circumstances we plan to operate with plenty of liquidity, with debt that is moderate in size and properly structured, and with an abundance of capital strength.

timeline.point: Berkshire borrowed ahead of need so it has firepower when credit is expensive or unavailable.
timeline.quote: The most attractive opportunities may present themselves at a time when credit is extremely expensive - or even unavailable. At such a time we want to have plenty of financial firepower.

timeline.point: With no new equity ideas, main capital moves were paying down debt and stockpiling funds.
timeline.quote: So our main capital allocation moves in 1986 were to pay off debt and stockpile funds.

timeline.point: Policies aim for certainty of meeting obligations under extraordinarily adverse conditions rather than optimal results in normal times.
timeline.quote: we adhere to policies - both in regard to debt and all other matters - that will allow us to achieve acceptable long-term results under extraordinarily adverse conditions, rather than optimal results under a normal range of conditions.

timeline.point: Arbitrage serves as an alternative to Treasury bills when cash exceeds good ideas.
timeline.quote: We prefer, of course, to make major long-term commitments, but we often have more cash than good ideas.

timeline.point: He resists doing something marginal just because Berkshire holds a lot of cash.
timeline.quote: we'll try to resist the temptation to do something marginal simply because we are long on cash.

timeline.point: Over $15 billion of cash equivalents at yearend; he wants a large acquisition to absorb it but sees none.
timeline.quote: Cash never makes us happy. But it's better to have the money burning a hole in Berkshire's pocket than resting comfortably in someone else's.

timeline.point: Default position is Treasury bills and repos; he never reaches for yield by lowering credit standards or extending maturities.
timeline.quote: No matter how low the yields on these instruments go, we never "reach" for a little more income by dropping our credit standards or by extending maturities.

timeline.point: Failing to find acquisitions or securities, Berkshire ended 2004 with $43 billion of cash equivalents.
timeline.quote: Berkshire therefore ended the year with $43 billion of cash equivalents, not a happy position.

timeline.point: He sold holdings he preferred to keep rather than let cash fall; Berkshire must never rely on others to meet obligations.
timeline.quote: We never want to count on the kindness of strangers in order to meet tomorrow's obligations.

timeline.point: Holding cash or long Treasuries at near-zero yields is a poor long-run policy despite crisis comfort.
timeline.quote: Clinging to cash equivalents or long-term government bonds at present yields is almost certainly a terrible policy if continued for long.

timeline.point: In the 2008 panic Berkshire was a supplier of liquidity, putting $15.5 billion to work.
timeline.quote: When the financial system went into cardiac arrest in September 2008, Berkshire was a supplier of liquidity and capital to the system, not a supplicant.

timeline.point: Cash fell from $44.3 billion to $30.6 billion as money was deployed during the crisis.
timeline.quote: We entered 2008 with $44.3 billion of cash-equivalents, and we have since retained operating earnings of $17 billion.

timeline.point: Formal pledge: at least $10 billion of cash outside the utility and railroad, usually $20 billion on hand.
timeline.quote: have pledged that we will hold at least $10 billion of cash, excluding that held at our regulated utility and railroad businesses.

timeline.point: Liquidity comes first: Treasury bills held despite poor rates; $20 billion working level, $10 billion minimum; buybacks stop below $20 billion.
timeline.quote: Our working level for liquidity is $20 billion; $10 billion is our absolute minimum.

timeline.point: Redundant liquidity and no collateral-posting derivatives cost returns most years but ensure survival.
timeline.quote: That reduces our returns in 99 years out of 100. But we will survive in the 100th while many others fail.

timeline.point: Cash is like oxygen; Berkshire always keeps at least $20 billion in Treasury bills, not cash substitutes.
timeline.quote: Cash, though, is to a business as oxygen is to an individual: never thought about when it is present, the only thing in mind when it is absent.

timeline.point: Cash and Treasury bills reached $116.0 billion, far above the level he wants; redeployment is the goal.
timeline.quote: This extraordinary liquidity earns only a pittance and is far beyond the level Charlie and I wish Berkshire to have.

timeline.point: With $112 billion in bills, he repeats the $20 billion floor and the fortress pledge.
timeline.quote: Berkshire will forever remain a financial fortress.

timeline.point: The minimum rises to more than $30 billion; $144 billion reflects failure to find qualifying businesses, not a preference for cash.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I have pledged that Berkshire (along with our subsidiaries other than BNSF and BHE) will always hold more than $30 billion of cash and equivalents.

timeline.point: Cash far above conventional needs lets Berkshire respond to market seizures with huge sums.
timeline.quote: Your company also holds a cash and U.S. Treasury bill position far in excess of what conventional wisdom deems necessary.

timeline.point: Despite a large cash position, most money stays in equities, and cash will never be preferred to good businesses.
timeline.quote: Berkshire will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses, whether controlled or only partially owned.

overview: In 1977-1979 Buffett praised Illinois National Bank, which earned about three times the return on assets of major banks, and regretted the forced 1980 divestiture under the Bank Holding Company Act. Wesco's Mutual Savings and Loan and the thrift crisis appear in the 1980s, with criticism of savings and loans that bought junk and zero-coupon bonds. In 1990 he called banking 'no favorite of ours' because 20:1 leverage magnifies mistakes, yet bought 10% of Wells Fargo cheaply, later adding M&T (First Empire), U.S. Bancorp, Bank of New York Mellon, JPMorgan and Bank of America. He attacked bank derivatives opacity (2002, 2008), reckless 2006-2008 lending and bank-merger folly, and in 2011 said the industry was back on its feet.
stance_basis: wary of the industry's leverage, lending herd behaviour, derivatives and acquisitions (1979, 1989-1990, 1992, 1998, 2002, 2006-2009, 2015), but positive on specific well-managed banks he owned (Illinois National 1977-1980, Wells Fargo 1990-2015, First Empire/M&T 1991-1997, Bank of America 2011-2016)
note: read = the 177 tagged passages (many are holdings or earnings tables) plus 5 untagged corpus hits read in full (1984_p0027, 2019_p0059, 2020_p0030, 2022_p0034, 2023_p0015); 2020-2023 bank holdings appear only in tables and brief mentions, without new commentary on the sector

timeline.point: Illinois National Bank earned about three times the return on assets of most large banks while paying top rates to savers and keeping low risk.
timeline.quote: In 1977 the Illinois National Bank continued to achieve a rate of earnings on assets about three times that of most large banks.

timeline.point: Record 2.3% return on assets; the Bank Holding Company Act forces divestiture by end-1980, and sale proceeds cannot replace the bank's earning power.
timeline.quote: You simply can't buy high quality businesses at the sort of price/earnings multiple likely to prevail on our bank sale.

timeline.point: The bank was divested by letting shareholders exchange Berkshire shares for Rockford Bancorp shares.
timeline.quote: On December 31, 1980 we completed the exchange of 41,086 shares of Rockford Bancorp Inc. (which owns 97.7% of Illinois National Bank) for a like number of shares of Berkshire Hathaway Inc.

timeline.point: Illinois National was sold; Rockford holders received about Berkshire's per-share intrinsic value, so the split was fair.
timeline.quote: When Rockford's liquidation is completed, its shareholders will have received per-share proceeds about equal to Berkshire's per-share intrinsic value at the time of the bank's sale.

timeline.point: Savings and loans that bought zero-coupon bonds with insured deposits booked phantom income, leaving taxpayers with the losses.
timeline.quote: Certain savings and loan associations were heavy buyers of such bonds, using cash that came from FSLIC-insured deposits.

timeline.point: Banking is not a favourite because 20:1 leverage lets small asset mistakes wipe out equity; he buys only well-managed banks at fair prices.
timeline.quote: The banking business is no favorite of ours. When assets are twenty times equity - a common ratio in this industry - mistakes that involve only a small portion of assets can destroy a major portion of equity.

timeline.point: Panic in bank stocks let Berkshire buy 10% of Wells Fargo for $290 million, under five times after-tax earnings.
timeline.quote: we purchased our 10% interest in Wells Fargo for $290 million, less than five times after-tax earnings, and less than three times pre-tax earnings.

timeline.point: Stress test: if 10% of Wells Fargo's loans went bad at 30% loss, the bank would roughly break even.
timeline.quote: these produced losses (including foregone interest) averaging 30% of principal, the company would roughly break even.

timeline.point: Wells Fargo produced a break-even look-through result, the low-level possibility he had described.
timeline.quote: we had a break-even result from our interest in Wells Fargo (dividends we received from the company were offset by negative retained earnings).

timeline.point: Berkshire's 13% of Wells Fargo is likened to owning a $7 billion bank earning about $100 million.
timeline.quote: bank, our 13% ownership translates into a $7 billion "Berkshire Bank" that earned about $100 million during 1994.

timeline.point: First Empire preferred is called; Berkshire keeps the converted common, citing comfort with well-run banks.
timeline.quote: We are comfortable owning stock in well-run banks, and we will convert and keep our First Empire common shares.

timeline.point: Big banks' derivatives disclosures leave even experienced readers unable to judge risk.
timeline.quote: When Charlie and I finish reading the long footnotes detailing the derivatives activities of major banks, the only thing we understand is that we don't understand how much risk the institution is running.

timeline.point: Weak lending practices and the house-price bubble exposed big financial institutions; Wells Fargo's earnings dipped slightly.
timeline.quote: what we are witnessing at some of our largest financial institutions is an ugly sight.

timeline.point: He lost 89% on $244 million of two Irish bank stocks bought in 2008.
timeline.quote: During 2008, I spent $244 million for shares of two Irish banks that appeared cheap to me. At yearend we wrote these holdings down to market: $27 million, for an 89% loss.

timeline.point: Boards of big financial institutions must hold the CEO responsible for risk; shareholders of failed institutions lost over $500 billion.
timeline.quote: a board of directors of a huge financial institution is derelict if it does not insist that its CEO bear full responsibility for risk control.

timeline.point: A well-run bank Berkshire owned made a value-destroying stock-for-stock purchase of a smaller bank.
timeline.quote: The owner of the small bank became richer, we became poorer, and the managers of the big bank - newly bigger - lived happily ever after.

timeline.point: Wells Fargo prospered through the recession, but Fed limits held its dividend down; he expects a large dividend increase.
timeline.quote: consistently prospering throughout the worst of the recession and currently enjoying enormous financial strength and earning power, has therefore been forced to maintain an artificially low payout.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought $5 billion of Bank of America preferred with warrants and added $1 billion of Wells Fargo; the industry has recovered.
timeline.quote: The banking industry is back on its feet, and Wells Fargo is prospering. Its earnings are strong, its assets solid and its capital at record levels.

timeline.point: Wells Fargo's reported earnings are depressed by a non-economic core-deposit amortization charge of about $1.5 billion.
timeline.quote: In no sense, except GAAP accounting, is this whopping charge an expense.

timeline.point: Bank of America warrant position is effectively Berkshire's fourth-largest equity investment.
timeline.quote: it is important for you to realize that Bank of America is, in effect, our fourth largest equity investment - and one we value highly.

timeline.point: Reckless mortgage origination and packaging by banks helped cause the 2008 panic.
timeline.quote: There is no question that reckless practices in home lending played a major role in bringing on the financial panic of 2008, which in turn led to the Great Recession.

timeline.point: Bank of America (9.5%) and Wells Fargo (9.8%) are among the five largest holdings, with large retained earnings.
timeline.quote: Far more important than the dividends, though, are the huge earnings that are annually retained by these companies.

timeline.point: Reaching for yield through risky loans helped the savings and loan industry destroy itself.
timeline.quote: Three decades ago, the once-mighty savings and loan industry destroyed itself, partly by ignoring that maxim.

timeline.point: He cites the 1863 Comptroller's warning that bankers cannot manage dishonest borrowers.
timeline.quote: Never deal with a rascal under the expectation that you can prevent him from cheating you.

overview: Across 48 letters (1977-2024) Buffett holds one core method: value stocks as pieces of businesses, buy what he understands with durable economics, able honest managers and a sensible price, keep a margin of safety, ignore forecasts, and use Mr. Market's swings rather than follow them. His view changed in one major way: from Graham's cheap 'cigar butts' to wonderful businesses at fair prices, stated as a lesson in 1983, 1987 and 1989 and credited to Munger in 2014 and 2023; in 1992 'very attractive price' became 'attractive price'. Constant themes are attacks on efficient-market theory and beta (1985-2022), risk as loss of purchasing power, concentration for skilled investors, low-cost index funds for others (1993-2016), and fear as the investor's friend.
stance_basis: the method is endorsed in every letter 1977-2024 (615 tagged passages); the main shift, from bargain 'cigar butts' to quality businesses at fair prices, was described as a lesson learned (1983, 1987, 1989, 2014, 2023), and the 1977 four-part creed was loosened only on price in 1992
note: more than 300 tagged passages: worked decade by decade from the annotation layer (all 615 summaries and stance quotes), read in full all 23 passages of the 1970s and 37-49 selected passages per later decade (241), plus 6 untagged corpus hits on index funds and the hedge-fund bet (2003_p0049, 2006_p0044, 2014_p0151, 2016_p0129, 2016_p0134, 2017_p0065); six decade parts precede this line

timeline.point: Four-part creed for buying stocks as if buying the whole business.
timeline.quote: We want the business to be (1) one that we can understand, (2) with favorable long-term prospects, (3) operated by honest and competent people, and (4) available at a very attractive price.

timeline.point: No attempt to forecast short-term prices; concentration in meaningful amounts.
timeline.quote: successfully forecasting short term stock price movements is something we think neither we nor anyone else can do.

timeline.point: Early lesson from Waumbec: good businesses at fair prices beat poor ones at bargains.
timeline.quote: "turnarounds" seldom turn, and that the same energies and talent are much better employed in a good business purchased at a fair price than in a poor business purchased at a bargain price.

timeline.point: First shift from Graham: from tangible-asset bargains to businesses with enduring goodwill.
timeline.quote: My own thinking has changed drastically from 35 years ago when I was taught to favor tangible assets and to shun businesses whose value depended largely upon economic Goodwill.

timeline.point: Graham's discount-to-value attitude bought Washington Post at a quarter of value while efficient-market believers ignored value.
timeline.quote: we had learned from Ben Graham that the key to successful investing was the purchase of shares in good businesses when market prices were at a large discount from underlying business values.

timeline.point: Contrarian rule for unpredictable fear and greed; owner earnings defined as the valuation measure.
timeline.quote: we simply attempt to be fearful when others are greedy and to be greedy only when others are fearful.

timeline.point: Mr. Market is to be used, not followed.
timeline.quote: Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you. It is his pocketbook, not his wisdom, that you will find useful.

timeline.point: Favorite holding period for outstanding businesses with outstanding managers.
timeline.quote: when we own portions of outstanding businesses with outstanding managements, our favorite holding period is forever.

timeline.point: Explicit rejection of cigar-butt investing after 25 years.
timeline.quote: It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price. Charlie understood this early; I was a slow learner.

timeline.point: Graham's margin of safety reaffirmed after the junk-bond losses.
timeline.quote: Forty-two years after reading that, I still think those are the right three words.

timeline.point: Only change to the 1977 creed: price standard relaxed because of size and markets.
timeline.quote: Because of both market conditions and our size, we now substitute "an attractive price" for "a very attractive price."

timeline.point: Value and growth are joined; margin of safety is the cornerstone.
timeline.quote: We believe this margin-of-safety principle, so strongly emphasized by Ben Graham, to be the cornerstone of investment success.

timeline.point: Index funds for investors who cannot analyze businesses; concentration for those who can; beta rejected.
timeline.quote: By periodically investing in an index fund, for example, the knownothing investor can actually out-perform most investment professionals.

timeline.point: Circle of competence and ten-year holding test.
timeline.quote: If you aren't willing to own a stock for ten years, don't even think about owning it for ten minutes.

timeline.point: Avoids tech because durable advantages cannot be identified there.
timeline.quote: If we have a strength, it is in recognizing when we are operating well within our circle of competence and when we are approaching the perimeter.

timeline.point: Value is discounted future cash; ratios and growth only clues; speculation rejected in the bubble.
timeline.quote: But value is destroyed, not created, by any business that loses money over its lifetime, no matter how high its interim valuation may get.

timeline.point: Few stocks attractive after the bubble; inactivity accepted.
timeline.quote: But occasionally successful investing requires inactivity.

timeline.point: Walter Schloss's Graham-style record refutes efficient-market theory.
timeline.quote: There is simply no possibility that what Walter achieved over 47 years was due to chance.

timeline.point: Buys in the panic, citing Graham.
timeline.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get.

timeline.point: Risk redefined as loss of purchasing power; productive assets beat currency instruments and gold.
timeline.quote: More succinctly, investing is forgoing consumption now in order to have the ability to consume more at a later date.

timeline.point: His will prescribes an index fund for his wife's trust.
timeline.quote: Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund.

timeline.point: Credits Munger for the shift away from Graham's cigar butts.
timeline.quote: Forget what you know about buying fair businesses at wonderful prices; instead, buy wonderful businesses at fair prices.

timeline.point: After the hedge-fund bet, all investors should use low-cost index funds.
timeline.quote: Both large and small investors should stick with low-cost index funds.

timeline.point: Against borrowing to own stocks, given four 37-59% falls in Berkshire shares.
timeline.quote: This table offers the strongest argument I can muster against ever using borrowed money to own stocks.

timeline.point: Stocks owned for long-term business performance.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I are not stock-pickers; we are business-pickers.

timeline.point: Markets misprice in both directions.
timeline.quote: "Efficient" markets exist only in textbooks.

timeline.point: Unchanged rule restated after Munger's death.
timeline.quote: One investment rule at Berkshire has not and will not change: Never risk permanent loss of capital.

timeline.point: Equities remain the main use of capital despite large cash.
timeline.quote: the great majority of your money remains in equities. That preference won't change.

overview: Buffett described Hurricane Andrew (1992) as the largest insured loss in history up to then: it added about four points to the industry's 1992 combined ratio, destroyed a few small insurers and exposed inadequate catastrophe reinsurance at larger ones. Berkshire, perhaps the largest super-cat writer, lost about $125 million, roughly equal to its 1992 super-cat premiums, so the line still lost only $2 million; GEICO's Andrew loss cut Berkshire's look-through earnings by about $25 million. He later used Andrew as a yardstick: a similar storm in 1994 could cost Berkshire $600 million, 1995 'dodged' a second Andrew, and in 2004 he compared its $15.5 billion industry loss with the WTC and a possible $100 billion event.
note: Thin event (5 tagged passages). 1995_p0053 ('a second Andrew was dodged') is not tagged with the event but was read and quoted.

timeline.point: Andrew added about four points to the industry's 1992 combined ratio, destroyed small insurers and showed larger ones their catastrophe reinsurance was inadequate.
timeline.quote: About four points in the industry's 1992 combined ratio can be attributed to Hurricane Andrew, which caused the largest insured loss in history.

timeline.point: He warned the damage could have been far worse had the storm hit 20-30 miles further north; companies would rethink reinsurance.
timeline.quote: All in all, many companies will rethink their reinsurance programs in light of the Andrew experience.

timeline.point: Berkshire's super-cat book lost about $125 million to Andrew, about its 1992 super-cat premiums, leaving a $2 million line loss; GEICO's loss cost Berkshire about $25 million of look-through earnings.
timeline.quote: we too took our lumps from Andrew, suffering losses from it of about $125 million, an amount roughly equal to our 1992 super-cat premium income.

timeline.point: Having expanded the super-cat business, he estimated a similar storm would now cost Berkshire $600 million.
timeline.quote: When Hurricane Andrew blew in 1992, we paid out about $125 million. Because we've since expanded our super-cat business, a similar storm today could cost us $600 million.

timeline.point: Hurricane Opal weakened before landfall, so a second Andrew was avoided; he warned the industry will not always be so lucky.
timeline.quote: the storm abated before hitting land, and so a second Andrew was dodged.

timeline.point: Andrew's $15.5 billion industry loss and the WTC's $35 billion rocked insurers; a $100 billion catastrophe remains possible and some reinsurers would not survive.
timeline.quote: Hurricane Andrew cost insurers about $15.5 billion in 1992 (though that loss would be far higher in today’s dollars). Both events rocked the insurance and reinsurance world.

overview: Buffett reported that $29 billion of Berkshire's $65 billion 2017 gain in net worth came not from operations but from Congress rewriting the tax code in December 2017. In 2018 he explained that cutting the corporate rate from 35% to 21% returned 40% (14/35ths) of the Treasury's 'AA share' interest in Berkshire's earnings, lifting after-tax earnings of the non-insurance businesses 47% versus 24% pre-tax and raising the intrinsic value of Berkshire and of most stocks it holds, though utility tax benefits pass to customers and the dividend tax rate was little changed. Later letters accrue deferred taxes at 21% and tie the equity outlook to corporate tax rates staying low.
note: Thin event (6 tagged passages, all in the 2017 and 2018 letters). 2018_p0059 and 2019_p0055 mention the 21% rate's consequences, are not tagged with the event, and were read; 2019_p0055 is quoted.

timeline.point: Of the $65 billion 2017 gain in net worth only $36 billion came from operations; $29 billion came from the December tax law.
timeline.quote: But only $36 billion came from Berkshire’s operations. The remaining $29 billion was delivered to us in December when Congress rewrote the U.S. Tax Code.

timeline.point: Non-insurance businesses' 2018 pre-tax income rose 24%, but after-tax income rose 47%, largely due to the corporate rate cut.
timeline.quote: But our after-tax gain in 2018 from these businesses was far greater – 47% – thanks in large part to the cut in the corporate tax rate

timeline.point: Cutting the rate from 35% to 21% returned 40% of the government's 'AA share' ownership and materially raised Berkshire's intrinsic value.
timeline.quote: 40% of the government’s “ownership” (14/35ths) was returned to Berkshire – free of charge – when the corporate tax rate was reduced to 21%.

timeline.point: Offsets: utility tax savings go to customers and the dividend tax rate stayed about 13%; overall the law made Berkshire's businesses and stocks more valuable.
timeline.quote: Overall, however, the new law made our businesses and the stocks we own considerably more valuable.

timeline.point: Deferred taxes on unrealized equity gains are accrued at the new 21% rate but will be paid at whatever rate prevails on sale.
timeline.quote: These liabilities are accrued in our financial statements at the current 21% corporate tax rate but will be paid at the rates prevailing when our investments are sold.

timeline.point: If low rates and low corporate taxes persist, he judged equities almost certain to beat long-term fixed-rate debt.
timeline.quote: if corporate tax rates also remain near the low level businesses now enjoy, it is almost certain that equities will over time perform far better than long-term, fixed-rate debt instruments.

overview: Berkshire bought FlightSafety International, the world leader in pilot training, in 1996 for about $1.5 billion in cash and A/B shares, structured to nudge holders toward cash. Buffett praised founder Al Ueltschi and later CEO Bruce Whitman and repeatedly called FlightSafety the runaway leader and 'gold standard' (about five times its nearest rival; training about 58% of U.S. corporate pilots by 2007). He also stressed its capital intensity: simulators cost up to $12-19 million, capex exceeds depreciation, so he used it to attack EBITDA. Earnings dipped after 9/11 and the corporate-aviation slowdown (2001-2003), recovered 2004-2007, and in 2007 he judged it 'excellent but not extraordinary' because growth needs heavy reinvestment.
note: Untagged passages 1996_p0010, 1997_p0075 and 2000_p0094 mention FlightSafety (headquarters jet joke, IDQ deal modeled on it, NetJets pilot training) and were read; earnings tables listing only 'Flight Services' were not counted.

timeline.point: Acquired FlightSafety, the world leader in pilot training, for about $1.5 billion, Berkshire's larger 1996 acquisition.
timeline.quote: Our other acquisition in 1996 - FlightSafety International, the world's leader in the training of pilots - was far larger, at about $1.5 billion

timeline.point: Deal gave holders cash or stock but nudged the tax-indifferent toward cash to limit share issuance: 51% cash, 41% A shares, 8% B shares.
timeline.quote: This nudge led to about 51% of FlightSafety's shares being exchanged for cash, 41% for Berkshire A and 8% for Berkshire B.

timeline.point: Unlike most Berkshire operations, the simulator-based business is capital intensive.
timeline.quote: Simulators are not cheap - they can cost as much as $19 million - so this business, unlike many of our operations, is capital intensive.

timeline.point: First full year: FlightSafety earned $139.5 million pre-tax.
FSI is about five times its nearest competitor, but high capital per revenue dollar means it needs high margins.
timeline.quote: the capital investment per dollar of revenue at FSI is exceptionally high. Operating margins must therefore also be high, if we are to earn a reasonable return on capital.

timeline.point: Spending $272 million on simulators, he argued depreciation is a real cost; growth prospects remain strong.
timeline.quote: should get an internship at a simulator company.

timeline.point: After 9/11 airline training fell; planned simulator spending of $162 million far exceeded $95 million depreciation, a rebuke to EBITDA.
timeline.quote: Those who believe that EBITDA is in any way equivalent to true earnings are welcome to pick up the tab.

timeline.point: Excluding a $60 million gain on selling its FlightSafety Boeing stake, training earnings fell slightly with business aviation; still the industry standard.
timeline.quote: FlightSafety training continues to be the gold standard for the industry, and we expect growth in the years to come.

timeline.point: Normal operating earnings fell from $183 million to $150 million as corporate aviation slowed, plus a $37 million simulator obsolescence loss.
timeline.quote: FlightSafety, our training operation, experienced a drop in “normal” operating earnings from $183 million to $150 million.

timeline.point: Profits recovered; up to $3.50 of capital per $1 of revenue makes utilization key; return on tangible equity rose to 15.1% from 8.4%.
timeline.quote: Last year, FlightSafety’s return on tangible equity improved to 15.1% from 8.4% in 2003.

timeline.point: Earnings improved with corporate aviation; heavy investment in new simulators and a Farnborough training center.
timeline.quote: In flight services, earnings improved at FlightSafety as corporate aviation continued its rebound.

timeline.point: Durable competitive advantage, but pre-tax earnings rose only $159 million on $509 million of incremental investment since 1996: excellent, not extraordinary.
timeline.quote: Consequently, if measured only by economic returns, FlightSafety is an excellent but not extraordinary business.

timeline.point: Record year: revenues up 14%, pre-tax earnings up 20%; trains about 58% of U.S. corporate pilots.
timeline.quote: FlightSafety, our pilot training business, gained 14% in revenues and 20% in pre-tax earnings.

overview: In 1989 Berkshire bought $358 million of USAir 9 1/4% convertible preferred. Buffett soon called it an 'unforced error': airline economics deteriorated through fare wars and bankruptcies, though he praised managers Colodny, Schofield and later Wolf. Dividends were suspended in 1994 and he wrote the stake down 75% to $89.5 million, calling it sloppy analysis that ignored a high-cost carrier's fate after deregulation. He twice tried to sell at about half of par and failed. A 5%-over-prime penalty clause on arrears, a 1996-97 recovery and conversion rights then produced a decent profit; he sold in 1998. Later letters cite USAir as proof airlines are a capital pit and as a near-disaster rescued by luck.
note: Untagged passages 1991_p0054 (block purchases list), 2022_p0020 and 2022_p0021 (USAir as a near-disaster rescued by luck) were read. Stance moved from cautious optimism (1989) to regret (1990-1995) to relief at a lucky profit (1996-1998), with the purchase itself always judged a mistake.

timeline.point: Bought $358 million of USAir preferred: 9 1/4% dividend, ten-year mandatory redemption, convertible at $60.
timeline.quote: We next purchased $358 million of USAir Group, Inc. preferred stock with mandatory redemption in ten years, a dividend of 9 1/4%, and the right to convert into common at $60 per share.

timeline.point: He could not forecast airline economics, so used a preferred structure; 'agnostics, not atheists' about the industry.
timeline.quote: we have no ability to forecast the economics of the investment banking business (in which we have a position through our 1987 purchase of Salomon convertible preferred), the airline industry, or the paper industry.

timeline.point: Called the purchase an unforced error made just as the airline hit industry trouble and Piedmont merger problems; stake worth substantially less than cost.
timeline.quote: In making the USAir purchase, your Chairman displayed exquisite timing: I plunged into the business at almost the exact moment that it ran into severe problems.

timeline.point: Kamikaze pricing showed that in a commodity business you cannot be much smarter than your dumbest competitor.
timeline.quote: In a business selling a commodity-type product, it's impossible to be a lot smarter than your dumbest competitor.

timeline.point: 1991 decimated the industry; the low USAir valuation reflects a real risk that airlines stay unprofitable, worsened by bankrupt carriers' low fares.
timeline.quote: Unfortunately 1991 was a decimating period for the industry, as Midway, Pan Am and America West all entered bankruptcy.

timeline.point: Praised Schofield's repositioning, but in airlines skill earns only survival, not prosperity; British Airways investment and board seats followed in 1993.
timeline.quote: Unfortunately, though, the near-term reward for skill in the airline business is simply survival, not prosperity.

timeline.point: Dividend suspended; he called it his top mistake, from sloppy analysis or hubris.
timeline.quote: Our $358 million purchase of USAir preferred stock, on which the dividend was suspended in September.

timeline.point: Wrote the stake down to $89.5 million, 25 cents on the dollar, sending a $269 million writedown through income; he and Munger left the board.
timeline.quote: Accordingly, we wrote our USAir investment down to $89.5 million, 25 cents on the dollar at yearend 1994.

timeline.point: Results improved and unpaid dividends compound at prime plus 5%, but it remains a weak credit; carried at 60% of par.
timeline.quote: We feel much better about our USAir preferred than we did a year ago, but your guess is as good as mine as to its ultimate value.

timeline.point: Admitted his analysis was superficial and wrong; USAir lost $2.4 billion in 1990-1994.
timeline.quote: But my analysis of USAir's business was both superficial and wrong.

timeline.point: The penalty-dividend clause he wrote in made arrears compound at 13.25%-14%; USAir resumed paying; he twice failed to sell cheaply.
timeline.quote: Mixed in with my many mistakes at USAir was one thing I got right

timeline.point: Preferred now probably worth par of $358 million, with $240.5 million of dividends collected over the years.
timeline.quote: the prices of USAir's publicly-traded securities tell us that our preferred stock is now probably worth its par value of $358 million, give or take a little.

timeline.point: Credited Stephen Wolf with a near-miraculous rebound; arrears made up and conversion rights made a decent profit almost certain.
timeline.quote: It is now almost certain that our US Airways shares will produce a decent profit -- that is, if my cost for Maalox is excluded -- and the gain could even prove indecent.

timeline.point: Called the purchase shameful participation in pouring capital into airlines; sold in 1998 at a hefty gain, after which the company went bankrupt twice.
timeline.quote: And I, to my shame, participated in this foolishness when I had Berkshire buy U.S. Air preferred stock in 1989.

timeline.point: Listed USAir with Salomon as near-disasters from which Berkshire escaped largely by luck.
timeline.quote: (Remember our escapes from near-disasters at USAir and Salomon? I certainly do.)

overview: Buffett first used convertible bonds as short-life alternatives to straight bonds (1979). In 1987-91 he bought five private convertible preferreds (Salomon, Gillette, USAir, Champion, First Empire) plus American Express Percs, calling them fixed-income securities with an equity kicker, used where he trusted management but could not forecast industry economics, and promised returns 'moderately above' fixed income. By 1992-95 he judged them inferior to open-market stock buying, ahead of bonds only thanks to Gillette; USAir broke his near-no-loss claim and taking Gillette preferred instead of common was a costly mistake. From 2008 he bought high-yield preferreds with equity sweeteners (Goldman Sachs, GE, Wrigley, Bank of America, Heinz, Occidental) and regretted their redemptions.
note: 12 untagged passages were found by search and read (1978_p0033, 1989_p0084, 1991_p0071, 2003_p0008, 2005_p0048, 2011_p0103, 2012_p0017, 2015_p0030, 2019_p0052, 2020_p0041, 2021_p0038, 2023_p0030). Stance is mixed: the 1987-91 group was judged disappointing apart from Gillette, while the 2008-2019 preferreds were described as very attractive high-yield commitments.

timeline.point: Fixed-dollar purchases limited to convertible bonds, whose conversion option effectively shortens their life and may offset losses in straight bonds.
timeline.quote: In the last several years our net fixed dollar commitments have been limited to the purchase of convertible bonds.

timeline.point: $700 million Salomon 9% convertible preferred, bought as convertible because investment banking economics are unpredictable; mainly a medium-term fixed-income holding.
timeline.quote: This unpredictability is one of the reasons why our participation is in the form of a convertible preferred.

timeline.point: Most of the Salomon preferred's value is fixed-income; conversion right may still prove valuable.
timeline.quote: However, the overwhelming portion of the preferred’s value resides in its fixed-income characteristics, not its equity characteristics.

timeline.point: Bought Gillette ($600M), USAir ($358M) and Champion ($300M) preferreds; structure chosen where industry economics could not be forecast.
timeline.quote: Our lack of strong convictions about these businesses, however, means that we must structure our investments in them differently

timeline.point: Expected money back plus dividends almost regardless, but satisfactory results only if the investees' common stocks do well.
timeline.quote: Under almost any conditions, we expect these preferreds to return us our money plus dividends.

timeline.point: Expected returns moderately above most fixed-income portfolios, below wonderful-business stocks or whole acquisitions.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I feel that our preferred stock investments should produce returns moderately above those achieved by most fixed-income portfolios

timeline.point: Rebutted the press: a convertible preferred is worth at least its value as a straight preferred, plus the option.
timeline.quote: most of the value of our convertible preferreds is derived from their fixed-income characteristics.

timeline.point: Added First Empire State 9% convertible preferred and American Express Percs, which convert into common with a capped value.
timeline.quote: Our American Express preferred is not a normal fixed-income security. Rather it is a "Perc," which carries a fixed dividend of 8.85% on our $300 million cost.

timeline.point: Negotiated preferreds, despite Gillette, did worse than open-market stock purchases, as expected.
timeline.quote: our overall performance with such purchases has been inferior to that we have achieved with purchases made in the secondary market.

timeline.point: USAir preferred, with dividend suspended, was his top mistake, possibly from false comfort in a senior security.
timeline.quote: a lapse that may have been caused by the fact that we were buying a senior security or by hubris.

timeline.point: Group beat fixed income only because of Gillette; his claim that losing money was almost impossible caused 'heartburn'.
timeline.quote: We beat this expectation - but only because of the performance of a single issue.

timeline.point: Choosing Gillette preferred over common cost about $625 million less $70 million of extra dividends.
timeline.quote: If I had negotiated for common rather than preferred, we would have been better off at yearend 1995 by $625 million, minus the "excess" dividends of about $70 million.

timeline.point: Excluding Gillette, the preferreds earned no more than the medium-term bonds they replaced.
timeline.quote: Overall, our preferreds have performed well, but that is true only because of one huge winner, Gillette.

timeline.point: All four remaining holdings rose sharply: Gillette $600M to $4.8B, First Empire $40M to $236M, Salomon and USAir revived.
timeline.quote: At yearend, the $600 million we put into Gillette in 1989 had appreciated to $4.8 billion

timeline.point: Bought $14.5 billion of high-yield Wrigley, Goldman Sachs and GE fixed-income securities with equity participations as a bonus.
timeline.quote: We very much like these commitments, which carry high current yields that, in themselves, make the investments more than satisfactory.

timeline.point: Five non-traded positions (Dow, GE, Goldman, Swiss Re, Wrigley) cost $21.1 billion and pay $2.1 billion a year.
timeline.quote: these holdings deliver us an aggregate of $2.1 billion annually in dividends and interest.

timeline.point: Redemptions by GE, Goldman and Swiss Re, though at premiums of about $1.4 billion, were unwelcome because earning power falls.
timeline.quote: but all of the redemptions are nevertheless unwelcome. After they occur, our earning power will be significantly reduced.

timeline.point: Bought $5 billion of Bank of America 6% preferred with warrants for 700 million shares at $7.14.
timeline.quote: a $5 billion 6% preferred stock of Bank of America that came with warrants allowing us to buy 700 million common shares at $7.14 per share

timeline.point: Heinz $8 billion 9% preferred, with features lifting its return to about 12%.
timeline.quote: we purchased $8 billion of Heinz preferred stock that carries a 9% coupon but also possesses other features that should increase the preferred’s annual return to 12% or so.

timeline.point: Kraft Heinz preferred paying $720 million a year likely redeemed for $8.32 billion: good for Kraft Heinz, bad for Berkshire.
timeline.quote: That will be good news for Kraft Heinz and bad news for Berkshire.

timeline.point: BofA preferred pays $300 million a year; the warrant showed a $10.5 billion profit and the preferred can fund its exercise.
timeline.quote: At yearend, that privilege would have delivered us a profit of $10.5 billion.

timeline.point: Holdings include a $10 billion Occidental Petroleum investment in preferred stock and warrants.
timeline.quote: Includes $10 billion investment in Occidental Petroleum Corporation consisting of preferred stock and warrants to buy common stock.

overview: Buffett's view has two sides. On the system, he was consistently negative: in 2002 he called derivatives 'time bombs' and 'financial weapons of mass destruction', citing mark-to-model ('mark-to-myth') accounting, collateral-call spirals, counterparty linkage and LTCM; in 2008 he said they made big banks impossible to analyze and that disclosure cannot fix this. Berkshire's own wind-down of Gen Re Securities (23,218 contracts, about $409 million of losses, 2002-2006) he called a costly lesson in his own dithering. Yet from the late 1990s he personally wrote contracts he judged mispriced (oil contracts, currency forwards, high-yield credit contracts, long-dated equity index puts), paid upfront so free of counterparty risk; these proved profitable, but once new contracts required collateral (2011-2014) he stopped writing them.
note: Two untagged earnings tables with Gen Re Securities losses (2003_p0098, 2004_p0078) were found and read. Stance is mixed by design: negative on derivatives for dealers and the financial system in every letter 2002-2008, positive on Berkshire's own uncollateralized, mispriced contracts 2006-2014.

timeline.point: Disclosed oil derivative contracts for 45.7 million barrels set up in 1994-95, with a $61.9 million pre-tax gain on settled contracts.
timeline.quote: The first was derivative contracts for 14.0 million barrels of oil, that being what was then left of a 45.7 million barrel position we established in 1994-95.

timeline.point: Charlie and he view derivatives and their trading as time bombs for both the parties and the economy.
timeline.quote: We view them as time bombs, both for the parties that deal in them and the economic system.

timeline.point: Gen Re Securities, an unwanted derivatives dealer acquired with Gen Re, is being terminated; like reinsurance, easy to enter and almost impossible to exit.
timeline.quote: Like Hell, both are easy to enter and almost impossible to exit.

timeline.point: Mark-to-model accounting lets traders and CEOs book illusory earnings and bonuses.
timeline.quote: In extreme cases, mark-to-model degenerates into what I would call mark-to-myth.

timeline.point: Credit risk is concentrated among a few dealers trading with each other; linkage can trigger systemic problems.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I believe, however, that the macro picture is dangerous and getting more so.

timeline.point: His summary judgment of derivatives.
timeline.quote: In our view, however, derivatives are financial weapons of mass destruction, carrying dangers that, while now latent, are potentially lethal.

timeline.point: Admitted that dithering on closing Gen Re Securities cost shareholders about $100 million pre-tax.
timeline.quote: I’m sure I could have saved you $100 million or so, pre-tax, if I had acted more promptly to shut down Gen Re Securities.

timeline.point: Lost $104 million in 2005 and $404 million in total exiting Gen Re's derivatives, even in a benign market.
timeline.quote: Our aggregate losses since we began this endeavor total $404 million.

timeline.point: Final report on the wind-down: 197 contracts left and $409 million cumulative pre-tax loss.
timeline.quote: Our cumulative pre-tax loss from this operation totals $409 million, but only $5 million occurred in 2006.

timeline.point: Berkshire writes a few large contracts he judges mispriced, free of counterparty risk, which have earned hundreds of millions.
timeline.quote: The answer is that derivatives, just like stocks and bonds, are sometimes wildly mispriced.

timeline.point: 94 contracts: high-yield default contracts ($3.2 billion premiums) and 15-20-year equity index puts ($4.5 billion premiums), expected to be profitable.
timeline.quote: I believe these contracts, in aggregate, will be profitable and that we will, in addition, receive substantial income from our investment of the premiums

timeline.point: Derivatives raised leverage and made banks, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac unanalyzable.
timeline.quote: Derivatives are dangerous. They have dramatically increased the leverage and risks in our financial system.

timeline.point: 251 contracts, each believed mispriced at inception; counterparties pay upfront, creating $8.1 billion of derivatives float.
timeline.quote: I believe each contract we own was mispriced at inception, sometimes dramatically so.

timeline.point: Black-Scholes, applied to long-dated puts, overstates the liability; Berkshire reported a $5.1 billion mark-to-market loss on the puts.
timeline.quote: If the formula is applied to extended time periods, however, it can produce absurd results.

timeline.point: Delighted with the contracts held; quarterly valuation swings were large but do not affect cash.
timeline.quote: We are delighted that we hold the derivatives contracts that we do.

timeline.point: High-yield credit contracts paid $2.5 billion of losses but will still earn an underwriting profit: 'we charged the right premium'.
timeline.quote: In short, we charged the right premium, and that protected us when business conditions turned terrible three years ago.

timeline.point: New rules require collateral, so no major new derivatives positions.
timeline.quote: Consequently, we will not be initiating any major derivatives positions.

timeline.point: Credit-protection contracts will earn about $1 billion pre-tax plus about $2 billion of average float.
timeline.quote: It’s now almost certain that our profit from these contracts will approximate $1 billion pre-tax.

timeline.point: Contracts proved quite profitable, but full collateralization of new contracts ended his interest regardless of profit.
timeline.quote: And that ended our interest in derivatives, regardless of what profit potential they might offer.

overview: From 1980 Buffett warned that underpriced reinsurance faced a 'bloodbath' in a super catastrophe. From 1989-90 Berkshire wrote huge catastrophe covers for its own account, perhaps the largest super-cat writer: priced to pay out about 90% of premiums, deliberately lumpy ('a lumpy 15% to a smooth 12%'), sold on unmatched financial strength, with a capped worst case (about $600 million after tax in 1994-1997). He cut volume whenever capital flooded in (cat bonds 1997, 2006, 2015). 9/11 exposed Gen Re's ignored terrorism risk. After the 2004-05 hurricanes he priced for possible climate change, and in 2011-2019 stressed that a $250-400 billion mega-cat would hurt others far more than Berkshire.
note: Nine untagged passages found by search were read (1985_p0105, 1990_p0084, 1994_p0053, 1997_p0009, 2001_p0037, 2005_p0008, 2007_p0011, 2007_p0012, 2018_p0057). Stance is mixed: he is eager to assume catastrophe risk at adequate prices and treats it as a Berkshire advantage, but consistently warns that mega-catastrophes are certain, mispricing is hidden for years, and he retreats when prices fall.

timeline.point: High interest rates lure amateurs into reinsurance; a super catastrophe could cause a bloodbath with some companies unable to pay.
timeline.quote: If we experience such a catastrophe, there could be a bloodbath with some companies not able to live up to contractual commitments.

timeline.point: Capacity withdrawals and better prices need a 'megadisaster' shock, which would bring great opportunity to well-capitalized insurers.
timeline.quote: Instead, major capacity withdrawals require a shock factor such as a natural or financial “megadisaster”.

timeline.point: After Hugo and the California quake, Berkshire offered up to $250 million of catastrophe cover and retains all of it rather than laying it off.
timeline.quote: Berkshire Hathaway offered to write up to $250 million of catastrophe coverage, advertising that proposition in trade publications.

timeline.point: A full $250 million loss in one quarter would cost about $165 million after tax, a blow to pride, not well-being.
timeline.quote: the damage would be a blow only to our pride, not to our well-being.

timeline.point: Super-cat results will be close to zero or 300% combined ratio in a given year: risk concentrated, not spread.
timeline.quote: Note that we are not spreading risk as insurers typically do; we are concentrating it.

timeline.point: Priced to pay out about 90% of premiums long term; annual GAAP results will look enormously profitable or unprofitable.
timeline.quote: We price this business expecting to pay out, over the long term, about 90% of the premiums we receive.

timeline.point: Past experience cannot simply be extrapolated: global warming and coastal growth shift the odds.
timeline.quote: If there is truly "global warming," for example, the odds would shift, since tiny changes in atmospheric conditions can produce momentous changes in weather patterns.

timeline.point: A loss-free year proves nothing: underpriced odds can win for years and still go broke.
timeline.quote: In fact, it will take decades for us to find out whether our underwriting judgment has been sound.

timeline.point: Worst-case super-cat loss about $600 million after tax; shareholders uncomfortable should sell before, not after, a mega-catastrophe.
timeline.quote: If you are not comfortable with this level of exposure, the time to sell your Berkshire stock is now, not after the inevitable mega-catastrophe.

timeline.point: A terrible super-cat year is certain; wrote record Florida hurricane and California Earthquake Authority covers.
timeline.quote: What you must understand, however, is that a truly terrible year in the super-cat business is not a possibility - it's a certainty.

timeline.point: Catastrophe bonds sold to 'innocents' depressed prices, so Berkshire will write less; worst case still about $600 million.
timeline.quote: The influx of "investor" money into catastrophe bonds -- which may well live up to their name -- has caused super-cat prices to deteriorate materially.

timeline.point: 9/11 showed Gen Re ignored terrorism and aggregation risk; he violated the 'Noah rule'.
timeline.quote: I violated the Noah rule: Predicting rain doesn’t count; building arks does.
