timeline.point: Still willing to lose $2-2.5 billion in one event if properly paid.
timeline.quote: We are perfectly willing to lose $2 billion to $2½ billion in a single event (as we did on September 11th) if we have been paid properly

timeline.point: A $100 billion industry loss is possible; Berkshire's 3-5% share would be covered by other earnings.
timeline.quote: When “the day after” arrives, Berkshire’s checks will clear.

timeline.point: After Katrina ($2.5 billion loss) and frequent strong storms, mega-cat cover only at far higher prices and limited aggregate exposure.
timeline.quote: we’ve concluded that we should now write mega-cat policies only at prices far higher than prevailed last year

timeline.point: Prepared to lose $6 billion in one event if paid, but cut wind exposure as capital flooded in.
timeline.quote: We remain prepared to lose $6 billion in a single event, if we have been paid appropriately for assuming that risk.

timeline.point: A $250 billion industry mega-catastrophe would leave Berkshire with a moderate profit while others face insolvency.
timeline.quote: Berkshire as a whole would likely record a moderate profit for the year because of its many streams of earnings.

timeline.point: Super-cat rates fell as climate change had not yet raised covered losses, so Berkshire backed away; one-year repricing limits climate risk.
timeline.quote: As a consequence, U.S. super-cat rates have fallen steadily in recent years, which is why we have backed away from that business.

timeline.point: Three hurricanes cost about $3 billion, roughly 3% of a $100 billion industry loss; a $400 billion event has about 2% annual odds.
timeline.quote: We believe that the annual probability of a U.S. mega-catastrophe causing $400 billion or more of insured losses is about 2%.

timeline.point: A catastrophe dwarfing Katrina will come, possibly a cyber attack; it will not strain Berkshire.
timeline.quote: “The Big One” may come from a traditional source, such as wind or earthquake, or it may be a total surprise involving, say, a cyber attack

timeline.point: Convective storm damage lifted pricing; a staggering loss will come, and one-year policies keep such risks manageable.
timeline.quote: Someday, any day, a truly staggering insurance loss will occur – and there is no guarantee that there will be only one per annum.

overview: Buffett's view of moats grew steadily more central and stayed positive. In the late 1970s he contrasted commodity textiles and insurance with See's and TV stations. His 1983 goodwill essay credited consumer franchises, unregulated government franchises and low-cost positions, and admitted he had moved from Graham's bargains to enduring goodwill. He first used the moat-around-a-castle image for GEICO's cost gap (1986), defined an economic franchise (1991), called Coke and Gillette 'Inevitables' (1996), made 'widening the moat' Berkshire's priority (2005) and gave his fullest test in 2007. He applied it critically too: insurance mostly lacks moats, media and newspaper franchises eroded from 1990-91 onward, Dexter's moat vanished, and tech advantages were unknowable to him.
note: Written from the decade parts. Tagged 435 passages (1970s 7, 1980s 132, 1990s 107, 2000s 83, 2010s 88, 2020s 18); all 7 of the 1970s and 18 of the 2020s and the 40 most relevant of each other decade were read in full (185), plus 5 untagged passages found by search (1991_p0035, 2007_p0048, 2012_p0110, 2015_p0071, 2017_p0017). The rest were reviewed through annotation summaries and stance quotes. Stance is positive in every decade on owning moat businesses; negative judgments concern specific industries (textiles, insurance generally, airlines, newspapers after 1990).

timeline.point: Undifferentiated, capital-intensive textile producers earn inadequate returns except under tight supply.
timeline.quote: The textile industry illustrates in textbook style how producers of relatively undifferentiated goods in capital intensive businesses must earn inadequate returns

timeline.point: Some businesses, like a network TV station, earn extraordinary returns almost unavoidably and may be worth their high price.
timeline.quote: Despite a fancy price tag, the “easy” business may be the better route to go.

timeline.point: In commodity industries only a wide, sustainable cost advantage, like GEICO's, earns good returns.
timeline.quote: a company with a wide and sustainable cost advantage.

timeline.point: Experience moved him from Graham's approach toward businesses with enduring goodwill and few tangible assets.
timeline.quote: produced my present strong preference for businesses that possess large amounts of enduring Goodwill and that utilize a minimum of tangible assets.

timeline.point: Sources of economic goodwill: consumer franchises, unregulated government franchises and enduring low-cost positions.
timeline.quote: Consumer franchises are a prime source of economic Goodwill.

timeline.point: Business economics matter more than management skill.
timeline.quote: a good managerial record (measured by economic returns) is far more a function of what business boat you get into than it is of how effectively you row

timeline.point: First moat image: GEICO's cost gap protects its business castle.
timeline.quote: The difference between GEICO’s costs and those of its competitors is a kind of moat that protects a valuable and muchsought-after business castle.

timeline.point: Learned to prefer wonderful companies at fair prices over bargains.
timeline.quote: It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price.

timeline.point: Defined an economic franchise; media were sliding from franchise to business.
timeline.quote: An economic franchise arises from a product or service that: (1) is needed or desired; (2) is thought by its customers to have no close substitute and; (3) is not subject to price regulation.

timeline.point: Brands, product attributes and distribution give Coke and Gillette a protective moat.
timeline.quote: setting up a protective moat around their economic castles.

timeline.point: Coke and Gillette are 'Inevitables', but for each there are dozens of Impostors.
timeline.quote: Thus, for every Inevitable, there are dozens of Impostors, companies now riding high but vulnerable to competitive attacks.

timeline.point: Avoided tech because he could not identify durable advantages there.
timeline.quote: we have no insights into which participants in the tech field possess a truly durable competitive advantage.

timeline.point: Widening the moat takes precedence over short-term earnings.
timeline.quote: But when short-term and long-term conflict, widening the moat must take precedence.

timeline.point: Newspaper fundamentals are eroding and will overwhelm managerial skill.
timeline.quote: And fundamentals are definitely eroding in the newspaper industry, a trend that has caused the profits of our Buffalo News to decline.

timeline.point: Fullest test: an enduring moat (low cost or a worldwide brand) protecting high returns, in a stable industry, not dependent on a superstar.
timeline.quote: A truly great business must have an enduring “moat” that protects excellent returns on invested capital.

timeline.point: Dexter's apparent durable advantage vanished within a few years, a costly mistake.
timeline.quote: What I had assessed as durable competitive advantage vanished within a few years.

timeline.point: Widening operating businesses' moats is one of Berkshire's four core goals.
timeline.quote: (2) widening the “moats” around our operating businesses that give them durable competitive advantages;

timeline.point: GEICO's low costs form an enduring moat competitors cannot cross.
timeline.quote: Its low costs create a moat – an enduring one – that competitors are unable to cross.

timeline.point: See's durable advantage gave significant pricing power with minimal reinvestment.
timeline.quote: a broad and durable competitive advantage that gave it significant pricing power.

timeline.point: P/c insurance has no trade secrets, patents or locational advantages.
timeline.quote: This is a business in which there are no trade secrets, patents, or locational advantages.

timeline.point: Goal restated: businesses with durable economic advantages and first-class CEOs.
timeline.quote: our goal is to have meaningful investments in businesses with both durable economic advantages and a first-class CEO.

timeline.point: Coke and Amex endured because their base franchises meet timeless needs worldwide.
timeline.quote: the consumption of liquids and the need for unquestioned financial trust are timeless essentials of our world.

overview: In the 1987 letter Buffett described the October 1987 crash as Mr. Market's "sudden, massive seizure" after a manic rampage, leaving the Dow up only 2.3% for the year. He blamed professional money managers who treat stocks as game tokens and especially "portfolio insurance," a mechanical stop-loss strategy with $60-90 billion of equities on a hair trigger. He argued such volatility helps any investor not forced to sell, but Berkshire found few bargains and could not buy meaningfully before prices rebounded. Later letters reuse the crash as a lesson: model-driven risk (1996), how fast a portfolio can fall (2005), and Berkshire's own 37.1% drop in October 1987 as an argument against borrowing to own stocks (2017).

timeline.point: Calls the 1987 market a year of excitement but little net movement (Dow +2.3%), with a manic rise until October and then a crash.
timeline.quote: Mr. Market was on a manic rampage until October and then experienced a sudden, massive seizure.

timeline.point: Blames professional money managers who focus on what other managers will do rather than on business results.
timeline.quote: For them, stocks are merely tokens in a game, like the thimble and flatiron in Monopoly.

timeline.point: Singles out portfolio insurance, an automatic stop-loss selling strategy, citing the Brady Report's estimate of equities exposed to it.
timeline.quote: According to the Brady Report, $60 billion to $90 billion of equities were poised on this hair trigger in midOctober of 1987.

timeline.point: Rejects the view that small investors cannot compete: irrational volatility creates chances for true investors who are not forced to sell.
timeline.quote: Such markets are ideal for any investor - small or large - so long as he sticks to his investment knitting.

timeline.point: Berkshire could not exploit the crash: a few stocks became interesting but rebounded before meaningful purchases were made.
timeline.quote: During the break in October, a few stocks fell to prices that interested us, but we were unable to make meaningful purchases before they rebounded.

timeline.point: Cites portfolio insurance in the 1987 crash as an example of how computer models give false security and cause debacles.
timeline.quote: Witness "portfolio insurance," whose destructive effects in the 1987 market crash led one wag to observe that it was the computers that should have been jumping out of windows.

timeline.point: Uses October 19, 1987 as the example of how quickly Berkshire's large portfolio could lose market value, which its capital must withstand.
timeline.quote: We also own a large investment portfolio whose market value could fall dramatically and quickly under certain conditions (as happened on October 19, 1987).

timeline.point: Lists the 10/2/87-10/27/87 fall of Berkshire stock (4,250 to 2,675, down 37.1%) among four major dips, arguing against borrowed money.
timeline.quote: This table offers the strongest argument I can muster against ever using borrowed money to own stocks.

overview: Moody's is a long-held but lightly discussed common-stock holding. Berkshire bought about 15% in 2000 and, per the 2008 letter, never bought another share; Moody's own buybacks lifted the stake above 20% by late 2008 (equity-method accounting). Berkshire sold some Moody's in 2009, then held 24,669,778 shares (about 11.5-13.3%) from 2013 through 2021, with market value rising from $1.9 billion to $9.6 billion. Buffett mostly lists it in holdings tables; his few judgments are favorable: among 'excellent businesses' (2003), a retained-earnings investee expected to yield capital gains (2019), Berkshire the largest owner (2022), and a 'very large and highly profitable' household name (2024). He never wrote a dedicated analysis of the company.

timeline.point: Moody's first appears in Berkshire's year-end common-stock table with 24 million shares.
timeline.quote: 24,000,000 Moody’s Corporation

timeline.point: Notes the Moody's position was last changed in 2000; calls the six largest holdings excellent businesses whose prices already reflect their quality.
timeline.quote: we last changed our position in Coca-Cola in 1994, American Express in 1998, Gillette in 1989, Washington Post in 1973, and Moody’s in 2000.

timeline.point: After a share split the holding is listed as 48 million shares, 16.2% of the company, market value $2,948 million.
timeline.quote: 48,000,000 Moody’s Corporation

timeline.point: Same 48 million shares, now 19.1% of Moody's, but market value down to $1,714 million at year-end 2007.
timeline.quote: 48,000,000 Moody’s Corporation

timeline.point: Berkshire bought 15% years earlier and never added; Moody's buybacks pushed the stake above 20%, so it is now carried at equity value.
timeline.quote: We purchased 15% of Moody’s some years ago and have not since bought a share.

timeline.point: Moody's was among Berkshire's largest stock sales of 2009.
timeline.quote: In 2009, our largest sales were in ConocoPhillips, Moody’s, Procter & Gamble and Johnson & Johnson

timeline.point: Holding reduced to 28.4 million shares, 12.7% of Moody's, market value $1,430 million.
timeline.quote: 28,415,250 Moody’s Corporation

timeline.point: Holding settles at 24,669,778 shares (11.5%), market $1,936 million; the share count stays unchanged through 2021.
timeline.quote: 24,669,778 Moody’s Corporation

timeline.point: Moody's (13.1% owned) is listed among investees whose retained earnings Buffett expects to produce at least equal capital gains.
timeline.quote: both logic and our past experience indicate that from the group we will realize capital gains at least equal to – and probably better than – the earnings of ours that they retained.

timeline.point: Same 24,669,778 shares (13.3%) now worth $9,636 million; buybacks raised Berkshire holders' indirect share of partly-owned firms like Moody's.
timeline.quote: 24,669,778 Moody’s Corporation

timeline.point: Berkshire is the largest owner of Moody's, one of eight large investees it leads.
timeline.quote: Berkshire was the largest owner of eight of these giants: American Express, Bank of America, Chevron, Coca-Cola, HP Inc., Moody’s, Occidental Petroleum and Paramount Global.

timeline.point: Names Moody's among very large, highly profitable household-name businesses earning high returns on net tangible equity.
timeline.quote: a dozen or so very large and highly profitable businesses with household names such as Apple, American Express, Coca-Cola and Moody’s.

overview: Blue Chip Stamps, a California trading-stamp company Buffett and Munger controlled from 1970, was Berkshire's main affiliate until 1983. Berkshire's stake grew to about 36.5% (1977), about 58% after the 1978 Diversified Retailing merger (then fully consolidated), about 60% in 1979-82, and 100% through a 1983 merger Buffett framed as a value-for-value exchange. Blue Chip was the vehicle that bought See's in 1972 and owned 80% of Wesco and the Buffalo News. The stamp business itself collapsed: sales fell from $126 million (1970) to $19.4 million (1980), $1.2 million (1991) and $25,920 (2006). Buffett calls trading stamps one of his misjudgments, while crediting the Blue Chip-See's purchase as Berkshire's 1972 turning point.

timeline.point: Berkshire keeps buying Blue Chip, reaching about 36.5%; Blue Chip earned about $12.9 million from operations plus $4.1 million securities gains.
timeline.quote: We again increased our equity interest in Blue Chip Stamps, and owned approximately 36 1/2% at the end of 1977.

timeline.point: The Diversified Retailing merger lifts ownership to about 58%, so Blue Chip is fully consolidated, which Buffett says obscures economic reality.
timeline.quote: After the merger, our ownership of Blue Chip Stamps increased to approximately 58%

timeline.point: The trading stamp business's liquidity needs are one reason Berkshire holds large marketable-securities positions.
timeline.quote: the liquidity requirements of our insurance and trading stamp businesses mandate major investments in marketable securities.

timeline.point: Announces a planned Berkshire-Blue Chip merger as a rare fair, value-for-value share exchange.
timeline.quote: One is to have a true business-value-for-business-value merger, such as the Berkshire-Blue Chip combination is intended to be.

timeline.point: The merger closes smoothly; Berkshire owns 100% of Blue Chip from mid-1983 and gains tax efficiency.
timeline.quote: The Blue Chip/Berkshire merger went off without a hitch.

timeline.point: The true cost of the merger exceeded the $51.7 million of goodwill booked, because the Berkshire shares given were worth more than their market price.
timeline.quote: what we truly paid in the Blue Chip merger for 40% of the Goodwill of See’s and the News was considerably more than the $51.7 million entered on our books

timeline.point: Admits the trading stamp cornerstone business shrank to about 5% of its size; only redeploying funds into better businesses overcame it.
timeline.quote: (3) shrunk in sales volume to about 5% its size at the time of our entry.

timeline.point: Contrasts collapsing stamp sales with See's growth since Blue Chip bought See's in 1972.
timeline.quote: The sales of trading stamps by Blue Chip thereafter declined from $102.5 million in 1972 to $1.2 million in 1991.

timeline.point: Excludes the affiliated Blue Chip and Diversified mergers when admitting that his other stock-only mergers cost shareholders money.
timeline.quote: If you aggregate all of our stock-only mergers (excluding those we did with two affiliated companies, Diversified Retailing and Blue Chip Stamps), you will find that our shareholders are slightly worse off

timeline.point: Lists trading stamps among businesses whose future economics he misjudged.
timeline.quote: I’m the fellow, remember, who thought he understood the future economics of trading stamps, textiles, shoes and second-tier department stores.

timeline.point: Recounts the decline: 1970 sales $126 million, 1980 $19.4 million, 1990 about $1.5 million.
timeline.quote: From the day Charlie and I stepped into the Blue Chip picture, the business went straight downhill.

timeline.point: Blue Chip contributed only $25,920 of Berkshire's $98 billion revenues.
timeline.quote: Last year, in Berkshire’s $98 billion of revenues, all of $25,920 (no zeros omitted) came from Blue Chip.

timeline.point: Calls 1972, when See's was bought for Blue Chip, a turning point that set Berkshire on Munger's blueprint of buying wonderful businesses.
timeline.quote: The year 1972 was a turning point for Berkshire

timeline.point: Recalls the 1983 merger enlarging the registered shareholder base and prompting the owner's manual of business principles.
timeline.quote: In 1983, Berkshire and Blue Chip merged, thereby expanding Berkshire’s base of registered shareholders from 1,900 to 2,900.

overview: Buffett long saw TV and media as franchises with extraordinary returns on tangible capital, and admired Capital Cities' Tom Murphy and Dan Burke. Berkshire bought Cap Cities in 1977, sold in 1978-80 (a blunder, he said), then in 1985-86 paid a 'full price' of $172.50 a share for 3 million shares, calling it permanent. From 1988-91 his view turned: media pricing power eroded and properties came to 'resemble businesses more than franchises', cutting the value of Cap Cities, Washington Post and the Buffalo News. He sold a third of Cap Cities in 1993 (regretted) and swapped the rest for Disney stock and cash in 1996. Later letters regret a declined TV station (2007) and note TV and internet eroding newspapers.

timeline.point: Berkshire invested $10.9 million in Capital Cities; Buffett prefers non-control ownership because he could not match its management.
timeline.quote: Capital Cities possesses both extraordinary properties and extraordinary management.

timeline.point: Network TV stations are cited as businesses that earn extraordinary returns on tangible capital almost automatically, and so sell at extraordinary prices.
timeline.quote: In some businesses - a network TV station, for example - it is virtually impossible to avoid earning extraordinary returns on tangible capital employed in the business.

timeline.point: In the goodwill appendix, communications businesses are the prime example of intangibles that thrive under inflation with minimal tangible investment.
timeline.quote: This phenomenon has been particularly evident in the communications business.

timeline.point: Buys 3 million Cap Cities/ABC shares at $172.50, praising Murphy and Burke as the best public-company management.
timeline.quote: I think it is the best of any publicly-owned company in the country.

timeline.point: Admits the purchase was at a full price amid near-mania for media properties, and that he had sold Cap Cities at $43 in 1978-80.
timeline.quote: Our Cap Cities purchase was made at a full price, reflecting the very considerable enthusiasm for both media stocks and media properties

timeline.point: Declares Cap Cities/ABC one of three permanent holdings, not to be sold even if overpriced.
timeline.quote: we expect to keep permanently our three primary holdings, Capital Cities/ABC, Inc., GEICO Corporation, and The Washington Post.

timeline.point: Industry conditions for the permanent holdings have become less favorable; management is superb but upside now looks smaller.
timeline.quote: at current prices, their upside potential looks considerably less exciting to us today than it did some years ago.

timeline.point: Surprised by media's vulnerability to recession; predicts lasting decline as ad dollars disperse over more channels.
timeline.quote: they will prove considerably less marvelous than I, the industry, or lenders thought would be the case only a few years ago.

timeline.point: Argues the decline is secular: media properties now act like ordinary businesses, which sharply lowers their valuation multiples.
timeline.quote: The fact is that newspaper, television, and magazine properties have begun to resemble businesses more than franchises in their economic behavior.

timeline.point: Strong, nearly debt-free Cap Cities and Washington Post soften the loss, and media still beats average business, but the old franchise era is over.
timeline.quote: But gone are the days of bullet-proof franchises and cornucopian economics.

timeline.point: Sold a third of the Cap Cities stake at a large gain, exceeding the retained earnings attributed to those shares.
timeline.quote: in 1986 we bought three million shares of Capital Cities/ABC for $172.50 per share and late last year sold one-third of that holding for $630 per share.

timeline.point: Calls the 1993 sale of 10 million Cap Cities shares at $63 (now $85.25) a costly mistake, repeating his 1978-80 sale.
timeline.quote: Now I've become a repeat offender.

timeline.point: Uses an early network TV station as the classic 'have-to-be-smart-once' business that thrives even with weak management.
timeline.quote: if you were smart enough to buy a network TV station very early in the game, you could put in a shiftless and backward nephew to run things, and the business would still do well for decades.

timeline.point: Cap Cities merges into Disney; Berkshire exchanges its shares for cash and Disney stock and buys more Disney.
timeline.quote: we exchanged our Cap Cities shares for a combination of cash and Disney stock.

timeline.point: Praises Murphy again and regrets selling a third of Cap Cities for $635 million versus $1.27 billion in the merger.
timeline.quote: If Murph should elect to run another business, don't bother to study its value - just buy the stock.

timeline.point: Notes newspapers are losing the battle for eyeballs to cable, satellite and internet.
timeline.quote: if cable and satellite broadcasting, as well as the internet, had come along first, newspapers as we know them probably would never have existed.

timeline.point: Recalls declining Murphy's offer of the Dallas-Fort Worth NBC station for $35 million around 1972, though he knew TV stations' economics.
timeline.quote: I knew that TV stations were See’s-like businesses that required virtually no capital investment and had excellent prospects for growth.

timeline.point: The declined station has since earned at least $1 billion and is worth about $800 million.
timeline.quote: In 2006, the station earned $73 million pre-tax, bringing its total earnings since I turned down the deal to at least $1 billion

timeline.point: Explains that television and the internet stripped newspapers of their primacy and much advertising, though local news remains their stronghold.
timeline.quote: In one area of interest after another, newspapers have therefore lost their “primacy.”

overview: See's, bought by Blue Chip Stamps in January 1972 for $25 million (Buffett nearly balked at $30 million), is Buffett's prototype 'dream business': a consumer franchise with untapped pricing power needing little capital. Pre-tax profit rose from about $4 million (1972) to $42 million (1991) and $82-83 million (2007, 2011); cumulative pre-tax earnings reached $1.9 billion by 2014 on only about $40 million of added investment, the cash funding other acquisitions. In the 1980s he reported flat or falling same-store poundage and cost pressure; volume grew only about 2% a year. He credits managers Chuck Huggins (1972-2005) and Brad Kinstler, says See's taught him the value of brands, but admits efforts to expand it largely failed.

timeline.point: Since Blue Chip bought See's in 1972, pre-tax earnings tripled with little added capital in a no-growth industry.
timeline.quote: pre-tax operating earnings have grown from $4.2 million to $12.6 million with little additional capital investment.

timeline.point: Calls results exceptional, but flags rising non-ingredient costs and stagnant poundage as problems.
timeline.quote: The business possesses a valuable and solid consumer franchise and a manager equally valuable and solid.

timeline.point: Same-store poundage fell about 8% cumulatively since 1979; See's no longer outperforms the industry in volume.
timeline.quote: The other problem we face, as the table suggests, is our recent inability to achieve meaningful gains in pounds sold.

timeline.point: The goodwill appendix uses See's as the example: high returns on tangible assets come from reputation, so economic goodwill grows while accounting goodwill is amortized.
timeline.quote: See’s last year earned $13 million after taxes on about $20 million of net tangible assets

timeline.point: Credits See's success, in an industry where most competitors earn little, to product and management.
timeline.quote: The success of See’s reflects the combination of an exceptional product and an exceptional manager, Chuck Huggins.

timeline.point: Despite unmatched store volumes, industry trends are poor and same-store poundage keeps slipping.
timeline.quote: unless we can stabilize per-shop poundage, profit margins will narrow.

timeline.point: Notes extreme seasonality: almost all profit is earned at Christmas.
timeline.quote: In 1988, the Company earned a record 90% of its full-year profits in December: $29 million out of $32.5 million before tax.

timeline.point: Volume rebounds with the first same-store poundage gains in years, helped by more advertising.
timeline.quote: At See's Candies we had an 8% increase in pounds sold, even though 1988 was itself a record year.

timeline.point: After 20 years, See's needed only $18 million of reinvested earnings and sent the rest to its owners.
timeline.quote: See's remaining pre-tax profits of $410 million were distributed to Blue Chip/Berkshire during the 20 years

timeline.point: Names the key insight of the purchase and admits the $25 million price limit was nearly a costly mistake.
timeline.quote: We saw that the business had untapped pricing power.

timeline.point: See's taught Buffett how to evaluate franchises, which paid off in stock investments.
timeline.quote: We've made significant money in certain common stocks because of the lessons we learned at See's.

timeline.point: Argues See's competitive position is durable because the reasons people buy its chocolates barely change.
timeline.quote: these motivations are not likely to change over the next 20 years, or even 50.

timeline.point: Record 24% operating margin; cumulative pre-tax earnings since purchase far exceed the price.
timeline.quote: Since we bought See’s for $25 million in 1972, it has earned $857 million pre-tax.

timeline.point: Businesses like See's are worth far more than their carrying value, so Berkshire's intrinsic value exceeds book value.
timeline.quote: Businesses such as See’s and Buffalo News are now worth fifteen to twenty times the value at which they are carried on our books.

timeline.point: Huggins retires after 34 years; Brad Kinstler takes over.
timeline.quote: Chuck’s love for the customer and the brand permeated the organization, which in his 34-year tenure produced a more-than-tenfold increase in profits.

timeline.point: Presents See's as the model of a great business: dominant earnings in a non-growing industry with little capital need.
timeline.quote: Let’s look at the prototype of a dream business, our own See’s Candy.

timeline.point: 2007 sales $383 million, pre-tax profit $82 million, capital $40 million; $1.35 billion pre-tax earned since 1972.
timeline.quote: This means we have had to reinvest only $32 million since 1972

timeline.point: See's cash, which it cannot reinvest itself, helped fund the BNSF purchase.
timeline.quote: two of our best-run businesses, but also two offering limited reinvestment opportunities

timeline.point: Record earnings; carrying value net of cash is below zero after Christmas.
timeline.quote: Last year See’s had record pre-tax earnings of $83 million, bringing its total since we bought it to $1.65 billion.

timeline.point: Calls 1972 a turning point; See's cash helped buy other businesses and taught him the value of brands.
timeline.quote: To date, See’s has earned $1.9 billion pre-tax, with its growth having required added investment of only $40 million.

timeline.point: Admits Berkshire could not profitably expand the candy business, so excess cash went elsewhere.
timeline.quote: But our many attempts to do so were largely futile.

timeline.point: At See's centennial, says Berkshire's job is not to meddle with a customer-driven consumer brand.
timeline.quote: the customer’s message to Berkshire remains clear: “Don’t mess with my candy.”

overview: Buffett was skeptical of bonds as a class in every decade: from 1979 he called long-term fixed-rate bonds obsolete contracts in an inflationary world ('bonds are as sound as a dollar'), regretted his own fifteen-year bonds, and warned in 2011-2024 that low yields made Treasuries riskier than stocks ('return-free risk'). He held mostly Treasury bills for liquidity and refused to reach for yield. Yet he bought specific mispriced debt when stigmatized: WPPSS (1983-84, beat most business acquisitions), Texaco, RJR Nabisco, fallen-angel and 2002 junk bonds ($8.3 billion), Treasury zeros (1997), cheap 2008-09 corporates; he condemned new-issue junk and zero-coupon abuses and called the $2 billion Energy Future Holdings purchase a big mistake.

timeline.point: Admits Berkshire's insurers erred by holding fifteen-year bonds as inflation rose; argues long fixed-price money contracts make no sense.
timeline.quote: It was a mistake to buy fifteen-year bonds, and yet we did

timeline.point: Refuses to fix a price for money decades ahead, just as he would not for candy or cloth.
timeline.quote: “Neither a short-term borrower nor a long-term lender be.”

timeline.point: Warns that insurers carrying bonds at amortized cost hide large losses that freeze investment and underwriting choices.
timeline.quote: Some of the largest and best known propertycasualty companies currently find themselves with nominal, or even negative, net worth when bond holdings are valued at market.

timeline.point: Explains buying stigmatized WPPSS bonds by valuing them as a business earning far more than typical acquisitions.
timeline.quote: Only a relatively few businesses earn the 16.3% after tax on unleveraged capital that our WPPSS investment does

timeline.point: Still dislikes most long-term bonds, fearing inflation and even a small chance of runaway inflation.
timeline.quote: bonds are as sound as a dollar - and we view the longterm outlook for dollars as dismal.

timeline.point: Bought about $700 million of medium-term tax-exempts only as the least objectionable alternative.
timeline.quote: at best, the bonds are mediocre investments.

timeline.point: WPPSS bonds, bought at about 17% after-tax yields, are now rated AA- and beat most 1983 business purchases, though his view of long bonds is unchanged.
timeline.quote: this purchase actually worked out better than did the general run of business acquisitions made in 1983

timeline.point: Condemns 1980s new-issue junk bonds while buying RJR Nabisco debt he judged mispriced.
timeline.quote: Mountains of junk bonds were sold by those who didn't care to those who didn't think - and there was no shortage of either.

timeline.point: Reports large gains and income from fixed-income bets such as Chrysler Financial, Texaco, Time-Warner, WPPSS and RJR Nabisco.
timeline.quote: Meanwhile, our fixed-income losses have been negligible: We've had thrills but so far no spills.

timeline.point: Discloses a large macro bet on long Treasury zeros, which gained $598.8 million as rates fell.
timeline.quote: our largest non-traditional position at yearend was $4.6 billion, at amortized cost, of long-term zero-coupon obligations of the U.S. Treasury.

timeline.point: Junk bonds are unsuitable for the public, but selective distressed-debt buying (WPPSS, Texaco, RJR, Finova) has paid off.
timeline.quote: And, so far, our 50-year experience in distressed debt has proven rewarding.

timeline.point: Took advantage of cheap junk bonds and loans in 2002.
timeline.quote: Overall, our commitments in this sector sextupled, reaching $8.3 billion by yearend.

timeline.point: Junk bonds rebounded quickly and now look unattractive.
timeline.quote: Yesterday’s weeds are today being priced as flowers.

timeline.point: Default holding is U.S. Treasury bills and repos; Berkshire will not stretch for yield.
timeline.quote: we never “reach” for a little more income by dropping our credit standards or by extending maturities.

timeline.point: Cites euro-denominated Amazon bonds bought at 57% of par as proof that bond markets can be inefficient.
timeline.quote: At the time, Amazon bonds were priced as “junk” credits, though they were anything but.

timeline.point: Says investors swung to overpricing risk, making near-zero-yield Treasuries a bubble and holding them a bad long-term policy.
timeline.quote: But the U.S. Treasury bond bubble of late 2008 may be regarded as almost equally extraordinary.

timeline.point: Regrets not buying more of the corporate and municipal bonds that were very cheap relative to Treasuries.
timeline.quote: When it’s raining gold, reach for a bucket, not a thimble.

timeline.point: Calls currency-based investments among the most dangerous assets because inflation erodes them; holds mainly T-bills for liquidity.
timeline.quote: Right now bonds should come with a warning label.

timeline.point: Energy Future Holdings bonds ended with an $873 million pre-tax loss.
timeline.quote: About $2 billion of the debt was purchased by Berkshire, pursuant to a decision I made without consulting with Charlie. That was a big mistake.

timeline.point: Uses the bet's Treasury strips, sold at a 0.88% yield in 2012, to argue bonds are riskier than stocks for long-term investors.
timeline.quote: Often, high-grade bonds in an investment portfolio increase its risk.

timeline.point: With the 10-year Treasury at 0.93%, down 94% from 1981, fixed-income investors face a bleak future.
timeline.quote: And bonds are not the place to be these days.

timeline.point: Berkshire will keep most money in equities; paper money can lose value through fiscal folly.
timeline.quote: Fixed-coupon bonds provide no protection against runaway currency.

overview: GEICO is Buffett's most consistently praised holding, positive in every decade: 'The Security I Like Best' (1951, repeated 2005) and the widest moat among his insurers. After its 1970s near-failure from under-reserving, Berkshire bought about a third in 1976-80 for roughly $47 million, judging the low-cost direct-selling advantage intact; buybacks lifted the stake to about 50%, and Berkshire paid $2.3 billion for the rest in January 1996. Under Tony Nicely, market share rose from 2.5% to about 12% (2016), making GEICO number two, with float growing from $2.5 billion to $22.1 billion by 2018. Admitted setbacks: wasted 2000 advertising, a failed credit-card venture, early-1980s reinsurance losses, and 'major repolishing' needed before 2024's sharp improvement.

timeline.point: Calls GEICO and SAFECO outstanding management groups giving Berkshire a large indirect insurance interest.
timeline.quote: we have a very large indirect interest in two truly outstanding management groups through our investments in SAFECO and GEICO.

timeline.point: With about 33% owned, calls GEICO a rare blend of durable business advantage and outstanding management.
timeline.quote: GEICO represents the best of all investment worlds - the coupling of a very important and very hard to duplicate business advantage with an extraordinary management

timeline.point: The mid-1970s crisis did not destroy GEICO's low-cost advantage; it was a franchise with a curable problem.
timeline.quote: Its troubles in the mid-70s were not produced by any diminution or disappearance of this essential economic advantage.

timeline.point: GEICO wrote at a 96 combined ratio versus the industry's 111 while Berkshire's own insurers did terribly.
timeline.quote: Geico’s performance during 1983 was as good as our own insurance performance was poor.

timeline.point: GEICO's 23.5% expense ratio forms a moat; it is one of three permanent holdings.
timeline.quote: The difference between GEICO’s costs and those of its competitors is a kind of moat that protects a valuable and muchsought-after business castle.

timeline.point: California's Proposition 103 threatens GEICO's large economic goodwill.
timeline.quote: But GEICO, because it is a low-cost producer able to earn high returns on equity, has a huge amount of economic goodwill at risk.

timeline.point: GEICO's underwriting profits make its float cost less than nothing.
timeline.quote: Essentially, GEICO's policyholders, in aggregate, pay the company interest on the float rather than the other way around.

timeline.point: Agrees to buy the remaining half for $2.3 billion, citing the same advantages as in 1951.
timeline.quote: Then, in 1995, we agreed to pay $2.3 billion for the half of the company we didn't own. That is a steep price.

timeline.point: Policy growth hit 16% and underwriting profit 8.1%, above the 4% target, so rates were cut.
timeline.quote: GEICO's underwriting profit for the year, though, was 8.1% of premiums, far above its average.

timeline.point: Admits stepped-up advertising failed to pay off as acquisition costs rose and growth stalled.
timeline.quote: I told you last year that we would get our money’s worth from stepped-up advertising at GEICO in 2000, but I was wrong.

timeline.point: A 1981-83 reinsured liability venture cost GEICO $94.1 million, mostly from unpaid reinsurers.
timeline.quote: GEICO’s losses from this venture now total a breathtaking $94.1 million or about 130,000% of the net premium it received.

timeline.point: Policies grew 12.1% and share reached about 6.1%; he restates his 1951 verdict.
timeline.quote: I called GEICO “The Security I Like Best.” And that’s what I still call it.

timeline.point: Share reached 7.2% versus 2.5% at acquisition, with ad spending up from $31 million to $751 million.
timeline.quote: GEICO possesses the widest moat of any of our insurers, one carefully protected and expanded by Tony Nicely, its CEO.

timeline.point: Underwriting profit in 13 of 14 years under Berkshire; float grew from $2.7 billion to $9.6 billion.
timeline.quote: GEICO has operated at an underwriting profit in 13 of the 14 years Berkshire has owned it.

timeline.point: Admits his GEICO credit-card idea lost about $50 million, against managers' advice.
timeline.quote: I subtly indicated that I was older and wiser.

timeline.point: Estimates GEICO's economic goodwill at about $14 billion versus $1.4 billion carried.
timeline.quote: Using the 97%-of-premium-volume yardstick we applied to our 1996 purchase, the real value today of GEICO’s economic goodwill is about $14 billion.

timeline.point: Flags driverless cars as a distant threat to premium volume.
timeline.quote: GEICO’s premium volume may shrink because of driverless cars.

timeline.point: Nicely retires as CEO after $15.5 billion of underwriting profit since 1996.
timeline.quote: By my estimate, Tony’s management of GEICO has increased Berkshire’s intrinsic value by more than $50 billion.

timeline.point: Todd Combs modernized GEICO's efficiency and underwriting, producing a spectacular 2024 improvement.
timeline.quote: GEICO was a long-held gem that needed major repolishing, and Todd has worked tirelessly in getting the job done.

overview: Berkshire bought $700 million of Salomon 9% convertible preferred in 1987. After the 1991 scandal Buffett served about ten months (August 1991 to June 1992) as Salomon's interim chairman, dealing with five government authorities; he credits Maughan, Denham, Howard, Macfarlane and lawyer Ron Olson with saving the firm. He called the post 'far from fun' but 'interesting and worthwhile' and later 'fascinating and instructional'. Financially he graded his bet on the conversion option 'very poor' (1995), though the preferred kept paying as a fixed-income security and the 1997 Travelers merger made results 'far better than I anticipated'. Later letters cite Salomon as a near-disaster rescued by luck and as a lesson about facing bad news promptly.

timeline.point: Elected Interim Chairman of Salomon on August 18, 1991, to protect Berkshire's investment.
timeline.quote: when I was elected Interim Chairman of Salomon Inc, it was a different story: I put my mouth where our money was.

timeline.point: Says Berkshire's managers are strong enough that his Salomon work does not hurt Berkshire's operations.
timeline.quote: Neither function is impeded by my work at Salomon.

timeline.point: Calls the Salomon situation his biggest surprise, yet the Salomon preferred rose slightly in value during 1991.
timeline.quote: Despite the company's travails, Charlie and I believe our Salomon preferred stock increased slightly in value during 1991.

timeline.point: Stepped down in June 1992 after ten months; glad to be back at Berkshire full time.
timeline.quote: Last June, I stepped down as Interim Chairman of Salomon Inc after ten months in the job.

timeline.point: Judges the post worthwhile: Salomon's reputation improved sharply and Salomon Brothers reported record pre-tax earnings.
timeline.quote: The Salomon post, though far from fun, was interesting and worthwhile

timeline.point: Credits four executives with the firm's survival.
timeline.quote: without the combined efforts of Salomon executives Deryck Maughan, Bob Denham, Don Howard, and John Macfarlane, the firm very probably would not have survived.

timeline.point: Describes the government matters: five authorities had concerns; lawyer Ron Olson was key.
timeline.quote: At least five authorities - the SEC, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the U.S. Treasury, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, and the Antitrust Division

timeline.point: Says the holding consumed far more management time than its economic weight justified.
timeline.quote: the amount of management time Charlie and I have devoted to this holding has been vastly greater than its economic significance to Berkshire.

timeline.point: Grades his decision to buy for the conversion option as very poor, while the 9% preferred still delivered as fixed income.
timeline.quote: my decision to go with Salomon because I saw value in the conversion option must be graded as very poor.

timeline.point: Salomon merged into Travelers; he credits Maughan and Denham with saving it after the 1991 scandal.
timeline.quote: playing key roles in saving Salomon from extinction following its 1991 scandal

timeline.point: Looks back: final results will be far better than he expected two years earlier; the experience was instructive.
timeline.quote: Looking back, I think of my Salomon experience as having been both fascinating and instructional

timeline.point: Draws a management lesson: delay in facing bad news nearly destroyed Salomon.
timeline.quote: A reluctance to face up immediately to bad news is what turned a problem at Salomon from one that could have easily been disposed of into one that almost caused the demise

timeline.point: Lists Salomon among bad moves rescued by luck.
timeline.quote: Remember our escapes from near-disasters at USAir and Salomon? I certainly do.

overview: Kirby, the vacuum-cleaner maker, came with the Scott Fetzer purchase (closed early 1986) and was reported as its own earnings line from 1986 to 1996. Buffett praised the product ('If you want the best, you buy a Kirby'), its direct-sales force and its unit growth, and put it among the 'Sainted Seven' businesses earning exceptional returns on capital under Ralph Schey. He highlighted fast export growth (international share of units from 5% to 20% by 1989) and the 1990 Generation 3 model, an 'unqualified success' though start-up costs held back earnings. Pre-tax earnings in the tables rose from $20.2 million (1986) to $58.5 million (1996). Every mention is favorable.

timeline.point: Kirby home-care systems named among the well-known products of newly acquired Scott Fetzer.
timeline.quote: Some well-known products are Kirby home-care systems, Campbell Hausfeld air compressors, and Wayne burners and water pumps.

timeline.point: Fourth straight year of unit volume gains; praises product quality and durability.
timeline.quote: Many 30- and 40-year-old Kirby cleaners are still in active duty. If you want the best, you buy a Kirby.

timeline.point: Kirby and World Book have handled the challenges facing direct sales well.
timeline.quote: So far, the record shows that both Kirby and World Book have responded most successfully.

timeline.point: Kirby counted among the 'Sainted Seven', which earned about 67% on average equity without leverage.
timeline.quote: this group earned about 67% on average equity capital.

timeline.point: Strong year with export sales booming; largest capital spending at Kirby ahead of a 1990 model change.
timeline.quote: International business has more than doubled in the last two years and quintupled in the past four; its share of unit sales has risen from 5% to 20%.

timeline.point: New Generation 3 vacuum lifted volume; start-up and learning-curve costs slowed earnings growth.
timeline.quote: Kirby unit volume grew substantially in 1990 with the help of our new vacuum cleaner, The Generation 3, which was an unqualified success.

timeline.point: Last separate earnings line: pre-tax earnings of $58.5 million versus $50.2 million in 1995.

overview: Two strands. As an insurer, Buffett moved from treating global warming as a hypothetical ('If there is truly global warming', 1992) to worry after the 2004-05 hurricanes (2005-06), to calling climate change 'highly likely' a major planetary problem (2015) while telling shareholders it should not worry them because policies reprice yearly; by 2023-24 he cites rising wildfire losses at BHE and convective storms ('Climate change may have been announcing its arrival'). As an owner, he consistently praises MidAmerican/BHE's retained-earnings build-out of wind, solar and transmission (wind spending of $1.8 billion in 2008 alone; renewables portfolio of $15-16 billion by 2013-15; Iowa wind self-sufficiency targeted for 2021) and BNSF's fuel efficiency versus trucks, always conditioned on reasonable regulated returns.

timeline.point: Super-cat pricing cannot rely on the past; global warming, if real, would shift the odds.
timeline.quote: If there is truly "global warming," for example, the odds would shift, since tiny changes in atmospheric conditions can produce momentous changes in weather patterns.

timeline.point: After Katrina he admits not knowing whether climate is changing storm patterns, so applies Pascal's wager and prices for the worse case.
timeline.quote: Or was it caused by changes in climate, water temperature or other variables we don't fully understand?

timeline.point: Warns that betting on benign atmospheric change would be a huge mistake for insurers.
timeline.quote: We do know that it would be a huge mistake to bet that evolving atmospheric changes are benign in their implications for insurers.

timeline.point: MidAmerican spent $1.8 billion on wind in 2008 and leads regulated utilities in wind ownership.
timeline.quote: In 2008 alone, MidAmerican spent $1.8 billion on wind generation at our two operations, and today the company is number one in the nation among regulated utilities in ownership of wind capacity.

timeline.point: Praises BNSF's fuel efficiency as both a cost edge and a cut in greenhouse emissions.
timeline.quote: our country gains because of reduced greenhouse emissions and a much smaller need for imported oil.

timeline.point: Renewables portfolio to cost $13 billion; he welcomes such commitments only with reasonable regulated returns.
timeline.quote: We relish making such commitments if they promise reasonable returns – and on that front, we put a large amount of trust in future regulation.

timeline.point: BHE pledged renewables in support of the Paris conference, calling it sensible for both environment and economics.
timeline.quote: Our fulfilling those promises will make great sense, both for the environment and for Berkshire's economics.

timeline.point: Notes subsidized renewables could erode high-cost incumbent utilities; BHE's efficiency keeps it competitive.
timeline.quote: Those tax credits, or other government-mandated help for renewables, may eventually erode the economics of the incumbent utility, particularly if it is a high-cost operator.

timeline.point: Responding to a proxy proposal, he calls climate change highly likely a major problem and backs early action.
timeline.quote: It seems highly likely to me that climate change poses a major problem for the planet.

timeline.point: But for Berkshire as an insurer, annual repricing means climate change is not a shareholder worry.
timeline.quote: But when you are thinking only as a shareholder of a major insurer, climate change should not be on your list of worries.

timeline.point: BHE expects wind self-sufficiency in Iowa by 2021, behind its low rates and high-tech customers.
timeline.quote: In other words, our utility will have attained wind self-sufficiency in the state of Iowa.

timeline.point: Western transmission build-out to carry remote wind and solar power; BHE to lead cleaner energy.
timeline.quote: Whatever the obstacles, BHE will be a leader in delivering ever-cleaner energy.

timeline.point: Defends BHE's renewables record as long-documented, not green-washing.
timeline.quote: The profile you will find there is not in any way one of those currently-fashionable "green-washing" stories.

timeline.point: Forest-fire losses at BHE and climate change raise doubts about utility investments in vulnerable western states.
timeline.quote: These costs arose from forest fires, whose frequency and intensity have increased – and will likely continue to increase – if convective storms become more frequent.

timeline.point: P/C pricing firmed on convective-storm damage; climate change may be arriving.
timeline.quote: Climate change may have been announcing its arrival.

overview: Bought at the start of 1986 for about $315 million after a failed banker-led sale, Scott Fetzer (World Book, Kirby, Campbell Hausfeld and other units) was Buffett's 'prototype' acquisition and one of his most praised. He used it in 1986 to explain purchase-price accounting and owner earnings, and in 1994 to contrast book and intrinsic value: earnings doubled while book value stayed flat, giving a Fortune-500-leading return on equity without leverage. He credits CEO Ralph Schey, under whom (1986-2000) it paid Berkshire $1.03 billion against a $230 million net price. The one weak spot named is World Book, hurt by CD-ROM and online rivals from 1995. Tables show it through 2002.

timeline.point: Acquired Scott Fetzer for about $320 million; calls it the model of what Berkshire wants to buy.
timeline.quote: Scott Fetzer is a prototype - understandable, large, well-managed, a good earner.

timeline.point: Praises CEO Ralph Schey's operating and capital-allocation record.
timeline.quote: Ralph's operating and capitalallocation record is superb, and we are delighted to be associated with him.

timeline.point: Uses Scott Fetzer to argue owner earnings exceed the GAAP figures depressed by purchase-price adjustments.
timeline.quote: we feel owner earnings of Scott Fetzer are considerably larger than the GAAP figures that we report.

timeline.point: Results beat expectations again: pre-tax earnings up 10% while capital employed fell.
timeline.quote: Pre-tax earnings rose 10% while average capital employed declined significantly.

timeline.point: Acquiring Schey mattered as much as the businesses; his units supply about 40% of non-insurance earnings.
timeline.quote: our acquisition of Ralph as a manager was fully as important as our acquisition of the businesses.

timeline.point: Record $110 million pre-tax on only $116 million of equity, with little debt.
timeline.quote: Scott Fetzer achieved such earnings while employing only $116 million of equity capital.

timeline.point: Return on equity would rank first in the Fortune 500 excluding bankruptcy windfalls.
timeline.quote: Scott Fetzer's return on equity would have ranked it first on the Fortune 500, well ahead of number two.

timeline.point: Carrying value halved by premium write-offs while earnings doubled, so intrinsic value far exceeds book.
timeline.quote: Yet Scott Fetzer is now earning about twice what it then did.

timeline.point: Names World Book, a Scott Fetzer unit, Berkshire's most difficult problem amid CD-ROM and online competition.
timeline.quote: Berkshire's most difficult problem is World Book, which operates in an industry beset by increasingly tough competition from CD-ROM and on-line offerings.

timeline.point: Scott Fetzer, the News and See's paid 100% of earnings to Berkshire, $1.8 billion in all.
timeline.quote: The News, See's and Scott Fetzer have alone paid us $1.8 billion, which we have gainfully employed elsewhere.

timeline.point: Record $96.5 million after-tax on $112 million net worth.
timeline.quote: earned a record $96.5 million after-tax on its $112 million net worth.

timeline.point: On Schey's retirement: $1.03 billion distributed against a $230 million net purchase price.
timeline.quote: Under his leadership, the company distributed $1.03 billion to Berkshire against our net purchase price of $230 million.

overview: His view moved in three phases. In 1998 he hailed the $22 billion stock-financed merger: General Re was 'first-class in every way'. In 1999-2002 it became the 'problem child': large underwriting losses, under-reserving ($800 million of prior-year losses recognized in 2001, $1.31 billion more in 2002), unpriced terrorism and nuclear aggregation exposed by September 11, and a derivatives unit (Gen Re Securities) whose wind-down cost over $400 million. He admitted being 'dead wrong' about its discipline. From 2003 under Joe Brandon and Tad Montross he declared it fixed, then a 'gem' with better-than-cost-free float of about $18-23 billion. In 2016 he still called paying for it with 21.8% more Berkshire shares 'a terrible mistake'.

timeline.point: Calls the two 1998 acquisitions, General Re and Executive Jet, first-class.
timeline.quote: The two companies we acquired in 1998, General Re and Executive Jet, are first-class in every way

timeline.point: Completes the $22 billion acquisition; praises General Re's reputation under Ron Ferguson.
timeline.quote: For many decades, General Re's name has stood for quality, integrity and professionalism in reinsurance

timeline.point: Huge, in his view aberrational, underwriting loss; business was badly underpriced.
timeline.quote: Our business was extremely underpriced, both domestically and internationally, a condition that is improving but not yet corrected.

timeline.point: Repricing under way; float cost should fall if no mega-catastrophe.
timeline.quote: Though our pricing is not fully corrected, we have significantly repriced business that was severely unprofitable or dropped it altogether.

timeline.point: Blames himself for letting General Re write business without a key safeguard before September 11.
timeline.quote: I allowed General Re to take on business without a safeguard I knew was important, and on September 11th, this error caught up with us.

timeline.point: Admits his earlier assurances of discipline were wrong; it broke all three underwriting rules.
timeline.quote: In the past I have assured you that General Re was underwriting with discipline – and I have been proven wrong.

timeline.point: Says Gen Re's culture had changed before the merger and it was grossly mispricing business.
timeline.quote: I was dead wrong. Gen Re's culture and practices had substantially changed and unbeknownst to management – and to me – the company was grossly mispricing its current business.

timeline.point: A further $1.31 billion charged in 2002 to correct earlier reserving errors.
timeline.quote: the company's 2002 underwriting results were penalized by an additional $1.31 billion that we recorded to correct the estimation mistakes of earlier years.

timeline.point: Declares the former problem child fixed under Brandon and Montross.
timeline.quote: That's behind us: Gen Re is fixed.

timeline.point: Confesses dithering over closing Gen Re Securities cost shareholders more than necessary.
timeline.quote: I'm sure I could have saved you $100 million or so, pre-tax, if I had acted more promptly to shut down Gen Re Securities.

timeline.point: Last report on the derivatives wind-down: cumulative pre-tax loss of $409 million.
timeline.quote: Our cumulative pre-tax loss from this operation totals $409 million, but only $5 million occurred in 2006.

timeline.point: Its old 'Tiffany' reputation outlived reality in 1998, a flaw he missed; luster now restored.
timeline.quote: This reputation, unfortunately, outlived its factual underpinnings, a flaw that I completely missed when I made the decision in 1998 to merge with General Re.

timeline.point: Calls the once-troubled unit a gleaming jewel after an outstanding underwriting year.
timeline.quote: Some years back this operation was troubled; now it is a gleaming jewel in our insurance crown.

timeline.point: Float better than cost-free under Montross; a headache turned treasure.
timeline.quote: In the first few years after we acquired it, General Re was a major headache. Now it's a treasure.

timeline.point: The early belief that he had made a huge mistake is long gone.
timeline.quote: That day is long gone. General Re is now a gem.

timeline.point: Still calls issuing 272,200 Berkshire shares to buy it a terrible mistake.
timeline.quote: It was, nevertheless, a terrible mistake on my part to issue 272,200 shares of Berkshire in buying General Re

overview: Consistent and confident, 1977-2024. Culture: extreme decentralization and autonomy for owner-minded managers who 'can't be hired' normally, a tiny headquarters, no budgets or committees, no mandatory retirement age, buying to keep, and shareholders treated as partners; he calls it self-propagating and 'rock-solid' (2014). Succession plans evolve: family control as a safeguard (1990, 1993); a board-chosen internal CEO from three or four candidates (2003-07); an investment succession plan (2006) filled by Todd Combs and Ted Weschler (2010-11); Howard Buffett proposed as non-executive chairman (2014); Ajit Jain and Greg Abel made vice chairmen (2018); Abel named the coming CEO (2023-24). He keeps about 99% of his net worth in Berkshire.

timeline.point: Decentralized trust lets Berkshire attract and keep talent that could not be hired normally.
timeline.quote: it enables us to attract and retain some extraordinarily talented individuals - people who simply can't be hired in the normal course of events

timeline.point: Defines his and Munger's two jobs: keep outstanding managers and allocate capital; stay out of managers' way.
timeline.quote: One is to attract and keep outstanding managers to run our various operations.

timeline.point: No mandatory retirement: superb managers are too scarce to discard for age.
timeline.quote: Superb managers are too scarce a resource to be discarded simply because a cake gets crowded with candles.

timeline.point: Succession plan: no stock would be sold at his death and like-minded owner and manager would follow.
timeline.quote: Both a controlling shareholder and a manager with philosophies similar to mine would follow me

timeline.point: Family members join the board to represent control but will not manage; 'prepared for the truck'.
timeline.quote: These family members will not be managers of the company in the future, but they will represent the controlling interest should anything happen to me.

timeline.point: Thirty years without a key manager leaving for another employer.
timeline.quote: Thinking back over the 1965-95 period, I can't recall that a single key manager has left Berkshire to join another employer.

timeline.point: Mandate to managers: run the business as if wholly owned, the family's only asset, unsellable for a century.
timeline.quote: Just run your business as if: 1) you own 100% of it; 2) it is the only asset in the world that you and your family have or will ever have

timeline.point: The board's main job is choosing his successor among four internal candidates who must keep the culture.
timeline.quote: The primary job of our directors is to select my successor, either upon my death or disability, or when I begin to lose my marbles.

timeline.point: Culture is ingrained, so operations would not miss a beat at his death; the board has agreed on a successor.
timeline.quote: The special Berkshire culture is deeply ingrained throughout our subsidiaries, and these operations won't miss a beat when I die.

timeline.point: Admits investment succession is less prepared; plans to hire a younger chief investment officer.
timeline.quote: Frankly, we are not as well-prepared on the investment side of our business.

timeline.point: Culture counts and self-propagates; he expects it to outlast himself and Munger.
timeline.quote: This culture grows stronger every year, and it will remain intact long after Charlie and I have left the scene.

timeline.point: Board is enthusiastic about the CEO successor; Combs and Weschler could run the whole portfolio later.
timeline.quote: When a transfer of responsibility is required, it will be seamless, and Berkshire's prospects will remain bright.

timeline.point: Proposes son Howard as non-executive chairman as a safety valve; successor CEO already identified.
timeline.quote: To further ensure continuation of our culture, I have suggested that my son, Howard, succeed me as a nonexecutive Chairman.

timeline.point: Warns the next CEO must fight arrogance, bureaucracy and complacency.
timeline.quote: My successor will need one other particular strength: the ability to fight off the ABCs of business decay, which are arrogance, bureaucracy and complacency.

timeline.point: Putting Jain over insurance and Abel over other operations made Berkshire better managed.
timeline.quote: Berkshire is now far better managed than when I alone was supervising operations.

timeline.point: Says Berkshire is fully prepared for his and Munger's departure.
timeline.quote: But Berkshire shareholders need not worry: Your company is 100% prepared for our departure.

timeline.point: Greg Abel runs non-insurance operations and is ready to be CEO.
timeline.quote: Greg Abel, who runs all non-insurance operations for Berkshire – and in all respects is ready to be CEO of Berkshire tomorrow

timeline.point: At 94, expects Abel to replace him soon and keep candid reporting to owners.
timeline.quote: At 94, it won't be long before Greg Abel replaces me as CEO and will be writing the annual letters.

overview: Buffett is consistently positive on branded consumer businesses across 1977-2023, in 46 letters. See's Candies (bought 1972 for $25 million) is his teaching case for pricing power and economic goodwill: $1.9 billion pre-tax by 2014 on $40 million of added capital, despite flat poundage he flagged in 1983-85 and failed expansion attempts. Coca-Cola (bought 1988-94 for $1.3 billion) and Gillette became his 'Inevitables' (1996), protected by a brand 'moat' (1993); Coke's dividend rose from $75 million to $704 million by 2022. Caveats he states: his costly Gillette preferred structure (1995), Gillette's value-destroying Duracell deal (2005), loss of focus as the main risk, online retail threats (2015) and the Kraft Heinz impairment (2018).

timeline.point: See's tripled pre-tax operating earnings since 1972 with little extra capital in a no-growth industry.
timeline.quote: pre-tax operating earnings have grown from $4.2 million to $12.6 million with little additional capital investment.

timeline.point: Branding protects economics in candy but not in commodity sugar.
timeline.quote: This works with candy bars (customers buy by brand name, not by asking for a “two-ounce candy bar”) but doesn’t work with sugar

timeline.point: See's economic goodwill grew even as accounting goodwill was amortized.
timeline.quote: while accounting Goodwill regularly decreased from the moment of purchase, economic Goodwill increased in irregular but very substantial fashion.

timeline.point: Candidly reports See's could not grow pounds sold.
timeline.quote: The other problem we face, as the table suggests, is our recent inability to achieve meaningful gains in pounds sold.

timeline.point: Explains the 1988-89 Coca-Cola purchase and praises Goizueta.
timeline.quote: With Roberto, the mesh of marketing and finance is perfect and the result is a shareholder's dream.

timeline.point: Calls Coca-Cola the world's most valuable franchise.
timeline.quote: the company increases our percentage ownership in what I regard to be the most valuable franchise in the world.

timeline.point: Key See's insight was its untapped pricing power.
timeline.quote: We saw that the business had untapped pricing power.

timeline.point: Brand might and distribution give Coke and Gillette a protective moat.
timeline.quote: The might of their brand names, the attributes of their products, and the strength of their distribution systems give them an enormous competitive advantage, setting up a protective moat around their economic castles.

timeline.point: Gillette is his best holding, but buying preferred rather than common was a costly mistake.
timeline.quote: Our best holding has been Gillette, which we told you from the start was a superior business.

timeline.point: Labels Coke and Gillette 'The Inevitables'; loss of focus is the key risk.
timeline.quote: Companies such as Coca-Cola and Gillette might well be labeled "The Inevitables."

timeline.point: Gillette's Duracell acquisition destroyed billions before Kilts repaired the company.
timeline.quote: Gillette’s acquisition of Duracell cost Gillette shareholders billions of dollars, a loss never made visible by conventional accounting.

timeline.point: See's is the prototype of a dream business.
timeline.quote: Let’s look at the prototype of a dream business, our own See’s Candy.

timeline.point: States the brand formula behind Coke, Wrigley and See's.
timeline.quote: “Buy commodities, sell brands” has long been a formula for business success.

timeline.point: See's taught him the value of powerful brands.
timeline.quote: through watching See’s in action, I gained a business education about the value of powerful brands that opened my eyes to many other profitable investments.

timeline.point: Heinz merged with Kraft; Berkshire owns about 27% at a $9.8 billion cost.
timeline.quote: Now we own 325.4 million shares of Kraft Heinz (about 27%) that cost us $9.8 billion.

timeline.point: Warns online retailing threatens some consumer brands.
timeline.quote: Online retailing threatens the business model of our retailers and certain of our consumer brands.

timeline.point: A $3.0 billion impairment came almost entirely from Kraft Heinz.
timeline.quote: a $3.0 billion non-cash loss from an impairment of intangible assets (arising almost entirely from our equity interest in Kraft Heinz)

timeline.point: Coke dividend grew from $75 million in 1994 to $704 million in 2022.
timeline.quote: The cash dividend we received from Coke in 1994 was $75 million. By 2022, the dividend had increased to $704 million.

timeline.point: Lesson from Coke: hold a truly wonderful business.
timeline.quote: When you find a truly wonderful business, stick with it.

overview: Buffett treated the 2005 hurricanes as a record loss that Berkshire could absorb but that changed its super-cat pricing. Katrina cost Berkshire about $2.5 billion and Rita and Wilma another $0.9 billion ($3.4 billion of hurricane losses), yet float was still costless in 2005 thanks to GEICO and other units. He openly asked whether climate or other changes had raised hurricane frequency, said he did not know, and, following Pascal's wager, would write mega-cat cover only at far higher prices with capped aggregate exposure. In 2006 the storms vanished and super-cat turned very profitable. Later letters use Katrina (about $3 billion, the largest loss to date) as the benchmark that a future 'Big One' will dwarf.

timeline.point: Katrina inflicted record losses on Berkshire and the industry; Berkshire estimated $2.5 billion from Katrina plus $0.9 billion from Rita and Wilma, yet the insurance business as a whole did well.
timeline.quote: We estimate our loss from Katrina at $2.5 billion – and her ugly sisters, Rita and Wilma, cost us an additional $.9 billion.

timeline.point: Despite $3.4 billion of hurricane losses as a mega-cat specialist, float was still costless in 2005 because of strong results elsewhere, especially GEICO.
timeline.quote: Nevertheless, our float was costless in 2005 because of the superb results we had in our other insurance activities, particularly at GEICO.

timeline.point: Seven Category 3+ storms hit in 2004-05 versus about 59 in the prior century; whether hurricane frequency or intensity has changed is an open question.
timeline.quote: It’s an open question whether atmospheric, oceanic or other causal factors have dramatically changed the frequency or intensity of hurricanes. Recent experience is worrisome.

timeline.point: Not knowing the answer, Berkshire follows Pascal's wager: mega-cat policies only at far higher prices and limited aggregate exposure, though it keeps the appetite to be the largest writer if prices are right.
timeline.quote: we’ve concluded that we should now write mega-cat policies only at prices far higher than prevailed last year

timeline.point: Katrina also showed why MidAmerican's diversified utilities are safer than a single utility, and why risks such as derivatives unwinds should be examined before the fact.
timeline.quote: A catastrophic event can render a single utility insolvent – witness what Katrina did to the local electric utility in New Orleans – no matter how conservative its debt policy.

timeline.point: In 2006 the hurricanes vanished and super-cat insurance swung from heavy losses to large profits, which Buffett called luck.
timeline.quote: After hammering us with hurricanes in 2004 and 2005 – storms that caused us to lose a bundle on super-cat insurance – she just vanished.

timeline.point: He warned that 2006's calm might precede devastating storms if 2004-05 signaled climate change, and that Katrina was far from a worst case.
timeline.quote: It’s naïve to think of Katrina as anything close to a worst-case event.

timeline.point: Katrina, about $3 billion, remained Berkshire's largest insurance loss and a reason to keep at least $20 billion of cash on hand.
timeline.quote: our largest to date having been about $3 billion from Katrina, the insurance industry’s most expensive catastrophe

timeline.point: Hurricane Sandy cost GEICO more than three times its Katrina loss, yet GEICO still earned an underwriting profit.
timeline.quote: Hurricane Sandy, which cost GEICO more than three times the loss it sustained from Katrina, the previous record-holder.

timeline.point: A future mega-catastrophe will dwarf Katrina and Michael; Berkshire will take big losses but look to add business the next day.
timeline.quote: A major catastrophe that will dwarf hurricanes Katrina and Michael will occur – perhaps tomorrow, perhaps many decades from now.

timeline.point: Repeated: handling such a loss will not strain Berkshire's resources.
timeline.quote: handling the loss will not come close to straining our resources, and we will be eager to add to our business the next day.

overview: In the 1989 and 1990 letters Buffett blamed the savings-and-loan and bank troubles on reckless lending and leverage: S&Ls bought zero-coupon and junk bonds with insured deposits and taxpayers will pay. He called banking 'no favorite of ours' because twenty-to-one leverage lets small mistakes destroy equity, and said banks followed each other into bad loans. Yet he used the chaotic market in bank stocks to buy 10% of Wells Fargo for $290 million, under five times after-tax earnings, judging that even severe California real-estate losses would only make the bank break even. He welcomed the near-50% price fall as a chance to buy more. In 1991 Wells Fargo did roughly break even, a result he had called a low-level possibility.

timeline.point: S&Ls used FSLIC-insured deposits to buy zero-coupon bonds and booked income never received; many are now in trouble and taxpayers will pay.
timeline.quote: In the many cases in which the loans will fail, the taxpayer will pick up the bill.

timeline.point: Banking is no favorite: at twenty times equity, small mistakes destroy equity, and many bankers imitated peers into bad loans.
timeline.quote: In their lending, many bankers played follow-the-leader with lemming-like zeal; now they are experiencing a lemming-like fate.

timeline.point: Because leverage magnifies management quality, Berkshire buys only well-managed banks at fair prices, never poorly run ones that look cheap.
timeline.quote: Instead, our only interest is in buying into well-managed banks at fair prices.

timeline.point: The flight from bank stocks let Berkshire buy 10% of Wells Fargo for $290 million at under five times after-tax earnings.
timeline.quote: Aided by their flight from bank stocks, we purchased our 10% interest in Wells Fargo for $290 million, less than five times after-tax earnings

timeline.point: He named the risks (earthquake, systemic panic, West Coast real-estate losses) but calculated that even heavy loan losses would only make Wells Fargo roughly break even.
timeline.quote: the market's major fear of the moment is that West Coast real estate values will tumble because of overbuilding and deliver huge losses to banks that have financed the expansion.

timeline.point: Fear of a New England-style California real-estate collapse halved Wells Fargo stock; Berkshire welcomed the decline to buy more.
timeline.quote: we welcomed the decline because it allowed us to pick up many more shares at the new, panic prices.

timeline.point: Debt-mania deals were financed partly by now-failed S&Ls, a cost borne by taxpayers.
timeline.quote: Many of the bonds that financed the purchase were sold to now-failed savings and loan associations; as a taxpayer, you are picking up the tab for this folly.

timeline.point: Wells Fargo produced a break-even result for Berkshire's look-through earnings in 1991, the outcome he had called unlikely.
timeline.quote: we had a break-even result from our interest in Wells Fargo (dividends we received from the company were offset by negative retained earnings).

overview: Berkshire bought H.H. Brown, the leading North American work-shoe maker, in mid-1991, largely because Frank Rooney agreed to stay as CEO. Buffett praised its unusually fine margins in a tough, import-dominated industry and its owner-like pay system (a $7,800 salary plus profits after a capital charge). Brown beat expectations (record profits in 1993, 35% above 1992), added Lowell Shoe and helped bring in Dexter. Shoe earnings fell cyclically in 1995 and import pressure grew; after Buffett's costly Dexter mistake, Dexter was placed under Brown's Rooney and Jim Issler, who turned it around by 2002. In 2009-2010 Brown raised profits on lower sales and then set sales and earnings records. His view of Brown itself stayed consistently positive.

timeline.point: Berkshire acquired H.H. Brown in 1991; by 1990 it had about 2,000 employees and earned about $25 million a year pre-tax.
timeline.quote: We made a sizable acquisition in 1991 - the H. H. Brown Company - and behind this business is an interesting history.

timeline.point: Much of Buffett's enthusiasm came from Frank Rooney continuing as CEO.
timeline.quote: Much of my enthusiasm for this purchase came from Frank's willingness to continue as CEO.

timeline.point: Brown leads North American work shoes with unusually fine margins in a tough industry where 85% of pairs are imported and most makers do poorly.
timeline.quote: it has a history of earning unusually fine margins on sales and assets

timeline.point: Its pay system, a small salary plus profits after a capital charge, makes managers stand in the shoes of owners.
timeline.quote: a designated percentage of the profits of the company after these are reduced by a charge for capital employed. These managers therefore truly stand in the shoes of owners.

timeline.point: Brown bought Lowell Shoe ($90 million of sales) at yearend, an add-on acquisition extending outstanding managers' domain. Brown earned $27.9 million pre-tax in 1992.
timeline.quote: At yearend, H. H. Brown purchased Lowell Shoe Company, a business with $90 million in sales that makes Nursemates

timeline.point: Brown exceeded high expectations, so Berkshire went on to buy Dexter Shoe; Brown's 1993 profits were a record, 35% above 1992.
