timeline.quote: Brown has been a real winner: Though we had high hopes to begin with, these expectations have been considerably exceeded

timeline.point: Dexter and Brown kept U.S. plants competitive against low-wage imports.
timeline.quote: someone forgot to tell this to the ingenious managements of Dexter and H. H. Brown and to their skilled labor forces

timeline.point: Shoe earnings were depressed industry-wide in 1995, but Berkshire's shoe units kept or widened their edge; he saw the drop as cyclical.
timeline.quote: you should view last year's figures as reflecting a cyclical problem, not a secular one.

timeline.point: With 93% of U.S. shoes imported, Dexter and Brown, the leading domestic makers, began sourcing more output abroad at significant severance costs.
timeline.quote: Nevertheless, in order to remain viable, we are sourcing more of our output internationally.

timeline.point: Shoes lost $46.2 million pre-tax in 2001 as Dexter's losses swamped Brown's and Justin's profits; Dexter was put under Brown's managers.
timeline.quote: We have now placed the Dexter operation – which is still substantial in size – under the management of Frank Rooney and Jim Issler at H.H. Brown.

timeline.point: Rooney and Issler turned Dexter around; shoes earned $24 million in 2002, a $70 million swing.
timeline.quote: Thanks to Frank Rooney and Jim Issler of H.H. Brown, the Dexter operation has been turned around.

timeline.point: Brown, under Jim Issler, was among the businesses whose profits improved in 2009 even as sales contracted.
timeline.quote: We had a number of companies at which profits improved even as sales contracted, always an exceptional managerial achievement.

timeline.point: Brown, best known for its Born brand, set a new record for sales and earnings in 2010.
timeline.quote: H. H. Brown, run by Jim Issler and best known for its Born brand, set a new record for sales and earnings

overview: HomeServices of America, a residential real estate brokerage, came to Berkshire with MidAmerican Energy in 2000. From 2001 he described it as the second-largest U.S. brokerage, built by Ron Peltier through acquisitions. He repeatedly called it highly cyclical yet viewed enthusiastically. Transaction volume grew from about $20 billion (2001) to $64 billion (2005); volume fell 9% and profits 50% in 2006, and 2008-2009 were terrible years for home sales, with only a modest profit in 2009, but Berkshire kept buying brokers at sensible prices. From 2012 it recovered, added the Prudential and Real Living franchises under the Berkshire name, and in 2017 bought Long and Foster, reaching 40,950 agents and $127 billion of sides.

timeline.point: MidAmerican also owns the second-largest U.S. residential brokerage, which handled about 106,000 transactions worth nearly $20 billion in 2001.
timeline.quote: At MidAmerican – this may surprise you – we also own the second-largest residential real estate brokerage business in the country.

timeline.point: Entered by accident but deliberately expanded; transactions doubled to $37 billion, mainly via acquisitions such as Prudential California Realty.
timeline.quote: On one side or the other (or both), we participated in $37 billion of transactions last year, up 100% from 2001.

timeline.point: Peltier raised revenues and profits dramatically; the business will always be cyclical, but Berkshire likes it.
timeline.quote: Though this business will always be cyclical, it’s one we like and in which we continue to have an appetite for sensible acquisitions.

timeline.point: Volume reached $48.6 billion in 2003; highly cyclical, yet viewed enthusiastically under an exceptional manager.
timeline.quote: Unlike our utility operations, this business is highly cyclical, but nevertheless one we view enthusiastically.

timeline.point: Called it a gem; 19,200 agents took part in $64 billion of transactions, up 6.5%, and the cooling market should bring acquisition chances.
timeline.quote: Somewhat incongruously, MidAmerican owns the second largest real estate brokerage firm in the U.S. And it’s a gem.

timeline.point: As housing turned, volume fell 9% to $58 billion and profits fell 50%, though acquisitions continued.
timeline.quote: Despite HomeServices’ purchase of two operations last year, the company’s overall volume fell 9% to $58 billion, and profits fell 50%.

timeline.point: 2008 was a terrible year for home sales and 2009 looked no better; Berkshire would still buy quality brokers at sensible prices.
timeline.quote: Last year was a terrible year for home sales, and 2009 looks no better.

timeline.point: Despite another terrible year, HomeServices earned a modest sum and bought a Chicago firm.
timeline.quote: Though last year was again a terrible year for home sales, HomeServices earned a modest sum.

timeline.point: Home-sale volume rose 33% to $42 billion; it bought 67% of the Prudential and Real Living franchisors, and earnings should rise as housing strengthens.
timeline.quote: Now, as the housing market continues to strengthen, we expect earnings to rise significantly.

timeline.point: Four acquisitions including Fox & Roach lifted agents 38% to 22,114; franchisees are being rebranded Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices.
timeline.quote: HomeServices now has 22,114 agents (listed by geography on page 112), up 38% from 2012.

timeline.point: With 38 realty companies and 29,000+ agents, owned realtors took part in $86 billion of sides; Berkshire is lucky it came with MidAmerican.
timeline.quote: But it came with our purchase of MidAmerican (now BHE) in 1999 – and we are lucky that it did.

timeline.point: Growth exploded with Long and Foster, Houlihan Lawrence and Gloria Nilson: 40,950 agents and $127 billion of sides, yet only about 3% of the U.S. market.
timeline.quote: Given sensible prices, we will keep adding brokers in this most fundamental of businesses.

overview: Buffett called the 1983 purchase of Nebraska Furniture Mart (90% per the 1983 letter, later 80%; $55 million, no audit) 'the ideal business'. His praise never wavered: rock-bottom operating costs (16.5% of sales vs. 35.6% at Levitz in 1984; 15% in 1990), low prices and a widening trade area. Single-store sales grew from $100 million (1983) to $300 million (1998). Mrs. B quit in 1989 over the carpet department and returned in 1992. NFM opened a Kansas City store in 2003; Omaha and Kansas City each sold about $400 million in 2007 and $450 million by 2013, earnings in 2011 were over ten times 1983 and its three stores set sales records in 2020.

timeline.point: Buying a majority of NFM was the high point of 1983; its one store sold over $100 million, more than all Omaha competitors combined.
timeline.quote: It’s the ideal business - one built upon exceptional value to the customer that in turn translates into exceptional economics for its owners.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought 90%, leaving 10% with family managers and optioning 10% to young family managers.
timeline.quote: We purchased 90% of the business - leaving 10% with members of the family who are involved in management

timeline.point: NFM's gross margin was about half of Levitz's 44.4%, and operating expenses about 16.5% of sales versus 35.6%.
timeline.quote: operating expenses (payroll, occupancy, advertising, etc.) are about 16.5% of sales versus 35.6% at Levitz.

timeline.point: Bought for a $55 million check with no audit, inventory or title checks, on Mrs. B's word.
timeline.quote: We gave Mrs. B a check for $55 million and she gave us her word.

timeline.point: NFM, See's and the Buffalo News earned $72 million pre-tax versus $8 million fifteen years earlier, with only about $40 million more capital, showing economic goodwill.
timeline.quote: although annual earnings are now $64 million greater, the businesses require only about $40 million more in invested capital to operate than was the case then.

timeline.point: Sales rose 10.2% to $132 million versus $44 million ten years earlier, as its territory widened.
timeline.quote: In 1986 net sales increased 10.2% to $132 million.

timeline.point: Sales of $142.6 million, up 8%; customers saved about $30 million by buying at NFM.
timeline.quote: Net sales of NFM were $142.6 million in 1987, up 8% from 1986.

timeline.point: Record sales and excellent earnings, but Mrs. B quit after a dispute over the carpet department; Buffett sided with the family.
timeline.quote: The Nebraska Furniture Mart had record sales and excellent earnings in 1989, but there was one sad note.

timeline.point: Sales of $159 million, up 4%; operating costs of 15% versus about 40% at Levitz let it price below all competitors.
timeline.quote: operating costs are rock-bottom - 15% in 1990 against about 40% for Levitz, the country's largest furniture retailer

timeline.point: Mrs. B sold her building and land to NFM, which added furniture space alongside her carpet business.
timeline.quote: I have always been a fan of hers, whether she was a partner or a competitor. But believe me, partner is better.

timeline.point: 1993 sales reached $200 million, far more than any other U.S. home-furnishings store.
timeline.quote: Last year the store had sales of $200 million, a larger amount by far than that recorded by any other home furnishings store in the United States.

timeline.point: NFM led, via the Blumkins, to R.C. Willey (1995), Star Furniture (1997) and Jordan's.
timeline.quote: Not only did Berkshire acquire three outstanding retailers; these deals also allowed me to become friends with some of the finest people you will ever meet.

timeline.point: NFM's new Kansas City store was hugely successful, probably the country's largest-volume home-furnishings store.
timeline.quote: Indeed, we believe the Kansas City store is the country’s largest-volume home-furnishings store.

timeline.point: Record earnings in a disastrous furniture year; Omaha and Kansas City each sold about $400 million.
timeline.quote: In a disastrous year for many furniture retailers, sales at Kansas City increased 8%, while in Omaha the gain was 6%.

timeline.point: Record earnings, more than ten times 1983; NFM bought 433 acres north of Dallas for what should be the highest-volume store.
timeline.quote: Nebraska Furniture Mart (80% owned) set an earnings record in 2011, netting more than ten times what it did in 1983, when we acquired our stake.

timeline.point: Omaha and Kansas City each do about $450 million a year; the 1.8 million sq ft Texas store should beat them, though it hardly moves Berkshire's needle.
timeline.quote: it takes more than a new store to move the needle on Berkshire’s $225 billion equity base.

timeline.point: NFM, worth $60 million when 80% was bought in 1983, now owns the three largest U.S. home-furnishings stores, each with record 2020 sales despite COVID closures.
timeline.quote: NFM now owns the three largest home-furnishings stores in the U.S. Each set a sales record in 2020

overview: Berkshire bought Coca-Cola from 1988, about $1 billion by 1989 and 400 million split-adjusted shares for $1.3 billion by 1994, and never sold. Buffett called it 'the most valuable franchise in the world', and praised Coke's moat, global share, low business risk and constant fundamentals ('The Inevitables'). He also warned that the stock can diverge from the business: the 1991 double-dip re-rating could not recur, earnings outran the price in 1991-93, and the holding fell from $13.4 billion (1998) to $8.1 billion (2005). From 2011 he stressed Coke's buybacks and retained earnings within the 'Big Four' and its dividend, rising every year from $75 million (1994) to $704 million (2022).

timeline.point: Major purchases of Coca-Cola in 1988 (14.2 million shares, $593 million cost), intended as a very long-term holding.
timeline.quote: when we own portions of outstanding businesses with outstanding managements, our favorite holding period is forever.

timeline.point: Holding rose to 23.35 million shares; Buffett said Coke had become a new company under Goizueta in 1981 and admitted he should have bought far earlier.
timeline.quote: Of course, we should have started buying Coke much earlier, soon after Roberto and Don began running things.

timeline.point: Coke's buybacks from retained earnings raise Berkshire's ownership more tax-efficiently than dividends would.
timeline.quote: the company increases our percentage ownership in what I regard to be the most valuable franchise in the world.

timeline.point: A sharp P/E rise in Coke and Gillette produced most of 1991's net-worth gain; such re-rating cannot recur annually.
timeline.quote: In effect, we got a double-dip benefit, delivered partly by the excellent earnings growth and even more so by the market's reappraisal of these stocks.

timeline.point: From 1991 to 1993 Coke's operating EPS rose 38% while its stock rose only 11%; long-run earnings are what count.
timeline.quote: From 1991 to 1993, Coke and Gillette increased their annual operating earnings per share by 38% and 37% respectively, but their market prices moved up only 11% and 6%.

timeline.point: Coke (about 44% of world soft drinks) carries far less long-term business risk than most companies; its moat makes beta a poor risk measure.
timeline.quote: The might of their brand names, the attributes of their products, and the strength of their distribution systems give them an enormous competitive advantage

timeline.point: Berkshire enlarged its Coke stake in 1994 to 100 million shares (7.8%), worth nearly $200 million of soft-drink earnings.
timeline.quote: Last year we went that direction by enlarging our holdings in Coca-Cola and American Express.

timeline.point: Coke and Gillette are 'The Inevitables', certain to dominate worldwide for an investment lifetime; the main risk is managers losing focus.
timeline.quote: no sensible observer - not even these companies' most vigorous competitors, assuming they are assessing the matter honestly - questions that Coke and Gillette will dominate their fields worldwide for an investment lifetime.

timeline.point: Past buybacks at low prices by Coke and others helped Berkshire more than today's at loftier prices.
timeline.quote: the repurchases that Coca-Cola, The Washington Post and Wells Fargo made in past years at very low prices benefitted Berkshire far more than do today's repurchases

timeline.point: He defended his independence as a Coke director: Berkshire's $8 billion Coke stake aligns him with Coke's owners.
timeline.quote: elementary arithmetic should make it clear that my heart and mind belong to the owners of Coke, not to its management.

timeline.point: The Coke holding rose from $1 billion to $13.4 billion by 1998 and then fell to $8.1 billion, unrealized moves outside earnings.
timeline.quote: our Coca-Cola holdings went from $1 billion in value early on to $13.4 billion at yearend 1998 and have since declined to $8.1 billion

timeline.point: Coke raised its dividend every year since 1995; $376 million expected in 2011, likely to double within ten years.
timeline.quote: Every year since, Coke has increased its dividend.

timeline.point: Coke's buybacks raised Berkshire's stake from 8.8% to 8.9%; Berkshire prefers part of a wonderful business to all of a so-so one.
timeline.quote: stock repurchases at Coca-Cola and American Express raised our percentage ownership. Our equity in Coca-Cola grew from 8.8% to 8.9%

timeline.point: The 400 million shares cost $1.3 billion; the dividend grew from $75 million (1994) to $704 million (2022) and the stake was worth $25 billion.
timeline.quote: The cash dividend we received from Coke in 1994 was $75 million. By 2022, the dividend had increased to $704 million.

timeline.point: No Coke shares bought or sold for over two decades; earnings and dividends rose again. Lesson: stick with a wonderful business.
timeline.quote: When you find a truly wonderful business, stick with it. Patience pays, and one wonderful business can offset the many mediocre decisions that are inevitable.

timeline.point: Coke remains among the household-name partial holdings, together valued at $272 billion, with very high returns on tangible equity.
timeline.quote: we own a small percentage of a dozen or so very large and highly profitable businesses with household names such as Apple, American Express, Coca-Cola and Moody’s.

overview: Buffett treats taxes as a permanent drag on returns, not a grievance. In 1979-81 he argued that inflation plus taxes (an 'investor's misery index') can leave owners with no real return. He criticised the 1986 Tax Reform Act as net negative for Berkshire, especially for insurers,. He explained deferred tax on unrealized gains as an interest-free Treasury loan, stressed the tax edge of owning 80%+ of a business, and repeatedly noted Berkshire's after-tax handicap versus the pre-tax S&P 500. From 1993 he called Berkshire's large tax payments fitting, criticised 2003 corporate tax breaks, counted the 2017 cut as a $29 billion gain, and hailed record payments ($26.8 billion in 2024).

timeline.point: Inflation plus the tax cost of extracting earnings forms an 'investor's misery index'; when it exceeds return on equity, owners lose purchasing power.
timeline.quote: When this index exceeds the rate of return earned on equity by the business, the investor’s purchasing power (real capital) shrinks even though he consumes nothing at all.

timeline.point: At current inflation, taxable individuals should expect no real long-term return from the average corporation.
timeline.quote: The average return on equity of corporations is fully offset by the combination of the implicit tax on capital levied by inflation and the explicit taxes levied both on dividends and gains

timeline.point: With tax-exempt bonds at 14%, a typical business earning 14% on equity is worth perhaps fifty cents on the dollar to a 50%-bracket owner.
timeline.quote: a typical American business is no longer worth one hundred cents on the dollar to owners who are individuals.

timeline.point: Proportionate redemptions (GEICO, General Foods) were taxed as dividends at the 6.9% intercorporate rate, a corporate tax advantage.
timeline.quote: the $21 million we received was taxed at only the 6.9% inter-corporate dividend rate

timeline.point: The 1986 Tax Reform Act is net negative: slower value growth, and shareholders keep 72 cents per dollar of gain instead of 80.
timeline.quote: Although we find much to praise in the Act, the net financial effect for Berkshire is negative

timeline.point: Who keeps a corporate tax cut depends on franchise strength and regulation; Berkshire's strong-franchise businesses largely keep it.
timeline.quote: What determines the outcome is the strength of the corporation’s business franchise and whether the profitability of that franchise is regulated.

timeline.point: He predicted the scheduled 1988 rates were unrealistic and would bring higher taxes or inflation within about five years.
timeline.quote: within, say, five years - either higher tax rates or higher inflation rates are almost certain to materialize.

timeline.point: Owning partial positions costs extra tax; the same business result can be up to 50% better from an 80%-or-more holding.
timeline.quote: a given business result can now deliver Berkshire financial results that are as much as 50% better if they come from an 80%-or-greater holding rather than from a lesser holding.

timeline.point: Deferred tax on unrealized gains (over $1.1 billion) is like an interest-free Treasury loan; the tax law gives buy-and-hold a mathematical edge.
timeline.quote: In economic terms, the liability resembles an interest-free loan from the U.S. Treasury that comes due only at our election

timeline.point: Berkshire's returns bear corporate tax while the S&P is pre-tax: an 18% index gain gives a corporate holder well under 13%.
timeline.quote: This is a structural disadvantage we simply have to live with; there is no antidote

timeline.point: Berkshire paid about $390 million of federal tax for 1993, which he and Munger accept as partly redressing market rewards.
timeline.quote: Speaking for our own shares, Charlie and I have absolutely no complaint about these taxes.

timeline.point: Berkshire paid $860 million in 1996 taxes; he called large payments fitting because Berkshire prospers in America.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I believe that large tax payments by Berkshire are entirely fitting.

timeline.point: Corporate capital gains are taxed at 35%, 75% more than an individual's rate; insurers' dividend exclusion is 59.5%, not 70%.
timeline.quote: This means that Berkshire’s tax on a long-term capital gain is fully 75% higher than what an individual would pay on an identical gain.

timeline.point: With a marketable stake the government is a partner twice (corporate tax plus dividend or gains tax), with an 80%-owned business only once.
timeline.quote: the government is our “partner” twice when we own part of a business through a stock investment, but only once when we own at least 80%.

timeline.point: Berkshire paid $3.3 billion, 2.5% of U.S. corporate tax, while many large firms pay far below 35%; he criticised the corporate tax breaks.
timeline.quote: If class warfare is being waged in America, my class is clearly winning.

timeline.point: Dividends are tax-inferior to shareholders selling shares, since all dividend cash is taxed but only the gain on a sale.
timeline.quote: Under the dividend program, all of the cash received by shareholders each year is taxed whereas the sell-off program results in tax on only the gain portion of the cash receipts.

timeline.point: Inside Berkshire, capital moves between businesses without taxes, and utilities can use tax credits thanks to other units' taxable income.
timeline.quote: At Berkshire, we can – without incurring taxes or much in the way of other costs – move huge sums from businesses that have limited opportunities

timeline.point: Of 2017's $65.3 billion net-worth gain, $29 billion came from the December tax-law rewrite.
timeline.quote: The remaining $29 billion was delivered to us in December when Congress rewrote the U.S. Tax Code.

timeline.point: Cutting the rate from 35% to 21% returned 14/35ths of the Treasury's 'AA shares' and materially raised intrinsic value.
timeline.quote: Last year, however, 40% of the government’s “ownership” (14/35ths) was returned to Berkshire – free of charge – when the corporate tax rate was reduced to 21%.

timeline.point: Berkshire paid $32 billion of federal income tax over 2012-21 and expects to pay much more, owing America no less.
timeline.quote: At Berkshire we hope and expect to pay much more in taxes during the next decade. We owe the country no less

timeline.point: Berkshire paid $26.8 billion to the IRS in 2024, about 5% of all U.S. corporate tax, a record for any company.
timeline.quote: Berkshire last year made four payments to the IRS that totaled $26.8 billion. That’s about 5% of what all of corporate America paid.

overview: Across 1977-2024 Buffett applied one consistent rule: retain earnings only if each dollar retained creates at least a dollar of market value, otherwise pay out or repurchase, and buy back stock only below intrinsic value. Berkshire paid one dividend (1967) and retained everything, which he credits for its growth. He valued investees' retained earnings and buybacks above dividends (look-through earnings, Coke, the Big Four) and redeployed See's-type surplus cash tax-free. He criticised CEOs' poor allocation, empire-building and options that reward withheld earnings. His practice evolved: textiles' futility in the 1980s, acceptance of capital-intensive utilities and rail from 2009, the 2012 sell-off-versus-dividend case, and a 2014 warning that excess earnings may eventually need distributing.

timeline.point: Retain where reinvestment returns are attractive; otherwise pay out or repurchase shares.
timeline.quote: then earnings should be paid out or used to repurchase shares - often by far the most attractive option for capital utilization.

timeline.point: Retained earnings are valued by their use, regardless of ownership share or accounting.
timeline.quote: the value of those retained earnings is determined by the use to which they are put and the subsequent level of earnings produced by that usage.

timeline.point: The one valid reason for retention is a dollar of market value created per dollar retained; Berkshire meets it, so pays nothing.
timeline.quote: for every dollar retained by the corporation, at least one dollar of market value will be created for owners.

timeline.point: Fixed-price options reward managers merely for retaining earnings.
timeline.quote: they have gained in value simply because management retained earnings, not because it did well with the capital in its hands.

timeline.point: Many CEOs lack capital-allocation skill despite deploying most of their firms' capital.
timeline.quote: The lack of skill that many CEOs have at capital allocation is no small matter

timeline.point: Capital allocation, including buybacks, must raise per-share intrinsic value.
timeline.quote: it's vital that they act in ways that increase per-share intrinsic value and avoid moves that decrease it.

timeline.point: Investees' undistributed earnings are more valuable than dividends because they reinvest at high returns.
timeline.quote: we regard the undistributed earnings of investees as more valuable to us than the portion paid out.

timeline.point: He graded his own 1999 capital allocation a D.
timeline.quote: My “one subject” is capital allocation, and my grade for 1999 most assuredly is a D.

timeline.point: Earnings of great businesses that can't reinvest internally should buy businesses elsewhere.
timeline.quote: There’s no rule that you have to invest money where you’ve earned it.

timeline.point: Shift: Berkshire now accepts capital-intensive businesses with decent incremental returns.
timeline.quote: we are today quite willing to enter businesses that regularly require large capital expenditures.

timeline.point: Buybacks only at a material discount to intrinsic value.
timeline.quote: The first law of capital allocation – whether the money is slated for acquisitions or share repurchases – is that what is smart at one price is dumb at another.

timeline.point: A sell-off policy beats dividends for owners in both cash and value.
timeline.quote: you would have both more cash to spend annually and more capital value.

timeline.point: Eventually excess earnings may need to be distributed via dividends or repurchases.
timeline.quote: Berkshire’s earnings and capital resources will reach a level that will not allow management to intelligently reinvest all of the company’s earnings.

timeline.point: A 100% payout would have left Berkshire with its 1965 $22 million.
timeline.quote: Had we instead followed a 100% payout policy, we would still be working with the $22 million with which we began fiscal 1965.

timeline.point: Investees' retained earnings delivered equal or greater capital gains over 56 years.
timeline.quote: Over our 56-year tenure, that expectation has been met.

timeline.point: Berkshire pays no dividends; repurchases are fully discretionary.
timeline.quote: Berkshire does not currently pay dividends, and its share repurchases are 100% discretionary.

timeline.point: One dividend in 60 years; continuous reinvestment built Berkshire.
timeline.quote: For sixty years, Berkshire shareholders endorsed continuous reinvestment and that enabled the company to build its taxable income.

overview: From 1983 Buffett says per-share intrinsic value, the discounted cash that can be taken out of a business, is what counts; book value only records what was put in. In 1964 Berkshire's $19.46 book value overstated intrinsic value (textile assets); by 1983 intrinsic value exceeded book, and the gap kept widening through economic goodwill, float, GEICO and businesses carried far below worth. For decades he used book value as a conservative proxy, set a 15% intrinsic-value growth goal (1989-1994), and from 1995 gave two quantitative pillars, per-share investments and operating earnings. Repurchase limits were tied to book (110% in 2011, 120% from 2012). In 2018 he dropped book value as the headline metric because it had lost relevance.
stance_basis: intrinsic value called the measure that counts in every discussion 1983-2022; book value endorsed as a useful proxy 1983-2016, then declared to have lost relevance and dropped in 2018

timeline.point: Book value grew from $19.46 (1964) to $335.85, 20.5% a year; the 1964 figure overstated intrinsic value.
timeline.quote: It probably also is fair to say that the quoted book value in 1964 somewhat overstated the intrinsic value of the enterprise

timeline.point: Share-issuance rule: Berkshire will not issue shares unless it receives as much intrinsic value as it gives.
timeline.quote: we will not issue shares unless we receive as much intrinsic business value as we give.

timeline.point: Defines the two terms: book value is an accounting input measure, intrinsic value discounted future cash output.
timeline.quote: Book value tells you what has been put in; intrinsic business value estimates what can be taken out.

timeline.point: Reports book value as a conservative proxy for intrinsic value, which now considerably exceeds book because of economic goodwill.
timeline.quote: it is a conservative but reasonably adequate proxy for growth in intrinsic business value - the measurement that really counts.

timeline.point: Business value probably grew faster than book; estimates are soft, observers could differ by more than 10%.
timeline.quote: business value is a soft number

timeline.point: Defines intrinsic value as all future cash flows discounted at prevailing interest rates.
timeline.quote: taking all future cash flows of a business - in and out - and discounting them at prevailing interest rates.

timeline.point: Sets the 15% goal for annual growth in intrinsic value; look-through earnings must grow at about that pace.
timeline.quote: Charlie Munger, Berkshire's Vice Chairman, and I have set a goal of attaining a 15% average annual increase in Berkshire's intrinsic value.

timeline.point: Uses the college-education analogy and Scott Fetzer: earnings doubled while carrying value fell below half its purchase level.
timeline.quote: In all cases, what is clear is that book value is meaningless as an indicator of intrinsic value.

timeline.point: Introduces a table of two value indices: per-share investments and per-share operating earnings excluding investment income.
timeline.quote: Last year, for the first time, we supplied you with a table that Charlie and I believe will help anyone trying to estimate Berkshire's intrinsic value.

timeline.point: Book value rose 48.3% mainly from share issuance at a premium; intrinsic value grew much less but still far exceeds book.
timeline.quote: it’s the per-share gain in intrinsic value that counts rather than the per-share gain in book value.

timeline.point: Goodwill amortization widens the gap; See's and Buffalo News are worth 15-20 times their carrying value.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I can assure you that it far exceeds our $57.8 billion book value.

timeline.point: Intrinsic value is all-important but imprecise; Berkshire's stable earnings help, its 68 businesses complicate.
timeline.quote: calculations of intrinsic value, though all-important, are necessarily imprecise and often seriously wrong.

timeline.point: Adds a third, qualitative element: how well retained earnings will be redeployed.
timeline.quote: Some companies will turn these retained dollars into fifty-cent pieces, others into two-dollar bills.

timeline.point: Repurchases at the 110%-of-book limit clearly raise per-share intrinsic value; float's true liability is far below its accounting liability.
timeline.quote: At our limit price of 110% of book value, repurchases clearly increase Berkshire’s per-share intrinsic value.

timeline.point: Raises the repurchase limit to 120% of book after a block became available at about 116%.
timeline.quote: we increased the limit to 120% in December when a large block became available at about 116% of book value.

timeline.point: The gap has widened as owned businesses are never revalued upward; intrinsic value gain about equals the 1,826,163% market gain.
timeline.quote: Consequently, the gap between Berkshire’s intrinsic value and its book value has materially widened.

timeline.point: Asymmetric accounting, writing down losers but never writing up winners, makes intrinsic value far exceed book.
timeline.quote: the large – and growing – unrecorded gains at our winners produce an intrinsic value for Berkshire’s shares that far exceeds their book value.

timeline.point: Drops book value from the letter's opening: it has lost relevance as operating businesses and buybacks above book grow.
timeline.quote: is a metric that has lost the relevance it once had.

timeline.point: Suggests estimating intrinsic value by summing four asset 'groves' minus taxes on securities gains.
timeline.quote: I believe Berkshire’s intrinsic value can be approximated by summing the values of our four asset-laden groves

timeline.point: Retained earnings and repurchasing about 5% of shares increased per-share intrinsic value despite no large acquisition.
timeline.quote: We did, though, increase Berkshire’s per-share intrinsic value by both retaining earnings and repurchasing about 5% of our shares.

overview: Berkshire agreed in 1999 to buy about 76% of MidAmerican Energy for about $2 billion cash, structured around PUHCA's 9.9% voting limit, with partners Walter Scott, David Sokol and Greg Abel. Buffett praised it every year to 2022: acquisitions (Kern River and Northern Natural 2002, PacifiCorp 2006, NV Energy 2013), full reinvestment with no dividends, wind and solar leadership, low Iowa rates, and earnings growing from $122 million in 2000 to a record $4 billion in 2021. Renamed BHE in 2014, it was one of the 'Powerhouse Five'. In 2023 he called its results a severe disappointment: wildfire losses and a broken regulatory pact in some states, a risk he failed to anticipate. In 2024 Berkshire bought the rest.
stance_basis: praised in every letter 1999-2022 (managers, reinvestment, rates, renewables); in 2023 a 'severe earnings disappointment' and a 'costly mistake' over regulatory and wildfire risk; 2024 improved but 'much left to accomplish'

timeline.point: Agrees to invest about $2 billion for about 76% of MidAmerican's equity but under 10% of votes because of PUHCA; hints at more utility deals.
timeline.quote: Though there are many regulatory constraints in the utility industry, it’s possible that we will make additional commitments in the field. If we do, the amounts involved could be large.

timeline.point: MEHC buys the Kern River and Northern Natural pipelines; it is Berkshire's largest non-insurance earnings stream.
timeline.quote: Already it has $18 billion of assets and delivers our largest stream of non-insurance earnings. It could well grow to be huge.

timeline.point: MidAmerican writes off its zinc recovery project at its California geothermal operations.
timeline.quote: In September, we threw in the towel.

timeline.point: Agrees to buy PacifiCorp; utilities give fair, not outsized, returns on large sums. PUHCA repeal allows consolidation.
timeline.quote: You can’t expect to earn outsized profits in regulated utilities, but the industry offers owners the opportunity to deploy large sums at fair returns

timeline.point: Recounts paying $35.05 a share in 1999; 2007 normalized earnings were about $15.01 a share.
timeline.quote: And yes, I’m glad I wilted and offered the extra nickel.

timeline.point: Record earnings; Iowa prices unchanged since purchase while wind reached almost 20% of capacity. Constellation breakup fee and profit added $1.09 billion.
timeline.quote: the company has kept electric prices unchanged since our purchase and has promised to hold them steady through 2013.

timeline.point: Describes the 'social compact' with regulators: invest heavily and earn a fair return. No dividends in ten years.
timeline.quote: We shouldn’t expect our regulators to live up to their end of the bargain unless we live up to ours.

timeline.point: Northern Natural rose from last (43 of 43) to second among pipelines; $5.4 billion invested or committed to wind.
timeline.quote: We can make this sort of investment because MidAmerican retains all of its earnings

timeline.point: MidAmerican buys NV Energy for $5.6 billion; ranks first in a customer-satisfaction poll of 52 holding companies.
timeline.quote: NV Energy will not be MidAmerican’s last major acquisition.

timeline.point: Renamed BHE; its utilities can use tax credits only because Berkshire produces large taxable income elsewhere.
timeline.quote: That gives Berkshire Hathaway Energy a major advantage over most public-utility companies in developing wind and solar projects.

timeline.point: Iowa retail rate 6.8¢ per kWh versus a 10.4¢ national average; efficiency let it operate 16 years without a rate increase.
timeline.quote: Our rock-bottom prices add up to real money for paycheck-strapped customers.

timeline.point: Calls the 2000 cash purchase of MidAmerican atonement for the share-financed General Re deal.
timeline.quote: Early in 2000, I atoned for that folly by buying 76% (since grown to 90%) of MidAmerican Energy

timeline.point: After 20 years BHE has retained $28 billion and never paid Berkshire a dividend; it is ready for $100 billion-plus projects.
timeline.quote: Our view: The more we can invest, the more we like it.

timeline.point: BHE ranks fourth among Berkshire's most valuable assets; earnings grew from $122 million to $3.4 billion in 21 years.
timeline.quote: What we have here is a very unusual utility business

timeline.point: Record $4 billion of earnings, up more than 30-fold since 2000; a leader in wind, solar and transmission.
timeline.quote: BHE, our final Giant, earned a record $4 billion in 2021.

timeline.point: Severe earnings disappointment: some states' regulatory climate and forest-fire losses threaten utility profitability.
timeline.quote: Our second and even more severe earnings disappointment last year occurred at BHE.

timeline.point: Admits he and his BHE partners did not anticipate adverse regulatory returns.
timeline.quote: I did not anticipate or even consider the adverse developments in regulatory returns

timeline.point: Berkshire raises its ownership from about 92% to 100% for roughly $3.9 billion; BHE operating earnings $3.73 billion vs $2.33 billion in 2023.
timeline.quote: Late in the year we increased our ownership of the utility operation from about 92% to 100%

overview: Buffett never forecasts the market but judges its price level, and his judgment moved with prices. In 1978 stocks were bargains ('a marvelous period for the value-oriented equity buyer'). From 1985 to 1989 he found no undervalued equities and warned of euphoria. In 1992 and 1999-2001 he predicted far lower future returns; he called the late-1990s market a bubble and later faulted himself for not selling. After 2002 he still found few cheap stocks. In 2008-2013 he urged buying on fear. In 2021 low rates kept prices high, and in 2023 he described casino-like markets. Throughout, he wants Berkshire's price near intrinsic value and treats Mr. Market's swings as an opportunity, not a guide.
stance_basis: positive on prices in the late 1970s (1977-1978) and the 2008 panic; negative on overvaluation in 1985-1989, 1996-2002 and 2021-2023; neutral 'no bargains' between

timeline.point: Insurance subsidiaries' equities rose about $112 million in three years while the Dow fell from 852 to 805; pension managers shunned stocks.
timeline.quote: It was a marvelous period for the value-oriented equity buyer.

timeline.point: With high interest rates, a typical American business is worth less than book to individual owners; equity capital adds no value for them.
timeline.quote: American equity capital, in aggregate, produces no value-added for individual investors.

timeline.point: Needs a moderately priced market; recalls 1972 when good businesses carried absurd prices.
timeline.quote: We need a moderately-priced stock market to assist us in this endeavor.

timeline.point: Can no longer find significantly undervalued equities, unlike a decade earlier when the only question was which bargain to choose.
timeline.quote: Today we cannot find significantly-undervalued equities to purchase for our insurance company portfolios.

timeline.point: Euphoria prevails; stocks cannot outperform the businesses they own forever.
timeline.quote: Bull markets can obscure mathematical laws, but they cannot repeal them.

timeline.point: Introduces Graham's Mr. Market: his quotes serve you but must not guide you.
timeline.quote: Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you.

timeline.point: The October crash, worsened by portfolio insurance, shows volatility helps a disciplined investor.
timeline.quote: Such markets are ideal for any investor - small or large - so long as he sticks to his investment knitting.

timeline.point: Major holdings priced high relative to intrinsic value and vulnerable to a market decline.
timeline.quote: While those prices may not yet cause nosebleeds, they are clearly vulnerable to a general market decline.

timeline.point: Predicts S&P returns in the next decade will be far below the past decade's.
timeline.quote: stocks cannot forever overperform their underlying businesses

timeline.point: Overpayment risk may now be quite high for virtually all stocks, even 'The Inevitables'.
timeline.quote: The overpayment risk surfaces periodically and, in our opinion, may now be quite high for the purchasers of virtually all stocks

timeline.point: Stocks not overvalued if rates and returns on equity hold, but the cheery consensus has eroded the margin of safety.
timeline.quote: Today's price levels, though, have materially eroded the "margin of safety" that Ben Graham identified as the cornerstone of intelligent investing.

timeline.point: With profits tied to roughly 5% nominal GDP growth, investors are wildly optimistic; a severe adjustment is likely.
timeline.quote: If investor expectations become more realistic — and they almost certainly will — the market adjustment is apt to be severe

timeline.point: Investors expected 19% a year; bubble companies were built to make money off investors.
timeline.quote: But a pin lies in wait for every bubble.

timeline.point: Expects only moderate returns; the Great Bubble ended March 10, 2000.
timeline.quote: today’s equity prices presage only moderate returns for investors.

timeline.point: After three years of falling prices, few stocks even mildly interest him.
timeline.quote: That dismal fact is testimony to the insanity of valuations reached during The Great Bubble.

timeline.point: Criticizes himself for only clucking about nose-bleed valuations in the bubble instead of selling.
timeline.quote: I talked when I should have walked.

timeline.point: Risk went from underpriced to overpriced; late-2008 Treasuries were a bubble.
timeline.quote: The investment world has gone from underpricing risk to overpricing it.

timeline.point: Bubbles in Internet stocks, houses and now gold come from bandwagon buying.
timeline.quote: But bubbles blown large enough inevitably pop.

timeline.point: Tumbling markets help investors with cash.
timeline.quote: A climate of fear is your friend when investing; a euphoric world is your enemy.

timeline.point: Finds little exciting to buy because low long-term rates push up prices of all productive assets.
timeline.quote: Long-term interest rates that are low push the prices of all productive investments upward

timeline.point: Markets now act more like a casino than in his youth; seizures may give Berkshire large opportunities.
timeline.quote: markets now exhibit far more casino-like behavior than they did when I was young.

overview: Buffett warned in the 2006 letter about weakened mortgage lending ('teaser' rates) and in 2007 blamed the belief that house prices would always rise. The 2008 letter covers the panic: frozen credit, a 'freefall in business activity', massive government action he called essential despite likely inflation, flawed history-based mortgage models, derivatives and the Fannie/Freddie regulatory failure. Berkshire supplied capital ($15.5-15.6 billion in weeks after Lehman: Goldman Sachs, GE, Wrigley), though he admits mistakes (ConocoPhillips, Irish banks) and says in 2009 he should have bought more bonds. Clayton's sensible lending held up. He predicted a housing recovery in 2010 and was 'dead wrong' in 2011. Later letters cite 2008 as proof that liquidity and fear-driven bargains matter.
stance_basis: negative on the crisis's causes (lending folly, Wall Street, derivatives, failed CEOs) in letters 2006-2015; positive on the government rescue (2008) and on panic-era buying (2008-2016); consistently optimistic on America's recovery

timeline.point: Housing slowdown stems partly from weakened lending: 'optional' contracts and teaser rates that defer payments; 'tomorrow' has arrived for many owners.
timeline.quote: The slowdown in residential real estate activity stems in part from the weakened lending practices of recent years.

timeline.point: Nearly all Americans believed house prices would forever rise; falling prices expose financial folly at large institutions.
timeline.quote: You only learn who has been swimming naked when the tide goes out

timeline.point: Credit market turned non-functional; by Q4 fear produced a freefall in business activity faster than he had ever seen.
timeline.quote: A freefall in business activity ensued, accelerating at a pace that I have never before witnessed.

timeline.point: Government's huge intervention was essential to avoid a total breakdown, though it will bring unwelcome aftereffects, likely inflation.
timeline.quote: strong and immediate action by government was essential last year if the financial system was to avoid a total breakdown.

timeline.point: Despite the crisis, he insists the U.S. has overcome far worse.
timeline.quote: America’s best days lie ahead.

timeline.point: Market disarray helped Berkshire buy: three large investments on terms unavailable in normal markets, adding about $1.5 billion of pre-tax earnings.
timeline.quote: When investing, pessimism is your friend, euphoria the enemy.

timeline.point: Clayton's low-FICO borrowers kept paying because loans fit their actual incomes; he calls for 10% down payments and verified income.
timeline.quote: they took out a mortgage with the intention of paying it off, whatever the course of home prices.

timeline.point: Mortgage-security losses came largely from history-based models that ignored skyrocketing prices and poor loan practices.
timeline.quote: the stupefying losses in mortgage-related securities came in large part because of flawed, history-based models used by salesmen, rating agencies and investors.

timeline.point: Admits buying ConocoPhillips near the oil peak cost several billion dollars; Irish bank shares lost 89%.
timeline.quote: the terrible timing of my purchase has cost Berkshire several billion dollars.

timeline.point: Risk swung from underpriced to overpriced; he calls late-2008 Treasuries a bubble comparable to Internet and housing bubbles.
timeline.quote: the U.S. Treasury bond bubble of late 2008 may be regarded as almost equally extraordinary.

timeline.point: Berkshire was a supplier, not supplicant: $15.5 billion poured in at the peak, $9 billion into three businesses and $6.5 billion for Wrigley.
timeline.quote: Berkshire was a supplier of liquidity and capital to the system, not a supplicant.

timeline.point: Says he should have bought far more of the cheap corporate and municipal bonds.
timeline.quote: When it’s raining gold, reach for a bucket, not a thimble.

timeline.point: Shareholders of failed institutions lost over $500 billion while CEOs and directors went largely unscathed; they need meaningful sticks.
timeline.quote: To say these owners have been “bailed-out” is to make a mockery of the term.

timeline.point: Leverage lessons: credit vanished overnight in September 2008 and nearly brought the country to its knees.
timeline.quote: Borrowers then learn that credit is like oxygen.

timeline.point: Concedes his 2010 forecast of a housing recovery was wrong; housing-related businesses remain depressed.
timeline.quote: Last year, I told you that “a housing recovery will probably begin within a year or so.” I was dead wrong.

timeline.point: Everyone shared the blame for the housing folly, built on the belief that home values would always rise.
timeline.quote: All of us participated in the destructive behavior – government, lenders, borrowers, the media, rating agencies, you name it.

timeline.point: Calls Berkshire a 'first responder' in the meltdown; supplied $15.6 billion in three weeks of late September-early October 2008.
timeline.quote: Berkshire played an important role as a “first responder” during the 2008-2009 meltdown

timeline.point: Reckless mortgage origination and securitization with no skin in the game played a major role in causing the panic and Great Recession.
timeline.quote: reckless practices in home lending played a major role in bringing on the financial panic of 2008, which in turn led to the Great Recession.

timeline.point: Berkshire shares fell 50.7% from September 2008 to March 2009, his strongest argument against borrowing to own stocks.
timeline.quote: This table offers the strongest argument I can muster against ever using borrowed money to own stocks.

timeline.point: In 2008 Berkshire relied on no commercial paper, bank lines or debt markets; it aims to help extinguish future financial fires.
timeline.quote: During the 2008 panic, Berkshire generated cash from operations and did not rely in any manner on commercial paper, bank lines or debt markets.

overview: Berkshire's original New England textile business (New Bedford, plus Waumbec Mills bought in 1975) was a drag from the start. In 1977-1978 Buffett called it a low-return commodity business but kept it for its role as an employer, honest management, cooperative labor and expected modest cash returns. Waumbec was 'a mistake' by 1979 and was closed in 1980. In July 1985 he shut the operation, admitting he was 'very wrong' about cash returns and should have quit sooner; the 1986 machinery auction netted less than zero. Later letters (1989-2024) use it as his first and defining mistake: buying a cheap but poor business, 'turnarounds seldom turn', the boat matters more than the rowing, and capital trapped for two decades.
stance_basis: negative on the business's economics in every letter 1977-2024; his decision changed from supporting it (1977-1978) to closing it (1985) and later calling the purchase a mistake

timeline.point: Another very poor year; he keeps the business for its role as an employer, its managers and the hope of modest profits.
timeline.quote: The textile business again had a very poor year in 1977. We have mistakenly predicted better results in each of the last two years.

timeline.point: Earnings of $1.3 million on $17 million of capital; textiles show how undifferentiated, capital-intensive producers earn inadequate returns.
timeline.quote: producers of relatively undifferentiated goods in capital intensive businesses must earn inadequate returns except under conditions of tight supply or real shortage.

timeline.point: States four conditions for staying in textiles, including modest cash returns, despite better uses for capital.
timeline.quote: we intend to continue to support our textile business despite more attractive alternative uses for capital.

timeline.point: The Waumbec purchase was a statistical bargain but a mistake; good businesses at fair prices beat poor ones at bargain prices.
timeline.quote: “turnarounds” seldom turn

timeline.point: Waumbec operations terminated; New Bedford looms cut by about one-third.
timeline.quote: Your Chairman made a costly mistake in not facing the realities of this situation sooner.

timeline.point: Decides in July to close the textile operation; admits his expectation of modest cash returns was wrong.
timeline.quote: It turned out that I was very wrong about (4).

timeline.point: Cost-cutting investments looked like winners individually but neutralized each other across the industry.
timeline.quote: Should you find yourself in a chronically-leaking boat, energy devoted to changing vessels is likely to be more productive than energy devoted to patching leaks.

timeline.point: Machinery that could cost $30-$50 million to replace sold for $163,122 gross, a lesson against weighting book or replacement value.
timeline.quote: Gross proceeds from our sale of this equipment came to $163,122.

timeline.point: Lists buying control of Berkshire, a known unpromising textile business bought because it looked cheap, as his first mistake.
timeline.quote: My first mistake, of course, was in buying control of Berkshire.

timeline.point: The 1964 book value of $19.46 overstated intrinsic value because all resources were tied up in sub-profitable textiles.
timeline.quote: all of the company's resources were tied up in a sub-profitable textile business.

timeline.point: Retells the 1962-1965 purchase as a 'cigar butt' that tied up capital; he struggled 18 years after 1966 before closing in 1985.
timeline.quote: In 1985, I finally threw in the towel and closed the operation.

timeline.point: Notes the human cost: the New Bedford operation struggled for 20 years before expiring, leaving older workers without options.
timeline.quote: our original New England textile operation, which struggled for 20 years before expiring.

timeline.point: The textile struggle taught him a part of a wonderful business beats all of a marginal one.
timeline.quote: my 20-year struggle with the textile operation I inherited at Berkshire

timeline.point: Calls taking control 60 years ago his mistake, one that plagued Berkshire for two decades.
timeline.quote: That move was a mistake – my mistake – and one that plagued us for two decades.

overview: Berkshire bought 80% of ISCAR, an Israeli maker of small consumable carbide cutting tools, for $4 billion in July 2006 after an unsolicited letter from chairman Eitan Wertheimer; it was Berkshire's first business bought outside the U.S. Buffett praised it in every letter from 2006 to 2015: 'managerial magicians', growth above high expectations, the 2008 Tungaloy purchase in the panic, profits through the 2009 recession while rivals lost money, a 159% profit rise in 2010 and record earnings in 2011. It was one of the 'Powerhouse Five' (2011-2015). In 2013 the Wertheimers sold the remaining 20% under a put. From 2014 he calls it IMC, and in 2017-2019 lists it only among the next five earners.
stance_basis: praised in every letter 2006-2015, never criticized; 2017-2019 mentions are neutral earnings groupings

timeline.point: Berkshire buys 80% of ISCAR for $4 billion; the Wertheimer family keeps 20%. First business bought outside the U.S.
timeline.quote: Berkshire purchased 80% of ISCAR for $4 billion.

timeline.point: Explains the economics: small consumable tools that make customers' expensive machines more productive.
timeline.quote: ISCAR makes money because it enables its customers to make more money. There is no better recipe for continued success.

timeline.point: Iscar performed magnificently in 2007 and opened a large plant in Dalian, China, near its tungsten supply.
timeline.quote: Iscar is as impressive a manufacturing operation as I’ve seen

timeline.point: Iscar buys Japan's Tungaloy in late November 2008; growth since purchase exceeded high expectations.
timeline.quote: Iscar’s growth since our purchase has exceeded our expectations – which were high – and the addition of Tungaloy will move performance to the next level.

timeline.point: Results fell significantly from 2008, but Iscar stayed profitable while its two main rivals operated at a loss.
timeline.quote: Nothing stops Israel-based Iscar – not wars, recessions or competitors.

timeline.point: Profits up 159%; may surpass pre-recession levels in 2011.
timeline.quote: At Iscar, profits were up 159% in 2010, and we may well surpass pre-recession levels in 2011.

timeline.point: Iscar is one of five large non-insurance businesses that all set operating-earnings records, more than $9 billion pre-tax combined.
timeline.quote: each of our five largest non-insurance companies – BNSF, Iscar, Lubrizol, Marmon Group and MidAmerican Energy – delivered record operating earnings.

timeline.point: The Wertheimer family exercised its put and sold Berkshire the remaining 20%; accounting required recording it below cost.
timeline.quote: the Wertheimer family elected to exercise a put option it held, selling us the 20% of the business it retained

timeline.point: Now called IMC, part of the 'Powerhouse Five' that earned a record $12.4 billion pre-tax.
timeline.quote: IMC (I’ve called it Iscar in the past)

timeline.point: Compares PCC's Mark Donegan to IMC's Jacob Harpaz, who turns ordinary materials into extraordinary products.
timeline.quote: the magic regularly performed by Jacob Harpaz at IMC, our remarkable Israeli manufacturer of cutting tools.

timeline.point: International Metalworking is listed among the next five subsidiaries, which earned $6.4 billion pre-tax combined.
timeline.quote: Clayton Homes, International Metalworking, Lubrizol, Marmon and Precision Castparts, had aggregate pre-tax income in 2018 of $6.4 billion

overview: Buffett treated the 2001-2002 scandals as a failure of managers, directors and auditors, not of law. In 2001 he condemned CEOs who walked away rich while shareholders lost billions, with Enron the symbol. The 2002 letter is his main treatment: pro-forma earnings, EBITDA, derivatives 'mark-to-myth', bloated pay, boardroom atmosphere, auditors serving the CEO, and the 1990s Senate fight against expensing options that he blamed for an 'anything-goes' era feeding the Great Bubble. He proposed four questions for audit committees, endorsed directors meeting without the CEO but doubted most new rules justified their cost, and gave investors three warnings. Later letters show follow-up: CEO pay as the 'acid test' (2003), and Enron bonds bought cheaply.
stance_basis: condemned the conduct in 2001 and at length in 2002; skeptical of most reforms except directors meeting without the CEO (endorsed 2002, adopted at Berkshire 2004)

timeline.point: Disgusted that executives behind the disasters walked away rich while shareholders lost billions; Enron named as the symbol of shareholder abuse.
timeline.quote: Though Enron has become the symbol for shareholder abuse, there is no shortage of egregious conduct elsewhere in corporate America.

timeline.point: Attacks 'pro-forma' earnings that show far more than auditors allow; reports Berkshire's own pro-forma earnings would have been lower.
timeline.quote: the CEO tells his owners “don’t count this, don’t count that – just count what makes earnings fat.”

timeline.point: Derivatives let energy and utility companies report large earnings that vanished when converted to cash.
timeline.quote: “Mark-to-market” then turned out to be truly “mark-to-myth.”

timeline.point: Managers' conduct declined as bubble prices rose: fudged numbers and obscene pay for mediocre results.
timeline.quote: As stock prices went up, the behavioral norms of managers went down.

timeline.point: Directors failed not for lack of laws but because of 'boardroom atmosphere'; over-reaching became common but few hands were slapped.
timeline.quote: Since I wrote that, over-reaching has become common but few hands have been slapped.

timeline.point: Endorses outside directors meeting without the CEO; doubts most other new governance rules are worth their costs.
timeline.quote: I doubt, however, that most of the other new governance rules and recommendations will provide benefits commensurate with the monetary and other costs they impose.

timeline.point: Audit committees cannot audit; their job is to make auditors divulge what they know. He proposes four questions to auditors.
timeline.quote: Audit committees can’t audit. Only a company’s outside auditor can determine whether the earnings that a management purports to have made are suspect.

timeline.point: Blames the Senate's defeat of option expensing and big auditors for an anything-goes era that pumped up the bubble.
timeline.quote: The licentious behavior that followed quickly became an air pump for The Great Bubble.

timeline.point: Advice to investors: beware weak accounting, unintelligible footnotes and companies that trumpet earnings projections.
timeline.quote: Managers that always promise to “make the numbers” will at some point be tempted to make up the numbers.

timeline.point: Rules prompted by the abuses would force Berkshire to consolidate Value Capital, which he calls inappropriate.
timeline.quote: Because of accounting abuses at Enron and elsewhere, rules will soon be instituted

timeline.point: Judges whether corporate America is reforming by CEO pay; results not encouraging.
timeline.quote: In judging whether Corporate America is serious about reforming itself, CEO pay remains the acid test. To date, the results aren’t encouraging.

timeline.point: Says two post-bubble reforms, including directors meeting without the CEO, proved useful at Berkshire.
timeline.quote: Two post-bubble governance reforms have been particularly useful at Berkshire

timeline.point: Berkshire profited from the wreckage: about $82 million of Enron bonds bought in 2002-2003 produced a $270 million overall gain.
timeline.quote: in 2002-2003 we spent about $82 million buying – of all things – Enron bonds

overview: Buffett's retail commentary centres on family-run Berkshire retailers he praised year after year: Associated Retail Stores (1978-82), Nebraska Furniture Mart (from 1983), Borsheim's (1989), Helzberg's and R.C. Willey (1995), Star (1997), Jordan's (1999) and Ben Bridge (2000), for rock-bottom costs, low prices and owner-managers. Alongside that praise he treated retailing as a hard industry: his early department-store buys (Diversified, Hochschild Kohn) were mistakes, 'in retailing, to coast is to fail' (1995), retailers were hit hard in 2008, the Tesco holding ended in a $444 million after-tax loss (2014), and in 2015 he named online retailing a threat to Berkshire's retailers.
stance_basis: positive on specific low-cost, family-managed retailers in letters 1978-2020; negative on retailing as an industry and on his department-store (1984, 1987, 1989) and Tesco (2014) investments

timeline.point: Associated Retail Stores, a women's apparel chain acquired with Diversified, had not grown but Ben Rosner earned returns on capital often near 20% after tax.
timeline.quote: Associated’s business has not grown, and it consistently has faced adverse demographic and retailing trends.

timeline.point: Praises Rosner for producing earnings in cash rather than in receivables and inventories, unlike many retailers.
timeline.quote: he produces very large earnings relative to capital employed - realized in cash and not in increased receivables and inventories as in many other retail businesses

timeline.point: Buys 90% of Nebraska Furniture Mart; calls it the ideal business, built on exceptional customer value.
timeline.quote: I’d rather wrestle grizzlies than compete with Mrs. B and her progeny.

timeline.point: NFM's cost advantage: operating expenses about half those of Levitz, letting it price far below competitors.
timeline.quote: operating expenses (payroll, occupancy, advertising, etc.) are about 16.5% of sales versus 35.6% at Levitz.

timeline.point: The department stores of Diversified Retailing, one of the three original businesses, shrank and lost money.
timeline.quote: shriveled in size while incurring large losses

timeline.point: Buys 80% of Borsheim's; same formula as NFM: one store, huge inventory, shrewd buying, very low expenses.
timeline.quote: The cornerstone for both enterprises is Mrs. B’s creed: “Sell cheap and tell the truth.”

timeline.point: Lists Hochschild Kohn, a Baltimore department store bought at a discount to book, among his mistakes.
timeline.quote: three years later I was lucky to sell the business for about what I had paid.

timeline.point: Borsheim's operating costs of about 18% of sales versus 40% at typical competitors; compares it with Wal-Mart.
timeline.quote: What works with diapers works with diamonds.

timeline.point: On buying Helzberg's and R.C. Willey: retailing is tough, many retailers are shooting stars, so management is decisive.
timeline.quote: In retailing, to coast is to fail.

timeline.point: Helzberg's earnings fell when expenses had been geared to same-store sales growth that did not come.
timeline.quote: Our only disappointment last year was in jewelry: Borsheim's did fine, but Helzberg's suffered a material decline in earnings.

timeline.point: After Star (1997) and Jordan's (1999), Berkshire's furniture retailers lead in six states.
timeline.quote: Each of our furniture operations is number one in its territory.

timeline.point: Recession year: jewelry same-store sales fell 7.6%, home furnishings flat, returns on capital still high.
timeline.quote: Considering the recessionary environment plaguing them, our retailing operations did well in 2001.

timeline.point: R.C. Willey's closed-on-Sunday stores outside Utah succeeded although he had doubted them.
timeline.quote: I would like to tell you that these stores were my idea. In truth, I thought they were mistakes.

timeline.point: NFM's Omaha and Kansas City stores each sold about $400 million, the two top home-furnishings stores in the country.
timeline.quote: In a disastrous year for many furniture retailers, sales at Kansas City increased 8%, while in Omaha the gain was 6%.

timeline.point: Economically sensitive businesses earned below potential; retailers among the hardest hit.
timeline.quote: Our retailers were hit particularly hard, as were our operations tied to residential construction.

timeline.point: Tesco: soured on management in 2013 but sold slowly; exited in 2014 with a $444 million after-tax loss.
timeline.quote: My leisurely pace in making sales would prove expensive.

timeline.point: Names online retailing among the threats Berkshire faces, though none is crucial to its long-term well-being.
timeline.quote: Online retailing threatens the business model of our retailers and certain of our consumer brands.

timeline.point: NFM, bought for a $60 million value in 1983, set sales records in 2020 despite six weeks of COVID closures.
timeline.quote: NFM now owns the three largest home-furnishings stores in the U.S.

overview: Housing enters the letters with the 1986 NHP stake and becomes a large Berkshire exposure in 2000-2003 (Acme Brick, Shaw, Benjamin Moore, Johns Manville, MiTek, HomeServices, Clayton Homes). Buffett liked these businesses and their managers but repeatedly attacked industry lending: manufactured housing in the 1990s and conventional mortgages in 2004-07 were made to 'buyers who shouldn't have bought'. The housing bust cut the building-products group's pre-tax earnings 82.5% from 2006 to 2009; he predicted a recovery 'within a year or so' in 2010 and admitted in 2011 he was 'dead wrong', while insisting housing would come back. Clayton's 100%-retained, down-payment-based lending held up and Clayton became America's largest home builder.
stance_basis: positive on Berkshire's housing businesses and long-run demand in letters 2000-2020; negative on industry mortgage practices (2003, 2008, 2015) and on the 2007-2011 downturn, with a recovery forecast he retracted in 2011

timeline.point: First housing-related stake: about half of NHP, a multifamily rental housing company.
timeline.quote: Last year we paid $23.7 million for about 50% of NHP, Inc., a developer, syndicator, owner and manager of multi-family rental housing.

timeline.point: Tax reform halted NHP's syndication model; low-income housing development depends on government policy.
timeline.quote: NHP will continue to seek ways to develop low- and moderate-income apartment housing, but will not likely meet success unless government policy changes.

timeline.point: In 2000 Berkshire bought Acme Brick, Shaw and Benjamin Moore and agreed to buy Johns Manville.
timeline.quote: we have embraced the 21st century by entering such cutting-edge industries as brick, carpet, insulation and paint.

timeline.point: HomeServices, acquired with MidAmerican, grew rapidly by acquisition; cyclical but liked.
timeline.quote: Though this business will always be cyclical, it’s one we like and in which we continue to have an appetite for sensible acquisitions.

timeline.point: Buys Clayton Homes; describes the manufactured-housing industry's securitization-fuelled bad lending of the 1990s.
timeline.quote: Much of its volume a few years back came from buyers who shouldn’t have bought, financed by lenders who shouldn’t have lent.

timeline.point: Manufactured-home sales at their lowest since 1962; Berkshire's funding lets Clayton keep lending.
timeline.quote: That era, characterized by irresponsible financing and naïve funders, was a fool’s paradise for the industry.

timeline.point: HomeServices volume fell 9% and profits 50%; blames teaser-rate and optional-payment mortgages.
timeline.quote: The slowdown in residential real estate activity stems in part from the weakened lending practices of recent years.

timeline.point: Housing downturn hits the building-products companies; he calls the setbacks minor and temporary (2007_p0008).
timeline.quote: Shaw, Acme Brick, Johns Manville and MiTek were all hurt in 2007 by the sharp housing downturn, with their pre-tax earnings declining 27%, 41%, 38%, and 9% respectively.

timeline.point: Clayton's low-FICO borrowers kept paying because loans fit their incomes; draws lessons for mortgage policy.
timeline.quote: Home purchases should involve an honest-to-God down payment of at least 10% and monthly payments that can be comfortably handled by the borrower’s income.

timeline.point: Construction-linked businesses suffered severely, though their competitive positions stayed intact.
timeline.quote: Combined pre-tax earnings of Shaw, Johns Manville, Acme Brick, and MiTek were $227 million, an 82.5% decline from $1.295 billion in 2006, when construction activity was booming.

timeline.point: Forecasts a recovery and keeps investing (bolt-ons at MiTek and Acme, new plants at Johns Manville and Shaw).
timeline.quote: A housing recovery will probably begin within a year or so. In any event, it is certain to occur at some point.

timeline.point: Admits the 2010 forecast was wrong; five housing companies earned $513 million versus $1.8 billion in 2006, but housing will come back.
timeline.quote: Last year, I told you that “a housing recovery will probably begin within a year or so.” I was dead wrong.

timeline.point: Clayton's $13.7 billion of mortgages to lower-income families performed well; Clayton is the largest U.S. home builder.
timeline.quote: the loans have performed well throughout the housing collapse, thereby validating our conviction that a reasonable down payment

timeline.point: Contrasts originate-and-sell lending before 2008 with Clayton keeping its loans; 8,444 foreclosures cost $157 million.
timeline.quote: At Clayton, our risk retention was, and is, 100%.

timeline.point: HomeServices' 2017 acquisitions brought it near the national lead, yet only about 3% of U.S. home brokerage.
timeline.quote: Given sensible prices, we will keep adding brokers in this most fundamental of businesses.

timeline.point: Clayton, bought in 2003 for $1.7 billion, now earns over $1 billion pre-tax a year.
timeline.quote: Today, Clayton and Pilot each have annual pre-tax earnings of more than $1 billion.

overview: Textiles are Buffett's longest-running cautionary tale. From 1977 he called the mills a low-return commodity business he kept for social reasons; the 1975 Waumbec purchase was a mistake, the operation was closed in 1985, and buying Berkshire itself was still called his mistake in 2024. Apparel and shoes fared better under good managers: Fechheimer (1986), H.H. Brown (1991), Fruit of the Loom (2002), Garan and Brooks. Dexter Shoe changed from 'one of the best-managed companies' (1993) to 'the worst deal I've made' (2007) as imports took the market, made worse because he paid in Berkshire stock. His view of commodity manufacturing is consistently negative; his view of individual managers is positive.
stance_basis: negative on textile manufacturing and on Dexter in letters 1977-2024; positive on Fechheimer, H.H. Brown, Fruit of the Loom and Brooks 1986-2012; view of Dexter reversed between 1993 and 2000

timeline.point: Keeps the textile mills for employment and management reasons while expecting only modest returns.
timeline.quote: this is the opposite case from our textile business where even very good management probably can average only modest results.

timeline.point: Commodity textiles earn inadequate returns while excess capacity persists; still commits to supporting the business.
timeline.quote: we intend to continue to support our textile business despite more attractive alternative uses for capital.

timeline.point: Calls the bargain-priced Waumbec Mills purchase a mistake.
timeline.quote: Both our operating and investment experience cause us to conclude that “turnarounds” seldom turn

timeline.point: Waumbec closed and New Bedford looms cut by about a third.
timeline.quote: Your Chairman made a costly mistake in not facing the realities of this situation sooner.

timeline.point: Closes the textile operation; condition (4) of 1978, modest cash returns, proved wrong after 1979.
timeline.quote: But in the end nothing worked and I should be faulted for not quitting sooner.

timeline.point: Burlington's $3 billion of capital spending left shareholders worse off: capital spending in a commodity industry neutralises itself.
timeline.quote: a textile company that allocates capital brilliantly within its industry is a remarkable textile company - but not a remarkable business.

timeline.point: Buys about 84% of Fechheimer, a uniform maker, at a $55 million valuation.
timeline.quote: Fechheimer is exactly the sort of business we like to buy.

timeline.point: Fechheimer earns high returns only because of the Heldman family's management.
timeline.quote: Neither furniture retailing nor uniform manufacturing has inherently attractive economics.

timeline.point: Buys H.H. Brown, the leading North American work-shoe maker, with fine margins under Frank Rooney.
timeline.quote: Shoes are a tough business - of the billion pairs purchased in the United States each year, about 85% are imported - and most manufacturers in the industry do poorly.

timeline.point: Acquires Dexter Shoe for Berkshire stock; expects shoe pre-tax earnings above $85 million in 1994.
timeline.quote: Dexter, I can assure you, needs no fixing: It is one of the best-managed companies Charlie and I have seen in our business lifetimes.

timeline.point: Shoe earnings fell in a depressed industry; he judges the problem cyclical.
timeline.quote: we believe you should view last year's figures as reflecting a cyclical problem, not a secular one.

timeline.point: Dexter is the exception in a good year; production shifting abroad with severance costs.
timeline.quote: In 1999, approximately 93% of the 1.3 billion pairs of shoes purchased in this country came from abroad, where extremely low-cost labor is the rule.

timeline.point: Keeping production in U.S. plants cost dearly; remaining Dexter goodwill charged off.
timeline.quote: I clearly made a mistake in paying what I did for Dexter in 1993.

timeline.point: Shoe operations lost $46.2 million pre-tax; lists three Dexter mistakes, including paying in stock.
timeline.quote: I concluded that Dexter could continue to cope with that problem, and I was wrong.

timeline.point: Fruit of the Loom and Garan acquired; Dexter turned around, shoes earned $24 million, a $70 million swing.
timeline.quote: Shoes are a tough business, but we have terrific managers and believe that in the future we will earn reasonable returns on the capital we employ in this operation.

timeline.point: Fruit of the Loom keeps gaining share in men's underwear and women's intimate apparel at mass marketers.
timeline.quote: we account for about 48.7% of the sales recorded by mass-marketers (Wal-Mart, Target, etc.).

timeline.point: Dexter, bought for $433 million in stock, cost shareholders about $3.5 billion in Berkshire shares.
timeline.quote: To date, Dexter is the worst deal that I’ve made.

timeline.point: Brooks, the running-shoe company, grows fast.
timeline.quote: Brooks is on fire: Its volume in 2012 grew 34%, and that was on top of a similar 34% gain in 2011.

timeline.point: Fifty-year review: Dexter's value went to zero and the shares given for it were worth about $5.7 billion.
timeline.quote: As a financial disaster, this one deserves a spot in the Guinness Book of World Records.

timeline.point: Sixty years on, calls buying control of the doomed northern textile company his mistake.
timeline.quote: That move was a mistake – my mistake – and one that plagued us for two decades.

overview: Bought in April 1977, the Buffalo News lost money through a costly Sunday-edition fight with the Courier-Express until 1982. From 1983 Buffett praised it as a dominant paper with the highest household penetration among large dailies, a 50% news hole he refused to cut, and superb management by Stan Lipsey; profits set records through 1989 and he said he would not sell it. From 1990-91 he wrote that secular change in media had materially reduced its intrinsic value, in 1995 that newspapers would gradually erode, and in 2006 that 'the days of lush profits' were over, though the News still outperformed most metropolitan papers in 2012.
stance_basis: losses and litigation 1978-1982; strongly positive 1983-1989; from 1990 positive on management but negative on newspaper economics (1990, 1991, 1995, 2006, 2012)

timeline.point: In the Sunday-paper battle the News lost money: a $2.9 million pre-tax loss in 1978.
Sunday circulation, started in 1977, now well above the old Courier-Express Sunday paper.
timeline.quote: The News now has Sunday circulation of 367,000, a 35% gain - even though the number of households within the primary circulation area has shown little change during the six years.

timeline.point: News is first in weekday penetration among the 100 largest papers; margin about 10% after tax in 1983.
timeline.quote: We believe a paper’s penetration ratio to be the best measure of the strength of its franchise.

timeline.point: Profits far above expectations; dominant papers profit whatever their quality, so the News sets its own standards.
timeline.quote: The economics of a dominant newspaper are excellent, among the very best in the business world.

timeline.point: Ten years after purchase, rewards far exceeded expectations; the News is a permanent holding.
timeline.quote: we would not sell See’s or Buffalo Evening News if someone were to offer us a price far above what we believe those businesses are worth.

timeline.point: Keeps a 50% news hole even if margins shrink; rejects flexible operating budgets.
timeline.quote: If we were to cut it to a more typical 40%, we would save approximately $4 million annually in newsprint costs. That interests us not at all
