timeline.point: Number one in household penetration, news hole 50.1%, and record profits while other papers slipped.
timeline.quote: the News set its seventh consecutive profit record.

timeline.point: Recession exposes media's vulnerability: advertising is dispersing and pricing power diminishing.
timeline.quote: These circumstances materially reduce the intrinsic value of our major media investments and also the value of our operating unit, Buffalo News - though all remain fine businesses.

timeline.point: Media intrinsic value fell because of secular change, but Berkshire will not sell permanent holdings.
timeline.quote: the intrinsic value of this investment has declined materially because of the secular transformation that the industry is experiencing.

timeline.point: Earnings fell in 1995; newspapers have lost another notch of economic attractiveness.
timeline.quote: Over time, we expect the competitive strength of newspapers to gradually erode, though the industry should nevertheless remain a fine business for many years to come.

timeline.point: The News paid out all its earnings to fund growth elsewhere in Berkshire.
timeline.quote: The News, See's and Scott Fetzer have alone paid us $1.8 billion, which we have gainfully employed elsewhere.

timeline.point: Cites the News as worth far more than its carrying value.
timeline.quote: Businesses such as See’s and Buffalo News are now worth fifteen to twenty times the value at which they are carried on our books.

timeline.point: Profits declining; the internet offers a fraction of print's old economics; Berkshire will stick with the paper (2006_p0075).
timeline.quote: And fundamentals are definitely eroding in the newspaper industry, a trend that has caused the profits of our Buffalo News to decline.

timeline.point: Among Berkshire's papers the News still did better than most big-city dailies; Lipsey retires.
timeline.quote: the two large papers we operated throughout the year – The Buffalo News and the Omaha World-Herald – held their revenue loss to 3%, which was also an above-average outcome.

timeline.point: Credits Stan Lipsey with saving the News during the 1977-1982 struggle.
timeline.quote: It’s no exaggeration for me to say that the News might now be extinct were it not for Stan.

overview: Berkshire bought $600 million of Gillette convertible preferred in 1989, converted it into 12 million common shares in 1991 after the company called it, and held the stake unchanged until Gillette merged into Procter & Gamble in 2005. Buffett praised Gillette as a business he understood, with over 60% of the world blade market (1993), one of 'The Inevitables' (1996), and in 1995 'our best holding'. His one criticism was of himself: buying preferred instead of common cost about $555 million. He also noted that Gillette had lost focus earlier and suffered capital-allocation blunders, notably Duracell, before Jim Kilts arrived in 2001.
stance_basis: praised as a superior, dominant business in letters 1989-2005 (and as a moat example in 2007); the only error named was his own preferred-stock structure (1995)

timeline.point: First of three 1989 convertible-preferred purchases.
timeline.quote: we purchased $600 million of The Gillette Co. preferred with an 8 3/4% dividend, a mandatory redemption in ten years, and the right to convert into common at $50 per share.

timeline.point: Unlike the airline and paper investments, Gillette is a business whose economics he understands; he joins its board.
timeline.quote: Gillette's business is very much the kind we like.

timeline.point: Preferred called; to be converted into 12 million common shares on April 1, 1991. CEO Colman Mockler died in January 1990.
timeline.quote: we can assess our holdings in Salomon and Champion at yearend 1990 as worth about what we paid, Gillette as worth somewhat more, and USAir as worth substantially less.

timeline.point: Coke and Gillette produced most of 1991's $2.1 billion book-value gain through a rise in their P/E ratios.
timeline.quote: Coca-Cola and Gillette are two of the best companies in the world and we expect their earnings to grow at hefty rates in the years ahead.

timeline.point: Earnings outran the stock from 1991 to 1993; what counts is the companies' earnings performance.
timeline.quote: From 1991 to 1993, Coke and Gillette increased their annual operating earnings per share by 38% and 37% respectively, but their market prices moved up only 11% and 6%.

timeline.point: Uses Coke and Gillette to argue that beta does not measure business risk.
timeline.quote: Gillette has more than a 60% share (in value) of the blade market.

timeline.point: Look-through view of the holding: about $250 million of 1994 blade and razor sales.
timeline.quote: by way of its Gillette stock, Berkshire has a 7% share of the world's razor and blade market (measured by revenues, not by units)

timeline.point: Best of the five convertible preferreds; without Gillette the preferreds did no better than fixed income (1995_p0097).
timeline.quote: Our best holding has been Gillette, which we told you from the start was a superior business.

timeline.point: His mistake: choosing preferred over common cost Berkshire about $555 million by yearend 1995.
timeline.quote: If I had negotiated for common rather than preferred, we would have been better off at yearend 1995 by $625 million, minus the "excess" dividends of about $70 million.

timeline.point: Expects Gillette to dominate its field worldwide for an investment lifetime; notes earlier loss of focus (1996_p0091).
timeline.quote: Companies such as Coca-Cola and Gillette might well be labeled "The Inevitables."

timeline.point: Gillette's common rose in line with excellent company performance.
timeline.quote: At yearend, the $600 million we put into Gillette in 1989 had appreciated to $4.8 billion

timeline.point: One of the 'Big Four' held about 12.5 years; its reported earnings omitted option costs.
timeline.quote: True, they were swelled because Gillette and Wells Fargo omitted option costs in their presentation of earnings

timeline.point: Credits Jim Kilts with restoring discipline before the P&G merger, which forced a meaningless $5.0 billion GAAP gain (2005_p0091).
timeline.quote: Before Jim Kilts arrived at Gillette in 2001, the company was struggling, having particularly suffered from capital-allocation blunders.

overview: World Book came with Scott Fetzer at the start of 1986 and was its largest unit. Buffett was openly enthusiastic in 1985-1990: the leading U.S. encyclopedia, low-priced, rising unit sales and pre-tax earnings near $22-32 million, run under Ralph Schey. Earnings then fell (from $31.9 million in 1990 to $8.8 million in 1995) as CD-ROM and on-line products arrived; in 1995 he called it 'Berkshire's most difficult problem'. In 1996 earnings recovered somewhat after distribution changes and overhead cuts, and he judged its long-term viability in print and electronic markets much improved. The letters do not discuss it after 1996.
stance_basis: praised in letters 1985-1990; earnings declines 1991-1995 and 'most difficult problem' in 1995; cautious recovery in 1996

timeline.point: World Book is about 40% of Scott Fetzer's sales.
timeline.quote: It also is by far the leader in its industry, selling more than twice as many encyclopedia sets annually as its nearest competitor.

timeline.point: Product quality at low prices was a reason to pay Scott Fetzer's asking price.
timeline.quote: This combination of exceptional products and modest prices at World Book, Inc. helped make us willing to pay the price demanded for Scott Fetzer

timeline.point: First year under Berkshire: $22.0 million pre-tax earnings.
timeline.quote: World Book’s unit volume increased for the fourth consecutive year, with encyclopedia sales up 7% over 1985 and 45% over 1982.

timeline.point: New edition launched; U.S. unit sales up a fifth straight year; pre-tax earnings $25.7 million.
timeline.quote: The outlook is good for Scott Fetzer operations in aggregate, and for World Book in particular.

timeline.point: One of the 'Sainted Seven'; pre-tax earnings $27.9 million.
timeline.quote: Unit sales at both Kirby and World Book were up significantly in 1988, with export business particularly strong.

timeline.point: Decentralising out of Chicago's Merchandise Mart as its lease expires.
timeline.quote: The expenses of this transition are significant; nevertheless profits in 1989 held up well.

timeline.point: Earnings improved to $31.9 million pre-tax despite slightly lower unit volume.
timeline.quote: World Book remains far and away the leader in United States encyclopedia sales and we are growing internationally, though from a small base.

timeline.point: Pre-tax earnings fall to $22.5 million from $31.9 million.
Pre-tax earnings fall to $19.9 million from $29.0 million in 1992.
Pre-tax earnings drop to $8.8 million; distribution changed, electronic products stepped up, overhead cut.
timeline.quote: Berkshire's most difficult problem is World Book, which operates in an industry beset by increasingly tough competition from CD-ROM and on-line offerings.

timeline.point: Earnings rose to $12.6 million though unit volume fell; heavy spending on a CD-ROM launched with IBM.
timeline.quote: Overall, the company has gone a long way toward assuring its long-term viability in both the print and electronic marketplaces.

overview: The letters contain no commentary by Buffett on healthcare or pharmaceuticals as an industry. The sector appears only through Berkshire's holdings tables: HCA (2003), Johnson & Johnson (2006-2011, peaking at about 64 million shares in 2007), Sanofi (2007-2016) and DaVita (2014-2015). The only prose is two notes that Berkshire sold Johnson & Johnson shares: in 2008 to fund the Wrigley, Goldman Sachs and General Electric commitments while keeping ample cash, and in 2009 among the year's largest sales. No stance on the sector can be drawn from the letters.
stance_basis: holdings tables 2003-2016 and two notes on selling Johnson & Johnson (2008, 2009); no evaluative statements

timeline.point: HCA appears among the itemized holdings (3.1% of the company).
Johnson & Johnson position enlarged to about 64 million shares (2.2%), cost $3.9 billion; Sanofi-Aventis added (2007_p0082).
Sold part of the J&J holding to fund the Wrigley, Goldman Sachs and GE commitments.
timeline.quote: I had to sell portions of some holdings that I would have preferred to keep (primarily Johnson & Johnson, Procter & Gamble and ConocoPhillips).

timeline.point: J&J was among 2009's largest sales, after building the position earlier in the year.
timeline.quote: In 2009, our largest sales were in ConocoPhillips, Moody’s, Procter & Gamble and Johnson & Johnson

timeline.point: DaVita HealthCare Partners appears among the fifteen largest holdings (8.6%).
timeline.quote: 18,513,482 DaVita HealthCare Partners Inc.

timeline.point: Sanofi still listed among the largest holdings.

note: Thin topic: almost all tagged passages are holdings tables; the timeline records positions, not opinions.

overview: Buffett reviews his own errors in nearly every letter. 1977-1989: buying cheap but poor businesses (Berkshire's textiles, Waumbec, Hochschild Kohn) taught him that turnarounds seldom turn and that a wonderful company at a fair price beats a fair company at a wonderful price; he also admitted insurance under-reserving (1984-1986). From 1989 he stressed costly errors of omission (Fannie Mae, Coca-Cola delayed, selling Disney and Cap Cities early). 1994-2007: USAir, Dexter Shoe paid in stock, General Re's reserving and derivatives, and dithering. Later: ConocoPhillips and Irish banks (2008), Energy Future bonds (2011-2013), Tesco (2014), overpaying for Precision Castparts (2020) and misjudging BHE regulation (2023). Recurring lessons: act promptly, avoid paying with Berkshire stock, stay within competence.
stance_basis: his own decisions judged negatively ('unforced errors') in letters 1977-2024, while candid post-mortems and learning from errors are praised (1985, 1991, 2000, 2024)

timeline.point: The key lesson, sometimes relearned: be in businesses with tailwinds, not headwinds like textiles.
timeline.quote: One of the lessons your management has learned - and, unfortunately, sometimes re-learned - is the importance of being in businesses where tailwinds prevail rather than headwinds.

timeline.point: Buying Waumbec Mills below working capital was a mistake; turnarounds seldom turn.
timeline.quote: “turnarounds” seldom turn, and that the same energies and talent are much better employed in a good business purchased at a fair price than in a poor business purchased at a bargain price.

timeline.point: Buying fifteen-year bonds was a mistake, and not selling them was worse.
timeline.quote: It was a mistake to buy fifteen-year bonds, and yet we did; we made an even more serious mistake in not selling them

timeline.point: His early bias toward tangible assets caused many costly mistakes of omission.
timeline.quote: This bias caused me to make many important business mistakes of omission, although relatively few of commission.

timeline.point: Insurance reserving errors repeatedly made underwriting look better than it was.
timeline.quote: my errors in reporting to you have been substantial and recently have always presented a better underwriting picture than was truly the case.

timeline.point: Closing textiles: he admits he should have quit sooner and believed what he preferred to believe.
timeline.quote: But in the end nothing worked and I should be faulted for not quitting sooner.

timeline.point: Mistakes of the first 25 years: the cigar-butt approach is foolish; buy wonderful companies at fair prices.
timeline.quote: It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price.

timeline.point: Worst mistakes were invisible omissions: big purchases he understood but passed on.
timeline.quote: For Berkshire's shareholders, myself included, the cost of this thumb-sucking has been huge.

timeline.point: Stopping and selling Fannie Mae purchases cost about $1.4 billion of gains.
timeline.quote: Typically, our most egregious mistakes fall in the omission, rather than the commission, category.

timeline.point: Selling Cap Cities early and the USAir preferred were 1994's 'mistake du jour' medal winners.
timeline.quote: Mistakes occur at the time of decision.

timeline.point: Stock-only mergers left shareholders slightly worse off; issuing stock cost owners money.
timeline.quote: Though it hurts me to say it, when I've issued stock, I've cost you money.

timeline.point: He foresaw terrorism risk at General Re before September 11 but did not act.
timeline.quote: I violated the Noah rule: Predicting rain doesn’t count; building arks does.

timeline.point: He believed Gen Re kept underwriting discipline at the 1998 merger and was dead wrong.
timeline.quote: I was dead wrong. Gen Re’s culture and practices had substantially changed

timeline.point: Dithering over Gen Re's derivatives exit cost money; problems need immediate action.
timeline.quote: When a problem exists, whether in personnel or in business operations, the time to act is now.

timeline.point: Dexter Shoe, paid in Berkshire stock, was his worst deal, costing about $3.5 billion.
timeline.quote: To date, Dexter is the worst deal that I’ve made.

timeline.point: Buying ConocoPhillips near the oil price peak cost several billion dollars.
timeline.quote: I bought a large amount of ConocoPhillips stock when oil and gas prices were near their peak.

timeline.point: About $2 billion of Energy Future Holdings bonds, bought without consulting Munger, lost $873 million pre-tax.
timeline.quote: That was a big mistake.

timeline.point: Dawdling in selling Tesco cost $444 million after tax.
timeline.quote: I made a big mistake with this investment by dawdling.

timeline.point: Buying National Indemnity for Berkshire rather than his partnership was his costliest blunder.
timeline.quote: I simply made a colossal mistake.

timeline.point: The $11 billion write-down reflects overpaying for Precision Castparts in 2016.
timeline.quote: That year, Berkshire purchased Precision Castparts (“PCC”), and I paid too much for the company.

timeline.point: He failed to anticipate adverse regulatory returns at BHE, a costly mistake.
timeline.quote: I did not anticipate or even consider the adverse developments in regulatory returns

timeline.point: The cardinal sin is delaying the correction of mistakes ('thumb-sucking').
timeline.quote: The cardinal sin is delaying the correction of mistakes or what Charlie Munger called “thumb-sucking.”

overview: Berkshire bought the Buffalo News in 1977; a Sunday-paper fight with the Courier-Express caused losses until the News won in 1982. In the 1980s Buffett called a dominant paper's economics among the best in business, praised the News for record profits, top household penetration and a 50% news hole, and the 1973 Washington Post stake as a bargain. From 1990-1991 he warned media franchises were eroding for secular reasons and becoming ordinary businesses; World Book struggled against CD-ROMs from 1995. In 2006 he said newspaper fundamentals were crumbling and lush profits were over. Yet in 2011-2012 Berkshire bought the Omaha World-Herald and 28 dailies at low prices, expecting falling earnings but viability for community papers with sensible Internet strategies.
stance_basis: dominant newspapers praised as superb businesses in letters 1983-1989; warnings of secular decline from 1990-1991, repeated in 1995, 2006, 2012 and 2015; cautious buying of local papers at low prices in 2011-2012

timeline.point: The Buffalo Evening News lost $4.6 million pre-tax in 1979 after a $2.9 million loss in 1978 (000s omitted).
timeline.quote: Buffalo Evening News ...... (4,617) (2,913)

timeline.point: Sunday circulation of the News reached 367,000, 35% above the old Courier-Express level, with flat households.
timeline.quote: The News now has Sunday circulation of 367,000, a 35% gain

timeline.point: Penetration ratio is the best measure of a paper's franchise; the News ranked first in weekday penetration.
timeline.quote: We believe a paper’s penetration ratio to be the best measure of the strength of its franchise.

timeline.point: Dominant papers earn excellent profits whether first-class or third-rate.
timeline.quote: The economics of a dominant newspaper are excellent, among the very best in the business world.

timeline.point: The Washington Post stake was bought in 1973 at no more than a quarter of business value.
timeline.quote: We bought all of our WPC holdings in mid-1973 at a price of not more than one-fourth of the then per-share business value of the enterprise.

timeline.point: Berkshire keeps a 50% news hole even though cutting to 40% would save about $4 million of newsprint yearly.
timeline.quote: If we were to cut it to a more typical 40%, we would save approximately $4 million annually in newsprint costs.

timeline.point: The News led major papers in penetration and set a seventh straight profit record while peers' profits slipped.
timeline.quote: the News set its seventh consecutive profit record.

timeline.point: Media proved more vulnerable to recession; many will stay marvels but less so than believed.
timeline.quote: they will prove considerably less marvelous than I, the industry, or lenders thought would be the case only a few years ago.

timeline.point: Media erosion is secular, not just cyclical; newspapers now behave more like businesses than franchises.
timeline.quote: newspaper, television, and magazine properties have begun to resemble businesses more than franchises in their economic behavior.

timeline.point: Media still beat the average business, but bullet-proof franchises are gone.
timeline.quote: But gone are the days of bullet-proof franchises and cornucopian economics.

timeline.point: Newspapers lost another notch of economic attractiveness; World Book faced CD-ROM and online competition.
timeline.quote: Today, the industry retains its excellent economics, but has lost still another notch.

timeline.point: See's and the Buffalo News are worth fifteen to twenty times their carrying value.
timeline.quote: Businesses such as See’s and Buffalo News are now worth fifteen to twenty times the value at which they are carried on our books.

timeline.point: Newspaper fundamentals are eroding; cable, satellite and the internet are winning the battle for eyeballs.
timeline.quote: if cable and satellite broadcasting, as well as the internet, had come along first, newspapers as we know them probably would never have existed.

timeline.point: Berkshire will keep the News unless it faces an irreversible cash drain, but the profit era has ended.
timeline.quote: But the days of lush profits from our newspaper are over.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought 28 dailies for $344 million while still predicting industry-wide decline.
timeline.quote: the circulation, advertising and profits of the newspaper industry overall are certain to decline. That prediction still holds.

timeline.point: Community papers with full local content and a paid Internet strategy should stay viable; cash earnings will still trend down.
timeline.quote: papers delivering comprehensive and reliable information to tightly-bound communities and having a sensible Internet strategy will remain viable for a long time.

timeline.point: Berkshire exchanged its Graham Holdings (former Washington Post Company) stock for operating businesses.
timeline.quote: we were pleased to exchange our Phillips 66 and Graham Holdings stock for operating businesses last year

timeline.point: Falling print circulation is listed among known threats, allowed for in the purchase prices.
timeline.quote: Circulation of our print newspapers will continue to fall

overview: Two different stories. Airlines: Buffett bought $358 million of USAir preferred in 1989, saying he could not forecast airline economics; the industry soon soured through 'kamikaze' pricing and bankruptcies, the dividend stopped in 1994 and he wrote the stake down 75%, calling it a mistake of sloppy analysis. USAir recovered in 1996-1997 and Berkshire exited at a gain, but from 1992 to 2007 he called airlines a capital-hungry business that has lost money since Kitty Hawk. Holdings tables list Delta, Southwest and United stakes in 2016-2019 without comment. Aviation services: he praised FlightSafety (bought 1996) as a durable leader needing heavy simulator spending, and NetJets (1998) as the dominant but long unprofitable fractional-jet operator until its 2009-2010 turnaround.
stance_basis: airlines criticized as a terrible business in letters 1990-2007 (USAir called his biggest mistake in 1994); FlightSafety and NetJets praised as industry leaders 1996-2011, with NetJets losses admitted 2001-2009

timeline.point: Berkshire bought a used corporate jet for $850,000; Buffett admits it is unclear whether it will earn its keep.
timeline.quote: Whether Berkshire will get its money’s worth from the plane is an open question

timeline.point: Berkshire bought $358 million of 9.25% USAir convertible preferred while admitting it cannot forecast airline economics.
timeline.quote: we have no ability to forecast the economics of the investment banking business (in which we have a position through our 1987 purchase of Salomon convertible preferred), the airline industry, or the paper industry.

timeline.point: Airline economics deteriorated after the purchase; in a commodity business you cannot outsmart the dumbest competitor.
timeline.quote: In a business selling a commodity-type product, it's impossible to be a lot smarter than your dumbest competitor.

timeline.point: Bankruptcies of Midway, Pan Am and America West; the airline industry has lost money in aggregate since Kitty Hawk.
timeline.quote: the industry, in aggregate, has posted a net loss since its birth after Kitty Hawk.

timeline.point: Growth destroyed value for airline investors: the more the industry grew, the worse for owners.
timeline.quote: The more the industry has grown, the worse the disaster for owners.

timeline.point: USAir dividend suspended; Buffett calls the purchase his top mistake, from sloppy analysis, and writes it down to 25 cents on the dollar.
timeline.quote: this was a case of sloppy analysis, a lapse that may have been caused by the fact that we were buying a senior security or by hubris.

timeline.point: He missed that high-cost carriers in an unregulated commodity business must cut costs or die.
timeline.quote: In an unregulated commodity business, a company must lower its costs to competitive levels or face extinction.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought FlightSafety, the world's leading pilot trainer, for about $1.5 billion.
timeline.quote: FlightSafety International, the world's leader in the training of pilots - was far larger, at about $1.5 billion

timeline.point: USAir turned profitable and paid arrears; the preferred was probably worth par, after his failed attempts to sell at a discount.
timeline.quote: the prices of USAir's publicly-traded securities tell us that our preferred stock is now probably worth its par value of $358 million

timeline.point: US Airways' rebound under Stephen Wolf was near miraculous; Buffett was wrong both to buy and to try to sell.
timeline.quote: I was wrong in originally purchasing the stock, and I was wrong later, in repeatedly trying to unload our holdings at 50 cents on the dollar.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought Executive Jet (NetJets) for $725 million; he sees fractional ownership's potential as barely tapped.
timeline.quote: Rich and I believe that the potential of fractional ownership has barely been scratched.

timeline.point: NetJets had a 75% industry share but lost money on European losses; the industry as a whole lost significant sums.
timeline.quote: The bald fact is that airplanes are costly to operate.

timeline.point: Airlines are the example of the worst business: fast growth, heavy capital needs, little or no profit.
timeline.quote: The worst sort of business is one that grows rapidly, requires significant capital to engender the growth, and then earns little or no money. Think airlines.

timeline.point: FlightSafety has a durable advantage but needs heavy reinvestment, so it is good, not sensational, economics.
timeline.quote: if measured only by economic returns, FlightSafety is an excellent but not extraordinary business.

timeline.point: NetJets lost $157 million in 11 years and its debt rose to $1.9 billion; Buffett says he failed shareholders.
timeline.quote: It’s clear that I failed you in letting NetJets descend into this condition.

timeline.point: Under Dave Sokol NetJets earned $207 million pre-tax, a $918 million swing from 2009.
timeline.quote: NetJets earned $207 million pre-tax in 2010, a swing of $918 million from 2009.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought Precision Castparts, the premier aerospace components supplier, for more than $32 billion.
timeline.quote: PCC has become the world’s premier supplier of aerospace components

timeline.point: Buffett lists USAir among bad moves rescued by luck.
timeline.quote: Remember our escapes from near-disasters at USAir and Salomon?

overview: Before 2000 the letters mention the U.S. economy only in passing: recessions hurting Buffalo (1983), the News and See's (1990-1991), and Berkshire prospering in America as nowhere else (1996, 1998). In 1999-2001 he tied profits to about 3% real GDP growth and warned stock prices implied only moderate returns. In 2004-2006 he worried about trade imbalances while calling the economy the world's strongest. In 2008 he expected the economy to be 'in shambles' through 2009 yet insisted 'America's best days lie ahead'. From 2010 the theme becomes a constant long-term bullish refrain: record U.S. capital spending, BNSF as an 'all-in wager' on America, 'never bet against America', and from 2018 'The American Tailwind' credited for much of Berkshire's success.
stance_basis: long-term optimism stated in letters 1996-2024, explicit 'America's best days lie ahead' or 'never bet against America' 2008-2022; near-term worries on trade imbalances (2005-2006) and the 2008-2009 recession

timeline.point: Buffalo's heavy-industry economy, hit hard by the recession, hurt the Buffalo News's retail advertisers.
timeline.quote: Buffalo has a concentration of heavy industry, a segment of the economy that was hit particularly hard by the recent recession and that has lagged the recovery.

timeline.point: Large tax payments are fitting because Berkshire owes its prosperity to America.
timeline.quote: Berkshire prospers in America as it would nowhere else.

timeline.point: Buffett ties corporate profit growth to about 3% real GDP growth plus 2% inflation and finds investors wildly optimistic.
timeline.quote: we see GDP growing at a real rate of about 3%.

timeline.point: American business will do fine, but equity prices imply only moderate returns after the market outran business.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I believe that American business will do fine over time but think that today’s equity prices presage only moderate returns for investors.

timeline.point: His currency bets do not reflect doubts about America, the world's strongest economy.
timeline.quote: Our economy is far and away the strongest in the world and will continue to be.

timeline.point: Americans will live better, but servicing the debtor position will force a 'tribute' abroad; a soft landing is wishful thinking.
timeline.quote: even though our course is unwise, Americans will live better ten or twenty years from now than they do today.

timeline.point: He expected the economy to stay in shambles through 2009 but said that did not predict the stock market.
timeline.quote: We’re certain, for example, that the economy will be in shambles throughout 2009 – and, for that matter, probably well beyond

timeline.point: Despite the crisis, the U.S. system has worked extraordinarily well and will keep doing so.
timeline.quote: Though the path has not been smooth, our economic system has worked extraordinarily well over time.

timeline.point: Berkshire spent 90% of $6 billion capex in the U.S. and planned a record $8 billion for 2011.
timeline.quote: Money will always flow toward opportunity, and there is an abundance of that in America.

timeline.point: Housing's own depression explains the lagging jobs recovery, but demographics will restore balance.
timeline.quote: Fortunately, demographics and our market system will restore the needed balance – probably before long.

timeline.point: While CEOs cited uncertainty, Berkshire spent a record $9.8 billion on plant and equipment, 88% in the U.S.
timeline.quote: Opportunities abound in America.

timeline.point: The 2009 BNSF purchase was an all-in wager on U.S. prosperity, which he calls close to a sure thing.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I have always considered a “bet” on ever-rising U.S. prosperity to be very close to a sure thing.

timeline.point: Even 2% real GDP growth lifts per-capita output about 34% in a generation; children will live better.
timeline.quote: The babies being born in America today are the luckiest crop in history.

timeline.point: Productivity gains have recently benefited mostly the wealthy and displace workers; he favors safety nets, not curbs.
timeline.quote: the productivity gains achieved in recent years have largely benefitted the wealthy.

timeline.point: Much of Berkshire's success is credited to 'The American Tailwind', which should supply most gains over the next 77 years.
timeline.quote: much of Berkshire’s success has simply been a product of what I think should be called The American Tailwind.

timeline.point: Despite severe interruptions, America's economic progress has been breathtaking.
timeline.quote: Our unwavering conclusion: Never bet against America.

timeline.point: After 80 years of investing he has never seen a time when a long-term bet against America made sense.
timeline.quote: I have yet to see a time when it made sense to make a long-term bet against America.

timeline.point: Capitalism has faults and abuses but works unmatched wonders; America is Exhibit A.
timeline.quote: It has its faults and abuses – in certain respects more egregious now than ever – but it also can work wonders unmatched by other economic systems.

overview: Four strands. Deficits: in 1984-1987 Buffett called huge deficits dangerous and predicted higher taxes or inflation; in 2004 he said budget deficits only redistribute output among Americans, unlike trade deficits; in 2018 he admitted his long deficit doom-preaching would have been costly; in 2022-2024 he pleaded ignorance on consequences yet warned fiscal folly can destroy paper money. Taxes: he detailed the 1986 Tax Reform Act (net negative), the 1993 rate rise and the 2017 cut (a $29 billion gain), and took pride in Berkshire's large tax payments. Crisis: in 2008 he called massive government action essential though likely inflationary. Pensions: from 2007 he warned of underfunded state and local promises.
stance_basis: warned against deficits and fiscal procrastination 1984-1987 and 2024; downplayed budget deficits in 2004 and conceded deficit doom-saying was wrong in 2018; praised 2008 rescue as essential; critical of public pension underfunding 2007-2013

timeline.point: Book value bought the same half ounce of gold as in 1964 because government can print money but not gold.
timeline.quote: government has been exceptionally able in printing money and creating promises, but is unable to print gold or create oil.

timeline.point: Huge deficits are dangerous and hard to reverse; without reversal high inflation is delayed, not avoided.
timeline.quote: we believe that present fiscal policy - featuring a huge deficit - is both extremely dangerous and difficult to reverse.

timeline.point: The Tax Reform Act of 1986 had praiseworthy parts but a net negative financial effect on Berkshire and its owners.
timeline.quote: Although we find much to praise in the Act, the net financial effect for Berkshire is negative

timeline.point: Scheduled 1988 tax rates look unrealistic; within about five years higher taxes or inflation, or both, are likely.
timeline.quote: within, say, five years - either higher tax rates or higher inflation rates are almost certain to materialize.

timeline.point: Government procrastination on fiscal problems, with foreigners holding U.S. claim checks, will almost inevitably cause inflation.
timeline.quote: almost inevitably, procrastination in facing up to fiscal problems will have inflationary consequences.

timeline.point: The corporate tax rate rise to 35% forced a 1% charge on unrealized gains, cutting net worth by $75 million.
timeline.quote: the corporate tax rate was raised in the third quarter of 1993 to 35%.

timeline.point: Berkshire's $860 million tax bill was so large that 2,000 such taxpayers would have balanced the federal budget.
timeline.quote: We were told to mail $860 million in income taxes to the U.S. Treasury.

timeline.point: Buffett criticized the Bush tax proposals; corporate tax had fallen to 7.4% of federal receipts from 32% in 1952.
timeline.quote: Corporate income taxes in fiscal 2003 accounted for 7.4% of all federal tax receipts, down from a post-war peak of 32% in 1952.

timeline.point: Budget deficits differ from trade deficits: they redistribute output among Americans and send nothing abroad.
timeline.quote: A budget deficit in no way reduces the portion of the national pie that goes to Americans.

timeline.point: Underfunded public pension promises are a long-fused time bomb for taxpayers that politicians avoid.
timeline.quote: Public pension promises are huge and, in many cases, funding is woefully inadequate.

timeline.point: The Treasury and Fed went 'all in'; likely to bring inflation, but strong action was essential to avoid financial breakdown.
timeline.quote: Whatever the downsides may be, strong and immediate action by government was essential last year if the financial system was to avoid a total breakdown.

timeline.point: Local governments face far tougher fiscal problems, with pension gaps that make insuring municipal bonds dangerous.
timeline.quote: Local governments are going to face far tougher fiscal problems in the future than they have to date.

timeline.point: State and local finances worsen because public entities promised pensions they could not afford.
timeline.quote: Local and state financial problems are accelerating, in large part because public entities promised pensions they couldn’t afford.

timeline.point: $29 billion of 2017's $65 billion net-worth gain came from Congress rewriting the tax code, not from operations.
timeline.quote: The remaining $29 billion was delivered to us in December when Congress rewrote the U.S. Tax Code.

timeline.point: The cut to a 21% rate returned 40% of the Treasury's 'AA share' interest to Berkshire, raising intrinsic value.
timeline.quote: 40% of the government’s “ownership” (14/35ths) was returned to Berkshire – free of charge – when the corporate tax rate was reduced to 21%.

timeline.point: Buffett conceded that fleeing stocks for gold over deficit fears, as he once preached, would have been a costly error.
timeline.quote: Those who regularly preach doom because of government budget deficits (as I regularly did myself for many years) might note that our country’s national debt has increased roughly 400-fold

timeline.point: The Treasury took in $32.3 trillion but spent $43.9 trillion in 2012-2021; Buffett pleads ignorance about consequences.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I plead ignorance and firmly believe that near-term economic and market forecasts are worse than useless.

timeline.point: Berkshire paid $26.8 billion to the IRS, about 5% of all corporate taxes, and urged government to keep the currency stable.
timeline.quote: Paper money can see its value evaporate if fiscal folly prevails.

overview: Berkshire, through Mutual Savings and Loan, bought Freddie Mac shares in 1988 up to the legal maximum, called it a long-term holding (favorite holding period 'forever') and carried it at cost. The position grew in 1991 and more than doubled in 1992, peaking around 8% ownership; holdings tables show it rising in value through 1999 and it counted in look-through earnings. Buffett also flagged it as exposed, with See's and Wells Fargo, to a big California earthquake. In 2000 Berkshire sold nearly all its Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae shares. Later letters were critical: in 2003 and 2008 he cited Freddie's accounting 'shenanigans' and OFHEO's failed oversight, and in 2009-2010 noted that FHA, Freddie and Fannie rules disadvantage manufactured-home buyers.
stance_basis: held and praised as a long-term holding 1988-1999; sold in 2000; criticized for massive accounting misstatements in 2003 and 2008

timeline.point: Major 1988 purchases of Freddie Mac preferred, at the legal maximum, meant as a very long-term holding.
timeline.quote: In 1988 we made major purchases of Federal Home Loan Mortgage Pfd. (“Freddie Mac”) and Coca Cola. We expect to hold these securities for a long time.

timeline.point: Yearend 1988 table: 2.4 million Freddie Mac preferred shares, cost $71.7 million, market $121.2 million; equivalent to common stock.
timeline.quote: *Although nominally a preferred stock, this security is financially equivalent to a common stock.

timeline.point: Freddie Mac was the one long-held stock whose share count rose in 1991.
timeline.quote: The exception is Federal Home Loan Mortgage ("Freddie Mac"), in which our shareholdings increased slightly.

timeline.point: Berkshire more than doubled its Freddie Mac position in 1992 (16.2 million shares, cost $414 million).
timeline.quote: we more than doubled our position in Freddie Mac

timeline.point: A major California quake could cut the value of See's, Wells Fargo and Freddie Mac along with insurance losses.
timeline.quote: they might well be accompanied by a major drop in the value of our holdings in See's, Wells Fargo and Freddie Mac.

timeline.point: Yearend 1997: 63,977,600 Freddie Mac shares, cost $329.4 million, market $2,683.1 million.
Berkshire sold nearly all its Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae shares in 2000.
timeline.quote: In 2000, we sold nearly all of our Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae shares

timeline.point: Freddie Mac's revealed accounting problems show investors cannot learn derivative risks from disclosures.
timeline.quote: the Freddie Mac shenanigans of mind-blowing size and audacity that were revealed last year

timeline.point: Derivatives let Fannie and Freddie misstate earnings for years while their regulator OFHEO missed it.
timeline.quote: They allowed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to engage in massive misstatements of earnings for years.

timeline.point: OFHEO kept calling both enterprises sound while they engaged in accounting shenanigans.
timeline.quote: In truth, both enterprises had engaged in massive accounting shenanigans for some time.

timeline.point: FHA, Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae loan rules favor site-built homes over Clayton's manufactured homes.
timeline.quote: Home-financing policies of our government, expressed through the loans found acceptable by FHA, Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae, favor site-built homes

overview: Real estate is a minor, mostly indirect topic. In 1986 Berkshire bought about 50% of NHP, a multi-family housing manager hurt by the end of tax-driven syndication. In 1990 Buffett judged West Coast real estate fears overdone for Wells Fargo and bought more at panic prices. From 2001 he praised HomeServices, MidAmerican's residential brokerage, as cyclical but a 'gem', blamed the 2006-2009 slump on lax mortgage lending, and kept buying brokers through 2017. In 2009 Berkshire took 50% of Berkadia despite expected commercial real estate trouble. From 2011 he named real estate, with farms and businesses, as a productive asset preferable to cash or gold, citing his 1993 NYU-area property.
stance_basis: real estate praised as a productive asset (2011, 2013, 2020) and HomeServices liked in letters 2002-2017; warnings about lending excess and housing slumps (2006-2009) and expected commercial real estate problems (2009)

timeline.point: Berkshire bought about half of NHP, a developer, syndicator, owner and manager of multi-family rental housing.
timeline.quote: Last year we paid $23.7 million for about 50% of NHP, Inc., a developer, syndicator, owner and manager of multi-family rental housing.

timeline.point: The Tax Reform Act of 1986 ended NHP's tax-driven syndication; residuals on some properties could gain if inflation rose.
timeline.quote: The tax-oriented syndication of properties to individuals has been halted by the Tax Reform Act of 1986.

timeline.point: Buffett judged a real estate decline unlikely to seriously hurt well-run banks such as Wells Fargo.
timeline.quote: even a meaningful drop in real estate values is unlikely to cause major problems for well-managed institutions

timeline.point: California real estate fears halved Wells Fargo's price; Berkshire welcomed the drop and bought more.
timeline.quote: fears of a California real estate disaster similar to that experienced in New England caused the price of Wells Fargo stock to fall almost 50% within a few months during 1990

timeline.point: HomeServices, MidAmerican's residential brokerage, grew fast; Buffett called it cyclical but a business Berkshire likes.
timeline.quote: Though this business will always be cyclical, it’s one we like and in which we continue to have an appetite for sensible acquisitions.

timeline.point: HomeServices, the second-largest U.S. brokerage, called a gem as a white-hot housing market cooled.
timeline.quote: Somewhat incongruously, MidAmerican owns the second largest real estate brokerage firm in the U.S. And it’s a gem.

timeline.point: Housing slowdown blamed partly on teaser-rate and optional-payment mortgages; HomeServices volume fell 9% and profits 50%.
timeline.quote: The slowdown in residential real estate activity stems in part from the weakened lending practices of recent years.

timeline.point: 2008 was a terrible year for home sales with no 2009 recovery expected; Berkshire kept buying brokers at sensible prices.
timeline.quote: Last year was a terrible year for home sales, and 2009 looks no better.

timeline.point: Berkshire took 50% of Berkadia, a big commercial mortgage servicer, despite expected commercial real estate trouble.
timeline.quote: Though commercial real estate will face major problems in the next few years, long-term opportunities for Berkadia are significant.

timeline.point: Buffett prefers productive assets, including real estate, over currency-based assets and gold.
timeline.quote: My own preference – and you knew this was coming – is our third category: investment in productive assets, whether businesses, farms, or real estate.

timeline.point: His 1993 NYU-area retail property came from the RTC after a commercial real estate bubble, at about a 10% unleveraged yield.
timeline.quote: Again, a bubble had popped – this one involving commercial real estate

timeline.point: He never considered selling the farm or New York property in the 2008 panic; fear is the investor's friend.
timeline.quote: I never gave a thought to selling my farm or New York real estate, even though a severe recession was clearly brewing

timeline.point: After buying Long and Foster and others, HomeServices had 40,950 agents but only about 3% of U.S. home brokerage.
timeline.quote: Given sensible prices, we will keep adding brokers in this most fundamental of businesses.

timeline.point: Farms, real estate and business ownership create wealth for patient, low-cost owners.
timeline.quote: Productive assets such as farms, real estate and, yes, business ownership produce wealth – lots of it.

overview: In the 1980s Berkshire held only WPPSS Projects 1-3 bonds, bought 1983-84 at about 16-17% tax-free and later rated AA-; he says he long shunned capital-intensive utilities as businesses. In 1999-2000 Berkshire bought 76% of MidAmerican Energy for cash; it added pipelines (2002), PacifiCorp (2006), NV Energy (2013) and AltaLink (2014), became Berkshire Hathaway Energy, never paid a dividend and led in renewables. From 2005 to 2021 he praised it repeatedly: fair regulated returns on huge sums, low Iowa rates, a 'social compact', earnings from $122 million (2000) to $4 billion (2021). Exceptions: the Energy Future Holdings bond loss (2011-2013) and, in 2023, wildfire losses and broken regulatory compacts he called a costly mistake. BHE became 100% owned in 2024.
stance_basis: praised the utility business in nearly every letter 2005-2021 after investing in 1999; turned cautious in 2023 over regulation and wildfire losses; earlier he says he shunned utilities as businesses and held only WPPSS bonds (1984-1992)

timeline.point: Bought WPPSS Projects 1-3 bonds after the Projects 4-5 default, judging risks more than compensated at the prices paid.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I judged the risks at the time we purchased the bonds and at the prices Berkshire paid (much lower than present prices) to be considerably more than compensated for by prospects of profit.

timeline.point: The $139 million WPPSS holding earns $22.7 million after tax, 16.3% on unleveraged capital, versus about double the price for a business.
timeline.quote: Only a relatively few businesses earn the 16.3% after tax on unleveraged capital that our WPPSS investment does

timeline.point: Regulated electric utilities pass tax changes through to prices rather than profits.
timeline.quote: as is the case with electric utilities, changes in corporate tax rates are largely reflected in prices, not in profits.

timeline.point: WPPSS worked out as expected: bought at about 17% after tax and unrated, now rated AA-.
timeline.quote: At the time of purchase, most of our bonds were yielding around 17% after taxes and carried no ratings, which had been suspended. Recently, the bonds were rated AA- by Standard & Poor’s.

timeline.point: Agreed to invest about $2 billion in MidAmerican for about 76% of equity but under 10% of votes, because of PUHCA.
timeline.quote: Though there are many regulatory constraints in the utility industry, it’s possible that we will make additional commitments in the field. If we do, the amounts involved could be large.

timeline.point: MidAmerican bought the Kern River and Northern Natural pipelines and became Berkshire's largest non-insurance earner.
timeline.quote: Already it has $18 billion of assets and delivers our largest stream of non-insurance earnings. It could well grow to be huge.

timeline.point: PacifiCorp purchase: utilities offer no outsized profits but let Berkshire deploy large sums at fair returns.
timeline.quote: You can’t expect to earn outsized profits in regulated utilities, but the industry offers owners the opportunity to deploy large sums at fair returns – and therefore, it makes good sense for Berkshire.

timeline.point: Utilities are a put-up-more-to-earn-more business: higher future earnings require many billions of new investment.
timeline.quote: We will earn considerably more money in this business ten years from now, but we will invest many billions to make it.

timeline.point: Utility earnings are uncorrelated with the economy; record 2008 results, plus $1.1 billion from the failed Constellation Energy deal.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I are equally enthusiastic about our utility business, which had record earnings last year and is poised for future gains.

timeline.point: He now accepts capital-intensive businesses like utilities if incremental investment earns decent returns.
timeline.quote: In earlier days, Charlie and I shunned capital-intensive businesses such as public utilities.

timeline.point: Iowa rates unchanged since 1999 while the rival raised prices over 70%; $5.4 billion committed to wind.
timeline.quote: Iowa rates have not increased since we purchased our operation there in 1999.

timeline.point: About $2 billion of Energy Future Holdings bonds, a Texas utility LBO tied to gas prices, was a big mistake.
timeline.quote: In tennis parlance, this was a major unforced error by your chairman.

timeline.point: Renewables portfolio will cost $13 billion; he trusts future regulation to allow reasonable returns.
timeline.quote: We relish making such commitments if they promise reasonable returns – and on that front, we put a large amount of trust in future regulation.

timeline.point: MidAmerican bought NV Energy for $5.6 billion, serving about 88% of Nevada's population.
timeline.quote: NV Energy, purchased for $5.6 billion by MidAmerican Energy, our utility subsidiary, supplies electricity to about 88% of Nevada’s population.

timeline.point: Utility economics are changing as subsidized renewables threaten high-cost incumbents; BHE's efficiency keeps it competitive.
timeline.quote: BHE’s long-established emphasis on efficiency – even when the company didn’t need it to attain authorized earnings – leaves us particularly competitive in today’s market

timeline.point: Buying MidAmerican for cash in 2000 atoned for the General Re stock deal and set Berkshire's course.
timeline.quote: Early in 2000, I atoned for that folly by buying 76% (since grown to 90%) of MidAmerican Energy

timeline.point: BHE has never paid a dividend and has retained $28 billion; it is ready for $100 billion-plus projects.
timeline.quote: Our view: The more we can invest, the more we like it.

timeline.point: BHE's annual earnings grew from $122 million to $3.4 billion over 21 years; $18 billion western grid project.
timeline.quote: What we have here is a very unusual utility business, whose annual earnings have grown from $122 million to $3.4 billion during our 21 years of ownership.

timeline.point: BHE earned a record $4 billion, more than 30 times its 2000 earnings.
timeline.quote: BHE, our final Giant, earned a record $4 billion in 2021.

timeline.point: BHE was a severe disappointment: regulation in some states raises the specter of zero profit or bankruptcy, plus wildfire losses.
timeline.quote: I did not anticipate or even consider the adverse developments in regulatory returns and, along with Berkshire’s two partners at BHE, I made a costly mistake in not doing so.

timeline.point: Raised ownership of the utility operation from about 92% to 100% for roughly $3.9 billion; BHE earnings recovered to $3.7 billion.
timeline.quote: Late in the year we increased our ownership of the utility operation from about 92% to 100% at a cost of roughly $3.9 billion

overview: Buffett's stance on leverage is consistently cautious from 1979 to 2024: Berkshire uses little debt, accepts lower returns for certainty, and he says his view has 'remained constant'. Debt is used only in bounded ways: long-term fixed-rate borrowing in advance of need (1980, 1987), zero-coupon convertibles (1989), borrowing to re-lend to Clayton's mortgage book at a 1-point markup (from 2003), non-guaranteed debt at the regulated utility and railroad, and yen bonds to hedge Japanese holdings (2020s). He attacked LBO and junk-bond excess and EBDIT (1989-1990), private equity's love of debt (2008, 2014), derivatives leverage (2002, 2008), and reckless mortgage lending (2006-2015), contrasting Clayton's down-payment lending. Repeatedly warns individuals never to buy stocks or Berkshire shares with borrowed money.
stance_basis: warns against leverage and describes Berkshire's low-debt policy in about 35 letters 1979-2024 with no change; accepts debt only where structured, non-recourse or matched to receivables

timeline.point: Berkshire's results were achieved with low financial and operating leverage.
timeline.quote: We have achieved this result while utilizing a low amount of leverage

timeline.point: Sold $60 million of 12 3/4% notes not for a current need but to have firepower when credit is expensive or unavailable.
timeline.quote: The most attractive opportunities may present themselves at a time when credit is extremely expensive - or even unavailable. At such a time we want to have plenty of financial firepower.

timeline.point: Owner principle: rarely use much debt, structure it long-term and fixed-rate, reject opportunities rather than over-leverage.
timeline.quote: We will reject interesting opportunities rather than over-leverage our balance sheet.

timeline.point: Sold $250 million of debentures; wants certainty of meeting obligations, not optimal results; says his debt views are unchanged.
timeline.quote: Our opinions about debt have remained constant.

timeline.point: Borrows ahead of need, because tight money creates the best acquisition opportunities.
timeline.quote: Our basic principle is that if you want to shoot rare, fast-moving elephants, you should always carry a loaded gun.

timeline.point: Attacks junk zero-coupon and PIK bonds and the EBDIT yardstick used to justify overleveraged deals.
timeline.quote: It is impossible to default on a promise to pay nothing.

timeline.point: Higher leverage would have raised returns, but a small chance of distress is not worth a large chance of extra return.
timeline.quote: A small chance of distress or disgrace cannot, in our view, be offset by a large chance of extra returns.

timeline.point: The junk-bond collapse refutes the claim that heavy debt makes managers more careful.
timeline.quote: The roads of business are riddled with potholes; a plan that requires dodging them all is a plan for disaster.

timeline.point: Called the 1989 convertibles; still averse to debt, especially short-term, but accepts modest well-structured debt.
timeline.quote: In general, we continue to have an aversion to debt, particularly the short-term kind.

timeline.point: Berkadia borrowed $5.6 billion, 90% guaranteed by Berkshire, to finance FINOVA; Berkshire had borrowed almost nothing from banks for decades.
timeline.quote: For the next three decades, we borrowed almost nothing from banks. (Debt is a four-letter word around Berkshire.)

timeline.point: Berkshire will borrow to fund Clayton's receivables and re-lend at cost plus one point, so the subsidiary pays its own way.
timeline.quote: We believe it’s appropriate to finance a soundly-selected book of interest-bearing receivables almost entirely with debt (just as a bank would).

timeline.point: Except for repos, receivables financing and MidAmerican's own debt, Berkshire shuns debt and wants total security.
timeline.quote: a long string of impressive numbers multiplied by a single zero always equals zero.

timeline.point: Private-equity buyers pile debt on acquirees, some now in mortal danger; Clayton's sensible lending kept borrowers paying.
timeline.quote: A number of these acquirees, purchased only two to three years ago, are now in mortal danger because of the debt piled on them by their private-equity buyers.

timeline.point: Housing lesson: real down payments of at least 10% and payments the borrower's verified income can carry.
timeline.quote: Home purchases should involve an honest-to-God down payment of at least 10% and monthly payments that can be comfortably handled by the borrower’s income.

timeline.point: NetJets' debt grew from $102 million to $1.9 billion; without Berkshire's guarantee it would have failed.
timeline.quote: Without Berkshire’s guarantee of this debt, NetJets would have been out of business.

timeline.point: 'Life and Debt': leverage is addictive and can produce zeroes; when credit vanishes only cash will do.
timeline.quote: Borrowers then learn that credit is like oxygen. When either is abundant, its presence goes unnoticed. When either is missing, that’s all that is noticed.

timeline.point: About $2 billion of Energy Future Holdings LBO debt, bought without consulting Charlie, produced an $873 million pre-tax loss.
timeline.quote: About $2 billion of the debt was purchased by Berkshire, pursuant to a decision I made without consulting with Charlie. That was a big mistake.

timeline.point: Borrowed money has no place in the investor's toolkit.
timeline.quote: Indeed, borrowed money has no place in the investor’s tool kit: Anything can happen anytime in markets.

timeline.point: Four Berkshire share drops of 37-59% are his strongest argument against owning stocks with borrowed money.
timeline.quote: This table offers the strongest argument I can muster against ever using borrowed money to own stocks.

timeline.point: Debt sits mostly at the railroad and energy subsidiaries, not guaranteed by Berkshire; leverage elsewhere would be madness.
timeline.quote: Rational people don’t risk what they have and need for what they don’t have and don’t need.

timeline.point: Repeats Munger's lesson that leverage is dangerous because nothing is a sure thing.
timeline.quote: There is no such thing as a 100% sure thing when investing. Thus, the use of leverage is dangerous.

timeline.point: Annual debt maturities are never material; most of the Japanese stake is financed with ¥1.3 trillion of bonds.
timeline.quote: Annual debt maturities are never material.

timeline.point: Yen borrowings increased, all fixed-rate, to stay roughly currency-neutral on the Japanese holdings.
timeline.quote: Berkshire has consistently – but not pursuant to any formula – increased its yen-denominated borrowings. All are at fixed rates, no “floaters.”

overview: From 1982 Buffett's rule never changed: issue shares only when Berkshire receives as much intrinsic business value as it gives, because issuing stock sells part of every business owned. He prefers cash deals and criticized acquirers who pay with undervalued stock or serially issue overpriced shares. He refused to split the stock (1983, 1992), but in 1995-1996 created Class B shares (1/30th of A) to block fee-laden Berkshire 'clone' trusts. He judged his own stock deals harshly: by 1997 they had cost shareholders money; Dexter (25,203 shares, 1993) was his worst error and General Re (272,200 shares, +21.8%, 1998) 'terrible'. BNSF (2009-2010, 6.1% more shares) he called a close but sensible exception. He remained averse through 2023.
stance_basis: against issuing shares below value and against splits in about 30 letters 1982-2023; only exceptions accepted are value-for-value deals (Blue Chip 1983, BNSF 2009) and the defensive 1996 B-share offering

timeline.point: Warns against companies that issue new shares to fund dividends they cannot otherwise pay.
timeline.quote: Other companies sell newly issued shares to Peter in order to pay dividends to Paul.

timeline.point: Sets the rule: Berkshire issues shares only when it receives as much intrinsic business value as it gives.
timeline.quote: we will not issue shares unless we receive as much intrinsic business value as we give.

timeline.point: Paying with stock worth half its intrinsic value means giving $2 of value to get $1.
timeline.quote: In effect, the acquirer must give up $2 of value to receive $1 of value.

timeline.point: Explains why Berkshire will not split: a split would attract less rational, short-term buyers.
timeline.quote: Were we to split the stock or take other actions focusing on stock price rather than business value, we would attract an entering class of buyers inferior to the exiting class of sellers.

timeline.point: After the Blue Chip merger, shares outstanding were nearly unchanged since 1965: virtually no net dilution.
timeline.quote: have been added to the original textile assets with virtually no net dilution to the original owners.

timeline.point: Reaffirms the no-split policy, crediting it for an unusually rational shareholder body.
timeline.quote: We hold to the view about stock splits that we set forth in the 1983 Annual Report.

timeline.point: Issued 25,203 shares to acquire Dexter Shoe, plus 3,944 on debenture conversion.
timeline.quote: we issued 25,203 shares when we acquired Dexter Shoe

timeline.point: Proposes Class B shares (1/30th of A) and a public offering, partly to block high-cost Berkshire 'clone' trusts; says the stock is not undervalued.
timeline.quote: Berkshire is selling at a price at which Charlie and I would not consider buying it.

timeline.point: Sold 517,500 B shares for $565 million with a 1.5% commission and open-ended size to deter flippers.
timeline.quote: The first was our sale in May of 517,500 shares of Class B Common, which generated net proceeds of $565 million.

timeline.point: Confession: his stock-only mergers left shareholders slightly worse off; he will be very reluctant to issue shares.
timeline.quote: Though it hurts me to say it, when I've issued stock, I've cost you money.

timeline.point: Bought Jordan's and MidAmerican for cash, the method he vastly prefers.
timeline.quote: We bought both for cash, issuing no Berkshire shares.

timeline.point: Paying with stock means selling part of everything the acquirer owns; his own such deals have cost shareholders.
timeline.quote: When a management proudly acquires another company for stock, the shareholders of the acquirer are concurrently selling part of their interest in everything they own.

timeline.point: Using stock for Dexter turned a $400 million mistake into a $3.5 billion one.
timeline.quote: By using Berkshire stock, I compounded this error hugely.

timeline.point: BNSF required about 95,000 new shares (6.1%); he hates issuing stock, and the decision was close.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I enjoy issuing Berkshire stock about as much as we relish prepping for a colonoscopy.

timeline.point: Trading a wonderful business's shares for a so-so business irreparably destroys value; successors will calculate value before issuing.
timeline.quote: You can’t get rich trading a hundred-dollar bill for eight tens

timeline.point: Companies bent on issuing shares signal promotion-minded management and overpriced stock; BPL and Berkshire avoid them.
timeline.quote: At both BPL and Berkshire, we have never invested in companies that are hell-bent on issuing shares.

timeline.point: Issuing 272,200 shares (+21.8%) for General Re in 1998 was a terrible mistake.
timeline.quote: It was, nevertheless, a terrible mistake on my part to issue 272,200 shares of Berkshire in buying General Re

timeline.point: Shares outstanding rose only 8.3% over 1999-2016, mostly for BNSF, which made good sense.
timeline.quote: That, I’m happy to say, was one issuance of stock that made good sense.

timeline.point: Conglomerates of the 1960s inflated their stock to use it as currency for pricey acquisitions.
timeline.quote: They simply needed to manufacture a vastly overvalued stock of their own that could be used as a “currency” for pricey acquisitions.

timeline.point: Doubling Berkshire is not possible in five years partly because it will not issue shares.
timeline.quote: we are highly averse to issuing shares (an act that immediately juices net worth).

timeline.point: Bought the last ~8% of the utility for about $3.9 billion, $2.9 billion in cash and the balance in B shares.
timeline.quote: of which $2.9 billion was paid in cash with a balance in Berkshire “B” shares.

overview: Buffett's view never changed across 1983-2023: trading costs and investment fees transfer owners' returns to intermediaries, so investors as a group must earn less than their businesses, and low-cost index funds are the best choice for most investors. He first framed this as 'frictional' costs of hyperactive markets (1983, 1986), recommended index funds to 'know-nothing' investors from 1993, attacked mutual-fund directors over fees (2002-2003), told the Gotrocks 'Helpers' parable (2005), criticized 2-and-20 hedge-fund fees (2006), and won a ten-year bet: an S&P 500 index fund gained 125.8% versus 2.8%-87.7% for five funds-of-funds (2008-2017). He also uses the index fund as Berkshire's own benchmark and willingly pays fees that deliver value (bankers, Todd Combs, Ted Weschler).
stance_basis: positive on low-cost index funds and negative on high fees and active trading in every letter that discusses them (about 25 letters, 1983-2023); no change over time

timeline.point: Heavy share turnover costs owners part of the business's earnings; active markets are a self-imposed tax.
timeline.quote: But investors should understand that what is good for the croupier is not good for the customer. A hyperactive stock market is the pickpocket of enterprise.

timeline.point: Trading costs and over $2 billion of annual management fees decide who eats the pie but do not enlarge it.
timeline.quote: These expensive activities may decide who eats the pie, but they don’t enlarge it.

timeline.point: Because of transaction and management costs, shareholders as a whole must underperform the companies they own.
timeline.quote: because of the heavy transaction and investment management costs they bear, stockholders as a whole and over the long term must inevitably underperform the companies they own.

timeline.point: First explicit index-fund recommendation: the investor who does not understand businesses should buy an index fund over time.
timeline.quote: By periodically investing in an index fund, for example, the knownothing investor can actually out-perform most investment professionals.

timeline.point: Class B shares were created partly to block fee-laden Berkshire 'clone' unit trusts sold to unsophisticated buyers.
timeline.quote: They would be sold by brokers working for big commissions, would impose other burdensome costs on their shareholders, and would be marketed en masse to unsophisticated buyers

timeline.point: Mutual-fund expenses of about 100 basis points cut investors' returns by 10% or more; an index fund beats most professionals.
timeline.quote: Most investors, both institutional and individual, will find that the best way to own common stocks is through an index fund that charges minimal fees.

timeline.point: Independent mutual-fund directors have failed for decades to replace weak managers or negotiate lower fees.
timeline.quote: Investment company directors have failed as well in negotiating management fees

timeline.point: After the fund-trading scandals, he calls very low-cost index funds such as Vanguard's the best choice for most equity investors.
timeline.quote: those index funds that are very low-cost (such as Vanguard’s) are investor-friendly by definition and are the best selection for most of those who wish to own equities.

timeline.point: Berkshire must beat the S&P 500 because shareholders can buy it cheaply through an index fund.
timeline.quote: Our shareholders can buy the S&P through an index fund at very low cost.

timeline.point: Gotrocks parable: frictional costs paid to 'Helpers' may take 20% of American business earnings from equity investors.
timeline.quote: the burden of paying Helpers may cause American equity investors, overall, to earn only 80% or so of what they would earn if they just sat still and listened to no one.

timeline.point: The 2-and-20 hedge-fund arrangement is lopsided: a 10% gross return leaves investors 6.4%.
timeline.quote: It’s a lopsided system whereby 2% of your principal is paid each year to the manager even if he accomplishes nothing

timeline.point: Passive investors earn the average minus low costs, so as a class active investors must trail them.
timeline.quote: That means that the passive group – the “know-nothings” – must win.

timeline.point: Hedge-fund partners who walk away rich after losses make their investors 'patsies'; Todd Combs's pay has deferrals to prevent this.
timeline.quote: Investors who put money with such managers should be labeled patsies, not partners.

timeline.point: His will tells the trustee to put 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund and 10% in short-term government bonds.
timeline.quote: Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. (I suggest Vanguard’s.)

timeline.point: Large institutions have long underperformed index investors, largely because of fees paid to consultants and managers.
timeline.quote: Many institutions pay substantial sums to consultants who, in turn, recommend high-fee managers. And that is a fool’s game.

timeline.point: Nine years into the bet, funds-of-funds averaged 2.2% a year; about 60% of their gains went to two layers of managers.
timeline.quote: Both large and small investors should stick with low-cost index funds.

timeline.point: He names Jack Bogle the person who has done the most for American investors.
timeline.quote: If a statue is ever erected to honor the person who has done the most for American investors, the handsdown choice should be Jack Bogle.

timeline.point: Final bet result: the S&P index fund averaged 8.5% a year against 0.3%-6.5% for the five funds-of-funds.
timeline.quote: Performance comes, performance goes. Fees never falter.

timeline.point: A 1% annual fee over 77 years would have halved an institution's gain from $5.3 billion to $2.65 billion.
timeline.quote: its gain would have been cut in half, to $2.65 billion.

timeline.point: Investors in productive assets need time, calm, diversification and minimal transactions and fees.
timeline.quote: investors must never forget that their expenses are Wall Street’s income.

timeline.point: Wall Street profits from feverish activity and will market whatever foolishness sells.
timeline.quote: what truly causes its denizens’ juices to flow is feverish activity.

overview: Marmon, the Pritzker family's industrial group (125-175 businesses; largest unit Union Tank Car), was agreed in 2007: $4.5 billion for 60%, the rest over about six years at a formula price, priced from financial statements alone with no advisors. Berkshire owned 64% in 2008, 80% in 2011, 90% in 2012 and 100% in 2013. Buffett praised CEO Frank Ptak (record 13.5% margin in 2009, record 2011 earnings, bolt-ons) and counted Marmon among the 'Powerhouse Five' (2011-2015). He repeatedly attacked GAAP for forcing write-offs ($614 million, $700 million) on the later purchases, arguing intrinsic value well exceeds carrying value. Railcar leasing moved to Finance in 2014; demand slowed sharply in 2016, yet he still 'very much' liked the business.
stance_basis: praised management, earnings and value in the 2007-2016 letters; only negatives are a 2016 railcar slowdown and criticism of the accounting rule, not of the business

timeline.point: Agreement to buy 60% of Marmon for $4.5 billion and nearly all the rest within six years at an earnings-based formula.
timeline.quote: We will soon purchase 60% of Marmon and will acquire virtually all of the balance within six years. Our initial outlay will be $4.5 billion

timeline.point: Priced from Marmon's financial statements alone, no advisors, and closed despite chaotic markets.
timeline.quote: We arrived at a price using only Marmon’s financial statements, employing no advisors and engaging in no nit-picking.

timeline.point: Closed the acquisition during market disarray; 64% owned, remaining stock to be bought over six years.
timeline.quote: We also closed on our Marmon acquisition (we own 64% of the company now and will purchase its remaining stock over the next six years).

timeline.point: Despite a 27% sales drop in the recession, Marmon earned a record 13.5% pre-tax margin under Frank Ptak.
timeline.quote: Frank Ptak’s Marmon delivered a 13.5% pre-tax profit margin, a record high.

timeline.point: Largest earner in manufacturing, service and retailing; scheduled purchase of 17% more for about $1.5 billion to reach 80%.
timeline.quote: Frank Ptak runs Marmon wonderfully, and we look forward to 100% ownership.

timeline.point: One of five large non-insurance companies with record operating earnings; ten of its eleven sectors gained.
timeline.quote: You can be confident of higher earnings from Marmon in the years ahead.

timeline.point: GAAP forced an immediate $614 million write-off on the extra 16% bought for $1.5 billion, which he calls meaningless.
timeline.quote: Obviously, this write-off had no connection to economic reality.

timeline.point: Another 10% bought; a $700 million write-off; the purchase implies $12.6 billion for 90% versus $8 billion carrying value.
timeline.quote: If we are correct, our Marmon holding is worth at least $4.6 billion more than its carrying value.

timeline.point: Union Tank Car and Procor own 97,000 tank cars; Marmon benefits from the U.S. oil-production revival.
timeline.quote: At both BNSF and Marmon, we are benefitting from the resurgence of U.S. oil production.

timeline.point: Purchases reached the 100% ownership agreed in 2008; $1.8 billion of charges for Marmon and Iscar minorities reduced net worth.
timeline.quote: In one case – Marmon – our purchases brought us to the 100% ownership we had signed up for in 2008.

timeline.point: Leasing (railcars, containers, cranes) moved to Finance; the rail fleet is worth considerably more than its $5 billion book value.
timeline.quote: Marmon’s rail fleet is worth considerably more than the $5 billion figure at which it is carried on our books.

timeline.point: Rail fleet grew to 133,220 units after buying 25,085 cars from General Electric; 97% leased.
timeline.quote: Marmon’s rail fleet expanded to 133,220 units by yearend, a number significantly increased by the company’s purchase of 25,085 cars from General Electric on September 30.

timeline.point: Railcar demand slowed sharply (utilization 91% vs 97%), so earnings will fall in 2017, but he still likes the business.
timeline.quote: Big swings in railcar demand have occurred in the past and they will continue. Nevertheless, we very much like this business and expect decent returns on equity capital over the years.

timeline.point: Grouped among the next five subsidiaries by earnings, which made $6.4 billion pre-tax in 2018.
timeline.quote: Lubrizol, Marmon and Precision Castparts, had aggregate pre-tax income in 2018 of $6.4 billion, up from the $5.5 billion these companies earned in 2017.

timeline.point: Marmon described as a holder of more than 100 operations, from railcar leasing to medical devices.
timeline.quote: Marmon has more than 100 individual business operations, ranging from the leasing of railroad cars to the manufacture of medical devices.

overview: Fechheimer Bros., a Cincinnati uniform maker and distributor, was Berkshire's only 1986 acquisition: about 84% bought on a $55 million valuation after its chairman Bob Heldman answered Buffett's annual-report 'ad'. Buffett called it a prototype acquisition with excellent economics whose only drawback was small size, and he praised the Heldman family's management for years, noting uniforms have no inherently attractive economics. It belonged to the 'Sainted Seven' units that earned high returns on equity without leverage. Pre-tax earnings rose from $8.4 million (part of 1986) to $13-17 million in 1987-1996; a large 1988 acquisition caused integration problems that dipped 1989 profits. After 1996 it appears only through manager moves (Brad Kinstler, 2000-2007).
stance_basis: praised as excellent economics and superb management in the 1986-1991 letters; no negative judgment anywhere, only a temporary 1989 profit dip noted

timeline.point: The year's one acquisition: excellent economics and good people, but small at about 2% of Berkshire's net worth.
timeline.quote: Fechheimer is a company with excellent economics, run by exactly the kind of people with whom we enjoy being associated. But it is relatively small, utilizing only about 2% of Berkshire’s net worth.

timeline.point: After a 1981 LBO the debt had been paid down; Berkshire bought about 84% on a $55 million valuation, the Heldmans keeping a stake.
timeline.quote: we quickly purchased about 84% of the stock for a price that was based upon a $55 million valuation for the entire business.

timeline.point: A prototype acquisition whose only flaw was size; the minimum earnings threshold for acquisitions was raised to $10 million.
timeline.quote: As a prototype for acquisitions, Fechheimer has only one drawback: size. We hope our next acquisition is at least several times as large but a carbon copy in all other respects.

timeline.point: First earnings line: $8.4 million pre-tax for the seven months after the June 1986 purchase.
timeline.quote: Fechheimer (Acquired 6/3/86) 8,400 --- 3,792 ---

timeline.point: Record profit in the purchase year and a substantial gain in 1987; Buffett credits the Heldman family, not the industry.
timeline.quote: There's nothing magic about the Uniform business; the only magic is in the Heldmans.

timeline.point: Uniforms lack attractive economics, so high returns depend on management; Buffett approved a sizable add-on acquisition unseen.
timeline.quote: Neither furniture retailing nor uniform manufacturing has inherently attractive economics. In these businesses, only exceptional managements can deliver high returns on invested capital.

timeline.point: As one of the 'Sainted Seven', it helped the group earn about 67% on average equity with no leverage.
timeline.quote: With no benefit from financial leverage, this group earned about 67% on average equity capital.

timeline.point: Profits fell somewhat while integrating the 1988 acquisition, but return on invested capital stayed splendid.
timeline.quote: Profits in 1989 were down somewhat because of problems the business experienced in integrating a major 1988 acquisition.

timeline.point: Integration problems largely solved; earnings flat on unusual items; 42 retail stores; prospects excellent.
timeline.quote: Fechheimer's operating performance improved considerably in 1990, as many of the problems we encountered in integrating the large acquisition we made in 1988 were moderated or solved.
