timeline.point: Fechheimer cited as the favorite acquisition pattern: owner-managers who take cash but stay on as owners.
timeline.quote: Our favorite form of purchase is one fitting the pattern through which we acquired Nebraska Furniture Mart, Fechheimer's and Borsheim's.

timeline.point: Last separate earnings line: $17.3 million pre-tax in 1996 versus $16.9 million in 1995.
Brad Kinstler moved from Cypress Insurance to run Fechheimer and is doing well.
timeline.quote: we needed a new manager at Fechheimer Bros., our Cincinnati-based uniform company, and called on Brad.

timeline.point: Kinstler, who had run Cypress and Fechheimer, became CEO of See's.
timeline.quote: Brad Kinstler, who previously had served Berkshire well while running Cypress Insurance and Fechheimer’s.

overview: Berkshire first appears as a Kraft Foods shareholder in the 2007-2011 holdings tables. In 2013 it and 3G Capital (Jorge Paulo Lemann) bought H. J. Heinz: Berkshire paid $4.25 billion for half the common and $8 billion for 9% preferred, calling it a partnership template and a permanent holding. Buffett praised 3G's managers and their cost-cutting as productivity gains. In 2015 Heinz merged with Kraft; Berkshire owned 325.4 million shares (about 27%) costing $9.8 billion, and the preferred was to be redeemed. From 2018 the tone turns factual and cooler: a $3.0 billion impairment from Kraft Heinz intangibles, and by 2019-2020 a market value ($10.5-11.3 billion) below the $13.3-13.8 billion carrying value. He gives no explicit later verdict.
stance_basis: praised the Heinz deal, partners and managers in the 2012-2015 letters; from 2018 reports an impairment and market value below carrying value without renewed praise

timeline.point: Kraft Foods appears among Berkshire's largest common-stock holdings: 124.4 million shares, 8.1% of the company, cost $4,152 million.
Agreement to buy 50% of the holding company that will own H. J. Heinz with Jorge Paulo Lemann's group, plus $8 billion of 9% preferred with warrants.
timeline.quote: Berkshire will also invest $8 billion in preferred shares that pay a 9% dividend.

timeline.point: Heinz deal completed; called a partnership template for future large acquisitions, and expected to prosper for a century.
timeline.quote: Both companies fit us well and will be prospering a century from now. With the Heinz purchase, moreover, we created a partnership template that may be used by Berkshire in future acquisitions of size.

timeline.point: Berkshire is the financing partner; unlike private equity it never intends to sell, and would like to buy more.
timeline.quote: Though the Heinz acquisition has some similarities to a “private equity” transaction, there is a crucial difference: Berkshire never intends to sell a share of the company.

timeline.point: Early results encouraging, but one-time purchase and restructuring charges of $1.3 billion kept 2013 earnings minor.
timeline.quote: Our partnership took control of Heinz in June, and operating results so far are encouraging.

timeline.point: Buffett says Heinz is run far better by 3G's managers than he would run it and expects more deals with 3G.
timeline.quote: I’m not embarrassed to admit that Heinz is run far better under Alex Behring, Chairman, and Bernardo Hees, CEO, than would be the case if I were in charge.

timeline.point: Heinz merged with Kraft: Berkshire now owns 325.4 million Kraft Heinz shares (about 27%) costing $9.8 billion.
timeline.quote: Now we own 325.4 million shares of Kraft Heinz (about 27%) that cost us $9.8 billion.

timeline.point: GAAP forced a $6.8 billion write-up although no shares were sold; the $8.32 billion preferred redemption is bad news for Berkshire.
timeline.quote: That will be good news for Kraft Heinz and bad news for Berkshire.

timeline.point: 3G's method of eliminating unnecessary costs praised as a productivity boost, though Berkshire's own path is hands-off.
timeline.quote: Their actions significantly boost productivity, the all-important factor in America’s economic growth over the past 240 years.

timeline.point: The Kraft-Heinz merger is cited as the rare total rebasing whose one-time costs deserved clear explanation to owners.
timeline.quote: when there is a total rebasing of a business, such as occurred when Kraft and Heinz merged, it is imperative that for several years the huge one-time costs of rationalizing the combined operations be explained clearly to owners.

timeline.point: Kraft Heinz carried on the equity method at $15.3 billion; yearend market value $28.4 billion against a $9.8 billion cost.
timeline.quote: are carried on our balance sheet at a GAAP figure of $15.3 billion and had a yearend market value of $28.4 billion.

timeline.point: 2018 GAAP earnings included a $3.0 billion non-cash impairment, almost entirely from Berkshire's equity interest in Kraft Heinz.
timeline.quote: a $3.0 billion non-cash loss from an impairment of intangible assets (arising almost entirely from our equity interest in Kraft Heinz)

timeline.point: Carrying value cut to $13.8 billion by its share of the write-off; market value $14 billion versus $9.8 billion cost.
timeline.quote: an amount reduced by our share of the large write-off of intangible assets taken by Kraft Heinz in 2018.

timeline.point: Market value of the Kraft Heinz shares fell below the GAAP carrying value.
timeline.quote: Please note, though, that the market value of our shares on that date was only $10.5 billion.

timeline.point: Still carried at $13.3 billion against a market value of only $11.3 billion.
timeline.quote: Please note, though, that the market value of our shares on that date was only $11.3 billion.

timeline.point: Berkshire owns 26.6% of Kraft Heinz, carried on the equity method at $13.1 billion.
timeline.quote: a 26.6% interest in Kraft Heinz (accounted for on the “equity” method, not market value, and carried at $13.1 billion)

timeline.point: Kraft Heinz is part of the non-controlled businesses (20-50% owned) line of operating earnings.
timeline.quote: such as Kraft Heinz, Occidental Petroleum and Berkadia.

overview: Buffett treated September 11 as the insurance industry's largest loss and as his own mistake: he had let General Re write business without a safeguard he knew was important, and the industry had priced on past experience, ignoring terrorism exposure. Berkshire's 2001 cost of float jumped to 12.8%, about half from World Trade Center losses. He drew lessons (price on exposure, limit aggregation) and said Berkshire would write some terrorism cover but cap total exposure. Side effects: airline training at FlightSafety fell, NetJets costs rose, FINOVA's aircraft collateral lost value, yet the XTRA purchase closed. Basis: negative and self-critical in the 2001 and 2002 letters; in 2004 the attack is cited as a $35 billion benchmark loss.

timeline.point: Buffett says he allowed General Re to take on business without a key safeguard and September 11 exposed the error.
timeline.quote: I allowed General Re to take on business without a safeguard I knew was important, and on September 11th, this error caught up with us.

timeline.point: Berkshire completed the XTRA tender although market closure on September 11 gave it the right to back away.
timeline.quote: he knew we had the option of backing away from our purchase.

timeline.point: The attack was the industry's largest loss and pushed Berkshire's 2001 cost of float to 12.8%, the worst since 1984.
timeline.quote: an event that delivered the insurance industry its largest loss in history. Our float cost therefore came in at a staggering 12.8%.

timeline.point: The whole industry, Berkshire included, priced property cover on past experience and took terrorism risk for free.
timeline.quote: all of us in the industry made a fundamental underwriting mistake by focusing on experience, rather than exposure, thereby assuming a huge terrorism risk for which we received no premium.

timeline.point: A close-to-worst-case attack (perhaps $1 trillion of damage) would destroy the industry unless it limits terrorism risk.
timeline.quote: Only the U.S. Government has the resources to absorb such a blow.

timeline.point: He had recognized the terrorism danger before the attack but did not act, leaving uncompensated risk at General Re.
timeline.quote: I violated the Noah rule: Predicting rain doesn't count; building arks does.

timeline.point: Berkshire will keep writing some terrorism cover, including large noncorrelated policies, but caps its total exposure.
timeline.quote: We will control our total exposure, no matter what the competition does.

timeline.point: After the attack Ajit Jain's speed in writing huge policies (refinery, airlines, Sears Tower) became a key advantage.
timeline.quote: After September 11th, his quickness to respond, always important, has become a major competitive advantage.

timeline.point: Commercial-airline pilot training at FlightSafety fell after the attack, while business-aviation training stayed near normal.
timeline.quote: After September 11th, training for commercial airlines fell, and today it remains depressed.

timeline.point: NetJets' cost of keeping its safety, security and service standards rose because of the attack.
timeline.quote: the cost of sticking to those standards was exacerbated by September 11th.

timeline.point: Berkshire withdrew its FINOVA bond offer when the NYSE closed; the attack also cut the value of FINOVA's aircraft collateral.
timeline.quote: Many of FINOVA's loans involve aircraft assets whose values were significantly diminished by the events of September 11th.

timeline.point: Looking back, about half of 2001's terrible 12.8% float cost came from World Trade Center losses.
timeline.quote: In 2001, however, our cost was terrible, coming in at 12.8%, about half of which was attributable to World Trade Center losses.

timeline.point: Gen Re's accumulated aggregation risk was so large the attack alone would have threatened an independent Gen Re.
timeline.quote: had Gen Re remained independent, the World Trade Center attack alone would have threatened the company's existence.

timeline.point: The attack remains the benchmark: the largest insured loss to date, about $35 billion, larger than Hurricane Andrew.
timeline.quote: The largest insured loss to date is the World Trade Center disaster, which cost the insurance industry an estimated $35 billion.

overview: XTRA, a truck-trailer lessor, was bought for cash in 2001 after Julian Robertson's Tiger Fund sold its block; the tender closed despite September 11. Buffett called trailer leasing cyclical but able to earn decent returns over time, and its reported earnings tracked the economy: poor in the 2002-03 recession, strong in 2005-06, down in 2007, hit hard in 2008-09, then recovering (utilization 63% to 75% in 2010; combined leasing profits $13 million in 2009 to $155 million in 2011). He consistently called XTRA a good business and industry leader that kept investing in equipment. From 2014 it appears mainly as one of three leasing operations with CORT and Marmon. Basis: positive remarks in letters 2001-2016, with the cyclicality stated openly.

timeline.point: XTRA came to Berkshire after Julian Robertson, liquidating Tiger Fund, decided in June 2001 to sell his block.
timeline.quote: One of these was XTRA, a leading lessor of truck trailers.

timeline.point: After completing the deal Buffett described trailer leasing as cyclical but capable of decent returns, and hoped to expand in leasing.
timeline.quote: Trailer leasing is a cyclical business but one in which we should earn decent returns over time.

timeline.point: XTRA and CORT had poor earnings for two years because the recession cut demand, though both stayed leaders.
timeline.quote: Both operations have had poor earnings during the past two years as the recession caused demand to drop considerably more than was anticipated.

timeline.point: Leasing rebounded; XTRA sold container and intermodal units to focus on trailers and earned decent profits under new CEO Bill Franz.
timeline.quote: XTRA disposed of its container and intermodal businesses in order to concentrate on trailer leasing, long its strong suit.

timeline.point: XTRA's earnings held at the high level reached in 2005; Berkshire sought tuck-in acquisitions for its lessors.
timeline.quote: CORT's earnings improved significantly last year, and XTRA's remained at the high level attained in 2005.

timeline.point: Lower trailer utilization cut XTRA's 2007 earnings, as did interest on $400 million it borrowed and paid to Berkshire.
timeline.quote: Utilization of trailers was down considerably in 2007 and that led to a drop in earnings at XTRA.

timeline.point: The recession hit CORT and XTRA severely with no rebound yet, though their competitive positions stayed strong.
timeline.quote: The table also illustrates how severely our furniture (CORT) and trailer (XTRA) leasing operations have been hit by the recession.

timeline.point: Recovery began: higher utilization roughly doubled XTRA's pre-tax earnings.
timeline.quote: XTRA increased the utilization of its equipment from 63% in 2009 to 75% in 2010, thereby raising pre-tax earnings to $35 million from $17 million in 2009.

timeline.point: XTRA and CORT's combined pre-tax earnings mirrored the non-housing economy's recovery.
timeline.quote: Their combined pre-tax earnings were $13 million in 2009, $53 million in 2010 and $155 million in 2011

timeline.point: XTRA kept investing in new trailers well above depreciation while competitors hesitated.
timeline.quote: Our expenditures for new rental equipment at XTRA totaled $256 million in 2012, more than double its depreciation expense.

timeline.point: XTRA and CORT, industry leaders, substantially raised earnings as the economy strengthened, helped by heavy equipment investment.
timeline.quote: Both companies have invested more money in new equipment than have many of their competitors, and that's paying off.

timeline.point: XTRA is listed with CORT and Marmon as Berkshire's three leasing and rental operations, each a leader.
timeline.quote: Each is the leader in its field.

overview: Bought in 1998 as Executive Jet for $725 million, half cash and half stock, NetJets was praised throughout as the inventor and runaway leader of fractional jet ownership, with safety and service standards Buffett's own family used. His financial view changed. Early letters stressed huge potential; 2001-2005 reported losses, largely from an expensive European build-out, and he admitted being dead wrong about 2005 profits. Profits came in 2006-07, but in 2009 he called NetJets Berkshire's major problem: an aggregate $157 million pre-tax loss over eleven years, debt up to $1.9 billion, survival only through Berkshire's guarantee. Under Dave Sokol, then Jordan Hansell, it earned $207 million in 2010 and $227 million in 2011.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought Executive Jet (EJA), by far the largest fractional-jet operator, for $725 million.
timeline.quote: we quickly made a $725 million deal, paying equal amounts of cash and stock.

timeline.point: EJA took 31% of world corporate-jet orders in 1997; Buffett saw fractional ownership as barely tapped.
timeline.quote: Rich and I believe that the potential of fractional ownership has barely been scratched.

timeline.point: Supply-constrained but growing fast, EJA was building critical mass in Europe at great expense.
timeline.quote: Though EJA was supply-constrained in 1999, its recurring revenues — monthly management fees plus hourly flight fees — increased 46%.

timeline.point: Recurring revenue grew 49% in 2000, but margins were slim, partly from European development costs.
timeline.quote: I also told you that this was a low-margin business, in which survivors will be few.

timeline.point: NetJets ran a small 2001 loss; scale gave it an edge, but Buffett expected only modest profits for a few years.
timeline.quote: Under the competitive conditions likely to prevail for a few years, however, our advantage will at best produce modest profits.

timeline.point: NetJets was the runaway leader of four firms, yet lost money again in 2002 as European losses exceeded U.S. profit.
timeline.quote: FAA records indicate that our industry share in 2002 was 75%

timeline.point: After a $41 million pre-tax loss in 2003, Buffett defended staying in Europe despite continuing losses there.
timeline.quote: The European loss is painful. But any company that forsakes Europe, as all of our competitors have done, is destined for second-tier status.

timeline.point: He admitted his forecast of 2005 profits was wrong; U.S. operations fell deep into the red as costs soared.
timeline.quote: I said last year that this business would earn money in 2005 – and I was dead wrong.

timeline.point: A turnaround: Europe became profitable under Mark Booth and NetJets earned $143 million pre-tax worldwide in 2006.
timeline.quote: Our U.S. operation also had a good year in 2006, which led to worldwide pre-tax earnings of $143 million at NetJets last year.

timeline.point: NetJets remained the unchallenged leader, with near 90% of the large-cabin market.
timeline.quote: We now operate 487 planes in the U.S. and 135 in Europe, a fleet more than twice the size of that operated by our three major competitors combined.

timeline.point: NetJets became Berkshire's major problem: operationally dominant but financially a failure, with debt soaring to $1.9 billion.
timeline.quote: In the eleven years that we have owned the company, it has recorded an aggregate pre-tax loss of $157 million.

timeline.point: Without Berkshire's guarantee NetJets would have been out of business; Buffett took the blame. It lost $711 million in 2009.
timeline.quote: It's clear that I failed you in letting NetJets descend into this condition.

timeline.point: Under Dave Sokol, and now paying a guarantee fee to Berkshire, NetJets became solidly profitable.
timeline.quote: NetJets earned $207 million pre-tax in 2010, a swing of $918 million from 2009.

timeline.point: Jordan Hansell delivered $227 million pre-tax in 2011; Buffett said the earlier problems were behind them.
timeline.quote: A few years ago NetJets was my number one worry: Its costs were far out of line with revenues, and cash was hemorrhaging.

timeline.point: NetJets now appears only as one of the tier of Berkshire's ten largest non-insurance earners.
timeline.quote: The next five, similarly ranked and listed (Berkshire Hathaway Automotive, Johns Manville, NetJets, Shaw and TTI) earned $1.9 billion last year

overview: Inflation is a persistent Buffett warning. In 1979-1981 he argued that inflation plus taxes can leave owners of even a 20%-return business with no real gain, called inflation a gigantic corporate tapeworm and said Berkshire had no corporate solution. In 1983 he explained why low-capital businesses with economic goodwill, like See's, withstand inflation best and asset-heavy ones do not. Through the 1980s it drove his aversion to long-term bonds and his view that insurance losses grow about 10% a year from monetary and social inflation. From 2008 he warned that stimulus and deficits invite inflation and that currency-based investments are riskier than productive assets. Basis: negative in letters 1977-2024; in 1979 he conceded his view might prove too negative.

timeline.point: Monetary and social inflation raise insurance costs about 1% a month, so underwriting margins shrink unless rates keep pace.
timeline.quote: costs involved in the insurance areas in which we operate rise at close to 1% per month.

timeline.point: Inflation turned bonds and savings accounts into purchasing-power losers and can do the same to a strong business.
timeline.quote: a business earning 20% on capital can produce a negative real return for its owners under inflationary conditions not much more severe than presently prevail.

timeline.point: He hedged his pessimism: very low inflation was possible if legislators responded.
timeline.quote: Inflation is man-made; perhaps it can be man-mastered.

timeline.point: Berkshire would not lock in a price on money for 2010-2020 any more than on candy or cloth, so it avoids long bonds.
timeline.quote: Neither a short-term borrower nor a long-term lender be.

timeline.point: Only purchasing-power gains are real earnings; inflation acts as a tax that raises the hurdle rate for real returns.
timeline.quote: High rates of inflation create a tax on capital that makes much corporate investment unwise

timeline.point: He applauded Volcker and moderating price indices but stayed as negative as ever on long-term inflation.
timeline.quote: Like virginity, a stable price level seems capable of maintenance, but not of restoration.

timeline.point: Inflation forces businesses to pour money into receivables, inventory and plant just to hold unit volume.
timeline.quote: For inflation acts as a gigantic corporate tapeworm.

timeline.point: The See's example: inflation hurts every business needing tangible assets, but asset-light ones least.
timeline.quote: Any unleveraged business that requires some net tangible assets to operate (and almost all do) is hurt by inflation.

timeline.point: Great inflation-era fortunes came from durable intangibles with small capital needs, such as communications.
timeline.quote: During inflation, Goodwill is the gift that keeps giving.

timeline.point: He disliked most long-term bonds because the dollar's outlook was dismal, with a small chance of runaway inflation.
timeline.quote: We believe substantial inflation lies ahead, although we have no idea what the average rate will turn out to be.

timeline.point: Insurance losses kept rising about 10% a year even with low general inflation, driven by social and judicial inflation.
timeline.quote: Today, social and judicial inflation are the major culprits; the cost of entering a courtroom has simply ballooned.

timeline.point: As a debtor nation borrowing in its own currency, the U.S. faces growing pressure to inflate.
timeline.quote: For the debtor government, the weapon of inflation is the economic equivalent of the "H" bomb

timeline.point: Berkshire keeps its aversion to long-term bonds; its only long bonds are WPPSS issues.
timeline.quote: We will become enthused about such securities only when we become enthused about prospects for long-term stability in the purchasing power of money.

timeline.point: Inflation is one of the factors in his definition of investment risk, measured in purchasing power.
timeline.quote: The levels of taxation and inflation that will be experienced and that will determine the degree by which an investor's purchasing-power return is reduced from his gross return.

timeline.point: Assuming about 3% real GDP growth and 2% inflation, he judged equity investors' return expectations wildly optimistic.
timeline.quote: In addition, we have hypothesized 2% inflation.

timeline.point: Though Berkshire bet against the dollar via currency contracts, its dollar-based assets favor price stability.
timeline.quote: both a strong dollar and a low-inflation environment are very much in our interest.

timeline.point: The Treasury and Fed went all in during the crisis; Buffett expected unwelcome aftereffects.
timeline.quote: one likely consequence is an onslaught of inflation.

timeline.point: Currency-based investments are among the most dangerous assets; inflation erased most of the dollar's value.
timeline.quote: the dollar has fallen a staggering 86% in value since 1965, when I took over management of Berkshire.

timeline.point: He prefers productive assets that keep purchasing power with little new capital; utilities fail that test.
timeline.quote: Farms, real estate, and many businesses such as Coca-Cola, IBM and our own See's Candy meet that double-barreled test.

timeline.point: A partial positive: at GEICO inflation in claim costs was matched by premiums, enlarging the business.
timeline.quote: paradoxically, the upward march in loss costs has made insurance companies far more valuable.

timeline.point: Berkshire aims for staying power in crises; its inflation protection is limited and deficits have consequences.
timeline.quote: Berkshire also offers some modest protection from runaway inflation, but this attribute is far from perfect.

timeline.point: Berkshire will keep most money in equities, since fixed-coupon bonds give no protection against runaway currency.
timeline.quote: Paper money can see its value evaporate if fiscal folly prevails.

overview: Buffett has endorsed share repurchases for over four decades, but only below intrinsic value. In 1980-1985 he praised investees such as GEICO, Washington Post and General Foods for buying stock at bargain prices, calling it the surest way to raise per-share value, while condemning greenmail. From 1999 he criticized buybacks made to pump the stock or offset option dilution. Berkshire paid no cash for buybacks for 40 years, set a 110%-of-book limit in 2011, raised it to 120% in 2012, then bought on his and Munger's value judgment: $5 billion in 2019, $24.7 billion in 2020, $51.7 billion over 2020-21. Investee buybacks (GEICO, Amex, Apple) raised its stakes at no cost. Basis: positive, always conditioned on price, in letters 1978-2024.

timeline.point: Companies that cannot reinvest at good returns should pay out earnings or buy back stock.
timeline.quote: then earnings should be paid out or used to repurchase shares - often by far the most attractive option for capital utilization.

timeline.point: He welcomes repurchases by investees when a fine business sells far below intrinsic value.
timeline.quote: what more certain or more profitable utilization of capital can there be than significant enlargement of the interests of all owners at that bargain price?

timeline.point: His endorsement covers only price-driven repurchases, never greenmail payments to a raider.
timeline.quote: a practice we find odious and repugnant.

timeline.point: Buybacks well below value immediately raise per-share value and show shareholder-minded management.
timeline.quote: When companies purchase their own stock, they often find it easy to get $2 of present value for $1.

timeline.point: Coca-Cola's buybacks raise Berkshire's ownership more tax-efficiently than dividends would, though reported earnings look smaller.
timeline.quote: When Coca-Cola uses retained earnings to repurchase its shares, the company increases our percentage ownership in what I regard to be the most valuable franchise in the world.

timeline.point: Berkshire's GEICO stake rose from 33.3% to about 50% without further purchases, thanks to GEICO's buybacks.
timeline.quote: Our interest in the company, nonetheless, grew to about 50% because it was a big repurchaser of its own shares.

timeline.point: Buybacks were once a sign of undervaluation; now many overpay departing holders at continuing holders' expense.
timeline.quote: Now, repurchases are all the rage, but are all too often made for an unstated and, in our view, ignoble reason: to pump or support the stock price.

timeline.point: Berkshire considered buying its own shares below $45,000 but set a strict value condition and would never prop the price.
timeline.quote: We will not repurchase shares unless we believe Berkshire stock is selling well below intrinsic value, conservatively calculated.

timeline.point: Fixed-price options tempt a CEO to withhold dividends and repurchase stock to enrich himself in a stagnant company.
timeline.quote: He should skip dividends entirely and instead use all of the company's earnings to repurchase stock.

timeline.point: Berkshire had retained all earnings for four decades rather than distribute them.
timeline.quote: not a dime of cash has left Berkshire for dividends or share repurchases during the past 40 years.

timeline.point: Berkshire set its first explicit buyback limit and bought only $67 million before the price rose past it.
timeline.quote: Last September, we announced that Berkshire would repurchase its shares at a price of up to 110% of book value.

timeline.point: Repurchases help continuing holders only below intrinsic value; offsetting dilution or excess cash is no justification.
timeline.quote: The first law of capital allocation – whether the money is slated for acquisitions or share repurchases – is that what is smart at one price is dumb at another.

timeline.point: The 110% limit proved unrealistic, so the board raised it.
timeline.quote: we increased the limit to 120% in December when a large block became available at about 116% of book value.

timeline.point: He rejected the claim that buybacks starve productive investment.
timeline.quote: I'm not aware of any enticing project that in recent years has died for lack of capital.

timeline.point: Investee buybacks keep enlarging Berkshire's stakes without new purchases.
timeline.quote: Meanwhile, our ownership increased from 12.6% to 17.9% because of repurchases made by the company.

timeline.point: Policy now rests on Buffett and Munger judging the stock cheap and Berkshire keeping ample cash afterwards.
timeline.quote: In 2019, the Berkshire price/value equation was modestly favorable at times, and we spent $5 billion in repurchasing about 1% of the company.

timeline.point: Berkshire's largest buyback year raised owners' stake in all its businesses by 5.2%.
timeline.quote: Last year we demonstrated our enthusiasm for Berkshire's spread of properties by repurchasing the equivalent of 80,998 "A" shares, spending $24.7 billion in the process.

timeline.point: Berkshire buys only at fair prices, unlike CEOs who buy more as prices rise.
timeline.quote: American CEOs have an embarrassing record of devoting more company funds to repurchases when prices have risen than when they have tanked.

timeline.point: With other uses unattractive, repurchases over two years left continuing owners with about 10% more of every business.
timeline.quote: we therefore repurchased 9% of the shares that were outstanding at yearend 2019 for a total cost of $51.7 billion.

timeline.point: Value-accretive buybacks harm no one; he attacked blanket claims that all buybacks are harmful.
timeline.quote: you are listening to either an economic illiterate or a silver-tongued demagogue

timeline.point: Berkshire's own buybacks raised indirect ownership of Coke and AMEX; the price caveat is repeated.
timeline.quote: What is sensible at a discount to business-value becomes stupid if done at a premium.

timeline.point: He praised the five Japanese trading houses for sensible repurchases alongside dividends and modest pay.
timeline.quote: they repurchase their shares when it is sensible to do so

overview: This sector covers American Express, Salomon, Freddie Mac, Moody's, Goldman Sachs, FINOVA/Berkadia and Gen Re Securities, plus Buffett's commentary on Wall Street. He was positive on select franchises: American Express since its 1960s salad-oil scandal, held largely untouched since the 1990s while Amex buybacks lifted the stake, and Berkadia's FINOVA financing, which made excellent money. He was repeatedly negative on investment-banking incentives (zero-coupon and junk-bond excesses, 1989-90), derivatives dealers (the costly Gen Re Securities wind-down, 2002-06), mutual-fund directors, and hedge-fund and private-equity fees, ending in his 2008-2017 bet won by an S&P 500 index fund. He admitted he could not forecast investment banking; Salomon brought the 1991 crisis he helped resolve. Basis: mixed across letters 1980-2024.

timeline.point: American Express after the 1964 salad-oil scandal, like GEICO in 1976, was a great franchise with a fixable problem.
timeline.quote: Both were one-of-a-kind companies, temporarily reeling from the effects of a fiscal blow that did not destroy their exceptional underlying economics.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought $700 million of Salomon convertible preferred because it could not forecast investment banking.
timeline.quote: We, of course, have no special insights regarding the direction or future profitability of investment banking.

timeline.point: Berkshire made a major purchase of Freddie Mac preferred, intending to hold it a long time.
timeline.quote: Our holdings of Freddie Mac are the maximum allowed by law

timeline.point: Wall Street embraced zero-coupon and PIK bonds because they let deals be priced above real earning power.
timeline.quote: Here, finally, was an instrument that would let the Street make deals at prices no longer limited by actual earning power.

timeline.point: Investment bankers should act as gatekeepers against promoters' excess, but many have abandoned that role.
timeline.quote: many leading investment firms have found bartender morality to be an intolerably restrictive standard.

timeline.point: After ten months as Salomon's interim chairman, Buffett credited its executives with saving the firm.
timeline.quote: without the combined efforts of Salomon executives Deryck Maughan, Bob Denham, Don Howard, and John Macfarlane, the firm very probably would not have survived.

timeline.point: The Salomon conversion option had proven worthless while the market doubled, though the 9% preferred paid as fixed income.
timeline.quote: my decision to go with Salomon because I saw value in the conversion option must be graded as very poor.

timeline.point: In 1994 he nearly sold the American Express Percs but kept them and bought up to 10%, now a $3 billion gain.
timeline.quote: Frank had convinced me that Amex's corporate card was a terrific franchise, and I had decided not to sell.

timeline.point: He warned that derivatives concentrate systemic risk among a few linked dealers.
timeline.quote: Large amounts of risk, particularly credit risk, have become concentrated in the hands of relatively few derivatives dealers, who in addition trade extensively with one other.

timeline.point: Independent mutual-fund directors have failed at both their jobs: picking managers and negotiating fees.
timeline.quote: their record has been absolutely pathetic.

timeline.point: Leucadia's fast liquidation of FINOVA extinguished Berkshire's $5.6 billion guarantee, cutting future income.
timeline.quote: Overall, Berkadia has made excellent money for us, and Joe and Ian have been terrific partners.

timeline.point: Exiting Gen Re Securities' derivatives cost $404 million through 2005; he blamed his own dithering.
timeline.quote: The hard fact is that I have cost you a lot of money by not moving immediately to close down

timeline.point: Money flooded to hedge funds charging 2-and-20, which leaves investors far less than the gross return.
timeline.quote: It's a lopsided system whereby 2% of your principal is paid each year to the manager even if he accomplishes nothing

timeline.point: Derivatives made large banks and investment banks impossible to analyze and hid accounting abuses at Fannie and Freddie.
timeline.quote: They allowed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to engage in massive misstatements of earnings for years.

timeline.point: Berkshire, with Leucadia, bought half of Capmark, renamed Berkadia, despite expected commercial real estate problems.
timeline.quote: At the end of 2009, we became a 50% owner of Berkadia Commercial Mortgage (formerly known as Capmark), the country's third-largest servicer of commercial mortgages.

timeline.point: Private-equity buyers are leveraged-buyout firms under a new name that load acquired companies with debt.
timeline.quote: Equity is dramatically reduced and debt is piled on in virtually all private-equity purchases.

timeline.point: The hedge-fund bet (funds-of-funds 2.2% a year versus the index fund's 7.1% through 2016) showed fees capture the gains.
timeline.quote: Both large and small investors should stick with low-cost index funds.

timeline.point: Final result: the index fund gained 125.8% versus 2.8%-87.7% for the five funds-of-funds over 2008-2017.
timeline.quote: Performance comes, performance goes. Fees never falter.

timeline.point: Without buying more shares, Berkshire's American Express stake grew through the company's repurchases.
timeline.quote: Meanwhile, our ownership increased from 12.6% to 17.9% because of repurchases made by the company.

timeline.point: Amex, bought for $1.3 billion by 1995, shows the payoff of holding a wonderful business.
timeline.quote: Annual dividends received from this investment have grown from $41 million to $302 million.

timeline.point: Amex and Coke prospered in their base businesses because their products traveled worldwide and meet lasting needs.
timeline.quote: the consumption of liquids and the need for unquestioned financial trust are timeless essentials of our world.

overview: Buffett's manufacturing story runs from Scott Fetzer (1986) through Iscar/IMC, Marmon, Lubrizol and Precision Castparts. He used Scott Fetzer to teach purchase accounting and owner earnings, and praised Ralph Schey for returns that would top the Fortune 500 and $1.03 billion of distributions against a $230 million net price. From 2006 Iscar drew his highest praise; Marmon, Lubrizol and later PCC joined Berkshire's largest earners. He also said uniform manufacturing lacks attractive economics, that his early bargain manufacturers and several small purchases were mistakes, and that he overpaid for PCC, written down by $11 billion in 2020. Basis: positive across letters 1985-2024; the manufacturing, service and retailing group earned roughly 16-24% after tax on tangible assets in 2007-2016.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought Scott Fetzer, 17 businesses with $700 million of sales, for about $320 million.
timeline.quote: Scott Fetzer is a prototype - understandable, large, well-managed, a good earner.

timeline.point: Using Scott Fetzer, he showed purchase-accounting charges understate economic earnings and defined owner earnings.
timeline.quote: we feel owner earnings of Scott Fetzer are considerably larger than the GAAP figures that we report.

timeline.point: He took 20 years to learn to buy good businesses rather than bargains such as farm-implement makers.
timeline.quote: My punishment was an education in the economics of short-line farm implement manufacturers, third-place department stores, and New England textile manufacturers.

timeline.point: Fechheimer earns high returns only because of exceptional management, not industry economics.
timeline.quote: Neither furniture retailing nor uniform manufacturing has inherently attractive economics.

timeline.point: Buying General Dynamics as an arbitrage, he switched to a long-term stake after studying CEO Bill Anders' strategy.
timeline.quote: In short order, I dumped my arbitrage thoughts and decided that Berkshire should become a long-term investor with Bill.

timeline.point: Scott Fetzer's earnings roughly doubled while book value stayed flat, without leverage, credited to Ralph Schey.
timeline.quote: Leaving aside such non-operating windfalls, Scott Fetzer's return on equity would have ranked it first on the Fortune 500, well ahead of number two.

timeline.point: Champion International's preferred was converted and sold back to the company for a moderate 19% after-tax gain.
timeline.quote: Charlie and I have never had a conviction about the paper industry

timeline.point: On Schey's retirement Buffett tallied Scott Fetzer's cash contribution, redeployed into other businesses.
timeline.quote: Under his leadership, the company distributed $1.03 billion to Berkshire against our net purchase price of $230 million.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought 80% of Israel's ISCAR for $4 billion, its first business purchase outside the U.S.
timeline.quote: ISCAR makes money because it enables its customers to make more money.

timeline.point: The manufacturing, service and retailing group earns well on tangible capital but only 9.8% on carrying value after premiums.
timeline.quote: earned a pleasing 23% on average tangible net worth last year.

timeline.point: In the recession Marmon posted a record 13.5% margin and Iscar stayed profitable while its two main rivals lost money.
timeline.quote: Nothing stops Israel-based Iscar – not wars, recessions or competitors.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought specialty-chemicals maker Lubrizol; Iscar, Lubrizol and Marmon were among five businesses with record earnings.
timeline.quote: with pre-tax profits increasing from $147 million to $1,085 million.

timeline.point: The sector's intrinsic value exceeds book overall, but not at many smaller companies he bought.
timeline.quote: I have made more than my share of mistakes buying small companies.

timeline.point: A few group businesses earn poor returns because he reverted to bargain hunting against Munger's rule.
timeline.quote: it was far better to buy a wonderful business at a fair price than to buy a fair business at a wonderful price.

timeline.point: Berkshire bought Precision Castparts, the premier aerospace components supplier, for more than $32 billion in cash.
timeline.quote: PCC fits perfectly into the Berkshire model and will substantially increase our normalized per-share earning power.

timeline.point: With Duracell and PCC added, the group employed $24 billion of net tangible assets with little debt.
timeline.quote: earned 24% after-tax on that capital.

timeline.point: An $11 billion write-down quantified his PCC mistake: a fine company bought at too high a price.
timeline.quote: That year, Berkshire purchased Precision Castparts ("PCC"), and I paid too much for the company.

timeline.point: Forest River, bought in 2005 after a two-page fax, outperformed every competitor under founder Pete Liegl.
timeline.quote: During the next 19 years, Pete shot the lights out. No competitor came close to his performance.
